Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verse 1–2 (part 1 of 2):

(p-2) Surat al-Tawba has one hundred and twenty-nine verses; it is Madani.

﴿A declaration of immunity from Allah and His Messenger to those among the polytheists with whom you made a covenant.﴾ ﴿So travel freely in the land for four months, and know that you cannot escape Allah, and that Allah will disgrace the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿And an announcement from Allah and His Messenger to the people on the day of the greater pilgrimage that Allah is free of obligation to the polytheists, and so is His Messenger. So if you repent, it is better for you; but if you turn away, then know that you cannot escape Allah. And give tidings of a painful punishment to those who disbelieve.﴾ [al-Tawba: 3] ﴿Except those among the polytheists with whom you made a covenant, then they have not failed you in anything nor have they supported anyone against you; so fulfil their covenant to their term. Indeed Allah loves the righteous.﴾ [al-Tawba: 4] ﴿Then when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them, take them captive, besiege them, and lie in wait for them at every place of ambush. But if they repent, establish the prayer and give the zakat, then let them go on their way. Indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ [al-Tawba: 5] ﴿And if any of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection until he hears the words of Allah, then convey him to his place of safety. That is because they are a people who do not know.﴾ [al-Tawba: 6] ﴿How can there be a covenant for the polytheists with Allah and with His Messenger, except those with whom you made a covenant at the Sacred Mosque? So as long as they remain upright toward you, remain upright toward them. Indeed Allah loves the righteous.﴾ [al-Tawba: 7] ﴿How, when if they gain the upper hand over you they would not observe any ties of kinship or covenant toward you? They please you with their mouths, but their hearts refuse, and most of them are defiantly disobedient.﴾ [al-Tawba: 8] ﴿They have sold the signs of Allah for a small price, and have barred [others] from His way. Indeed, evil is what they have been doing.﴾ [al-Tawba: 9] ﴿They observe no tie of kinship or covenant regarding a believer, and it is they who are the transgressors.﴾ [al-Tawba: 10] ﴿But if they repent, establish the prayer and give the zakat, then they are your brothers in religion. We detail the signs for a people who know.﴾ [al-Tawba: 11] ﴿And if they break their oaths after their covenant and revile your religion, then fight the leaders of disbelief, for they have no oaths, so that they may desist.﴾ [al-Tawba: 12] ﴿Will you not fight a people who broke their oaths, and who resolved to expel the Messenger, and who began the attack against you the first time? Do you fear them? Allah has more right that you should fear Him, if you are believers.﴾ [al-Tawba: 13] ﴿Fight them; Allah will punish them by your hands, disgrace them, give you victory over them, and heal the breasts of a believing people.﴾ [al-Tawba: 14] ﴿And He will remove the rage from their hearts. Allah turns in forgiveness to whom He wills, and Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾ [al-Tawba: 15] ﴿Or did you suppose that you would be left alone, when Allah has not yet known those of you who strove and did not take, besides Allah and His Messenger and the believers, any intimate friend? Allah is All-Aware of what you do.﴾ [al-Tawba: 16] ﴿It is not for the polytheists to maintain the mosques of Allah while bearing witness against themselves of disbelief. Those, their deeds have become void, and in the Fire they will abide forever.﴾ [al-Tawba: 17] ﴿Only one who believes in Allah and the Last Day, establishes the prayer, gives the zakat, and fears none but Allah maintains the mosques of Allah. It is those who may be among the guided.﴾ [al-Tawba: 18] ﴿Have you made the providing of water for the pilgrims and the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque equal to one who believes in Allah and the Last Day and strives in the way of Allah? They are not equal in the sight of Allah, and Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾ [al-Tawba: 19] ﴿Those who believed, emigrated, and strove in the way of Allah with their wealth and their lives are greater in rank in the sight of Allah, and it is they who are the triumphant.﴾ [al-Tawba: 20] ﴿Their Lord gives them good tidings of mercy from Him, approval, and gardens for them wherein is enduring bliss.﴾ [al-Tawba: 21] ﴿Abiding therein forever. Indeed, with Allah is a great reward.﴾ [al-Tawba: 22] ﴿O you who believe, do not take your fathers and your brothers as allies if they prefer disbelief over faith. And whoever of you allies with them, then it is they who are the wrongdoers.﴾ [al-Tawba: 23] ﴿Say: If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your spouses, your kindred, the wealth you have acquired, the commerce you fear will decline, and the dwellings you are pleased with are dearer to you than Allah and His Messenger and striving in His way, then wait until Allah brings His command. And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.﴾ [al-Tawba: 24] ﴿Allah has already given you victory in many battlefields, and on the day of Hunayn, when your large numbers pleased you, but they did not avail you at all, and the earth, for all its vastness, was confining for you, and then you turned back in retreat.﴾ [al-Tawba: 25] ﴿Then Allah sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers, and sent down hosts you did not see, and punished those who disbelieved. That is the recompense of the disbelievers.﴾ [al-Tawba: 26] ﴿Then Allah turns in forgiveness after that to whom He wills, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ [al-Tawba: 27] ﴿O you who believe, the polytheists are only impure, so let them not approach the Sacred Mosque after this their year. And if you fear poverty, Allah will enrich you from His bounty if He wills. Indeed Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾ [al-Tawba: 28] ﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah or in the Last Day, and who do not forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden, and who do not adopt the religion of truth from among those who were given the Book, until they pay the jizya willingly while they are humbled.﴾ [al-Tawba: 29] ﴿And the Jews say, "Ezra is the son of Allah," and the Christians say, "The Messiah is the son of Allah." That is their statement from their mouths; they imitate the saying of those who disbelieved before them. May Allah destroy them; how are they deluded?﴾ [al-Tawba: 30] (p-3) Al-marsad: a noun of place from rasada, yarsudu, meaning to watch for; it can be a verbal noun, a time, or a place. Amir ibn al-Tufayl said:
Indeed you know, and I do not think you forget, that death for the youth is at the ambush.

Al-ill: oath and supplication; from it is the saying of Abu Jahl:
For an oath upon us, a binding duty we do not neglect, its strength firm, its rope not unraveled.
When they made pacts and alliances they raised their voices with it and proclaimed it; it derives from al-al, which is supplication, and he has an ulil, that is a moan, by which he raises his voice. It was also said: kinship. Abu Ubayda cited for kinship the verse of a poet:
The most corrupt of people are successors who have cut off the ill and the roots of kinship.
The apparent meaning of the verse is that it refers to covenant. From kinship is the saying of Hassan:
By your life, your ill among Quraysh is like the ill of the young camel among the ostrich's chicks.
It was named ill because it binds what a covenant does not bind. It was also said: from alla al-barq, meaning the lightning flashed. Al-Azhari said: al-ulail is brightness; one says alla yauul, meaning he was clear and shone. Al-Qurtubi said: it is derived from sharpness; from it comes al-illa, a spear; and an ear that is mu'allala is sharpened. When it is said of covenant, supplication, or kinship that it is ill, the meaning is that the ear is directed toward the direction it is sharpened for. A covenant is called ill for its purity. Its plural in the paucity form is al-all, and in the abundance form al-ull; the original of the paucity plural is uull, and the unstressed hamza that is the first radical was made easy, changing it to alif, and the lam was assimilated into the lam.

Al-dhimma: covenant. Abu Ubayda said: security. Al-Asma'i said: everything that must be guarded and protected.

Aba ya'ba: refused. He said:
He refused oppression while al-Nu'man's hand burns upon him, and he kept away while the swords were his strongholds.
And he said:
God refused except His justice and His faithfulness, so the unknown is not known nor is the known lost.
The present form of this verb in the pattern fa'ala with an open ayn is anomalous; from it is "aabi al-lahm" for a man among the Companions.

Shafahu: he removed his illness. Al-'ashira: a group bound by a cause, a contract, or affection, like the bond of a clan. Iqtaraf: he earned. Kasada al-shay' kasadan wa kusudan: it went unsold and had no demand. Al-mawtin: the position and the standing place. The poet said:
How many a position, had I not been there, would have made you fall as falls what plunges from the top of a steep cliff.
Similarly is al-watan.

Hunayn: a valley between Makka and al-Ta'if; it was also said: a valley beside Dhu al-Majaz. Al-'ayla: poverty; 'aala ya'ilu: he became poor. He said:
The poor man does not know when his wealth will come, and the rich man does not know when he will become poor.
Al-jizya: what is taken from the people of protection in exchange for their residence in the lands of Islam. It was named so because they pay it (yajzunaha), that is, they discharge it; or because they are repaid for it by being granted exemption from killing.

Al-mudahat: likeness and imitation. The Thaqif say al-mudaha'a with a hamza, and "dahva'tu" [I imitated]; so its root differs from the one before it, unless dahat is claimed to have an original hamza, as in their saying in tawadda'tu, qara'tu, and akhta'tu: tawaddaytu, qaraytu, and akhtaytu; this is possible. As for dahya' with a hamza, short, its hamza is extra, like the hamza of 'arafi'a; or long, its hamza is extra for feminine marking; or long with a feminine ta' after it. Al-Buhturi related this from Abu 'Amr al-Shaybani in al-Nawadir, and he said: he combined two feminine markers. The meaning of this word in its three forms is the woman who does not menstruate, or who has no breast, who resembles men in that. Whoever claims that al-mudahat is derived from dahya' is wrong, because the two roots differ: the hamza of al-mudaha'a is original, and the hamza of dahya' is extra in its three forms.

﴿A declaration of immunity from Allah and His Messenger to those among the polytheists with whom you made a covenant﴾ ﴿So travel freely in the land for four months, and know that you cannot escape Allah, and that Allah will disgrace the disbelievers﴾; this surah is entirely Madani. It was said: except two verses at its end, which were revealed in Makka; this is the view of the majority. The exegetes mentioned for it a name, and disagreement about the reason it begins without the basmala, and a difference from the Companions: is it and al-Anfal one surah, or two surahs? The meaning of the wording has no bearing on that, so we have left it out of our book; it may be consulted in the books of the exegetes.

It is said: I became free of so-and-so, abra'u bara'a; that is, the bond of protection was severed between us; from it: bari'tu min al-dayn, I was discharged from the debt. "Baraa'a" is in the nominative as the subject, and the predicate is "ila alladhina 'aahadtum"; "min Allah" is a qualifying phrase that permits beginning with an indefinite noun; or it is by supposing an omitted subject, that is: this is a declaration of immunity. 'Isa ibn 'Umar read "baraa'atan" in the accusative; Ibn 'Atiyya said: that is, adhere to it, and it carries the sense of urging; al-Zamakhshari said: listen to a declaration of immunity.

He said: If you ask, with what is the declaration of immunity connected: with Allah and His Messenger, and the covenant with the Muslims? I say: Allah had first permitted a covenant with the polytheists, so the Muslims with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ made covenants with them; when they broke the covenant, Allah made it obligatory to cast it back at them, so the Muslims were addressed with what had newly occurred, and it was said to them: know that Allah and His Messenger have become free of what you covenanted with the polytheists. Ibn 'Atiyya said: since the covenant of the Messenger ﷺ was binding on all his community, it was fitting to say "you made a covenant." Ibn Ishaq and others said: the Arabs had been bound by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in a general covenant that no one would be barred from the Sacred House, and similar truces; this was annulled by this verse, and a period of four months was granted to all of them. Whoever had a particular covenant with the Messenger and had less than four months remaining was informed to complete it; whoever had a longer term had his covenant completed for him; and whoever was among those counted as having broken the covenant was limited to four months. Whoever had no particular covenant was granted the four months to travel (yasih) in the land, that is, to go about in it freely and safely.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verses 1–2 (part 2 of 2):

The apparent meaning of the phrase (min al-mushrikin, "from the polytheists") is generality. Thus everyone with whom the Muslims had a covenant is included, whether from the polytheists of Makkah or others. It is narrated that they all broke the covenant except Banu Damrah and Kinanah, so the covenant was annulled for those who had broken it.

Muqatil said: "The polytheists referred to here are three tribes of the Arabs: Khuza'ah, Banu Mudlij, and Banu Khuzaymah." It was also said: this verse concerns the people of Makkah. The Messenger ﷺ had made a truce with Quraysh at the time of al-Hudaybiyah, that they would lay down war for ten years, during which people would be safe. Khuza'ah entered into the covenant of the Messenger, and Banu Bakr ibn Abd Manat entered into the covenant of Quraysh. The Banu al-Dil of Banu Bakr had a blood debt owed to Khuza'ah, so they seized the opportunity of Khuza'ah's heedlessness. Nawfal ibn Mu'awiyah al-Dili went out with those of Banu Bakr who obeyed him, and they attacked Khuza'ah by night, and they fought. Quraysh aided Banu Bakr with weapons, and a group helped them with their own persons. Khuza'ah were defeated and retreated to the Sacred Precinct (al-haram). That was a violation of the truce of al-Hudaybiyah. So Budayl ibn Warqa' and Amr ibn Salim of Khuza'ah went out with some of their people and came to the Messenger ﷺ seeking help. Amr recited to him:

O Lord, I appeal to Muhammad
the covenant of our father and his father, the ancient one.
You have been a father to us, and we have been sons;
then we embraced Islam and did not withdraw our hand.
So help us, may Allah guide you, with a mighty help,
and call the servants of Allah, they will come with reinforcements.
Among them is the Messenger of Allah, who has come forth,
white like the sun, rising high.
If his face is seen dark with dust, it turns black,
in a host like a sea flowing in foam.
Indeed Quraysh have broken their promise to you
and violated your firm covenant.
They claimed that you do not call anyone,
while they are more humiliated and fewer in number.
They attacked us by night at al-Hatim, while we slept,
and they killed us while bowing and prostrating.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "May I not be helped if I do not help you." So he prepared to march on Makkah and conquered it in the year eight. Then he went out to the expedition of Tabuk, and those among the hypocrites who stayed behind spread rumours and false reports. The polytheists began to break their covenants, so Allah the Exalted commanded him to announce their covenant to them and permitted war.

(Fasihu, "so travel freely") is a command of permission, and within it is a threat. It is a shift (iltifat) from the third person to the second person; that is, say to them: "Travel." One says: sahа siyahatan wa sawhan wa sayahanan, and from it comes sayh al-ma' (the flowing, spread-out water), which is the running, spreading water. Tarafah said:

Had I feared this from you, you would not have reached me until you saw horses before me galloping.

Ibn Abbas and al-Zuhri said: the first of the months was Shawwal until the verse was revealed, and its end was the end of Muharram after the day of the proclamation (yawm al-adhan) by fifty days. So the term for those who had a covenant was four months from the day of revelation, and the term for the remaining polytheists was fifty nights from the day of the proclamation. Al-Suddi and others said: its beginning is the day of the proclamation, and its end is the ten days of Rabi' al-Akhir. It was also said: it is the ten days of Dhu al-Qa'dah to the twentieth of Rabi' al-Awwal, because the Hajj in that year fell at that time due to the nasi' (intercalation) practised among them, and then in the second year it fell in Dhu al-Hijjah.

(Ghayru mu'jizi Allah), meaning you will not escape Him, even if He gives you respite, and He will disgrace you; that is, He will humiliate you in this world by killing, capture, and plunder, and in the Hereafter by punishment. Abu Amr related from the people of Najran that they recited (min Allah) with a kasra on the nun, according to the original principle of meeting two sakin letters, and by following the kasra of the nun.

(p-2) Surat al-Tawba has one hundred and twenty-nine verses; it is Madani.

Do you fear them? Allah has more right that you should fear Him, if you are believers.﴾ [al-Tawba: 13] ﴿Fight them; Allah will punish them by your hands, disgrace them, give you victory over them, and heal the breasts of a believing people.﴾ [al-Tawba: 14] ﴿And He will remove the rage from their hearts. And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.﴾ [al-Tawba: 24] ﴿Allah has already given you victory in many battlefields, and on the day of Hunayn, when your large numbers pleased you, but they did not avail you at all, and the earth, for all its vastness, was confining for you, and then you turned back in retreat.﴾ [al-Tawba: 25] ﴿Then Allah sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers, and sent down hosts you did not see, and punished those who disbelieved. That is the recompense of the disbelievers.﴾ [al-Tawba: 26] ﴿Then Allah turns in forgiveness after that to whom He wills, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ [al-Tawba: 27] ﴿O you who believe, the polytheists are only impure, so let them not approach the Sacred Mosque after this their year. And if you fear poverty, Allah will enrich you from His bounty if He wills. Indeed Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾ [al-Tawba: 28] ﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah or in the Last Day, and who do not forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden, and who do not adopt the religion of truth from among those who were given the Book, until they pay the jizya willingly while they are humbled.﴾ [al-Tawba: 29] ﴿And the Jews say, "Ezra is the son of Allah," and the Christians say, "The Messiah is the son of Allah." That is their statement from their mouths; they imitate the saying of those who disbelieved before them. May Allah destroy them; how are they deluded?﴾ [al-Tawba: 30] (p-3) Al-marsad: a noun of place from rasada, yarsudu, meaning to watch for; it can be a verbal noun, a time, or a place. Amir ibn al-Tufayl said:
Indeed you know, and I do not think you forget, that death for the youth is at the ambush.

Al-ill: oath and supplication; from it is the saying of Abu Jahl:
For an oath upon us, a binding duty we do not neglect, its strength firm, its rope not unraveled.
When they made pacts and alliances they raised their voices with it and proclaimed it; it derives from al-al, which is supplication, and he has an ulil, that is a moan, by which he raises his voice. It was also said: kinship. Abu Ubayda cited for kinship the verse of a poet:
The most corrupt of people are successors who have cut off the ill and the roots of kinship.
The apparent meaning of the verse is that it refers to covenant. From kinship is the saying of Hassan:
By your life, your ill among Quraysh is like the ill of the young camel among the ostrich's chicks.
It was named ill because it binds what a covenant does not bind. It was also said: from alla al-barq, meaning the lightning flashed. Al-Azhari said: al-ulail is brightness; one says alla yauul, meaning he was clear and shone. Al-Qurtubi said: it is derived from sharpness; from it comes al-illa, a spear; and an ear that is mu'allala is sharpened. When it is said of covenant, supplication, or kinship that it is ill, the meaning is that the ear is directed toward the direction it is sharpened for. A covenant is called ill for its purity. Its plural in the paucity form is al-all, and in the abundance form al-ull; the original of the paucity plural is uull, and the unstressed hamza that is the first radical was made easy, changing it to alif, and the lam was assimilated into the lam.

Al-dhimma: covenant. Abu Ubayda said: security. Al-Asma'i said: everything that must be guarded and protected.

Aba ya'ba: refused. He said:
He refused oppression while al-Nu'man's hand burns upon him, and he kept away while the swords were his strongholds.
And he said:
God refused except His justice and His faithfulness, so the unknown is not known nor is the known lost.
The present form of this verb in the pattern fa'ala with an open ayn is anomalous; from it is "aabi al-lahm" for a man among the Companions.

Shafahu: he removed his illness. Al-'ashira: a group bound by a cause, a contract, or affection, like the bond of a clan. Iqtaraf: he earned. Kasada al-shay' kasadan wa kusudan: it went unsold and had no demand. Al-mawtin: the position and the standing place. The poet said:
How many a position, had I not been there, would have made you fall as falls what plunges from the top of a steep cliff.
Similarly is al-watan.

Hunayn: a valley between Makka and al-Ta'if; it was also said: a valley beside Dhu al-Majaz. Al-'ayla: poverty; 'aala ya'ilu: he became poor. He said:
The poor man does not know when his wealth will come, and the rich man does not know when he will become poor.
Al-jizya: what is taken from the people of protection in exchange for their residence in the lands of Islam. It was named so because they pay it (yajzunaha), that is, they discharge it; or because they are repaid for it by being granted exemption from killing.

Al-mudahat: likeness and imitation. The Thaqif say al-mudaha'a with a hamza, and "dahva'tu" [I imitated]; so its root differs from the one before it, unless dahat is claimed to have an original hamza, as in their saying in tawadda'tu, qara'tu, and akhta'tu: tawaddaytu, qaraytu, and akhtaytu; this is possible. As for dahya' with a hamza, short, its hamza is extra, like the hamza of 'arafi'a; or long, its hamza is extra for feminine marking; or long with a feminine ta' after it. Al-Buhturi related this from Abu 'Amr al-Shaybani in al-Nawadir, and he said: he combined two feminine markers. The meaning of this word in its three forms is the woman who does not menstruate, or who has no breast, who resembles men in that. Whoever claims that al-mudahat is derived from dahya' is wrong, because the two roots differ: the hamza of al-mudaha'a is original, and the hamza of dahya' is extra in its three forms.

﴿A declaration of immunity from Allah and His Messenger to those among the polytheists with whom you made a covenant﴾ ﴿So travel freely in the land for four months, and know that you cannot escape Allah, and that Allah will disgrace the disbelievers﴾; this surah is entirely Madani. It was said: except two verses at its end, which were revealed in Makka; this is the view of the majority. The exegetes mentioned for it a name, and disagreement about the reason it begins without the basmala, and a difference from the Companions: is it and al-Anfal one surah, or two surahs? The meaning of the wording has no bearing on that, so we have left it out of our book; it may be consulted in the books of the exegetes.

It is said: I became free of so-and-so, abra'u bara'a; that is, the bond of protection was severed between us; from it: bari'tu min al-dayn, I was discharged from the debt. "Baraa'a" is in the nominative as the subject, and the predicate is "ila alladhina 'aahadtum"; "min Allah" is a qualifying phrase that permits beginning with an indefinite noun; or it is by supposing an omitted subject, that is: this is a declaration of immunity. 'Isa ibn 'Umar read "baraa'atan" in the accusative; Ibn 'Atiyya said: that is, adhere to it, and it carries the sense of urging; al-Zamakhshari said: listen to a declaration of immunity.

He said: If you ask, with what is the declaration of immunity connected: with Allah and His Messenger, and the covenant with the Muslims? I say: Allah had first permitted a covenant with the polytheists, so the Muslims with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ made covenants with them; when they broke the covenant, Allah made it obligatory to cast it back at them, so the Muslims were addressed with what had newly occurred, and it was said to them: know that Allah and His Messenger have become free of what you covenanted with the polytheists. Ibn 'Atiyya said: since the covenant of the Messenger ﷺ was binding on all his community, it was fitting to say "you made a covenant." Ibn Ishaq and others said: the Arabs had been bound by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in a general covenant that no one would be barred from the Sacred House, and similar truces; this was annulled by this verse, and a period of four months was granted to all of them. Whoever had a particular covenant with the Messenger and had less than four months remaining was informed to complete it; whoever had a longer term had his covenant completed for him; and whoever was among those counted as having broken the covenant was limited to four months. Whoever had no particular covenant was granted the four months to travel (yasih) in the land, that is, to go about in it freely and safely.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verses 1–2 (part 2 of 2):

The apparent meaning of the phrase (min al-mushrikin, "from the polytheists") is generality. Thus everyone with whom the Muslims had a covenant is included, whether from the polytheists of Makkah or others. It is narrated that they all broke the covenant except Banu Damrah and Kinanah, so the covenant was annulled for those who had broken it.

Muqatil said: "The polytheists referred to here are three tribes of the Arabs: Khuza'ah, Banu Mudlij, and Banu Khuzaymah." It was also said: this verse concerns the people of Makkah. The Messenger ﷺ had made a truce with Quraysh at the time of al-Hudaybiyah, that they would lay down war for ten years, during which people would be safe. Khuza'ah entered into the covenant of the Messenger, and Banu Bakr ibn Abd Manat entered into the covenant of Quraysh. The Banu al-Dil of Banu Bakr had a blood debt owed to Khuza'ah, so they seized the opportunity of Khuza'ah's heedlessness. Nawfal ibn Mu'awiyah al-Dili went out with those of Banu Bakr who obeyed him, and they attacked Khuza'ah by night, and they fought. Quraysh aided Banu Bakr with weapons, and a group helped them with their own persons. Khuza'ah were defeated and retreated to the Sacred Precinct (al-haram). That was a violation of the truce of al-Hudaybiyah. So Budayl ibn Warqa' and Amr ibn Salim of Khuza'ah went out with some of their people and came to the Messenger ﷺ seeking help. Amr recited to him:

O Lord, I appeal to Muhammad
the covenant of our father and his father, the ancient one.
You have been a father to us, and we have been sons;
then we embraced Islam and did not withdraw our hand.
So help us, may Allah guide you, with a mighty help,
and call the servants of Allah, they will come with reinforcements.
Among them is the Messenger of Allah, who has come forth,
white like the sun, rising high.
If his face is seen dark with dust, it turns black,
in a host like a sea flowing in foam.
Indeed Quraysh have broken their promise to you
and violated your firm covenant.
They claimed that you do not call anyone,
while they are more humiliated and fewer in number.
They attacked us by night at al-Hatim, while we slept,
and they killed us while bowing and prostrating.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "May I not be helped if I do not help you." So he prepared to march on Makkah and conquered it in the year eight. Then he went out to the expedition of Tabuk, and those among the hypocrites who stayed behind spread rumours and false reports. The polytheists began to break their covenants, so Allah the Exalted commanded him to announce their covenant to them and permitted war.

(Fasihu, "so travel freely") is a command of permission, and within it is a threat. It is a shift (iltifat) from the third person to the second person; that is, say to them: "Travel." One says: sahа siyahatan wa sawhan wa sayahanan, and from it comes sayh al-ma' (the flowing, spread-out water), which is the running, spreading water. Tarafah said:

Had I feared this from you, you would not have reached me until you saw horses before me galloping.

Ibn Abbas and al-Zuhri said: the first of the months was Shawwal until the verse was revealed, and its end was the end of Muharram after the day of the proclamation (yawm al-adhan) by fifty days. So the term for those who had a covenant was four months from the day of revelation, and the term for the remaining polytheists was fifty nights from the day of the proclamation. Al-Suddi and others said: its beginning is the day of the proclamation, and its end is the ten days of Rabi' al-Akhir. It was also said: it is the ten days of Dhu al-Qa'dah to the twentieth of Rabi' al-Awwal, because the Hajj in that year fell at that time due to the nasi' (intercalation) practised among them, and then in the second year it fell in Dhu al-Hijjah.

(Ghayru mu'jizi Allah), meaning you will not escape Him, even if He gives you respite, and He will disgrace you; that is, He will humiliate you in this world by killing, capture, and plunder, and in the Hereafter by punishment. Abu Amr related from the people of Najran that they recited (min Allah) with a kasra on the nun, according to the original principle of meeting two sakin letters, and by following the kasra of the nun.

﴿And a proclamation from Allah and His Messenger to the people on the day of the greater pilgrimage (al-hajj al-akbar) that Allah is free of obligation to the polytheists, and so is His Messenger﴾. Al-Dahhak, Ikrimah and Abu al-Mutawakkil recited (wa-idhnun) with a kasra on the hamza and sukun on the dhal. Al-Hasan and al-A'raj recited (inna Allah) with a kasra on the hamza. The fath (opening vowel) is based on the assumption of "bi-anna" (that), while the kasra is based, according to the Basran school, on an implied "qawl" (saying), or, according to the Kufan school, because al-adhan (the proclamation) carries the meaning of "qawl" (saying), so it takes the kasra.

Ibn Abi Ishaq, Isa ibn Umar and Zayd ibn Ali recited (wa-rasulahu) in the accusative, as a coordination with the position of the noun following inna (ism inna). Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be accusative as a direct object with (ma'a) (ma'iyya construction). It was also recited in the genitive, which is anomalous (shadhdh). It is reported from al-Hasan, and it is explained as coordination by proximity (al-'atf 'ala al-jiwar), just as they used adjectives and emphatics by proximity. It was also said that it is the waw of oath (wa al-qasam). It is reported that a Bedouin heard someone reciting with the genitive and said: "If Allah is free of obligation to His Messenger, then I am free of it too." The reciter seized him and brought him to Umar, and the Bedouin related the recitation as he had heard it. At that, Umar ordered the teaching of Arabic grammar (al-'arabiyya). As for the recitation of the majority with the nominative, it is based on the inchoative (al-ibtida', the subject), and the predicate (khabar) is omitted, meaning: "and His Messenger is free of obligation to them." It was omitted because what precedes it indicates it. They permitted that it be coordinated with the pronoun concealed in "bari'" (free). Its acceptability is supported by the fact that a prepositional phrase, "min al-mushrikin" (to the polytheists), intervenes between the one who bears the pronoun and the coordinated word. Whoever permits coordination with the position of the noun after the kasra-inna permits it also with the fath-inna. Others permit it with the kasra-inna but forbid it with the fath-inna. Ibn Atiyya said: The position of our teacher, Abu al-Hasan ibn al-Babadhish, following the implication of the words of Sibawayh, is that there is no position (mahall, grammatical place) for what follows inna, since it is inflected and the effect of the governing word has appeared in it, and that there is no difference between inna and layta (would that). The consensus is that there is no position for what follows these, and that is the end of his words. This statement is open to criticism, because the reason that inna has no position for what follows it is not the appearance of the governing word's effect, as shown by "laysa Zaydun bi-qa'im" (Zayd is not standing) and "ma fi al-dar min rajul" (there is no man in the house), where the governing word's effect has appeared and yet they have a position. His words "and the consensus..." to the end mean that layta has no grammatical position by consensus, and that is not so, because al-Farra' disagreed and made the rule of layta, la'alla, ka'anna and lakinna the same as the rule of inna regarding the position of their noun.

The grammatical analysis (i'rab) of (wa-adhanun) is like that of (bara'ah) on both readings. Then the sentence is coordinated with a similar sentence, and there is no basis for the view of whoever said that it is coordinated with (bara'ah), just as one does not say "'Amr is coordinated with Zayd" in "Zayd qama wa-'Amr qa'id" (Zayd stood and 'Amr is sitting).

Al-adhan means al-iidhan, which is notification, just as al-aman (security) and al-'ata' (giving) are used with the meanings of al-iman (granting security) and al-i'ta' (giving). Making it a predicate for (wa-adhanun) is weak if we analyse it as a subject; rather, the predicate is his words "ila al-nas" (to the people). The inchoative with an indefinite noun is permitted because it is qualified by his words "min Allah wa-rasulihi" (from Allah and His Messenger).

(Yawma) is in the accusative, governed by what is connected to (ila al-nas). Some permitted its accusative governed by (wa-adhanun), but this is remote, for two reasons: the verbal noun, when it is qualified before it governs its complement, may not govern what follows the qualifier; and it may not be made a predicate until it has governed its complement, yet it has been made a predicate by his words "ila al-nas."

It was reported: When it was the ninth year (of the Hijra), the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wished to perform the pilgrimage, but he disliked seeing the polytheists circumambulating the House naked. So he sent Abu Bakr as commander over the pilgrimage season, then followed him with Ali to recite these verses (p-7) to the people of the season, riding his she-camel al-'Adba'. It was said to him: "If only you had sent them with Abu Bakr." He said: "None shall deliver on my behalf except a man from me." When they met, Abu Bakr said: "Are you a commander or one who is commanded?" He said: "One who is commanded." When the day of tarwiya came, Abu Bakr gave the sermon, and Ali stood on the day of sacrifice after the Jamrat al-'Aqaba and said: "O people, I am the messenger of the Messenger of Allah to you." They said: "With what?" He recited to them thirty or forty verses. And from Mujahid: thirteen. Then he said: "I have been commanded with four things: that no polytheist should approach the House after this year, that no naked person should circumambulate the House, that none shall enter Paradise except a believing soul, and that the covenant of everyone who has a covenant be fulfilled for him until its term." At that they said: "O Ali, tell your cousin that we have cast the covenant behind our backs, and there is between us and him no covenant except spear-thrusts and sword-blows." It was said: The custom of the Arabs in breaking their covenants was that a man from the tribe should undertake it; had Abu Bakr undertaken it, they would have said: "This contradicts what is known of us regarding breaking covenants," so for this reason he made Ali undertake it. Abu Hurayra was with Ali, and whenever Ali's voice became hoarse, Abu Hurayra would call out.

The apparent meaning is that (yawm al-hajj al-akbar) is the day of Uhud. Umar, Ibn al-Zubayr, Abu Juhayfa, Tawus, 'Ata' and Ibn al-Musayyab said: it is the day of 'Arafa. It is related with a chain going back to the Messenger (ﷺ). Abu Musa, Ibn Abi Awfa, al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba, Ibn Jubayr, Ikrimah, al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, al-Zuhri, Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi said: it is the day of sacrifice (yawm al-nahr). It was also said that (yawm al-hajj al-akbar) means all the days of the pilgrimage, as Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said. Ibn Atiyya said: What the hadiths converge upon is that Ali proclaimed those verses on the day of 'Arafa following Abu Bakr's sermon, then he saw that he had not reached all the people by making them hear, so he followed them with the proclamation on the day of sacrifice. On that day Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, sent someone to assist him with them, such as Abu Hurayra and others, and they also went after the markets of the Arabs, such as Dhu al-Majaz and others, and with this the saying of Sufyan is strengthened. He said: This was the day of Siffin and the day of the Camel, meaning all its days. Mujahid said: the day of the greater pilgrimage is all the days of Mina, and the gatherings of the polytheists when they were at Dhu al-Majaz, 'Ukaz and Majanna, until it was proclaimed among them: that Muslims and polytheists shall not gather after this year of theirs.

As for describing it as "the greater": al-Hasan and Abdullah ibn al-Harith ibn Nawfal said: because in that year both Muslims and polytheists performed the pilgrimage, and it coincided with the festival of the Jews and Christians, and this did not happen before or after it, so it became great in the heart of every believer and unbeliever. This view is weakened by the fact that the Exalted does not describe it as "the greater" for this reason. Al-Hasan also said: because Abu Bakr performed the pilgrimage in it, and the covenants were cast off in it. Ibn Atiyya said: This is the view that resembles al-Hasan's reasoning, and its explanation is that this day was the opening with truth and the sign of Islam through the leadership of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), the covenants were cast off in it, religion was honoured in it, and polytheism was humbled in it, and this did not happen in the year eight when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) appointed 'Attab ibn Asad, who was the commander of the Arabs, over its beginning. So every pilgrimage after the pilgrimage of Abu Bakr is built upon it, and it deserves to be called "the greater," end of quote. As for whoever said it is the day of 'Arafa, it was called "the greater" because it is the greatest of the obligations of the pilgrimage, for if it is missed the pilgrimage is missed. As for whoever said it is the day of Mina, that is because the greatest part of the pilgrimage is in it, and the completion of its acts: circumambulation, sacrifice, shaving and stoning. It was also said: it was described as "the greater" because the 'umra is called "the lesser pilgrimage." Mundhir ibn Sa'id and others said: People used to be dispersed on the day of 'Arafa when the Hums would stand at Muzdalifa, and the gathering was on the day of sacrifice at Mina, and for this reason they called it "the day of the greater pilgrimage," i.e., the greater as opposed to the lesser in which they were dispersed. Al-Mahdawi mentioned that the Hums and those who followed them stood at Muzdalifa in the pilgrimage of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him. Al-Qurtubi related from Ibn Sirin that by "the day of the greater pilgrimage" is meant the year in which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) performed the Farewell Pilgrimage and the nations performed the pilgrimage with him. This requires an implied element, as if he said: this proclamation's ruling is established on the day of the greater pilgrimage, which is the year of the pilgrimage of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), end of quote. It was called "the greater" because in it the rites of the pilgrimage were established, and he said in it: "Take your rites from me."

The clause (bara'atun min Allah wa-rasulihi) is a statement (p-8) of the establishment of disavowal, and the clause ﴿And a proclamation from Allah and His Messenger﴾ is a statement of the obligation to notify what has been established, so the two differ. The disavowal is attached to the covenant-holders, because it is specific to them, both those who broke their covenants and those who did not, while the proclamation is attached to "the people" because it includes the covenant-holder and other than him, the one who broke the covenant and other than him, the Muslim and the unbeliever. This is the view of the majority. It was said: It is permissible that the address be to the unbelievers, by the evidence of the end of the verse, and by the evidence of Ali's proclaiming the four sentences, whose apparent meaning is that those addressed by these sentences are the unbelievers. Since the prepositional phrase is a predicate of (wa-adhanun), it takes (ila), meaning: it is directed and reaches to the people. Had the prepositional phrase been in the position of the object, it would have taken (li) (for).

The (min) in (min al-mushrikin) is connected to (bari') as the connection of a complement, as one says: "bari'tu minka" (I am free of you) and "bari'tu min al-din" (I am free of the religion). This is unlike the (min) in his words "bara'atun min Allah," for that is in the position of a qualifier.

﴿So if you repent﴾, i.e., from the polytheism that necessitates Allah and His Messenger's disavowal of you, ﴿then it is better for you﴾, i.e., the repentance, ﴿in this world, for the protection of your souls, children and wealth, and in the Hereafter, for your entry into Paradise and your deliverance from the Fire. ﴿But if you turn away﴾, i.e., from Islam, ﴿then know that you cannot escape Allah﴾, i.e., you will not outrun Him from the vengeance that will befall you, ﴿and give tidings of painful punishment to those who disbelieve﴾. He made the warning into good news by way of mockery of them. "Those who disbelieve" is general, including the idol-worshipping polytheists and others. In this is a great threat regarding what will befall them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verses 4–8 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Except those among the polytheists with whom you made a covenant, who have not failed you in anything and have not supported anyone against you. So fulfil their covenant to them until their term. Indeed, Allah loves the righteous.﴾ Some scholars said: this is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), meaning: "But those with whom you made a covenant and who remained steadfast in the covenant, fulfil their covenant to them." Others, among them al-Zajjaj, said: it is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil) from His words: ﴿to those among the polytheists with whom you made a covenant﴾ (al-Tawbah: 1). Al-Zamakhshari said: its aspect is that it is an exception from His words: ﴿So travel freely in the land﴾ (al-Tawbah: 2), because the speech is addressed to the Muslims. Its meaning is: "A declaration of disavowal from Allah and His Messenger to those among the polytheists with whom you made a covenant. So say to them: Travel freely, except those of them with whom you made a covenant, who have not broken it, so fulfil their covenant to them." The exception here carries the sense of a corrective qualification (istidrak), as if it were said, after they had been commanded regarding the covenant-breakers: "But those who did not break their covenant, fulfil their covenant to them, do not treat them as you treat them, and do not equate the faithful with the treacherous." It was also said that it is a connected exception, and before it there is an omitted clause whose estimate is: "Kill the polytheists who have a covenant, except those with whom you made a covenant." This is a very weak view. The most apparent position is that it is disconnected, because of the long separation by many clauses between what could be the excepted item and the exception.

Mujahid and others said: they are a people who had a covenant with the Messenger for a fixed term, so he was commanded to honour it for them. From Ibn Abbas: when Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) recited "Bara'ah" (the opening of the surah), he said to the Banu Damrah, a clan of Kinanah, and a clan of Sulaym: "Allah has excluded you," and then he recited this verse.

The apparent meaning of His words "until their term" is that it refers to the term that existed between them and the Messenger, so they were commanded to fulfil the covenant until the full term was complete. From Ibn Abbas: nine months remained for a clan of Kinanah, so their covenant was to be fulfilled for them. Also from him: "until their term" means until the four months mentioned in the verse. This is far-fetched, because then the exception would not establish a renewed ruling, since the ruling for these excepted people would be the same as the ruling for the rest of the covenant-holders who did not display the same qualities, namely not failing and not supporting others against the Muslims.

ʿAtaʾ ibn al-Sa'ib al-Kufi, Ikrimah, Abu Zayd, and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read: ﴿yanquḍūkum﴾ with the dad marked (ض), which suits "covenant" (ʿahd). Its meaning is the same as the reading of the majority, because whoever falls short in the covenant has fallen short in the appointed term. It is by omission of a modifier (muḍāf), meaning: "and they did not break your covenant," so the modifier was omitted and the modified (muḍāf ilayhi) was placed in its position, because the context indicates it. Al-Karmani said: the reading with dad is closer to the sense of "covenant," but the reading with ṣad is better, so that in contrast to it stands the word "completion" (tamām) in His words: ﴿fa-atimmū ilayhim﴾ ("fulfil to them"), and completion is the opposite of shortfall.

The word ﴿shay'an﴾ ("in anything") is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: not even a little shortfall, nor much.

﴿And have not supported anyone against you﴾, as Quraysh did with the Banu Bakr when they aided them with weapons against Khuza'ah. The verb ﴿ataw﴾ (here: fulfil) is followed by "to" (ilā) because it includes the sense of ﴿fa-addū﴾ (render), meaning: render it to them complete and whole. Qatadah's statement that the excepted people were Quraysh with whom a covenant was made at the time of al-Hudaybiyyah is rejected, because Quraysh embraced Islam at the Conquest before the permission for all this was given. His words ﴿Indeed, Allah loves the righteous﴾ are an alert that fulfilling the covenant is part of piety (taqwa), and that part of piety is not to treat the two groups as equal.

﴿So when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them, seize them, besiege them, and lie in wait for them at every place of ambush.﴾ The discussion of ﴿insalakha﴾ ("has passed") was already given in His words: ﴿fa-insalakha﴾. Abu al-Haytham said: one says "we sighted the crescent of such-and-such month," meaning we entered it and wore it. So each night we increase in wearing it until half of it has passed, then after the half is complete we strip it off ourselves bit by bit until we have stripped the whole of it from ourselves, and so it "passes." He recited:

"When you strip off the month, you sight its like,
The stripping of months and the sighting suffices as a killer."

The apparent meaning is that these months are those in which the covenant-breakers were permitted to travel freely, and they are described as sacred (ḥurum) because fighting is forbidden in them. The disagreement about their beginning and end has already been mentioned.

When an indefinite noun (nakira) is mentioned first and then repeated, the proper way is to refer back to it with a pronoun, as in: "I met a man and struck him." It is also permissible to repeat the word with the definite article (al-), as in: "I met a man and struck the man." But it is not permissible to describe it with a description that implies difference. If you said: "I met a man and struck the blue man," while meaning the man you met, it would not be correct; rather, that would refer to someone else, and the one struck would not be the one met. But if you describe it with a description that does not imply difference, it is permissible, as in: "I met a man and struck the aforementioned man." Here the phrase ﴿the sacred months﴾ came, because this description is understood from His words: ﴿So travel freely in the land for four months﴾ (al-Tawbah: 2), since the estimate is: "four months that are sacred, in which you will not be attacked." So "sacred" is not a description that implies difference. It was also said: the sacred months are other than these four, namely the months in which Allah has forbidden fighting since He created the heavens and the earth. These are what a hadith mentions, in which the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed time has returned to its original form on the day Allah created the heavens and the earth. The year is twelve months, of which four are sacred: Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, al-Muharram, and Rajab." In that case the four would be drawn from two years. It was also said: the first of them is al-Muharram, so they would be from one year.

The command to kill was given as encouragement and as a strengthening of resolve, and to show that they have no defence against being killed. The unrestricted command to kill is evidence for killing them by any means. Abu Bakr killed the apostates by burning with fire, by stoning, by throwing them from mountain tops, and by inverting them into wells. Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) also burned a group of the people of apostasy, relying on the general wording of this verse. Sound hadiths have also come forbidding mutilation (muthlah). The word ﴿polytheists﴾ is general and covers every polytheist. The Sunnah, however, made exceptions for children, monks, and elderly people who are not men of military judgment, and whoever among them fights is killed. Al-Zamakhshari said: it means those who broke the covenant and supported others against you.

The phrase ﴿wherever you find them﴾ is general across places, whether within the sacred territory or outside it. ﴿Seize them﴾ is an expression for capture, and "the captive" (al-akhidh) is the prisoner. Evidence for permissibility of capturing them is ﴿besiege them﴾: confine them and prevent them from moving freely in the lands. It was also said: enslave them. It was also said: its meaning is "lay siege to them if they fortify themselves." The reading ﴿fa-ḥāṣirūhum﴾ ("then besiege them") is attested as an irregular reading (shādhdh), and this view is also reported from Ibn Abbas. Also from him: keep them away from the Sacred Mosque. It was also said: prevent them from entering the lands of Islam and from acting in them except with permission. Al-Qurtubi said, concerning His words ﴿and lie in wait for them at every place of ambush﴾: this indicates the permissibility of ambushing them before the call (to Islam), because the meaning is "lie in wait for them at the places where they are off guard." This is an alert that the aim is to inflict harm on them by every means, whether by fighting or by ambush. The Muslims have agreed on the permissibility of stealing from the wealth of the people of war, hamstringing their horses, and destroying their livestock if they cannot be taken out to the abode of Islam, unless they make peace on such terms.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿kulla marṣad﴾ ("every place of ambush") means every passage and route where you lie in wait for them. It is in the accusative as an adverb of place, like His words: ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾ (al-A'raf: 16), end of quotation. This is what al-Zajjaj also said; he said: ﴿kulla marṣad﴾ is an adverb of place, like your saying: "I went a way." Abu Ali (al-Farisi) rejected this, because a ﴿marṣad﴾ is a specific place in which the enemy is watched, so it is a particular place from which the preposition is not dropped except by transmitted usage, as Sibawayh related: "I entered the house," and as the fox "made the path smooth" (ʿasala al-ṭarīq). End of quotation. I say: its accusative as an adverb of place is valid, because His words ﴿and lie in wait for them﴾ do not mean literal sitting, but rather: watch them in every place where one watches. Since it carries this meaning, it is analogically permissible to drop the preposition from it, as the poet said: "They sat at all its passages, every sitting place." So whenever the governing verb of a specific place-adverb is either from the same root or has the same meaning, it may reach the adverb without the intermediary "in" (fī). Thus it is permissible to say "I sat the seat of Zayd" and "I sat the seat of Zayd," meaning "in the seat of Zayd." Just as a verb may govern a verbal noun not of its own root when it has the same meaning, so too it may govern an adverb of place. Al-Akhfash said: the meaning is "upon every place of ambush," so "upon" was omitted and the verb took effect, and the verb reaches its governed object in the accusative. Our companions restrict this to poetry, and they cited:

"It longs and reveals what is in it of passion,
And hides what, were it not for grief, would have ended me."

That is: would have ended me (qaḍā 'alayya), that is, would have decided my fate.

﴿Then if they repent, establish prayer, and give zakat, let them go their way. Indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ That is, from disbelief and treachery. Repentance includes faith and abandoning the sins they were engaged in. Then He drew attention to the greatest of the Islamic rites, which is the establishment of prayer, the best of physical acts, and the giving of zakat, the best of financial acts. By these two the practical strength becomes evident, just as by repentance the intellectual strength becomes evident in place of ignorance. ﴿Let them go their way﴾ is an expression for refraining from them and treating them in the same way as Muslims in their affairs, wherever they wish, without your interfering with them, as the poet said: "Let go the path for one through whom the minaret will be built." Or the meaning may be: release them from captivity and confinement. The first meaning is the apparent one, because the ruling covers both the one who was taken captive and others.

Ibn Zayd said: prayer and zakat were made obligatory together, and Allah refused that prayer be accepted without zakat. He also said: may Allah have mercy on Abu Bakr, how deeply understanding he was in his statement: "I will surely fight whoever distinguishes between prayer and zakat." The mention of the attributes of forgiveness and mercy from Him, the Exalted, fits those who repent from disbelief and commit themselves to the laws of Islam. The hafiz Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi said: there is no disagreement among Muslims that whoever abandons prayer and the rest of the obligatory duties while considering them permissible becomes a disbeliever, is buried in the graveyard of disbelievers, and his property becomes spoils (fay'). Whoever abandons the sunan (recommended practices) commits sin (fisq), and whoever abandons the supererogatory acts (nawafil) is not blamed, unless he denies their merit, in which case he becomes a disbeliever, because he becomes one who rejects what the Prophet (ﷺ) brought and reported. End of quotation. The apparent view is that the implication of the conditional clause does not establish with certainty that whoever deliberately abandons prayer and zakat, without considering it lawful and while able to do so, must be killed; because releasing the way may be achieved by imprisonment or other means, so killing is not specifically required. Scholars differed on this. Makhul, Malik, al-Shafi'i, Hammad ibn Zayd, Waki', and Abu Thawr said: he is to be killed. Ibn Shihab, Abu Hanifah, and Dawud said: he is to be imprisoned and beaten, and not killed. A group of the Companions and the Successors said: he is killed as a disbeliever, his property is the property of an apostate, and Ishaq held this view. Ishaq said: this has been the position of the people of knowledge from the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) until our time.

﴿And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection until he hears the word of Allah, then deliver him to his place of safety. That is because they are a people who do not know.﴾ Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: it has been abrogated (mansukhah) by the verse commanding the killing of the polytheists. Al-Hasan and Mujahid said: it is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated) until the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Jubayr reported: a man came to Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) and said: If one of us wants to come to Muhammad after the end of this term in order to hear the word of Allah, or to come to him for some need, will he be killed? He said: No, because Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection﴾, to the end of the verse. End of quotation. It was also said: the ruling of this verse applied only during the four months that were set as their term. The apparent view, however, is that it is muhkam.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verses 4–8 (part 2 of 2):

When God commanded the killing of the polytheists wherever they are found, their capture, their confinement, and the pursuit of their unguarded moments, He mentioned to them a state in which they are neither killed nor captured but taken as prisoners. This is the state in which one of them comes seeking guidance, seeking proof and evidence for what he calls to of the religion. The meaning is: ﴿If anyone among the polytheists seeks your protection﴾; that is, asks you to grant him protection. This is after the sacred months have passed, so that he may hear the word of God and what it contains of monotheism, and may learn what you were sent with. So grant him protection until he hears the word of God and reflects on it, and becomes aware of the reality of the matter. Then convey him to his abode, where he is safe if he does not become Muslim. Then fight him if you wish, without treachery or betrayal.

The word حَتَّى (ḥattā, "until") may be a particle of limit, meaning "until he hears." It may also be a particle of causation (ta'līl, "so that"). In both cases it is connected with فَأَجِرْهُ (fa-ajirhu, "grant him protection"). It is not valid for it to be an instance of al-tanāzuʿ (the grammatical construction in which two verbs compete for one object). Although in terms of meaning it is valid for it to be connected with اسْتَجَارَكَ (istajāraka, "seeks your protection") or with فَأَجِرْهُ, this is prevented by a verbal obstacle: if the first verb were made to govern, it would place a pronoun in the second, and حَتَّى does not govern a pronoun. For this reason it is not valid to treat it as al-tanāzuʿ. However, those grammarians who held that حَتَّى governs a pronoun may consider it al-tanāzuʿ in their view. The position that حَتَّى does not govern a pronoun is that of the majority.

Since the Qur'an is the greatest of the miracles, hearing is linked to it, and hearing is mentioned because it is the path to understanding. Hearing may sometimes mean understanding. You say to someone you addressed who did not accept from you: "You did not hear," meaning "You did not understand." كَلَامَ اللَّهِ (kalām Allāh, "the word of God") is an annexation (iḍāfah) of an attribute to the thing described, not an annexation of a created thing to its Creator. مَأْمَنَهُ (ma'manahu, "his place of safety") means the place of his safety. It was said that مَأْمَنَهُ is a verbal noun, meaning: "then convey to him his safety."

The Mu'tazilah (a theological school) used the phrase ﴿until he hears the word of God﴾ as evidence that the speech of God is created, because only letters and sounds are heard, and it is known by necessity that these are originated. This is discussed in ʿilm al-kalām (scholastic theology).

In this verse is evidence that reflection on monotheism is among the highest stations, since the blood of the disbeliever, whose blood was forfeit, is protected by his request for reflection and inference. It also obliges the Messenger to convey him to his place of safety. In it is also evidence that taqlīd (blind imitation) is not sufficient in religion, since he is not given respite; rather, it is said to him: either you embrace Islam or you will be killed. In it is further evidence that after he hears the word of God, he is not allowed to remain in the land of Islam; rather, he is conveyed to his place of safety. And it is obligatory to protect him and to safeguard him for a period in which he hears the word of God.

The address in ﴿اسْتَجَارَكَ﴾ (istajāraka, "seeks your protection") and ﴿فَأَجِرْهُ﴾ (fa-ajirhu, "grant him protection") shows that the safe-conduct granted by the ruler is valid. As for others: the safe-conduct of a free man is binding. Ibn Ḥabīb said that the imam considers it. As for a slave: al-Awzāʿī, al-Thawrī, al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, Isḥāq, Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan, Abū Thawr, and Dāwūd said that he has the right to grant safe-conduct, and this is the well-known position of Mālik. Abū Ḥanīfah said that he has no safe-conduct, and this is also a view in the school of Mālik. According to the majority, a free woman has the right to grant safe-conduct. ʿAbd al-Malik ibn al-Mājishūn said no, unless the imam grants it, but his view is anomalous. A child who is able to fight, his safe-conduct is valid.

﴿That is because they are a people who do not know﴾; that is, that command, to grant protection and convey him to safety, is because they are an ignorant people who do not know what Islam is or what the reality of what you call to is. Therefore it is necessary to give them safe-conduct until they hear and understand the truth, as al-Zamakhsharī said. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: it is a reference to this gentleness in granting protection, in making them hear, and in conveying them to safety. The phrase ﴿they do not know﴾ negates their knowledge of their right path in following the Messenger (ﷺ).

﴿How can there be a covenant for the polytheists with God and with His Messenger, except for those with whom you made a covenant at the Sacred Mosque? So as long as they are upright toward you, be upright toward them. Indeed, God loves the righteous.﴾

This is an interrogative whose meaning is wonder, disapproval, and disbelief. Al-Tabrīzī and al-Kirmānī said its meaning is negation; that is, there can be no covenant for them while they are hostile to you. He pointed out the reason for the absence of a covenant by the attribute that they possess, which is polytheism. Al-Qurṭubī said: in the verse there is an ellipsis; that is, how can there be a covenant for the polytheists while they hide treachery and breach of covenant? End of quote. The interrogative is often used to mean negation, and from it is the poet's saying:

"Here are swords, O Hudā ibn Mālik, many,
but none strikes with the sword."

That is, none strikes with the sword. Since the interrogative means negation, the exception may come after it. The exception may be connected (muttaṣil) or disconnected (munqaṭiʿ). That is, "but those among them with whom you made a covenant at the Sacred Mosque." Al-Ḥawfī said: it is valid for ﴿الَّذِينَ﴾ (alladhīna, "those who") to be in the genitive case as a substitute (badal) for ﴿الْمُشْرِكِينَ﴾ (al-mushrikīn, "the polytheists"), because the meaning of what preceded is negation. That is, there is no covenant for the polytheists except with those who did not break it. Ibn ʿAbbās said they are Quraysh. Al-Suddī said they are Banū Judhaymah ibn al-Dīl. Ibn Isḥāq said they are the tribes of Banū Bakr, who had entered, at the time of al-Ḥudaybiyyah, into the truce that was between the Messenger (ﷺ) and Quraysh. Al-Zamakhsharī said they are like Banū Kinānah and Banū Ḍamrah. Some, including Mujāhid, said they are Khuzāʿah, and this was refuted by their conversion to Islam in the year of the conquest. Ibn Zayd said they are Quraysh. The verse was revealed, but they were not upright, so after that they were given a respite of four months. This view was weakened on the grounds that, four months after the proclamation, there were none left among Quraysh except Muslims, and that was a year after the conquest of Makkah. Likewise for Khuzāʿah, as al-Ṭabarī said.

﴿So as long as they are upright toward you﴾ in the covenant, ﴿be upright toward them﴾ in fulfilling it.

Abū al-Baqāʾ permitted that كَيْفَ (kayfa, "how") be the predicate of يَكُونُ (yakūnu, "there is"), as in His saying ﴿how was the end of their scheming﴾ (27:51). He also permitted that لِلْمُشْرِكِينَ (lil-mushrikīn, "for the polytheists") be the predicate. عِنْدَ (ʿinda, "with" / "in the presence of") in these two cases is an adverbial complement (ẓarf) of الْعَهْدُ (al-ʿahd, "the covenant"), or of يَكُونُ, or it is a circumstantial (ḥāl), or it is a qualifier of الْعَهْدُ. The predicate may also be عِنْدَ اللَّهِ (ʿinda Allāh, "with God"), and لِلْمُشْرِكِينَ is a clarification or is connected with يَكُونُ. And كَيْفَ is a circumstantial element from الْعَهْدُ. End of quote.

The apparent view is that مَا (mā) in ﴿مَا اسْتَقَامُوا﴾ (mā istaqāmū, "as long as they are upright") is a temporal verbal noun (maṣdariyyah ẓarfiyyah), meaning: "be upright toward them for the duration of their uprightness." It is not conditional. Abū al-Baqāʾ said it is conditional, like His saying ﴿Whatever mercy God grants to people﴾ (35:2). So the meaning would be: "For whatever period they are upright toward you, be upright toward them." Al-Ḥawfī said مَا is a conditional in the nominative position as a subject, with اسْتَقَامُوا as its predicate, and لَكُم connected with اسْتَقَامُوا, and فَاسْتَقِيمُوا لَهُمْ with the فَ being the response of the condition. So the meaning would be: "Whatever time they are upright toward you, be upright toward them." He permitted it to be conditional because of the presence of the فَ in فَاسْتَقِيمُوا, since a temporal verbal noun does not require the فَ. Ibn Mālik permitted the temporal verbal noun to be conditional and to apocopate the verb, and he cited poetry whose apparent meaning supports his claim. We have mentioned that in our book al-Takmīl, and we interpreted the verse he cited. So according to his view, it is temporal and conditional.

﴿Indeed God loves the righteous﴾ means that fulfilling the covenant is among the traits of the righteous, and waiting for these people, if they remain upright, is among the deeds of the believers. Piety includes faith and fulfilling the covenant.

﴿How [can there be a covenant]? If they gain the upper hand over you, they will not observe toward you any tie of kinship or covenant. They please you with their mouths, but their hearts refuse, and most of them are defiantly disobedient.﴾

كَيْفَ (kayfa, "how") here is an emphasis negating their steadfastness in the covenant. The verb omitted after it is apparently of the same type as the nearest verb mentioned before it, and it was omitted because its meaning is known from the earlier كَيْفَ. The estimate is: "How can there be a covenant for them while this is their state?" The omission of the verb after كَيْفَ occurs when the meaning indicates it, as in His saying ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness?﴾ (4:41). The poet said:

"You told me that death is in the villages,
so how [did he die] while here are a hill and a sand dune?"

That is: "so how did he die, when he was not in a village?" Al-Ḥuṭay'ah said:

"So how [can you blame me], when I did not know them to have forsaken you over a grave matter, and that they had cut up your hide?"

That is: "So how can you blame me for praising them?" He dispensed with that, because what occurred in the poem indicated what was omitted. Abū al-Baqāʾ estimated the omitted verb after كَيْفَ as: "How can you feel reassured about them?" Others estimated it as: "How will they not kill them?"

The وَ (wa, "and") in ﴿وَإِنْ يَظْهَرُوا﴾ (wa-in yaẓharū, "if they gain the upper hand") is the waw of circumstance. The discussion of the conditional clause occurring as a circumstantial clause has already been treated in His saying ﴿And if an offer like it comes to them, they will take it﴾ (7:169). The meaning of ظُهُور (ẓuhūr, "gaining the upper hand") is superiority and victory. You say: ظَهَرْتُ عَلَى فُلَانٍ (ẓahartu ʿalā fulān, "I prevailed over so-and-so"), meaning "I overcame him." The meaning here is: if they gain power over you and triumph over you. Zayd ibn ʿAlī read ﴿وَإِنْ يُظْهَرُوا﴾ (wa-in yuẓharū, in the passive voice).

لَا يَرْقُبُوا (lā yarqubū, "they do not observe") means: they do not preserve or respect. إِلًّا (illan) means: a covenant, or kinship, or an alliance, or a political bond, or God, or jiʾār (raising the voice in supplication). These are the views given. Mujāhid and Abū Mijlaz said that إِلٌّ (il) is the name of God in Syriac, which was Arabized. From this is the saying of Abū Bakr when he heard the speech of Musaylimah: "This is a speech that did not come out of il." One group read أَلًّا (allan), with a fatḥah on the hamzah, as a verbal noun from the verb ألَّ, which means "covenant." ʿIkrimah read إِيلًا (īlan), with a kasrah on the hamzah and a yāʾ after it. It was said that this is the name of God. It may also mean إِلًى (ilan), in which one of the doubled letters was replaced by a yāʾ, as they said in إِمَّا (immā) → إِيمَا (īmā). The poet said:

"Would that our mother had raised her ostrich,
[to be taken] either to Paradise or to the Fire."

Ibn Jinnī said: it may also be derived from آلَ يَئُولُ (āla yaʾūlu, "to govern"), when it means "to manage affairs," with the waw changed to a yāʾ because it is quiescent and the letter before it is kasrah. That is: they do not observe in you any political management, nor conciliation, nor covenant. Whoever holds that الإِلّ (al-ill) means the covenant makes both words, al-ill and al-dhimmah, two words for one meaning or for closely related meanings. Whoever holds that al-ill is other than the covenant, then they are two different words.

When He mentioned their conduct toward the believers if they gain the upper hand over them, He mentioned their conduct toward them when they are not dominant, saying: ﴿They please you with their mouths﴾. He began this statement anew; that is, their outward state is contrary to their inward state. All of this is an affirmation and a making improbable of the steadfastness of their hearts in the covenant. إِبَاءُ الْقَلْبِ (ibāʾ al-qalb, "the refusal of the heart") is its opposition to what runs on the tongue of good speech.

It was said: ﴿They please you with their mouths﴾ refers to their promises of faith, while their hearts refuse except disbelief. It was said: they please you in obedience, while their hearts refuse except disobedience. The apparent view is to keep أَكْثَرُهُم (aktharuhum, "most of them") on its literal meaning. It was said: "most of them" is used because among them is one for whom God decreed faith. It was also said: it is used because among them is one who has restraint in observing good conduct, abstaining from what damages honor and invites evil talk. As for "most of them," they are people of corrupt souls, who go out in evil; no manliness restrains them, and no praiseworthy disposition holds them back. They do not guard against lying, deceit, or treachery. Whoever has this description is blamed among people and in all religions. Do you not see the people of al-Jāhiliyyah (the period of ignorance before Islam), who were disbelievers, how they praise themselves for chastity, truthfulness, fulfilling covenants, and good morals? It was also said: the meaning of "most of them" is "all of them are defiantly disobedient." This was said by Ibn ʿAṭiyyah and al-Kirmānī.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verses 4–8 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Except those among the polytheists with whom you made a covenant, who have not failed you in anything and have not supported anyone against you. So fulfil their covenant to them until their term. Indeed, Allah loves the righteous.﴾ Some scholars said: this is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), meaning: "But those with whom you made a covenant and who remained steadfast in the covenant, fulfil their covenant to them." Others, among them al-Zajjaj, said: it is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil) from His words: ﴿to those among the polytheists with whom you made a covenant﴾ (al-Tawbah: 1). Al-Zamakhshari said: its aspect is that it is an exception from His words: ﴿So travel freely in the land﴾ (al-Tawbah: 2), because the speech is addressed to the Muslims. Its meaning is: "A declaration of disavowal from Allah and His Messenger to those among the polytheists with whom you made a covenant. So say to them: Travel freely, except those of them with whom you made a covenant, who have not broken it, so fulfil their covenant to them." The exception here carries the sense of a corrective qualification (istidrak), as if it were said, after they had been commanded regarding the covenant-breakers: "But those who did not break their covenant, fulfil their covenant to them, do not treat them as you treat them, and do not equate the faithful with the treacherous." It was also said that it is a connected exception, and before it there is an omitted clause whose estimate is: "Kill the polytheists who have a covenant, except those with whom you made a covenant." This is a very weak view. The most apparent position is that it is disconnected, because of the long separation by many clauses between what could be the excepted item and the exception.

Mujahid and others said: they are a people who had a covenant with the Messenger for a fixed term, so he was commanded to honour it for them. From Ibn Abbas: when Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) recited "Bara'ah" (the opening of the surah), he said to the Banu Damrah, a clan of Kinanah, and a clan of Sulaym: "Allah has excluded you," and then he recited this verse.

The apparent meaning of His words "until their term" is that it refers to the term that existed between them and the Messenger, so they were commanded to fulfil the covenant until the full term was complete. From Ibn Abbas: nine months remained for a clan of Kinanah, so their covenant was to be fulfilled for them. Also from him: "until their term" means until the four months mentioned in the verse. This is far-fetched, because then the exception would not establish a renewed ruling, since the ruling for these excepted people would be the same as the ruling for the rest of the covenant-holders who did not display the same qualities, namely not failing and not supporting others against the Muslims.

ʿAtaʾ ibn al-Sa'ib al-Kufi, Ikrimah, Abu Zayd, and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read: ﴿yanquḍūkum﴾ with the dad marked (ض), which suits "covenant" (ʿahd). Its meaning is the same as the reading of the majority, because whoever falls short in the covenant has fallen short in the appointed term. It is by omission of a modifier (muḍāf), meaning: "and they did not break your covenant," so the modifier was omitted and the modified (muḍāf ilayhi) was placed in its position, because the context indicates it. Al-Karmani said: the reading with dad is closer to the sense of "covenant," but the reading with ṣad is better, so that in contrast to it stands the word "completion" (tamām) in His words: ﴿fa-atimmū ilayhim﴾ ("fulfil to them"), and completion is the opposite of shortfall.

The word ﴿shay'an﴾ ("in anything") is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: not even a little shortfall, nor much.

﴿And have not supported anyone against you﴾, as Quraysh did with the Banu Bakr when they aided them with weapons against Khuza'ah. The verb ﴿ataw﴾ (here: fulfil) is followed by "to" (ilā) because it includes the sense of ﴿fa-addū﴾ (render), meaning: render it to them complete and whole. Qatadah's statement that the excepted people were Quraysh with whom a covenant was made at the time of al-Hudaybiyyah is rejected, because Quraysh embraced Islam at the Conquest before the permission for all this was given. His words ﴿Indeed, Allah loves the righteous﴾ are an alert that fulfilling the covenant is part of piety (taqwa), and that part of piety is not to treat the two groups as equal.

﴿So when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them, seize them, besiege them, and lie in wait for them at every place of ambush.﴾ The discussion of ﴿insalakha﴾ ("has passed") was already given in His words: ﴿fa-insalakha﴾. Abu al-Haytham said: one says "we sighted the crescent of such-and-such month," meaning we entered it and wore it. So each night we increase in wearing it until half of it has passed, then after the half is complete we strip it off ourselves bit by bit until we have stripped the whole of it from ourselves, and so it "passes." He recited:

"When you strip off the month, you sight its like,
The stripping of months and the sighting suffices as a killer."

The apparent meaning is that these months are those in which the covenant-breakers were permitted to travel freely, and they are described as sacred (ḥurum) because fighting is forbidden in them. The disagreement about their beginning and end has already been mentioned.

When an indefinite noun (nakira) is mentioned first and then repeated, the proper way is to refer back to it with a pronoun, as in: "I met a man and struck him." It is also permissible to repeat the word with the definite article (al-), as in: "I met a man and struck the man." But it is not permissible to describe it with a description that implies difference. If you said: "I met a man and struck the blue man," while meaning the man you met, it would not be correct; rather, that would refer to someone else, and the one struck would not be the one met. But if you describe it with a description that does not imply difference, it is permissible, as in: "I met a man and struck the aforementioned man." Here the phrase ﴿the sacred months﴾ came, because this description is understood from His words: ﴿So travel freely in the land for four months﴾ (al-Tawbah: 2), since the estimate is: "four months that are sacred, in which you will not be attacked." So "sacred" is not a description that implies difference. It was also said: the sacred months are other than these four, namely the months in which Allah has forbidden fighting since He created the heavens and the earth. These are what a hadith mentions, in which the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed time has returned to its original form on the day Allah created the heavens and the earth.
