The year is twelve months, of which four are sacred: Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, al-Muharram, and Rajab." In that case the four would be drawn from two years. It was also said: the first of them is al-Muharram, so they would be from one year.

The command to kill was given as encouragement and as a strengthening of resolve, and to show that they have no defence against being killed. The unrestricted command to kill is evidence for killing them by any means. Abu Bakr killed the apostates by burning with fire, by stoning, by throwing them from mountain tops, and by inverting them into wells. Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) also burned a group of the people of apostasy, relying on the general wording of this verse. Sound hadiths have also come forbidding mutilation (muthlah). The word ﴿polytheists﴾ is general and covers every polytheist. The Sunnah, however, made exceptions for children, monks, and elderly people who are not men of military judgment, and whoever among them fights is killed. Al-Zamakhshari said: it means those who broke the covenant and supported others against you.

The phrase ﴿wherever you find them﴾ is general across places, whether within the sacred territory or outside it. ﴿Seize them﴾ is an expression for capture, and "the captive" (al-akhidh) is the prisoner. Evidence for permissibility of capturing them is ﴿besiege them﴾: confine them and prevent them from moving freely in the lands. It was also said: enslave them. It was also said: its meaning is "lay siege to them if they fortify themselves." The reading ﴿fa-ḥāṣirūhum﴾ ("then besiege them") is attested as an irregular reading (shādhdh), and this view is also reported from Ibn Abbas. Also from him: keep them away from the Sacred Mosque. It was also said: prevent them from entering the lands of Islam and from acting in them except with permission. Al-Qurtubi said, concerning His words ﴿and lie in wait for them at every place of ambush﴾: this indicates the permissibility of ambushing them before the call (to Islam), because the meaning is "lie in wait for them at the places where they are off guard." This is an alert that the aim is to inflict harm on them by every means, whether by fighting or by ambush. The Muslims have agreed on the permissibility of stealing from the wealth of the people of war, hamstringing their horses, and destroying their livestock if they cannot be taken out to the abode of Islam, unless they make peace on such terms.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿kulla marṣad﴾ ("every place of ambush") means every passage and route where you lie in wait for them. It is in the accusative as an adverb of place, like His words: ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾ (al-A'raf: 16), end of quotation. This is what al-Zajjaj also said; he said: ﴿kulla marṣad﴾ is an adverb of place, like your saying: "I went a way." Abu Ali (al-Farisi) rejected this, because a ﴿marṣad﴾ is a specific place in which the enemy is watched, so it is a particular place from which the preposition is not dropped except by transmitted usage, as Sibawayh related: "I entered the house," and as the fox "made the path smooth" (ʿasala al-ṭarīq). End of quotation. I say: its accusative as an adverb of place is valid, because His words ﴿and lie in wait for them﴾ do not mean literal sitting, but rather: watch them in every place where one watches. Since it carries this meaning, it is analogically permissible to drop the preposition from it, as the poet said: "They sat at all its passages, every sitting place." So whenever the governing verb of a specific place-adverb is either from the same root or has the same meaning, it may reach the adverb without the intermediary "in" (fī). Thus it is permissible to say "I sat the seat of Zayd" and "I sat the seat of Zayd," meaning "in the seat of Zayd." Just as a verb may govern a verbal noun not of its own root when it has the same meaning, so too it may govern an adverb of place. Al-Akhfash said: the meaning is "upon every place of ambush," so "upon" was omitted and the verb took effect, and the verb reaches its governed object in the accusative. Our companions restrict this to poetry, and they cited:

"It longs and reveals what is in it of passion,
And hides what, were it not for grief, would have ended me."

That is: would have ended me (qaḍā 'alayya), that is, would have decided my fate.

﴿Then if they repent, establish prayer, and give zakat, let them go their way. Indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ That is, from disbelief and treachery. Repentance includes faith and abandoning the sins they were engaged in. Then He drew attention to the greatest of the Islamic rites, which is the establishment of prayer, the best of physical acts, and the giving of zakat, the best of financial acts. By these two the practical strength becomes evident, just as by repentance the intellectual strength becomes evident in place of ignorance. ﴿Let them go their way﴾ is an expression for refraining from them and treating them in the same way as Muslims in their affairs, wherever they wish, without your interfering with them, as the poet said: "Let go the path for one through whom the minaret will be built." Or the meaning may be: release them from captivity and confinement. The first meaning is the apparent one, because the ruling covers both the one who was taken captive and others.

Ibn Zayd said: prayer and zakat were made obligatory together, and Allah refused that prayer be accepted without zakat. He also said: may Allah have mercy on Abu Bakr, how deeply understanding he was in his statement: "I will surely fight whoever distinguishes between prayer and zakat." The mention of the attributes of forgiveness and mercy from Him, the Exalted, fits those who repent from disbelief and commit themselves to the laws of Islam. The hafiz Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi said: there is no disagreement among Muslims that whoever abandons prayer and the rest of the obligatory duties while considering them permissible becomes a disbeliever, is buried in the graveyard of disbelievers, and his property becomes spoils (fay'). Whoever abandons the sunan (recommended practices) commits sin (fisq), and whoever abandons the supererogatory acts (nawafil) is not blamed, unless he denies their merit, in which case he becomes a disbeliever, because he becomes one who rejects what the Prophet (ﷺ) brought and reported. End of quotation. The apparent view is that the implication of the conditional clause does not establish with certainty that whoever deliberately abandons prayer and zakat, without considering it lawful and while able to do so, must be killed; because releasing the way may be achieved by imprisonment or other means, so killing is not specifically required. Scholars differed on this. Makhul, Malik, al-Shafi'i, Hammad ibn Zayd, Waki', and Abu Thawr said: he is to be killed. Ibn Shihab, Abu Hanifah, and Dawud said: he is to be imprisoned and beaten, and not killed. A group of the Companions and the Successors said: he is killed as a disbeliever, his property is the property of an apostate, and Ishaq held this view. Ishaq said: this has been the position of the people of knowledge from the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) until our time.

﴿And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection until he hears the word of Allah, then deliver him to his place of safety. That is because they are a people who do not know.﴾ Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: it has been abrogated (mansukhah) by the verse commanding the killing of the polytheists. Al-Hasan and Mujahid said: it is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated) until the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Jubayr reported: a man came to Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) and said: If one of us wants to come to Muhammad after the end of this term in order to hear the word of Allah, or to come to him for some need, will he be killed? He said: No, because Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection﴾, to the end of the verse. End of quotation. It was also said: the ruling of this verse applied only during the four months that were set as their term. The apparent view, however, is that it is muhkam.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verses 4–8 (part 2 of 2):

When God commanded the killing of the polytheists wherever they are found, their capture, their confinement, and the pursuit of their unguarded moments, He mentioned to them a state in which they are neither killed nor captured but taken as prisoners. This is the state in which one of them comes seeking guidance, seeking proof and evidence for what he calls to of the religion. The meaning is: ﴿If anyone among the polytheists seeks your protection﴾; that is, asks you to grant him protection. This is after the sacred months have passed, so that he may hear the word of God and what it contains of monotheism, and may learn what you were sent with. So grant him protection until he hears the word of God and reflects on it, and becomes aware of the reality of the matter. Then convey him to his abode, where he is safe if he does not become Muslim. Then fight him if you wish, without treachery or betrayal.

The word حَتَّى (ḥattā, "until") may be a particle of limit, meaning "until he hears." It may also be a particle of causation (ta'līl, "so that"). In both cases it is connected with فَأَجِرْهُ (fa-ajirhu, "grant him protection"). It is not valid for it to be an instance of al-tanāzuʿ (the grammatical construction in which two verbs compete for one object). Although in terms of meaning it is valid for it to be connected with اسْتَجَارَكَ (istajāraka, "seeks your protection") or with فَأَجِرْهُ, this is prevented by a verbal obstacle: if the first verb were made to govern, it would place a pronoun in the second, and حَتَّى does not govern a pronoun. For this reason it is not valid to treat it as al-tanāzuʿ. However, those grammarians who held that حَتَّى governs a pronoun may consider it al-tanāzuʿ in their view. The position that حَتَّى does not govern a pronoun is that of the majority.

Since the Qur'an is the greatest of the miracles, hearing is linked to it, and hearing is mentioned because it is the path to understanding. Hearing may sometimes mean understanding. You say to someone you addressed who did not accept from you: "You did not hear," meaning "You did not understand." كَلَامَ اللَّهِ (kalām Allāh, "the word of God") is an annexation (iḍāfah) of an attribute to the thing described, not an annexation of a created thing to its Creator. مَأْمَنَهُ (ma'manahu, "his place of safety") means the place of his safety. It was said that مَأْمَنَهُ is a verbal noun, meaning: "then convey to him his safety."

The Mu'tazilah (a theological school) used the phrase ﴿until he hears the word of God﴾ as evidence that the speech of God is created, because only letters and sounds are heard, and it is known by necessity that these are originated. This is discussed in ʿilm al-kalām (scholastic theology).

In this verse is evidence that reflection on monotheism is among the highest stations, since the blood of the disbeliever, whose blood was forfeit, is protected by his request for reflection and inference. It also obliges the Messenger to convey him to his place of safety. In it is also evidence that taqlīd (blind imitation) is not sufficient in religion, since he is not given respite; rather, it is said to him: either you embrace Islam or you will be killed. In it is further evidence that after he hears the word of God, he is not allowed to remain in the land of Islam; rather, he is conveyed to his place of safety. And it is obligatory to protect him and to safeguard him for a period in which he hears the word of God.

The address in ﴿اسْتَجَارَكَ﴾ (istajāraka, "seeks your protection") and ﴿فَأَجِرْهُ﴾ (fa-ajirhu, "grant him protection") shows that the safe-conduct granted by the ruler is valid. As for others: the safe-conduct of a free man is binding. Ibn Ḥabīb said that the imam considers it. As for a slave: al-Awzāʿī, al-Thawrī, al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, Isḥāq, Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan, Abū Thawr, and Dāwūd said that he has the right to grant safe-conduct, and this is the well-known position of Mālik. Abū Ḥanīfah said that he has no safe-conduct, and this is also a view in the school of Mālik. According to the majority, a free woman has the right to grant safe-conduct. ʿAbd al-Malik ibn al-Mājishūn said no, unless the imam grants it, but his view is anomalous. A child who is able to fight, his safe-conduct is valid.

﴿That is because they are a people who do not know﴾; that is, that command, to grant protection and convey him to safety, is because they are an ignorant people who do not know what Islam is or what the reality of what you call to is. Therefore it is necessary to give them safe-conduct until they hear and understand the truth, as al-Zamakhsharī said. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: it is a reference to this gentleness in granting protection, in making them hear, and in conveying them to safety. The phrase ﴿they do not know﴾ negates their knowledge of their right path in following the Messenger (ﷺ).

﴿How can there be a covenant for the polytheists with God and with His Messenger, except for those with whom you made a covenant at the Sacred Mosque? So as long as they are upright toward you, be upright toward them. Indeed, God loves the righteous.﴾

This is an interrogative whose meaning is wonder, disapproval, and disbelief. Al-Tabrīzī and al-Kirmānī said its meaning is negation; that is, there can be no covenant for them while they are hostile to you. He pointed out the reason for the absence of a covenant by the attribute that they possess, which is polytheism. Al-Qurṭubī said: in the verse there is an ellipsis; that is, how can there be a covenant for the polytheists while they hide treachery and breach of covenant? End of quote. The interrogative is often used to mean negation, and from it is the poet's saying:

"Here are swords, O Hudā ibn Mālik, many,
but none strikes with the sword."

That is, none strikes with the sword. Since the interrogative means negation, the exception may come after it. The exception may be connected (muttaṣil) or disconnected (munqaṭiʿ). That is, "but those among them with whom you made a covenant at the Sacred Mosque." Al-Ḥawfī said: it is valid for ﴿الَّذِينَ﴾ (alladhīna, "those who") to be in the genitive case as a substitute (badal) for ﴿الْمُشْرِكِينَ﴾ (al-mushrikīn, "the polytheists"), because the meaning of what preceded is negation. That is, there is no covenant for the polytheists except with those who did not break it. Ibn ʿAbbās said they are Quraysh. Al-Suddī said they are Banū Judhaymah ibn al-Dīl. Ibn Isḥāq said they are the tribes of Banū Bakr, who had entered, at the time of al-Ḥudaybiyyah, into the truce that was between the Messenger (ﷺ) and Quraysh. Al-Zamakhsharī said they are like Banū Kinānah and Banū Ḍamrah. Some, including Mujāhid, said they are Khuzāʿah, and this was refuted by their conversion to Islam in the year of the conquest. Ibn Zayd said they are Quraysh. The verse was revealed, but they were not upright, so after that they were given a respite of four months. This view was weakened on the grounds that, four months after the proclamation, there were none left among Quraysh except Muslims, and that was a year after the conquest of Makkah. Likewise for Khuzāʿah, as al-Ṭabarī said.

﴿So as long as they are upright toward you﴾ in the covenant, ﴿be upright toward them﴾ in fulfilling it.

Abū al-Baqāʾ permitted that كَيْفَ (kayfa, "how") be the predicate of يَكُونُ (yakūnu, "there is"), as in His saying ﴿how was the end of their scheming﴾ (27:51). He also permitted that لِلْمُشْرِكِينَ (lil-mushrikīn, "for the polytheists") be the predicate. عِنْدَ (ʿinda, "with" / "in the presence of") in these two cases is an adverbial complement (ẓarf) of الْعَهْدُ (al-ʿahd, "the covenant"), or of يَكُونُ, or it is a circumstantial (ḥāl), or it is a qualifier of الْعَهْدُ. The predicate may also be عِنْدَ اللَّهِ (ʿinda Allāh, "with God"), and لِلْمُشْرِكِينَ is a clarification or is connected with يَكُونُ. And كَيْفَ is a circumstantial element from الْعَهْدُ. End of quote.

The apparent view is that مَا (mā) in ﴿مَا اسْتَقَامُوا﴾ (mā istaqāmū, "as long as they are upright") is a temporal verbal noun (maṣdariyyah ẓarfiyyah), meaning: "be upright toward them for the duration of their uprightness." It is not conditional. Abū al-Baqāʾ said it is conditional, like His saying ﴿Whatever mercy God grants to people﴾ (35:2). So the meaning would be: "For whatever period they are upright toward you, be upright toward them." Al-Ḥawfī said مَا is a conditional in the nominative position as a subject, with اسْتَقَامُوا as its predicate, and لَكُم connected with اسْتَقَامُوا, and فَاسْتَقِيمُوا لَهُمْ with the فَ being the response of the condition. So the meaning would be: "Whatever time they are upright toward you, be upright toward them." He permitted it to be conditional because of the presence of the فَ in فَاسْتَقِيمُوا, since a temporal verbal noun does not require the فَ. Ibn Mālik permitted the temporal verbal noun to be conditional and to apocopate the verb, and he cited poetry whose apparent meaning supports his claim. We have mentioned that in our book al-Takmīl, and we interpreted the verse he cited. So according to his view, it is temporal and conditional.

﴿Indeed God loves the righteous﴾ means that fulfilling the covenant is among the traits of the righteous, and waiting for these people, if they remain upright, is among the deeds of the believers. Piety includes faith and fulfilling the covenant.

﴿How [can there be a covenant]? If they gain the upper hand over you, they will not observe toward you any tie of kinship or covenant. They please you with their mouths, but their hearts refuse, and most of them are defiantly disobedient.﴾

كَيْفَ (kayfa, "how") here is an emphasis negating their steadfastness in the covenant. The verb omitted after it is apparently of the same type as the nearest verb mentioned before it, and it was omitted because its meaning is known from the earlier كَيْفَ. The estimate is: "How can there be a covenant for them while this is their state?" The omission of the verb after كَيْفَ occurs when the meaning indicates it, as in His saying ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness?﴾ (4:41). The poet said:

"You told me that death is in the villages,
so how [did he die] while here are a hill and a sand dune?"

That is: "so how did he die, when he was not in a village?" Al-Ḥuṭay'ah said:

"So how [can you blame me], when I did not know them to have forsaken you over a grave matter, and that they had cut up your hide?"

That is: "So how can you blame me for praising them?" He dispensed with that, because what occurred in the poem indicated what was omitted. Abū al-Baqāʾ estimated the omitted verb after كَيْفَ as: "How can you feel reassured about them?" Others estimated it as: "How will they not kill them?"

The وَ (wa, "and") in ﴿وَإِنْ يَظْهَرُوا﴾ (wa-in yaẓharū, "if they gain the upper hand") is the waw of circumstance. The discussion of the conditional clause occurring as a circumstantial clause has already been treated in His saying ﴿And if an offer like it comes to them, they will take it﴾ (7:169). The meaning of ظُهُور (ẓuhūr, "gaining the upper hand") is superiority and victory. You say: ظَهَرْتُ عَلَى فُلَانٍ (ẓahartu ʿalā fulān, "I prevailed over so-and-so"), meaning "I overcame him." The meaning here is: if they gain power over you and triumph over you. Zayd ibn ʿAlī read ﴿وَإِنْ يُظْهَرُوا﴾ (wa-in yuẓharū, in the passive voice).

لَا يَرْقُبُوا (lā yarqubū, "they do not observe") means: they do not preserve or respect. إِلًّا (illan) means: a covenant, or kinship, or an alliance, or a political bond, or God, or jiʾār (raising the voice in supplication). These are the views given. Mujāhid and Abū Mijlaz said that إِلٌّ (il) is the name of God in Syriac, which was Arabized. From this is the saying of Abū Bakr when he heard the speech of Musaylimah: "This is a speech that did not come out of il." One group read أَلًّا (allan), with a fatḥah on the hamzah, as a verbal noun from the verb ألَّ, which means "covenant." ʿIkrimah read إِيلًا (īlan), with a kasrah on the hamzah and a yāʾ after it. It was said that this is the name of God. It may also mean إِلًى (ilan), in which one of the doubled letters was replaced by a yāʾ, as they said in إِمَّا (immā) → إِيمَا (īmā). The poet said:

"Would that our mother had raised her ostrich,
[to be taken] either to Paradise or to the Fire."

Ibn Jinnī said: it may also be derived from آلَ يَئُولُ (āla yaʾūlu, "to govern"), when it means "to manage affairs," with the waw changed to a yāʾ because it is quiescent and the letter before it is kasrah. That is: they do not observe in you any political management, nor conciliation, nor covenant. Whoever holds that الإِلّ (al-ill) means the covenant makes both words, al-ill and al-dhimmah, two words for one meaning or for closely related meanings. Whoever holds that al-ill is other than the covenant, then they are two different words.

When He mentioned their conduct toward the believers if they gain the upper hand over them, He mentioned their conduct toward them when they are not dominant, saying: ﴿They please you with their mouths﴾. He began this statement anew; that is, their outward state is contrary to their inward state. All of this is an affirmation and a making improbable of the steadfastness of their hearts in the covenant. إِبَاءُ الْقَلْبِ (ibāʾ al-qalb, "the refusal of the heart") is its opposition to what runs on the tongue of good speech.

It was said: ﴿They please you with their mouths﴾ refers to their promises of faith, while their hearts refuse except disbelief. It was said: they please you in obedience, while their hearts refuse except disobedience. The apparent view is to keep أَكْثَرُهُم (aktharuhum, "most of them") on its literal meaning. It was said: "most of them" is used because among them is one for whom God decreed faith. It was also said: it is used because among them is one who has restraint in observing good conduct, abstaining from what damages honor and invites evil talk. As for "most of them," they are people of corrupt souls, who go out in evil; no manliness restrains them, and no praiseworthy disposition holds them back. They do not guard against lying, deceit, or treachery. Whoever has this description is blamed among people and in all religions. Do you not see the people of al-Jāhiliyyah (the period of ignorance before Islam), who were disbelievers, how they praise themselves for chastity, truthfulness, fulfilling covenants, and good morals? It was also said: the meaning of "most of them" is "all of them are defiantly disobedient." This was said by Ibn ʿAṭiyyah and al-Kirmānī.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verses 4–8 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Except those among the polytheists with whom you made a covenant, who have not failed you in anything and have not supported anyone against you. So fulfil their covenant to them until their term. Indeed, Allah loves the righteous.﴾ Some scholars said: this is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), meaning: "But those with whom you made a covenant and who remained steadfast in the covenant, fulfil their covenant to them." Others, among them al-Zajjaj, said: it is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil) from His words: ﴿to those among the polytheists with whom you made a covenant﴾ (al-Tawbah: 1). Al-Zamakhshari said: its aspect is that it is an exception from His words: ﴿So travel freely in the land﴾ (al-Tawbah: 2), because the speech is addressed to the Muslims. Its meaning is: "A declaration of disavowal from Allah and His Messenger to those among the polytheists with whom you made a covenant. So say to them: Travel freely, except those of them with whom you made a covenant, who have not broken it, so fulfil their covenant to them." The exception here carries the sense of a corrective qualification (istidrak), as if it were said, after they had been commanded regarding the covenant-breakers: "But those who did not break their covenant, fulfil their covenant to them, do not treat them as you treat them, and do not equate the faithful with the treacherous." It was also said that it is a connected exception, and before it there is an omitted clause whose estimate is: "Kill the polytheists who have a covenant, except those with whom you made a covenant." This is a very weak view. The most apparent position is that it is disconnected, because of the long separation by many clauses between what could be the excepted item and the exception.

Mujahid and others said: they are a people who had a covenant with the Messenger for a fixed term, so he was commanded to honour it for them. From Ibn Abbas: when Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) recited "Bara'ah" (the opening of the surah), he said to the Banu Damrah, a clan of Kinanah, and a clan of Sulaym: "Allah has excluded you," and then he recited this verse.

The apparent meaning of His words "until their term" is that it refers to the term that existed between them and the Messenger, so they were commanded to fulfil the covenant until the full term was complete. From Ibn Abbas: nine months remained for a clan of Kinanah, so their covenant was to be fulfilled for them. Also from him: "until their term" means until the four months mentioned in the verse. This is far-fetched, because then the exception would not establish a renewed ruling, since the ruling for these excepted people would be the same as the ruling for the rest of the covenant-holders who did not display the same qualities, namely not failing and not supporting others against the Muslims.

ʿAtaʾ ibn al-Sa'ib al-Kufi, Ikrimah, Abu Zayd, and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read: ﴿yanquḍūkum﴾ with the dad marked (ض), which suits "covenant" (ʿahd). Its meaning is the same as the reading of the majority, because whoever falls short in the covenant has fallen short in the appointed term. It is by omission of a modifier (muḍāf), meaning: "and they did not break your covenant," so the modifier was omitted and the modified (muḍāf ilayhi) was placed in its position, because the context indicates it. Al-Karmani said: the reading with dad is closer to the sense of "covenant," but the reading with ṣad is better, so that in contrast to it stands the word "completion" (tamām) in His words: ﴿fa-atimmū ilayhim﴾ ("fulfil to them"), and completion is the opposite of shortfall.

The word ﴿shay'an﴾ ("in anything") is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: not even a little shortfall, nor much.

﴿And have not supported anyone against you﴾, as Quraysh did with the Banu Bakr when they aided them with weapons against Khuza'ah. The verb ﴿ataw﴾ (here: fulfil) is followed by "to" (ilā) because it includes the sense of ﴿fa-addū﴾ (render), meaning: render it to them complete and whole. Qatadah's statement that the excepted people were Quraysh with whom a covenant was made at the time of al-Hudaybiyyah is rejected, because Quraysh embraced Islam at the Conquest before the permission for all this was given. His words ﴿Indeed, Allah loves the righteous﴾ are an alert that fulfilling the covenant is part of piety (taqwa), and that part of piety is not to treat the two groups as equal.

﴿So when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them, seize them, besiege them, and lie in wait for them at every place of ambush.﴾ The discussion of ﴿insalakha﴾ ("has passed") was already given in His words: ﴿fa-insalakha﴾. Abu al-Haytham said: one says "we sighted the crescent of such-and-such month," meaning we entered it and wore it. So each night we increase in wearing it until half of it has passed, then after the half is complete we strip it off ourselves bit by bit until we have stripped the whole of it from ourselves, and so it "passes." He recited:

"When you strip off the month, you sight its like,
The stripping of months and the sighting suffices as a killer."

The apparent meaning is that these months are those in which the covenant-breakers were permitted to travel freely, and they are described as sacred (ḥurum) because fighting is forbidden in them. The disagreement about their beginning and end has already been mentioned.

When an indefinite noun (nakira) is mentioned first and then repeated, the proper way is to refer back to it with a pronoun, as in: "I met a man and struck him." It is also permissible to repeat the word with the definite article (al-), as in: "I met a man and struck the man." But it is not permissible to describe it with a description that implies difference. If you said: "I met a man and struck the blue man," while meaning the man you met, it would not be correct; rather, that would refer to someone else, and the one struck would not be the one met. But if you describe it with a description that does not imply difference, it is permissible, as in: "I met a man and struck the aforementioned man." Here the phrase ﴿the sacred months﴾ came, because this description is understood from His words: ﴿So travel freely in the land for four months﴾ (al-Tawbah: 2), since the estimate is: "four months that are sacred, in which you will not be attacked." So "sacred" is not a description that implies difference. It was also said: the sacred months are other than these four, namely the months in which Allah has forbidden fighting since He created the heavens and the earth. These are what a hadith mentions, in which the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed time has returned to its original form on the day Allah created the heavens and the earth. The year is twelve months, of which four are sacred: Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, al-Muharram, and Rajab." In that case the four would be drawn from two years. It was also said: the first of them is al-Muharram, so they would be from one year.

The command to kill was given as encouragement and as a strengthening of resolve, and to show that they have no defence against being killed. The unrestricted command to kill is evidence for killing them by any means. Abu Bakr killed the apostates by burning with fire, by stoning, by throwing them from mountain tops, and by inverting them into wells. Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) also burned a group of the people of apostasy, relying on the general wording of this verse. Sound hadiths have also come forbidding mutilation (muthlah). The word ﴿polytheists﴾ is general and covers every polytheist. The Sunnah, however, made exceptions for children, monks, and elderly people who are not men of military judgment, and whoever among them fights is killed. Al-Zamakhshari said: it means those who broke the covenant and supported others against you.

The phrase ﴿wherever you find them﴾ is general across places, whether within the sacred territory or outside it. ﴿Seize them﴾ is an expression for capture, and "the captive" (al-akhidh) is the prisoner. Evidence for permissibility of capturing them is ﴿besiege them﴾: confine them and prevent them from moving freely in the lands. It was also said: enslave them. It was also said: its meaning is "lay siege to them if they fortify themselves." The reading ﴿fa-ḥāṣirūhum﴾ ("then besiege them") is attested as an irregular reading (shādhdh), and this view is also reported from Ibn Abbas. Also from him: keep them away from the Sacred Mosque. It was also said: prevent them from entering the lands of Islam and from acting in them except with permission. Al-Qurtubi said, concerning His words ﴿and lie in wait for them at every place of ambush﴾: this indicates the permissibility of ambushing them before the call (to Islam), because the meaning is "lie in wait for them at the places where they are off guard." This is an alert that the aim is to inflict harm on them by every means, whether by fighting or by ambush. The Muslims have agreed on the permissibility of stealing from the wealth of the people of war, hamstringing their horses, and destroying their livestock if they cannot be taken out to the abode of Islam, unless they make peace on such terms.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿kulla marṣad﴾ ("every place of ambush") means every passage and route where you lie in wait for them. It is in the accusative as an adverb of place, like His words: ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾ (al-A'raf: 16), end of quotation. This is what al-Zajjaj also said; he said: ﴿kulla marṣad﴾ is an adverb of place, like your saying: "I went a way." Abu Ali (al-Farisi) rejected this, because a ﴿marṣad﴾ is a specific place in which the enemy is watched, so it is a particular place from which the preposition is not dropped except by transmitted usage, as Sibawayh related: "I entered the house," and as the fox "made the path smooth" (ʿasala al-ṭarīq). End of quotation. I say: its accusative as an adverb of place is valid, because His words ﴿and lie in wait for them﴾ do not mean literal sitting, but rather: watch them in every place where one watches. Since it carries this meaning, it is analogically permissible to drop the preposition from it, as the poet said: "They sat at all its passages, every sitting place." So whenever the governing verb of a specific place-adverb is either from the same root or has the same meaning, it may reach the adverb without the intermediary "in" (fī). Thus it is permissible to say "I sat the seat of Zayd" and "I sat the seat of Zayd," meaning "in the seat of Zayd." Just as a verb may govern a verbal noun not of its own root when it has the same meaning, so too it may govern an adverb of place. Al-Akhfash said: the meaning is "upon every place of ambush," so "upon" was omitted and the verb took effect, and the verb reaches its governed object in the accusative. Our companions restrict this to poetry, and they cited:

"It longs and reveals what is in it of passion,
And hides what, were it not for grief, would have ended me."

That is: would have ended me (qaḍā 'alayya), that is, would have decided my fate.

﴿Then if they repent, establish prayer, and give zakat, let them go their way. Indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ That is, from disbelief and treachery. Repentance includes faith and abandoning the sins they were engaged in. Then He drew attention to the greatest of the Islamic rites, which is the establishment of prayer, the best of physical acts, and the giving of zakat, the best of financial acts. By these two the practical strength becomes evident, just as by repentance the intellectual strength becomes evident in place of ignorance. ﴿Let them go their way﴾ is an expression for refraining from them and treating them in the same way as Muslims in their affairs, wherever they wish, without your interfering with them, as the poet said: "Let go the path for one through whom the minaret will be built." Or the meaning may be: release them from captivity and confinement. The first meaning is the apparent one, because the ruling covers both the one who was taken captive and others.

Ibn Zayd said: prayer and zakat were made obligatory together, and Allah refused that prayer be accepted without zakat. He also said: may Allah have mercy on Abu Bakr, how deeply understanding he was in his statement: "I will surely fight whoever distinguishes between prayer and zakat." The mention of the attributes of forgiveness and mercy from Him, the Exalted, fits those who repent from disbelief and commit themselves to the laws of Islam. The hafiz Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi said: there is no disagreement among Muslims that whoever abandons prayer and the rest of the obligatory duties while considering them permissible becomes a disbeliever, is buried in the graveyard of disbelievers, and his property becomes spoils (fay'). Whoever abandons the sunan (recommended practices) commits sin (fisq), and whoever abandons the supererogatory acts (nawafil) is not blamed, unless he denies their merit, in which case he becomes a disbeliever, because he becomes one who rejects what the Prophet (ﷺ) brought and reported. End of quotation. The apparent view is that the implication of the conditional clause does not establish with certainty that whoever deliberately abandons prayer and zakat, without considering it lawful and while able to do so, must be killed; because releasing the way may be achieved by imprisonment or other means, so killing is not specifically required. Scholars differed on this. Makhul, Malik, al-Shafi'i, Hammad ibn Zayd, Waki', and Abu Thawr said: he is to be killed. Ibn Shihab, Abu Hanifah, and Dawud said: he is to be imprisoned and beaten, and not killed. A group of the Companions and the Successors said: he is killed as a disbeliever, his property is the property of an apostate, and Ishaq held this view. Ishaq said: this has been the position of the people of knowledge from the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) until our time.

﴿And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection until he hears the word of Allah, then deliver him to his place of safety. That is because they are a people who do not know.﴾ Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: it has been abrogated (mansukhah) by the verse commanding the killing of the polytheists. Al-Hasan and Mujahid said: it is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated) until the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Jubayr reported: a man came to Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) and said: If one of us wants to come to Muhammad after the end of this term in order to hear the word of Allah, or to come to him for some need, will he be killed? He said: No, because Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection﴾, to the end of the verse. End of quotation. It was also said: the ruling of this verse applied only during the four months that were set as their term. The apparent view, however, is that it is muhkam.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verses 4–8 (part 2 of 2):

When God commanded the killing of the polytheists wherever they are found, their capture, their confinement, and the pursuit of their unguarded moments, He mentioned to them a state in which they are neither killed nor captured but taken as prisoners. This is the state in which one of them comes seeking guidance, seeking proof and evidence for what he calls to of the religion. The meaning is: ﴿If anyone among the polytheists seeks your protection﴾; that is, asks you to grant him protection. This is after the sacred months have passed, so that he may hear the word of God and what it contains of monotheism, and may learn what you were sent with. So grant him protection until he hears the word of God and reflects on it, and becomes aware of the reality of the matter. Then convey him to his abode, where he is safe if he does not become Muslim. Then fight him if you wish, without treachery or betrayal.

The word حَتَّى (ḥattā, "until") may be a particle of limit, meaning "until he hears." It may also be a particle of causation (ta'līl, "so that"). In both cases it is connected with فَأَجِرْهُ (fa-ajirhu, "grant him protection"). It is not valid for it to be an instance of al-tanāzuʿ (the grammatical construction in which two verbs compete for one object). Although in terms of meaning it is valid for it to be connected with اسْتَجَارَكَ (istajāraka, "seeks your protection") or with فَأَجِرْهُ, this is prevented by a verbal obstacle: if the first verb were made to govern, it would place a pronoun in the second, and حَتَّى does not govern a pronoun. For this reason it is not valid to treat it as al-tanāzuʿ. However, those grammarians who held that حَتَّى governs a pronoun may consider it al-tanāzuʿ in their view. The position that حَتَّى does not govern a pronoun is that of the majority.

Since the Qur'an is the greatest of the miracles, hearing is linked to it, and hearing is mentioned because it is the path to understanding. Hearing may sometimes mean understanding. You say to someone you addressed who did not accept from you: "You did not hear," meaning "You did not understand." كَلَامَ اللَّهِ (kalām Allāh, "the word of God") is an annexation (iḍāfah) of an attribute to the thing described, not an annexation of a created thing to its Creator. مَأْمَنَهُ (ma'manahu, "his place of safety") means the place of his safety. It was said that مَأْمَنَهُ is a verbal noun, meaning: "then convey to him his safety."

The Mu'tazilah (a theological school) used the phrase ﴿until he hears the word of God﴾ as evidence that the speech of God is created, because only letters and sounds are heard, and it is known by necessity that these are originated. This is discussed in ʿilm al-kalām (scholastic theology).

In this verse is evidence that reflection on monotheism is among the highest stations, since the blood of the disbeliever, whose blood was forfeit, is protected by his request for reflection and inference. It also obliges the Messenger to convey him to his place of safety. In it is also evidence that taqlīd (blind imitation) is not sufficient in religion, since he is not given respite; rather, it is said to him: either you embrace Islam or you will be killed. In it is further evidence that after he hears the word of God, he is not allowed to remain in the land of Islam; rather, he is conveyed to his place of safety. And it is obligatory to protect him and to safeguard him for a period in which he hears the word of God.

The address in ﴿اسْتَجَارَكَ﴾ (istajāraka, "seeks your protection") and ﴿فَأَجِرْهُ﴾ (fa-ajirhu, "grant him protection") shows that the safe-conduct granted by the ruler is valid. As for others: the safe-conduct of a free man is binding. Ibn Ḥabīb said that the imam considers it. As for a slave: al-Awzāʿī, al-Thawrī, al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, Isḥāq, Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan, Abū Thawr, and Dāwūd said that he has the right to grant safe-conduct, and this is the well-known position of Mālik. Abū Ḥanīfah said that he has no safe-conduct, and this is also a view in the school of Mālik. According to the majority, a free woman has the right to grant safe-conduct. ʿAbd al-Malik ibn al-Mājishūn said no, unless the imam grants it, but his view is anomalous. A child who is able to fight, his safe-conduct is valid.

﴿That is because they are a people who do not know﴾; that is, that command, to grant protection and convey him to safety, is because they are an ignorant people who do not know what Islam is or what the reality of what you call to is. Therefore it is necessary to give them safe-conduct until they hear and understand the truth, as al-Zamakhsharī said. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: it is a reference to this gentleness in granting protection, in making them hear, and in conveying them to safety. The phrase ﴿they do not know﴾ negates their knowledge of their right path in following the Messenger (ﷺ).

﴿How can there be a covenant for the polytheists with God and with His Messenger, except for those with whom you made a covenant at the Sacred Mosque? So as long as they are upright toward you, be upright toward them. Indeed, God loves the righteous.﴾

This is an interrogative whose meaning is wonder, disapproval, and disbelief. Al-Tabrīzī and al-Kirmānī said its meaning is negation; that is, there can be no covenant for them while they are hostile to you. He pointed out the reason for the absence of a covenant by the attribute that they possess, which is polytheism. Al-Qurṭubī said: in the verse there is an ellipsis; that is, how can there be a covenant for the polytheists while they hide treachery and breach of covenant? End of quote. The interrogative is often used to mean negation, and from it is the poet's saying:

"Here are swords, O Hudā ibn Mālik, many,
but none strikes with the sword."

That is, none strikes with the sword. Since the interrogative means negation, the exception may come after it. The exception may be connected (muttaṣil) or disconnected (munqaṭiʿ). That is, "but those among them with whom you made a covenant at the Sacred Mosque." Al-Ḥawfī said: it is valid for ﴿الَّذِينَ﴾ (alladhīna, "those who") to be in the genitive case as a substitute (badal) for ﴿الْمُشْرِكِينَ﴾ (al-mushrikīn, "the polytheists"), because the meaning of what preceded is negation. That is, there is no covenant for the polytheists except with those who did not break it. Ibn ʿAbbās said they are Quraysh. Al-Suddī said they are Banū Judhaymah ibn al-Dīl. Ibn Isḥāq said they are the tribes of Banū Bakr, who had entered, at the time of al-Ḥudaybiyyah, into the truce that was between the Messenger (ﷺ) and Quraysh. Al-Zamakhsharī said they are like Banū Kinānah and Banū Ḍamrah. Some, including Mujāhid, said they are Khuzāʿah, and this was refuted by their conversion to Islam in the year of the conquest. Ibn Zayd said they are Quraysh. The verse was revealed, but they were not upright, so after that they were given a respite of four months. This view was weakened on the grounds that, four months after the proclamation, there were none left among Quraysh except Muslims, and that was a year after the conquest of Makkah. Likewise for Khuzāʿah, as al-Ṭabarī said.

﴿So as long as they are upright toward you﴾ in the covenant, ﴿be upright toward them﴾ in fulfilling it.

Abū al-Baqāʾ permitted that كَيْفَ (kayfa, "how") be the predicate of يَكُونُ (yakūnu, "there is"), as in His saying ﴿how was the end of their scheming﴾ (27:51). He also permitted that لِلْمُشْرِكِينَ (lil-mushrikīn, "for the polytheists") be the predicate. عِنْدَ (ʿinda, "with" / "in the presence of") in these two cases is an adverbial complement (ẓarf) of الْعَهْدُ (al-ʿahd, "the covenant"), or of يَكُونُ, or it is a circumstantial (ḥāl), or it is a qualifier of الْعَهْدُ. The predicate may also be عِنْدَ اللَّهِ (ʿinda Allāh, "with God"), and لِلْمُشْرِكِينَ is a clarification or is connected with يَكُونُ. And كَيْفَ is a circumstantial element from الْعَهْدُ. End of quote.

The apparent view is that مَا (mā) in ﴿مَا اسْتَقَامُوا﴾ (mā istaqāmū, "as long as they are upright") is a temporal verbal noun (maṣdariyyah ẓarfiyyah), meaning: "be upright toward them for the duration of their uprightness." It is not conditional. Abū al-Baqāʾ said it is conditional, like His saying ﴿Whatever mercy God grants to people﴾ (35:2). So the meaning would be: "For whatever period they are upright toward you, be upright toward them." Al-Ḥawfī said مَا is a conditional in the nominative position as a subject, with اسْتَقَامُوا as its predicate, and لَكُم connected with اسْتَقَامُوا, and فَاسْتَقِيمُوا لَهُمْ with the فَ being the response of the condition. So the meaning would be: "Whatever time they are upright toward you, be upright toward them." He permitted it to be conditional because of the presence of the فَ in فَاسْتَقِيمُوا, since a temporal verbal noun does not require the فَ. Ibn Mālik permitted the temporal verbal noun to be conditional and to apocopate the verb, and he cited poetry whose apparent meaning supports his claim. We have mentioned that in our book al-Takmīl, and we interpreted the verse he cited. So according to his view, it is temporal and conditional.

﴿Indeed God loves the righteous﴾ means that fulfilling the covenant is among the traits of the righteous, and waiting for these people, if they remain upright, is among the deeds of the believers. Piety includes faith and fulfilling the covenant.

﴿How [can there be a covenant]? If they gain the upper hand over you, they will not observe toward you any tie of kinship or covenant. They please you with their mouths, but their hearts refuse, and most of them are defiantly disobedient.﴾

كَيْفَ (kayfa, "how") here is an emphasis negating their steadfastness in the covenant. The verb omitted after it is apparently of the same type as the nearest verb mentioned before it, and it was omitted because its meaning is known from the earlier كَيْفَ. The estimate is: "How can there be a covenant for them while this is their state?" The omission of the verb after كَيْفَ occurs when the meaning indicates it, as in His saying ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness?﴾ (4:41). The poet said:

"You told me that death is in the villages,
so how [did he die] while here are a hill and a sand dune?"

That is: "so how did he die, when he was not in a village?" Al-Ḥuṭay'ah said:

"So how [can you blame me], when I did not know them to have forsaken you over a grave matter, and that they had cut up your hide?"

That is: "So how can you blame me for praising them?" He dispensed with that, because what occurred in the poem indicated what was omitted. Abū al-Baqāʾ estimated the omitted verb after كَيْفَ as: "How can you feel reassured about them?" Others estimated it as: "How will they not kill them?"

The وَ (wa, "and") in ﴿وَإِنْ يَظْهَرُوا﴾ (wa-in yaẓharū, "if they gain the upper hand") is the waw of circumstance. The discussion of the conditional clause occurring as a circumstantial clause has already been treated in His saying ﴿And if an offer like it comes to them, they will take it﴾ (7:169). The meaning of ظُهُور (ẓuhūr, "gaining the upper hand") is superiority and victory. You say: ظَهَرْتُ عَلَى فُلَانٍ (ẓahartu ʿalā fulān, "I prevailed over so-and-so"), meaning "I overcame him." The meaning here is: if they gain power over you and triumph over you. Zayd ibn ʿAlī read ﴿وَإِنْ يُظْهَرُوا﴾ (wa-in yuẓharū, in the passive voice).

لَا يَرْقُبُوا (lā yarqubū, "they do not observe") means: they do not preserve or respect. إِلًّا (illan) means: a covenant, or kinship, or an alliance, or a political bond, or God, or jiʾār (raising the voice in supplication). These are the views given. Mujāhid and Abū Mijlaz said that إِلٌّ (il) is the name of God in Syriac, which was Arabized. From this is the saying of Abū Bakr when he heard the speech of Musaylimah: "This is a speech that did not come out of il." One group read أَلًّا (allan), with a fatḥah on the hamzah, as a verbal noun from the verb ألَّ, which means "covenant." ʿIkrimah read إِيلًا (īlan), with a kasrah on the hamzah and a yāʾ after it. It was said that this is the name of God. It may also mean إِلًى (ilan), in which one of the doubled letters was replaced by a yāʾ, as they said in إِمَّا (immā) → إِيمَا (īmā). The poet said:

"Would that our mother had raised her ostrich,
[to be taken] either to Paradise or to the Fire."

Ibn Jinnī said: it may also be derived from آلَ يَئُولُ (āla yaʾūlu, "to govern"), when it means "to manage affairs," with the waw changed to a yāʾ because it is quiescent and the letter before it is kasrah. That is: they do not observe in you any political management, nor conciliation, nor covenant. Whoever holds that الإِلّ (al-ill) means the covenant makes both words, al-ill and al-dhimmah, two words for one meaning or for closely related meanings. Whoever holds that al-ill is other than the covenant, then they are two different words.

When He mentioned their conduct toward the believers if they gain the upper hand over them, He mentioned their conduct toward them when they are not dominant, saying: ﴿They please you with their mouths﴾. He began this statement anew; that is, their outward state is contrary to their inward state. All of this is an affirmation and a making improbable of the steadfastness of their hearts in the covenant. إِبَاءُ الْقَلْبِ (ibāʾ al-qalb, "the refusal of the heart") is its opposition to what runs on the tongue of good speech.

It was said: ﴿They please you with their mouths﴾ refers to their promises of faith, while their hearts refuse except disbelief. It was said: they please you in obedience, while their hearts refuse except disobedience. The apparent view is to keep أَكْثَرُهُم (aktharuhum, "most of them") on its literal meaning. It was said: "most of them" is used because among them is one for whom God decreed faith. It was also said: it is used because among them is one who has restraint in observing good conduct, abstaining from what damages honor and invites evil talk. As for "most of them," they are people of corrupt souls, who go out in evil; no manliness restrains them, and no praiseworthy disposition holds them back. They do not guard against lying, deceit, or treachery. Whoever has this description is blamed among people and in all religions. Do you not see the people of al-Jāhiliyyah (the period of ignorance before Islam), who were disbelievers, how they praise themselves for chastity, truthfulness, fulfilling covenants, and good morals? It was also said: the meaning of "most of them" is "all of them are defiantly disobedient." This was said by Ibn ʿAṭiyyah and al-Kirmānī.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verses 4–8 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Except those among the polytheists with whom you made a covenant, who have not failed you in anything and have not supported anyone against you. So fulfil their covenant to them until their term. Indeed, Allah loves the righteous.﴾ Some scholars said: this is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), meaning: "But those with whom you made a covenant and who remained steadfast in the covenant, fulfil their covenant to them." Others, among them al-Zajjaj, said: it is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil) from His words: ﴿to those among the polytheists with whom you made a covenant﴾ (al-Tawbah: 1). Al-Zamakhshari said: its aspect is that it is an exception from His words: ﴿So travel freely in the land﴾ (al-Tawbah: 2), because the speech is addressed to the Muslims. Its meaning is: "A declaration of disavowal from Allah and His Messenger to those among the polytheists with whom you made a covenant. So say to them: Travel freely, except those of them with whom you made a covenant, who have not broken it, so fulfil their covenant to them." The exception here carries the sense of a corrective qualification (istidrak), as if it were said, after they had been commanded regarding the covenant-breakers: "But those who did not break their covenant, fulfil their covenant to them, do not treat them as you treat them, and do not equate the faithful with the treacherous." It was also said that it is a connected exception, and before it there is an omitted clause whose estimate is: "Kill the polytheists who have a covenant, except those with whom you made a covenant." This is a very weak view. The most apparent position is that it is disconnected, because of the long separation by many clauses between what could be the excepted item and the exception.

Mujahid and others said: they are a people who had a covenant with the Messenger for a fixed term, so he was commanded to honour it for them. From Ibn Abbas: when Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) recited "Bara'ah" (the opening of the surah), he said to the Banu Damrah, a clan of Kinanah, and a clan of Sulaym: "Allah has excluded you," and then he recited this verse.

The apparent meaning of His words "until their term" is that it refers to the term that existed between them and the Messenger, so they were commanded to fulfil the covenant until the full term was complete. From Ibn Abbas: nine months remained for a clan of Kinanah, so their covenant was to be fulfilled for them. Also from him: "until their term" means until the four months mentioned in the verse. This is far-fetched, because then the exception would not establish a renewed ruling, since the ruling for these excepted people would be the same as the ruling for the rest of the covenant-holders who did not display the same qualities, namely not failing and not supporting others against the Muslims.

ʿAtaʾ ibn al-Sa'ib al-Kufi, Ikrimah, Abu Zayd, and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read: ﴿yanquḍūkum﴾ with the dad marked (ض), which suits "covenant" (ʿahd). Its meaning is the same as the reading of the majority, because whoever falls short in the covenant has fallen short in the appointed term. It is by omission of a modifier (muḍāf), meaning: "and they did not break your covenant," so the modifier was omitted and the modified (muḍāf ilayhi) was placed in its position, because the context indicates it. Al-Karmani said: the reading with dad is closer to the sense of "covenant," but the reading with ṣad is better, so that in contrast to it stands the word "completion" (tamām) in His words: ﴿fa-atimmū ilayhim﴾ ("fulfil to them"), and completion is the opposite of shortfall.

The word ﴿shay'an﴾ ("in anything") is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: not even a little shortfall, nor much.

﴿And have not supported anyone against you﴾, as Quraysh did with the Banu Bakr when they aided them with weapons against Khuza'ah. The verb ﴿ataw﴾ (here: fulfil) is followed by "to" (ilā) because it includes the sense of ﴿fa-addū﴾ (render), meaning: render it to them complete and whole. Qatadah's statement that the excepted people were Quraysh with whom a covenant was made at the time of al-Hudaybiyyah is rejected, because Quraysh embraced Islam at the Conquest before the permission for all this was given. His words ﴿Indeed, Allah loves the righteous﴾ are an alert that fulfilling the covenant is part of piety (taqwa), and that part of piety is not to treat the two groups as equal.

﴿So when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them, seize them, besiege them, and lie in wait for them at every place of ambush.﴾ The discussion of ﴿insalakha﴾ ("has passed") was already given in His words: ﴿fa-insalakha﴾. Abu al-Haytham said: one says "we sighted the crescent of such-and-such month," meaning we entered it and wore it. So each night we increase in wearing it until half of it has passed, then after the half is complete we strip it off ourselves bit by bit until we have stripped the whole of it from ourselves, and so it "passes." He recited:

"When you strip off the month, you sight its like,
The stripping of months and the sighting suffices as a killer."

The apparent meaning is that these months are those in which the covenant-breakers were permitted to travel freely, and they are described as sacred (ḥurum) because fighting is forbidden in them. The disagreement about their beginning and end has already been mentioned.

When an indefinite noun (nakira) is mentioned first and then repeated, the proper way is to refer back to it with a pronoun, as in: "I met a man and struck him." It is also permissible to repeat the word with the definite article (al-), as in: "I met a man and struck the man." But it is not permissible to describe it with a description that implies difference. If you said: "I met a man and struck the blue man," while meaning the man you met, it would not be correct; rather, that would refer to someone else, and the one struck would not be the one met. But if you describe it with a description that does not imply difference, it is permissible, as in: "I met a man and struck the aforementioned man." Here the phrase ﴿the sacred months﴾ came, because this description is understood from His words: ﴿So travel freely in the land for four months﴾ (al-Tawbah: 2), since the estimate is: "four months that are sacred, in which you will not be attacked." So "sacred" is not a description that implies difference. It was also said: the sacred months are other than these four, namely the months in which Allah has forbidden fighting since He created the heavens and the earth. These are what a hadith mentions, in which the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed time has returned to its original form on the day Allah created the heavens and the earth. The year is twelve months, of which four are sacred: Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, al-Muharram, and Rajab." In that case the four would be drawn from two years. It was also said: the first of them is al-Muharram, so they would be from one year.

The command to kill was given as encouragement and as a strengthening of resolve, and to show that they have no defence against being killed. The unrestricted command to kill is evidence for killing them by any means. Abu Bakr killed the apostates by burning with fire, by stoning, by throwing them from mountain tops, and by inverting them into wells. Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) also burned a group of the people of apostasy, relying on the general wording of this verse. Sound hadiths have also come forbidding mutilation (muthlah). The word ﴿polytheists﴾ is general and covers every polytheist. The Sunnah, however, made exceptions for children, monks, and elderly people who are not men of military judgment, and whoever among them fights is killed. Al-Zamakhshari said: it means those who broke the covenant and supported others against you.

The phrase ﴿wherever you find them﴾ is general across places, whether within the sacred territory or outside it. ﴿Seize them﴾ is an expression for capture, and "the captive" (al-akhidh) is the prisoner. Evidence for permissibility of capturing them is ﴿besiege them﴾: confine them and prevent them from moving freely in the lands. It was also said: enslave them. It was also said: its meaning is "lay siege to them if they fortify themselves." The reading ﴿fa-ḥāṣirūhum﴾ ("then besiege them") is attested as an irregular reading (shādhdh), and this view is also reported from Ibn Abbas. Also from him: keep them away from the Sacred Mosque. It was also said: prevent them from entering the lands of Islam and from acting in them except with permission. Al-Qurtubi said, concerning His words ﴿and lie in wait for them at every place of ambush﴾: this indicates the permissibility of ambushing them before the call (to Islam), because the meaning is "lie in wait for them at the places where they are off guard." This is an alert that the aim is to inflict harm on them by every means, whether by fighting or by ambush. The Muslims have agreed on the permissibility of stealing from the wealth of the people of war, hamstringing their horses, and destroying their livestock if they cannot be taken out to the abode of Islam, unless they make peace on such terms.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿kulla marṣad﴾ ("every place of ambush") means every passage and route where you lie in wait for them. It is in the accusative as an adverb of place, like His words: ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾ (al-A'raf: 16), end of quotation. This is what al-Zajjaj also said; he said: ﴿kulla marṣad﴾ is an adverb of place, like your saying: "I went a way." Abu Ali (al-Farisi) rejected this, because a ﴿marṣad﴾ is a specific place in which the enemy is watched, so it is a particular place from which the preposition is not dropped except by transmitted usage, as Sibawayh related: "I entered the house," and as the fox "made the path smooth" (ʿasala al-ṭarīq). End of quotation. I say: its accusative as an adverb of place is valid, because His words ﴿and lie in wait for them﴾ do not mean literal sitting, but rather: watch them in every place where one watches. Since it carries this meaning, it is analogically permissible to drop the preposition from it, as the poet said: "They sat at all its passages, every sitting place." So whenever the governing verb of a specific place-adverb is either from the same root or has the same meaning, it may reach the adverb without the intermediary "in" (fī). Thus it is permissible to say "I sat the seat of Zayd" and "I sat the seat of Zayd," meaning "in the seat of Zayd." Just as a verb may govern a verbal noun not of its own root when it has the same meaning, so too it may govern an adverb of place. Al-Akhfash said: the meaning is "upon every place of ambush," so "upon" was omitted and the verb took effect, and the verb reaches its governed object in the accusative. Our companions restrict this to poetry, and they cited:

"It longs and reveals what is in it of passion,
And hides what, were it not for grief, would have ended me."

That is: would have ended me (qaḍā 'alayya), that is, would have decided my fate.

﴿Then if they repent, establish prayer, and give zakat, let them go their way. Indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ That is, from disbelief and treachery. Repentance includes faith and abandoning the sins they were engaged in. Then He drew attention to the greatest of the Islamic rites, which is the establishment of prayer, the best of physical acts, and the giving of zakat, the best of financial acts. By these two the practical strength becomes evident, just as by repentance the intellectual strength becomes evident in place of ignorance. ﴿Let them go their way﴾ is an expression for refraining from them and treating them in the same way as Muslims in their affairs, wherever they wish, without your interfering with them, as the poet said: "Let go the path for one through whom the minaret will be built." Or the meaning may be: release them from captivity and confinement. The first meaning is the apparent one, because the ruling covers both the one who was taken captive and others.

Ibn Zayd said: prayer and zakat were made obligatory together, and Allah refused that prayer be accepted without zakat. He also said: may Allah have mercy on Abu Bakr, how deeply understanding he was in his statement: "I will surely fight whoever distinguishes between prayer and zakat." The mention of the attributes of forgiveness and mercy from Him, the Exalted, fits those who repent from disbelief and commit themselves to the laws of Islam. The hafiz Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi said: there is no disagreement among Muslims that whoever abandons prayer and the rest of the obligatory duties while considering them permissible becomes a disbeliever, is buried in the graveyard of disbelievers, and his property becomes spoils (fay'). Whoever abandons the sunan (recommended practices) commits sin (fisq), and whoever abandons the supererogatory acts (nawafil) is not blamed, unless he denies their merit, in which case he becomes a disbeliever, because he becomes one who rejects what the Prophet (ﷺ) brought and reported. End of quotation. The apparent view is that the implication of the conditional clause does not establish with certainty that whoever deliberately abandons prayer and zakat, without considering it lawful and while able to do so, must be killed; because releasing the way may be achieved by imprisonment or other means, so killing is not specifically required. Scholars differed on this. Makhul, Malik, al-Shafi'i, Hammad ibn Zayd, Waki', and Abu Thawr said: he is to be killed. Ibn Shihab, Abu Hanifah, and Dawud said: he is to be imprisoned and beaten, and not killed. A group of the Companions and the Successors said: he is killed as a disbeliever, his property is the property of an apostate, and Ishaq held this view. Ishaq said: this has been the position of the people of knowledge from the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) until our time.

﴿And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection until he hears the word of Allah, then deliver him to his place of safety. That is because they are a people who do not know.﴾ Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: it has been abrogated (mansukhah) by the verse commanding the killing of the polytheists. Al-Hasan and Mujahid said: it is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated) until the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Jubayr reported: a man came to Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) and said: If one of us wants to come to Muhammad after the end of this term in order to hear the word of Allah, or to come to him for some need, will he be killed? He said: No, because Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection﴾, to the end of the verse. End of quotation. It was also said: the ruling of this verse applied only during the four months that were set as their term. The apparent view, however, is that it is muhkam.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verses 4–8 (part 2 of 2):

When God commanded the killing of the polytheists wherever they are found, their capture, their confinement, and the pursuit of their unguarded moments, He mentioned to them a state in which they are neither killed nor captured but taken as prisoners. This is the state in which one of them comes seeking guidance, seeking proof and evidence for what he calls to of the religion. The meaning is: ﴿If anyone among the polytheists seeks your protection﴾; that is, asks you to grant him protection. This is after the sacred months have passed, so that he may hear the word of God and what it contains of monotheism, and may learn what you were sent with. So grant him protection until he hears the word of God and reflects on it, and becomes aware of the reality of the matter. Then convey him to his abode, where he is safe if he does not become Muslim. Then fight him if you wish, without treachery or betrayal.

The word حَتَّى (ḥattā, "until") may be a particle of limit, meaning "until he hears." It may also be a particle of causation (ta'līl, "so that"). In both cases it is connected with فَأَجِرْهُ (fa-ajirhu, "grant him protection"). It is not valid for it to be an instance of al-tanāzuʿ (the grammatical construction in which two verbs compete for one object). Although in terms of meaning it is valid for it to be connected with اسْتَجَارَكَ (istajāraka, "seeks your protection") or with فَأَجِرْهُ, this is prevented by a verbal obstacle: if the first verb were made to govern, it would place a pronoun in the second, and حَتَّى does not govern a pronoun. For this reason it is not valid to treat it as al-tanāzuʿ. However, those grammarians who held that حَتَّى governs a pronoun may consider it al-tanāzuʿ in their view. The position that حَتَّى does not govern a pronoun is that of the majority.

Since the Qur'an is the greatest of the miracles, hearing is linked to it, and hearing is mentioned because it is the path to understanding. Hearing may sometimes mean understanding. You say to someone you addressed who did not accept from you: "You did not hear," meaning "You did not understand." كَلَامَ اللَّهِ (kalām Allāh, "the word of God") is an annexation (iḍāfah) of an attribute to the thing described, not an annexation of a created thing to its Creator. مَأْمَنَهُ (ma'manahu, "his place of safety") means the place of his safety. It was said that مَأْمَنَهُ is a verbal noun, meaning: "then convey to him his safety."

The Mu'tazilah (a theological school) used the phrase ﴿until he hears the word of God﴾ as evidence that the speech of God is created, because only letters and sounds are heard, and it is known by necessity that these are originated. This is discussed in ʿilm al-kalām (scholastic theology).

In this verse is evidence that reflection on monotheism is among the highest stations, since the blood of the disbeliever, whose blood was forfeit, is protected by his request for reflection and inference. It also obliges the Messenger to convey him to his place of safety. In it is also evidence that taqlīd (blind imitation) is not sufficient in religion, since he is not given respite; rather, it is said to him: either you embrace Islam or you will be killed. In it is further evidence that after he hears the word of God, he is not allowed to remain in the land of Islam; rather, he is conveyed to his place of safety. And it is obligatory to protect him and to safeguard him for a period in which he hears the word of God.

The address in ﴿اسْتَجَارَكَ﴾ (istajāraka, "seeks your protection") and ﴿فَأَجِرْهُ﴾ (fa-ajirhu, "grant him protection") shows that the safe-conduct granted by the ruler is valid. As for others: the safe-conduct of a free man is binding. Ibn Ḥabīb said that the imam considers it. As for a slave: al-Awzāʿī, al-Thawrī, al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, Isḥāq, Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan, Abū Thawr, and Dāwūd said that he has the right to grant safe-conduct, and this is the well-known position of Mālik. Abū Ḥanīfah said that he has no safe-conduct, and this is also a view in the school of Mālik. According to the majority, a free woman has the right to grant safe-conduct. ʿAbd al-Malik ibn al-Mājishūn said no, unless the imam grants it, but his view is anomalous. A child who is able to fight, his safe-conduct is valid.

﴿That is because they are a people who do not know﴾; that is, that command, to grant protection and convey him to safety, is because they are an ignorant people who do not know what Islam is or what the reality of what you call to is. Therefore it is necessary to give them safe-conduct until they hear and understand the truth, as al-Zamakhsharī said. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: it is a reference to this gentleness in granting protection, in making them hear, and in conveying them to safety. The phrase ﴿they do not know﴾ negates their knowledge of their right path in following the Messenger (ﷺ).

﴿How can there be a covenant for the polytheists with God and with His Messenger, except for those with whom you made a covenant at the Sacred Mosque? So as long as they are upright toward you, be upright toward them. Indeed, God loves the righteous.﴾

This is an interrogative whose meaning is wonder, disapproval, and disbelief. Al-Tabrīzī and al-Kirmānī said its meaning is negation; that is, there can be no covenant for them while they are hostile to you. He pointed out the reason for the absence of a covenant by the attribute that they possess, which is polytheism. Al-Qurṭubī said: in the verse there is an ellipsis; that is, how can there be a covenant for the polytheists while they hide treachery and breach of covenant? End of quote. The interrogative is often used to mean negation, and from it is the poet's saying:

"Here are swords, O Hudā ibn Mālik, many,
but none strikes with the sword."

That is, none strikes with the sword. Since the interrogative means negation, the exception may come after it. The exception may be connected (muttaṣil) or disconnected (munqaṭiʿ). That is, "but those among them with whom you made a covenant at the Sacred Mosque." Al-Ḥawfī said: it is valid for ﴿الَّذِينَ﴾ (alladhīna, "those who") to be in the genitive case as a substitute (badal) for ﴿الْمُشْرِكِينَ﴾ (al-mushrikīn, "the polytheists"), because the meaning of what preceded is negation. That is, there is no covenant for the polytheists except with those who did not break it. Ibn ʿAbbās said they are Quraysh. Al-Suddī said they are Banū Judhaymah ibn al-Dīl. Ibn Isḥāq said they are the tribes of Banū Bakr, who had entered, at the time of al-Ḥudaybiyyah, into the truce that was between the Messenger (ﷺ) and Quraysh. Al-Zamakhsharī said they are like Banū Kinānah and Banū Ḍamrah. Some, including Mujāhid, said they are Khuzāʿah, and this was refuted by their conversion to Islam in the year of the conquest. Ibn Zayd said they are Quraysh. The verse was revealed, but they were not upright, so after that they were given a respite of four months. This view was weakened on the grounds that, four months after the proclamation, there were none left among Quraysh except Muslims, and that was a year after the conquest of Makkah. Likewise for Khuzāʿah, as al-Ṭabarī said.

﴿So as long as they are upright toward you﴾ in the covenant, ﴿be upright toward them﴾ in fulfilling it.

Abū al-Baqāʾ permitted that كَيْفَ (kayfa, "how") be the predicate of يَكُونُ (yakūnu, "there is"), as in His saying ﴿how was the end of their scheming﴾ (27:51). He also permitted that لِلْمُشْرِكِينَ (lil-mushrikīn, "for the polytheists") be the predicate. عِنْدَ (ʿinda, "with" / "in the presence of") in these two cases is an adverbial complement (ẓarf) of الْعَهْدُ (al-ʿahd, "the covenant"), or of يَكُونُ, or it is a circumstantial (ḥāl), or it is a qualifier of الْعَهْدُ. The predicate may also be عِنْدَ اللَّهِ (ʿinda Allāh, "with God"), and لِلْمُشْرِكِينَ is a clarification or is connected with يَكُونُ. And كَيْفَ is a circumstantial element from الْعَهْدُ. End of quote.

The apparent view is that مَا (mā) in ﴿مَا اسْتَقَامُوا﴾ (mā istaqāmū, "as long as they are upright") is a temporal verbal noun (maṣdariyyah ẓarfiyyah), meaning: "be upright toward them for the duration of their uprightness." It is not conditional. Abū al-Baqāʾ said it is conditional, like His saying ﴿Whatever mercy God grants to people﴾ (35:2). So the meaning would be: "For whatever period they are upright toward you, be upright toward them." Al-Ḥawfī said مَا is a conditional in the nominative position as a subject, with اسْتَقَامُوا as its predicate, and لَكُم connected with اسْتَقَامُوا, and فَاسْتَقِيمُوا لَهُمْ with the فَ being the response of the condition. So the meaning would be: "Whatever time they are upright toward you, be upright toward them." He permitted it to be conditional because of the presence of the فَ in فَاسْتَقِيمُوا, since a temporal verbal noun does not require the فَ. Ibn Mālik permitted the temporal verbal noun to be conditional and to apocopate the verb, and he cited poetry whose apparent meaning supports his claim. We have mentioned that in our book al-Takmīl, and we interpreted the verse he cited. So according to his view, it is temporal and conditional.

﴿Indeed God loves the righteous﴾ means that fulfilling the covenant is among the traits of the righteous, and waiting for these people, if they remain upright, is among the deeds of the believers. Piety includes faith and fulfilling the covenant.

﴿How [can there be a covenant]? If they gain the upper hand over you, they will not observe toward you any tie of kinship or covenant. They please you with their mouths, but their hearts refuse, and most of them are defiantly disobedient.﴾

كَيْفَ (kayfa, "how") here is an emphasis negating their steadfastness in the covenant. The verb omitted after it is apparently of the same type as the nearest verb mentioned before it, and it was omitted because its meaning is known from the earlier كَيْفَ. The estimate is: "How can there be a covenant for them while this is their state?" The omission of the verb after كَيْفَ occurs when the meaning indicates it, as in His saying ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness?﴾ (4:41). The poet said:

"You told me that death is in the villages,
so how [did he die] while here are a hill and a sand dune?"

That is: "so how did he die, when he was not in a village?" Al-Ḥuṭay'ah said:

"So how [can you blame me], when I did not know them to have forsaken you over a grave matter, and that they had cut up your hide?"

That is: "So how can you blame me for praising them?" He dispensed with that, because what occurred in the poem indicated what was omitted. Abū al-Baqāʾ estimated the omitted verb after كَيْفَ as: "How can you feel reassured about them?" Others estimated it as: "How will they not kill them?"

The وَ (wa, "and") in ﴿وَإِنْ يَظْهَرُوا﴾ (wa-in yaẓharū, "if they gain the upper hand") is the waw of circumstance. The discussion of the conditional clause occurring as a circumstantial clause has already been treated in His saying ﴿And if an offer like it comes to them, they will take it﴾ (7:169). The meaning of ظُهُور (ẓuhūr, "gaining the upper hand") is superiority and victory. You say: ظَهَرْتُ عَلَى فُلَانٍ (ẓahartu ʿalā fulān, "I prevailed over so-and-so"), meaning "I overcame him." The meaning here is: if they gain power over you and triumph over you. Zayd ibn ʿAlī read ﴿وَإِنْ يُظْهَرُوا﴾ (wa-in yuẓharū, in the passive voice).

لَا يَرْقُبُوا (lā yarqubū, "they do not observe") means: they do not preserve or respect. إِلًّا (illan) means: a covenant, or kinship, or an alliance, or a political bond, or God, or jiʾār (raising the voice in supplication). These are the views given. Mujāhid and Abū Mijlaz said that إِلٌّ (il) is the name of God in Syriac, which was Arabized. From this is the saying of Abū Bakr when he heard the speech of Musaylimah: "This is a speech that did not come out of il." One group read أَلًّا (allan), with a fatḥah on the hamzah, as a verbal noun from the verb ألَّ, which means "covenant." ʿIkrimah read إِيلًا (īlan), with a kasrah on the hamzah and a yāʾ after it.
