The situation of the Arab disbelievers and the enemies of the Messenger of God ﷺ required that the reference to them first be with the phrase "leaders of disbelief," and they were included under the term at that time. The one who undertakes the fighting against the Prophet ﷺ and the repelling of him at the beginning of his law is the imam of every one who disbelieves in that law until the Day of Resurrection. Then in each generation of disbelievers there come leaders specific to each generation. End of quote. It has been said that the covenant means Islam, so the meaning is: they disbelieved after their Islam. For this reason some read "wa-in nakathu iymanahum" with a kasra on the alif (meaning "their faith"), and this is the view of al-Zamakhshari, who said: His saying ﴿then fight the leaders of disbelief⟩ means "then fight them," and so He placed "leaders of disbelief" in the position of their pronoun, to indicate that when they broke faith while in the state of polytheism, out of rebellion, transgression, and abandoning the customs of the noble and faithful among the Arabs, and then believed, established prayer, gave zakat, and became brothers to the Muslims in religion, then returned and apostatized from Islam, broke the faith they had pledged with regard to faith and fidelity to covenants, and sat reviling the religion of God, saying that Muhammad's religion is nothing, then they are the leaders of disbelief and those of leadership and precedence in it, and no disbeliever can match their dust. The well-known position of the school of Malik is that a dhimmi (a non-Muslim under protection) who reviles the religion, doing something such as denying the law or insulting the Prophet ﷺ or the like, is killed. It has been said: if he openly does something among what is known of his belief and disbelief, he is disciplined for the open act and left alone, but if he disbelieves in something that is not of his belief, such as insulting, or the like, he is killed. Abu Hanifa said: he is asked to repent. It is disputed: if a dhimmi insults and then embraces Islam to escape being killed (taqiyya, or precautionary dissimulation under threat). The well-known position of the school of Malik is that he is left alone, because Islam erases what came before it. In al-'Utbiyya (a book in the Maliki school) it is said that he is killed, and he is not in a better position than a Muslim.

Al-Haramayn (Ibn Kathir and Nafi'), and Abu 'Amr, read by replacing the second hamza with a ya'. It is reported from Nafi' that he prolonged the hamza. The rest of the seven readers, and Ibn Abi Uways from Nafi', read with two hamzas, and Hisham inserted an alif between them. The origin is "ii'imma," on the pattern of "af'ila," the plural of "imam." They assimilated the mim into the mim, so its vowel was moved to the hamza before it. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, how is the wording "a'imma"? I say: it is a hamza followed by a hamza, pronounced "bayn bayn" (an intermediate sound between the hamza and the ya'), that is, between the place of articulation of the hamza and the ya'. Pronouncing the hamza fully is a well-known reading, though it is not accepted by the Basran grammarians. As for pronouncing it explicitly as ya', that is not a recitation and cannot be one. Whoever pronounces it that way is a grammatical misreader and a distorter. End of quote. This is his habit of finding fault with the readers. How could that be a mistake when it was recited by the head of the Basran grammarians, Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala', the reciter of Mecca Ibn Kathir, and the reciter of the city of the Messenger, Nafi'? He negated their faith when they did not remain steadfast in it nor fulfilled it, so they were treated as having no oaths. Or it is by omission of the qualifier, meaning: they have no oaths that they fulfill. The majority read with a fatha on the hamza. Al-Hasan, 'Ata', Zayd ibn 'Ali, and Ibn 'Amir read "la iman lahum," meaning they have no Islam and no acceptance of truth. Abu 'Ali said: this is not strong, because it is repetitive, since He had already described the leaders of disbelief as having no faith. The better reading with a kasra on the alif is that it is the verbal noun of "amanahu iman" (he granted him security), and from it is His saying ﴿and gave them security from fear⟩ [Quraysh: 4]. The meaning is that they do not grant security to the people of the dhimma, since the polytheists had only Islam or the sword. Abu Hatim said: al-Hasan explained his reading as "la islam lahum" (they have no Islam). Al-Zamakhshari followed him in this, saying: it is read "la iman lahum," meaning "la islam lahum," and they are not given safe conduct after apostasy and breaking the covenant, and there is no way to it. The reading with a fatha was used by Abu Hanifa as evidence that the oath of a disbeliever is not an oath, while according to al-Shafi'i their oath is an oath. He said: its meaning is that they do not fulfill it, as evidenced by the fact that He described them as breakers of oaths.

﴿So that they may desist⟩ is connected to His saying ﴿then fight the leaders of disbelief⟩. That is: let your purpose in fighting them, after such great wrongs have been committed by them, be their desisting from what they are in. This is from His generosity, His bounty, and His returning to the wrongdoer with mercy.

﴿Will you not fight a people who broke their oaths, and resolved to expel the Messenger, and they began against you first? Do you fear them? God has more right that you fear Him, if you are believers.⟩ ("Ala") is a particle of urging, and its meaning here is to incite them to fight. They claimed that it is composed of the interrogative hamza and the negative la, so that it carries the sense of specification. Al-Zamakhshari said: the hamza entered for affirmation of the negation of fighting, and its meaning is urging to it in the manner of emphasis. When God commanded the killing of the people of disbelief, He followed it with the cause that moves one to fight them, which is three things they combined, each of which on its own is sufficient to urge fighting them. The meaning of "they broke their oaths" is that they violated the covenant. Al-Suddi, Ibn Ishaq, and al-Kalbi said: it was revealed about the disbelievers of Mecca, who broke their oaths after the treaty of al-Hudaybiyya and aided Banu Bakr against Khuza'a. Their resolution was the resolution of Quraysh to expel the Messenger from Mecca when they deliberated in the Dar al-Nadwa (the council house), so God permitted the migration, and he went out by himself. Or it was Banu Bakr's resolution to expel him from Medina because of what they undertook of consultation and gathering. Or the Jews resolved to betray the Messenger ﷺ, broke his covenant, and aided the hypocrites in expelling him from Medina. These are three opinions, the first of which is that of al-Suddi. Al-Hasan said: from Medina. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is consistent for the battle of Uhud, the confederates, and others, and they are the ones who initiated the fighting, because the Messenger of God ﷺ first came to them with the clear Book and challenged them with it, but they turned away from contesting it because they were unable to, and turned to fighting. So they were the initiators, and the initiator is the more unjust. What prevents you, then, from fighting them with the same, striking them with evil as they struck you? He rebuked them for abandoning the fight and urged them to it, then described them with what necessitates urging it. It is established that whoever has attributes like theirs, breaking covenants, expelling the Messenger, and beginning fighting without any justification, deserves that his assault not be left unanswered, and that whoever neglects it be rebuked. This was said by al-Zamakhshari, and it is an exaggeration. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "the first time" (awwal marra) has been said to mean their deeds in Mecca against the Prophet ﷺ and the believers. Mujahid said: it is what Quraysh began with, the aid they gave Banu Bakr, their allies, against Khuza'a, the allies of the Prophet, and this was the beginning of the breaking. Al-Tabari said: it means their act on the day of Badr. End of quote.

Zayd ibn 'Ali read "badawkum" without a hamza. Its basis is that he softened the hamza of "bada'tu" by changing it to ya', just as they said "qarayt" for "qara'tu," making it like "ramayt." When the verb was attached to the waw of the pronoun, the ya' dropped, giving "badawkum," just as you say "ramawkum." ("Atakhshawnahum") is an affirmation of the fear of them and a rebuke for it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verse 9–16 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Allah has more right that you fear Him﴾ [so that you would fight His enemies]. The word "Allah" (lafz al-jalalah) is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is "more right" (ahaqq). "That you fear Him" (an takhshawhu) is a substitute (badal) for "Allah"; that is, the fear of Allah is more deserving than their fear [of others]. "That you fear Him" is in the position of nominative case (raf'). It is permissible that it be in the position of accusative (nasb) or genitive (jarr) according to the disagreement [of the grammarians] when the preposition is elided, and its underlying form is: "by that you fear Him"; that is, He is more deserving than other than Him that you fear Him. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "that you fear Him" be the subject, and "more right" its predicate placed before it. Ibn 'Atiyya permitted that "more right" (ahaqq) be the subject and its predicate "that you fear Him," and the clause is a predicate for the first [subject]. The use of an indefinite noun as subject is acceptable because it is an elative (af'al al-tafdil), and Sibawayh permitted that a definite noun be the predicate of an indefinite noun in such a construction as: "Aim at a man whose father is better than him."

﴿if you are believers﴾; that is, those whose faith is complete, because they were believers. Al-Zamakhshari said: he means that the requirement of sound faith is that the believer fears none but his Lord and does not care for anyone else, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they fear none but Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 39].

﴿Fight them, and Allah will punish them by your hands and will disgrace them and give you victory over them and heal the breasts of a believing people﴾ ﴿and remove the rage of their hearts. And Allah turns in forgiveness to whom He wills. And Allah is Knowing and Wise﴾. The verses before this established the deeds of the disbelievers that necessitate fighting them, and the urging to fight; the command to fight is forbidden in this [context]. Their punishment by the hands of the believers is in this world by killing, capture and plunder. These are promises that strengthened their hearts and rectified their intentions. Their disgrace is their humiliation and abasement. "And will give you victory" means He will make you triumph over them. The healing of the breasts is by the elevation of the religion of Allah and the punishment and disgrace of the disbelievers.

Zayd ibn 'Ali read "wa-nashfi" with the nun, by way of iltifat (shift of person). The phrasing "breasts of a believing people" came to include the addressees and every believer, because what befalls the people of disbelief of punishment and disgrace is a healing for the breast of every believer. It was said: the intended people are specific ones. Ibn 'Abbas said: "They are clans from Yemen and Saba' who came to Makkah and embraced Islam, and they met from its people severe harm, so they sent to the Messenger of Allah complaining to him, and he said: 'Rejoice, for relief is near.'" Mujahid and al-Suddi said: they are Khuza'ah. The reason for specifying them is that they were the ones against whom the covenant was broken and upon whom war fell, and at that time there were many believers among Khuza'ah. Do you not see the saying of the Khuza'i seeking the help of the Prophet (ﷺ):

"There we became Muslims and did not withdraw a hand,"

and at the end of the verse:

"And they killed us while bowing and prostrating."

Removing rage is by what the disbelievers suffered of hardship. This clause is like an emphasis for the one before it, because the healing of the breast from the cause of rage is the removal of rage. A group read "wa-yadhhabu" as an intransitive verb with "rage" (ghayz) as its subject. Zayd ibn 'Ali likewise read it, except that he raised the letter ba' (ghayzu). All these promises were fulfilled, and this was a proof of the truthfulness of the Messenger and the soundness of his prophethood. It begins first with what results from victory, namely Allah's punishment of the disbelievers and their disgrace at the hands of the believers, since the beginning with what afflicts the disbelievers of evil is what gladdens the believers. Then He mentioned the cause, which is Allah's victory of the believers over the disbelievers. Then He mentioned what also results from victory, the healing of the believers' breasts and the removal of their rage, completing the blessings. So He mentioned what results from victory with respect to the disbelievers, and mentioned what befalls the Muslims of joy and happiness in attaining vengeance, and did not mention what they gained of spoils and provisions, because the Arabs are a people created with zeal and pride, so their desire to attain vengeance and kill enemies is what suits their nature:

"Verily the lions, the lions of the thicket, their resolve
on the day of battle is in the one despoiled, not in the spoils."

Al-Jumhur read "wa-yatubu Allahu" with raf' (nominative), and it is a resumptive statement that some of the people of Makkah and others will turn from their disbelief, and many of them did so, and their Islam was good. Al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and Abu al-Fath said: this is an existing matter whether they were fought or not, so there is no way to include "today" in the answer of the condition in "fight them." End of quote. Zayd ibn 'Ali, al-A'raj, Ibn Abi Ishaq, 'Isa al-Thaqafi, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, 'Umar ibn Qa'id, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub, as transmitted from them, read "wa-yatuba Allahu" with nasb of the ba', making it included in the answer of the command by way of meaning. It was said: it is possible that repentance is included in the reward. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is valid in my view if it is taken that repentance is meant as: the killing of the disbelievers and jihad in the way of Allah is a repentance for you, O believers, and a perfection of your faith, so repentance on this view enters into the condition of fighting. Others said: when He commanded them to fight, that was difficult for some of them, so when they proceeded to fight, that action served as repentance from that aversion. It was said: the existence of disbelief and abundance of wealth is a pleasure sought by a forbidden way, so when a lawful way was gained for them, that was a motive for them to repent of what preceded, so repentance became connected with that fighting. End of quote. What they established about repentance entering under the answer of the command concerns the believers who were commanded to fight the disbelievers, but what appears is that it concerns the disbelievers: the meaning is "upon whom He wills of the disbelievers," because fighting the disbelievers and the Muslims' overcoming them may result in the Islam of many people, even if they had no desire for Islam and no inclination before the fighting. Do you not see how the fighting of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) against the people of Makkah was a cause of their Islam, because one who enters Islam may enter it with insight, and may enter it with reluctance and compulsion, and then his condition may become good in Islam. Do you not see how 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Sarh's condition was first in Islam, then his affair came to the best state, and he died the best death in prostration in his prayer, and he was among the best of the Companions? "And Allah is Knowing" knows what will be just as He knows what has been, and in that is an affirmation of what He arranged of those promises, and that they will certainly occur. "Wise" in directing His servants from state to state according to what His wisdom, exalted is He, requires.

﴿Or do you think that you will be left alone while Allah has not yet known those of you who strove and did not take, other than Allah and His Messenger and the believers, an intimate (walijah)﴾. The explanation of a parallel of this clause was given earlier, and the meaning is: you will not be left as you are until the sincere among you are distinguished, who are the strivers in the way of Allah, who did not take as intimates anyone other than Allah from among others.

﴿and did not take, other than Allah and His Messenger and the believers, an intimate (walijah)﴾. "And did not take" is coordinated with "strove" (jahadu), meaning: not taking an intimate. The walijah is an pattern (fa'ilah) from walaja, like al-dakhilah from dakhala, and it is the inner circle and the entrance into which one enters secretly; hypocrisy was likened to it. Qatadah said: the walijah is betrayal; al-Dahhak said: deception; 'Ata' said: the enemies; al-Hasan said: disbelief and hypocrisy. Abu 'Ubaydah said: everything you introduce into something while it is not of it is a walijah, and a man who is among a people while not of them is a walijah; it is used for the singular, dual and plural with one form. A man's walijah is the one who is specially entrusted with the secret of his affair from among the people; its plural is wala'ij and wulj, like sahifah, sahaif and suhuf. 'Ubadah ibn Safwan al-Ghanawi said:

"And their intimates in every open and gathering,
to everyone who is hoped for and everyone who is feared."

In this verse is a reproach of the hypocrites who took intimates, especially at the imposition of fighting. The meaning: you must be tested, O believers, as in His saying: ﴿Do people think that they will be left to say, "We believe," and they will not be tested?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 2]. Since a man may fight while being a hypocrite, He negated this description of him, and explained that jihad necessarily requires sincerity, free of hypocrisy, showing off, and cultivating friendship with the disbelievers.

﴿And Allah is Aware of what you do﴾. Al-Jumhur read with the ta' as address, in harmony with His saying "Or do you think," and al-Hasan, Ya'qub in one narration from Ruways, and Sallam read with the ya' as the third person by way of iltifat.

(p-14) The apparent reading is that the pronoun refers to the polytheists mentioned before, who were commanded to be fought. The meaning is: they bartered the Qur'an and the Islam it calls to for a small price, which is following desires and whims, since those desires abandoned the religion of God and preferred disbelief. That was like buying and selling. Mujahid said: they were the Bedouin Arabs whom Abu Sufyan gathered for his food. Abu Salih said: they were a people of the Jews, and "the signs of God" are the Torah. Ibn Abbas said: they were the people of al-Ta'if, who would give people money to keep them from entering Islam. "They turned away from His way" means they turned themselves away from the religion of God and deviated from it. The apparent reading is that "sa'a" (evil is) here has been converted into a verb. Its class follows the manner of "bi'sa" (how wretched), but it may also remain in its original descriptive form, in which case it is transitive, meaning: "what they used to do grieved them." The object is then omitted because the meaning is understood.

﴿They do not observe regarding any believer a bond of kinship or a covenant, and those are the transgressors.﴾ This is a warning about the attribute that necessitates enmity, which is faith. Since His saying ﴿they do not observe regarding you⟩ [al-Tawba: 8] could be taken to apply only to the addressees, He drew attention to the cause of this, namely that the reason for the hostility is faith. "Those" refers to those who combine these blameworthy attributes, and they are "the transgressors," those who exceed the limit in wrongdoing, evil, and breaking covenants.

﴿But if they repent, establish prayer, and give zakat, then they are your brothers in religion.⟩ That is: if they repent of disbelief and breaking the covenant, and commit to the rulings of Islam, then they are your brothers, meaning they are your brothers. "Ikhwan" and "ikhwa" are plurals of "akh" (brother), whether by lineage or by religion. Whoever claims that "ikhwa" is used for lineage and "ikhwan" for friendship has erred. God said: ﴿The believers are only brothers⟩ [al-Hujurat: 10], and He said: ﴿or the houses of your brothers⟩ [al-Nur: 61]. He made the establishment of brotherhood in religion depend on the combination of all three conditions. It appears that the implied meaning of the conditional is not intended.

﴿And We explain the signs for a people who know.⟩ That is, We clarify and make them plain. This clause is a parenthetical insertion between the two conditionals: between His saying ﴿But if they repent⟩ and His saying "And if they break their oaths," as an urging and encouragement to reflect on the rulings God has detailed. He said ﴿for a people who know⟩ because only those who have knowledge and understanding reflect on their details.

﴿And if they break their oaths after their covenant and revile your religion, then fight the leaders of disbelief, for they have no oaths, so that they may desist.⟩ That is: if they violate their pledges after they had made covenants and sworn oaths not to break them. "Wa-taʿanu" (and they reviled) means they found fault with it, disparaged it, and belittled it. The word "ta'n" (reviling) here is figurative; its original sense is striking with a spear, a stick, or the like. Here it means blame, as in the hadith about the leadership of Usama: "If you revile his leadership, you have already reviled the leadership of his father before him," meaning you found fault with it and belittled it. The apparent view is that this division between the two conditions concerns disbelievers originally, because whoever embraced Islam and then apostatized would be covered by His saying "fight the leaders of disbelief," meaning the chiefs and leaders of disbelief. The meaning is: fight the disbelievers. He singled out the leaders for mention because they are the ones who incite the followers to remain in disbelief. Al-Karmani said: every disbeliever is an imam of himself, so the meaning is: fight every disbeliever. It has been said that whoever undertakes to break a covenant and revile the religion becomes a head of disbelief and is therefore one of the leaders of disbelief. Ibn Abbas said: the leaders of disbelief are the chiefs of Quraysh. Al-Qurtubi said: this is far-fetched, because the verse is in the surah of Bara'a (al-Tawba), and by the time it was revealed God had uprooted the power of Quraysh, and none of them remained except a Muslim or one at peace. Qatada said: the intended ones are Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, Utba ibn Rabi'a, and others. This is weak unless it is taken as an example, because the verse was revealed long after Badr. It is reported from Hudhayfa that he said: "These have not yet come," meaning they have not yet died out, so they keep coming and fighting. Ibn Atiyya said: the best thing that can be said about this is that it does not refer to a specific individual, but rather that the command was pushed toward fighting the leaders of those who break covenants among the disbelievers until the Day of Resurrection, without specification. The situation of the Arab disbelievers and the enemies of the Messenger of God ﷺ required that the reference to them first be with the phrase "leaders of disbelief," and they were included under the term at that time. The one who undertakes the fighting against the Prophet ﷺ and the repelling of him at the beginning of his law is the imam of every one who disbelieves in that law until the Day of Resurrection. Then in each generation of disbelievers there come leaders specific to each generation. End of quote. It has been said that the covenant means Islam, so the meaning is: they disbelieved after their Islam. For this reason some read "wa-in nakathu iymanahum" with a kasra on the alif (meaning "their faith"), and this is the view of al-Zamakhshari, who said: His saying ﴿then fight the leaders of disbelief⟩ means "then fight them," and so He placed "leaders of disbelief" in the position of their pronoun, to indicate that when they broke faith while in the state of polytheism, out of rebellion, transgression, and abandoning the customs of the noble and faithful among the Arabs, and then believed, established prayer, gave zakat, and became brothers to the Muslims in religion, then returned and apostatized from Islam, broke the faith they had pledged with regard to faith and fidelity to covenants, and sat reviling the religion of God, saying that Muhammad's religion is nothing, then they are the leaders of disbelief and those of leadership and precedence in it, and no disbeliever can match their dust. The well-known position of the school of Malik is that a dhimmi (a non-Muslim under protection) who reviles the religion, doing something such as denying the law or insulting the Prophet ﷺ or the like, is killed. It has been said: if he openly does something among what is known of his belief and disbelief, he is disciplined for the open act and left alone, but if he disbelieves in something that is not of his belief, such as insulting, or the like, he is killed. Abu Hanifa said: he is asked to repent. It is disputed: if a dhimmi insults and then embraces Islam to escape being killed (taqiyya, or precautionary dissimulation under threat). The well-known position of the school of Malik is that he is left alone, because Islam erases what came before it. In al-'Utbiyya (a book in the Maliki school) it is said that he is killed, and he is not in a better position than a Muslim.

Or the Jews resolved to betray the Messenger ﷺ, broke his covenant, and aided the hypocrites in expelling him from Medina. These are three opinions, the first of which is that of al-Suddi. Al-Hasan said: from Medina. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is consistent for the battle of Uhud, the confederates, and others, and they are the ones who initiated the fighting, because the Messenger of God ﷺ first came to them with the clear Book and challenged them with it, but they turned away from contesting it because they were unable to, and turned to fighting. So they were the initiators, and the initiator is the more unjust. What prevents you, then, from fighting them with the same, striking them with evil as they struck you? He rebuked them for abandoning the fight and urged them to it, then described them with what necessitates urging it. It is established that whoever has attributes like theirs, breaking covenants, expelling the Messenger, and beginning fighting without any justification, deserves that his assault not be left unanswered, and that whoever neglects it be rebuked. This was said by al-Zamakhshari, and it is an exaggeration. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "the first time" (awwal marra) has been said to mean their deeds in Mecca against the Prophet ﷺ and the believers. Mujahid said: it is what Quraysh began with, the aid they gave Banu Bakr, their allies, against Khuza'a, the allies of the Prophet, and this was the beginning of the breaking. Al-Tabari said: it means their act on the day of Badr. End of quote.

Zayd ibn 'Ali read "badawkum" without a hamza. Its basis is that he softened the hamza of "bada'tu" by changing it to ya', just as they said "qarayt" for "qara'tu," making it like "ramayt." When the verb was attached to the waw of the pronoun, the ya' dropped, giving "badawkum," just as you say "ramawkum." ("Atakhshawnahum") is an affirmation of the fear of them and a rebuke for it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verse 9–16 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Allah has more right that you fear Him﴾ [so that you would fight His enemies]. The word "Allah" (lafz al-jalalah) is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is "more right" (ahaqq). "That you fear Him" (an takhshawhu) is a substitute (badal) for "Allah"; that is, the fear of Allah is more deserving than their fear [of others]. "That you fear Him" is in the position of nominative case (raf'). It is permissible that it be in the position of accusative (nasb) or genitive (jarr) according to the disagreement [of the grammarians] when the preposition is elided, and its underlying form is: "by that you fear Him"; that is, He is more deserving than other than Him that you fear Him. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "that you fear Him" be the subject, and "more right" its predicate placed before it. Ibn 'Atiyya permitted that "more right" (ahaqq) be the subject and its predicate "that you fear Him," and the clause is a predicate for the first [subject]. The use of an indefinite noun as subject is acceptable because it is an elative (af'al al-tafdil), and Sibawayh permitted that a definite noun be the predicate of an indefinite noun in such a construction as: "Aim at a man whose father is better than him."

﴿if you are believers﴾; that is, those whose faith is complete, because they were believers. Al-Zamakhshari said: he means that the requirement of sound faith is that the believer fears none but his Lord and does not care for anyone else, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they fear none but Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 39].

﴿Fight them, and Allah will punish them by your hands and will disgrace them and give you victory over them and heal the breasts of a believing people﴾ ﴿and remove the rage of their hearts. And Allah turns in forgiveness to whom He wills. And Allah is Knowing and Wise﴾. The verses before this established the deeds of the disbelievers that necessitate fighting them, and the urging to fight; the command to fight is forbidden in this [context]. Their punishment by the hands of the believers is in this world by killing, capture and plunder. These are promises that strengthened their hearts and rectified their intentions. Their disgrace is their humiliation and abasement. "And will give you victory" means He will make you triumph over them. The healing of the breasts is by the elevation of the religion of Allah and the punishment and disgrace of the disbelievers.

Zayd ibn 'Ali read "wa-nashfi" with the nun, by way of iltifat (shift of person). The phrasing "breasts of a believing people" came to include the addressees and every believer, because what befalls the people of disbelief of punishment and disgrace is a healing for the breast of every believer. It was said: the intended people are specific ones. Ibn 'Abbas said: "They are clans from Yemen and Saba' who came to Makkah and embraced Islam, and they met from its people severe harm, so they sent to the Messenger of Allah complaining to him, and he said: 'Rejoice, for relief is near.'" Mujahid and al-Suddi said: they are Khuza'ah. The reason for specifying them is that they were the ones against whom the covenant was broken and upon whom war fell, and at that time there were many believers among Khuza'ah. Do you not see the saying of the Khuza'i seeking the help of the Prophet (ﷺ):

"There we became Muslims and did not withdraw a hand,"

and at the end of the verse:

"And they killed us while bowing and prostrating."

Removing rage is by what the disbelievers suffered of hardship. This clause is like an emphasis for the one before it, because the healing of the breast from the cause of rage is the removal of rage. A group read "wa-yadhhabu" as an intransitive verb with "rage" (ghayz) as its subject. Zayd ibn 'Ali likewise read it, except that he raised the letter ba' (ghayzu). All these promises were fulfilled, and this was a proof of the truthfulness of the Messenger and the soundness of his prophethood. It begins first with what results from victory, namely Allah's punishment of the disbelievers and their disgrace at the hands of the believers, since the beginning with what afflicts the disbelievers of evil is what gladdens the believers. Then He mentioned the cause, which is Allah's victory of the believers over the disbelievers. Then He mentioned what also results from victory, the healing of the believers' breasts and the removal of their rage, completing the blessings. So He mentioned what results from victory with respect to the disbelievers, and mentioned what befalls the Muslims of joy and happiness in attaining vengeance, and did not mention what they gained of spoils and provisions, because the Arabs are a people created with zeal and pride, so their desire to attain vengeance and kill enemies is what suits their nature:

"Verily the lions, the lions of the thicket, their resolve
on the day of battle is in the one despoiled, not in the spoils."

Al-Jumhur read "wa-yatubu Allahu" with raf' (nominative), and it is a resumptive statement that some of the people of Makkah and others will turn from their disbelief, and many of them did so, and their Islam was good. Al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and Abu al-Fath said: this is an existing matter whether they were fought or not, so there is no way to include "today" in the answer of the condition in "fight them." End of quote. Zayd ibn 'Ali, al-A'raj, Ibn Abi Ishaq, 'Isa al-Thaqafi, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, 'Umar ibn Qa'id, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub, as transmitted from them, read "wa-yatuba Allahu" with nasb of the ba', making it included in the answer of the command by way of meaning. It was said: it is possible that repentance is included in the reward. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is valid in my view if it is taken that repentance is meant as: the killing of the disbelievers and jihad in the way of Allah is a repentance for you, O believers, and a perfection of your faith, so repentance on this view enters into the condition of fighting. Others said: when He commanded them to fight, that was difficult for some of them, so when they proceeded to fight, that action served as repentance from that aversion. It was said: the existence of disbelief and abundance of wealth is a pleasure sought by a forbidden way, so when a lawful way was gained for them, that was a motive for them to repent of what preceded, so repentance became connected with that fighting. End of quote. What they established about repentance entering under the answer of the command concerns the believers who were commanded to fight the disbelievers, but what appears is that it concerns the disbelievers: the meaning is "upon whom He wills of the disbelievers," because fighting the disbelievers and the Muslims' overcoming them may result in the Islam of many people, even if they had no desire for Islam and no inclination before the fighting. Do you not see how the fighting of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) against the people of Makkah was a cause of their Islam, because one who enters Islam may enter it with insight, and may enter it with reluctance and compulsion, and then his condition may become good in Islam. Do you not see how 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Sarh's condition was first in Islam, then his affair came to the best state, and he died the best death in prostration in his prayer, and he was among the best of the Companions? "And Allah is Knowing" knows what will be just as He knows what has been, and in that is an affirmation of what He arranged of those promises, and that they will certainly occur. "Wise" in directing His servants from state to state according to what His wisdom, exalted is He, requires.

﴿Or do you think that you will be left alone while Allah has not yet known those of you who strove and did not take, other than Allah and His Messenger and the believers, an intimate (walijah)﴾. The explanation of a parallel of this clause was given earlier, and the meaning is: you will not be left as you are until the sincere among you are distinguished, who are the strivers in the way of Allah, who did not take as intimates anyone other than Allah from among others.

﴿and did not take, other than Allah and His Messenger and the believers, an intimate (walijah)﴾. "And did not take" is coordinated with "strove" (jahadu), meaning: not taking an intimate. The walijah is an pattern (fa'ilah) from walaja, like al-dakhilah from dakhala, and it is the inner circle and the entrance into which one enters secretly; hypocrisy was likened to it. Qatadah said: the walijah is betrayal; al-Dahhak said: deception; 'Ata' said: the enemies; al-Hasan said: disbelief and hypocrisy. Abu 'Ubaydah said: everything you introduce into something while it is not of it is a walijah, and a man who is among a people while not of them is a walijah; it is used for the singular, dual and plural with one form. A man's walijah is the one who is specially entrusted with the secret of his affair from among the people; its plural is wala'ij and wulj, like sahifah, sahaif and suhuf. 'Ubadah ibn Safwan al-Ghanawi said:

"And their intimates in every open and gathering,
to everyone who is hoped for and everyone who is feared."

In this verse is a reproach of the hypocrites who took intimates, especially at the imposition of fighting. The meaning: you must be tested, O believers, as in His saying: ﴿Do people think that they will be left to say, "We believe," and they will not be tested?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 2]. Since a man may fight while being a hypocrite, He negated this description of him, and explained that jihad necessarily requires sincerity, free of hypocrisy, showing off, and cultivating friendship with the disbelievers.

﴿And Allah is Aware of what you do﴾. Al-Jumhur read with the ta' as address, in harmony with His saying "Or do you think," and al-Hasan, Ya'qub in one narration from Ruways, and Sallam read with the ya' as the third person by way of iltifat.

(p-14) The apparent reading is that the pronoun refers to the polytheists mentioned before, who were commanded to be fought. The meaning is: they bartered the Qur'an and the Islam it calls to for a small price, which is following desires and whims, since those desires abandoned the religion of God and preferred disbelief. That was like buying and selling. Mujahid said: they were the Bedouin Arabs whom Abu Sufyan gathered for his food. Abu Salih said: they were a people of the Jews, and "the signs of God" are the Torah. Ibn Abbas said: they were the people of al-Ta'if, who would give people money to keep them from entering Islam. "They turned away from His way" means they turned themselves away from the religion of God and deviated from it. The apparent reading is that "sa'a" (evil is) here has been converted into a verb. Its class follows the manner of "bi'sa" (how wretched), but it may also remain in its original descriptive form, in which case it is transitive, meaning: "what they used to do grieved them." The object is then omitted because the meaning is understood.

﴿They do not observe regarding any believer a bond of kinship or a covenant, and those are the transgressors.﴾ This is a warning about the attribute that necessitates enmity, which is faith. Since His saying ﴿they do not observe regarding you⟩ [al-Tawba: 8] could be taken to apply only to the addressees, He drew attention to the cause of this, namely that the reason for the hostility is faith. "Those" refers to those who combine these blameworthy attributes, and they are "the transgressors," those who exceed the limit in wrongdoing, evil, and breaking covenants.

﴿But if they repent, establish prayer, and give zakat, then they are your brothers in religion.⟩ That is: if they repent of disbelief and breaking the covenant, and commit to the rulings of Islam, then they are your brothers, meaning they are your brothers. "Ikhwan" and "ikhwa" are plurals of "akh" (brother), whether by lineage or by religion. Whoever claims that "ikhwa" is used for lineage and "ikhwan" for friendship has erred. God said: ﴿The believers are only brothers⟩ [al-Hujurat: 10], and He said: ﴿or the houses of your brothers⟩ [al-Nur: 61]. He made the establishment of brotherhood in religion depend on the combination of all three conditions. It appears that the implied meaning of the conditional is not intended.

﴿And We explain the signs for a people who know.⟩ That is, We clarify and make them plain. This clause is a parenthetical insertion between the two conditionals: between His saying ﴿But if they repent⟩ and His saying "And if they break their oaths," as an urging and encouragement to reflect on the rulings God has detailed. He said ﴿for a people who know⟩ because only those who have knowledge and understanding reflect on their details.

﴿And if they break their oaths after their covenant and revile your religion, then fight the leaders of disbelief, for they have no oaths, so that they may desist.⟩ That is: if they violate their pledges after they had made covenants and sworn oaths not to break them. "Wa-taʿanu" (and they reviled) means they found fault with it, disparaged it, and belittled it. The word "ta'n" (reviling) here is figurative; its original sense is striking with a spear, a stick, or the like. Here it means blame, as in the hadith about the leadership of Usama: "If you revile his leadership, you have already reviled the leadership of his father before him," meaning you found fault with it and belittled it. The apparent view is that this division between the two conditions concerns disbelievers originally, because whoever embraced Islam and then apostatized would be covered by His saying "fight the leaders of disbelief," meaning the chiefs and leaders of disbelief. The meaning is: fight the disbelievers. He singled out the leaders for mention because they are the ones who incite the followers to remain in disbelief. Al-Karmani said: every disbeliever is an imam of himself, so the meaning is: fight every disbeliever. It has been said that whoever undertakes to break a covenant and revile the religion becomes a head of disbelief and is therefore one of the leaders of disbelief. Ibn Abbas said: the leaders of disbelief are the chiefs of Quraysh. Al-Qurtubi said: this is far-fetched, because the verse is in the surah of Bara'a (al-Tawba), and by the time it was revealed God had uprooted the power of Quraysh, and none of them remained except a Muslim or one at peace. Qatada said: the intended ones are Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, Utba ibn Rabi'a, and others. This is weak unless it is taken as an example, because the verse was revealed long after Badr. It is reported from Hudhayfa that he said: "These have not yet come," meaning they have not yet died out, so they keep coming and fighting. Ibn Atiyya said: the best thing that can be said about this is that it does not refer to a specific individual, but rather that the command was pushed toward fighting the leaders of those who break covenants among the disbelievers until the Day of Resurrection, without specification. The situation of the Arab disbelievers and the enemies of the Messenger of God ﷺ required that the reference to them first be with the phrase "leaders of disbelief," and they were included under the term at that time. The one who undertakes the fighting against the Prophet ﷺ and the repelling of him at the beginning of his law is the imam of every one who disbelieves in that law until the Day of Resurrection. Then in each generation of disbelievers there come leaders specific to each generation. End of quote. It has been said that the covenant means Islam, so the meaning is: they disbelieved after their Islam. For this reason some read "wa-in nakathu iymanahum" with a kasra on the alif (meaning "their faith"), and this is the view of al-Zamakhshari, who said: His saying ﴿then fight the leaders of disbelief⟩ means "then fight them," and so He placed "leaders of disbelief" in the position of their pronoun, to indicate that when they broke faith while in the state of polytheism, out of rebellion, transgression, and abandoning the customs of the noble and faithful among the Arabs, and then believed, established prayer, gave zakat, and became brothers to the Muslims in religion, then returned and apostatized from Islam, broke the faith they had pledged with regard to faith and fidelity to covenants, and sat reviling the religion of God, saying that Muhammad's religion is nothing, then they are the leaders of disbelief and those of leadership and precedence in it, and no disbeliever can match their dust. The well-known position of the school of Malik is that a dhimmi (a non-Muslim under protection) who reviles the religion, doing something such as denying the law or insulting the Prophet ﷺ or the like, is killed. It has been said: if he openly does something among what is known of his belief and disbelief, he is disciplined for the open act and left alone, but if he disbelieves in something that is not of his belief, such as insulting, or the like, he is killed. Abu Hanifa said: he is asked to repent. It is disputed: if a dhimmi insults and then embraces Islam to escape being killed (taqiyya, or precautionary dissimulation under threat). The well-known position of the school of Malik is that he is left alone, because Islam erases what came before it. In al-'Utbiyya (a book in the Maliki school) it is said that he is killed, and he is not in a better position than a Muslim.

Al-Haramayn (Ibn Kathir and Nafi'), and Abu 'Amr, read by replacing the second hamza with a ya'. It is reported from Nafi' that he prolonged the hamza. The rest of the seven readers, and Ibn Abi Uways from Nafi', read with two hamzas, and Hisham inserted an alif between them. The origin is "ii'imma," on the pattern of "af'ila," the plural of "imam." They assimilated the mim into the mim, so its vowel was moved to the hamza before it. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, how is the wording "a'imma"? I say: it is a hamza followed by a hamza, pronounced "bayn bayn" (an intermediate sound between the hamza and the ya'), that is, between the place of articulation of the hamza and the ya'. Pronouncing the hamza fully is a well-known reading, though it is not accepted by the Basran grammarians. As for pronouncing it explicitly as ya', that is not a recitation and cannot be one. Whoever pronounces it that way is a grammatical misreader and a distorter. End of quote. This is his habit of finding fault with the readers. How could that be a mistake when it was recited by the head of the Basran grammarians, Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala', the reciter of Mecca Ibn Kathir, and the reciter of the city of the Messenger, Nafi'? He negated their faith when they did not remain steadfast in it nor fulfilled it, so they were treated as having no oaths. Or it is by omission of the qualifier, meaning: they have no oaths that they fulfill. The majority read with a fatha on the hamza. Al-Hasan, 'Ata', Zayd ibn 'Ali, and Ibn 'Amir read "la iman lahum," meaning they have no Islam and no acceptance of truth. Abu 'Ali said: this is not strong, because it is repetitive, since He had already described the leaders of disbelief as having no faith. The better reading with a kasra on the alif is that it is the verbal noun of "amanahu iman" (he granted him security), and from it is His saying ﴿and gave them security from fear⟩ [Quraysh: 4]. The meaning is that they do not grant security to the people of the dhimma, since the polytheists had only Islam or the sword. Abu Hatim said: al-Hasan explained his reading as "la islam lahum" (they have no Islam). Al-Zamakhshari followed him in this, saying: it is read "la iman lahum," meaning "la islam lahum," and they are not given safe conduct after apostasy and breaking the covenant, and there is no way to it. The reading with a fatha was used by Abu Hanifa as evidence that the oath of a disbeliever is not an oath, while according to al-Shafi'i their oath is an oath. He said: its meaning is that they do not fulfill it, as evidenced by the fact that He described them as breakers of oaths.

﴿So that they may desist⟩ is connected to His saying ﴿then fight the leaders of disbelief⟩. That is: let your purpose in fighting them, after such great wrongs have been committed by them, be their desisting from what they are in. This is from His generosity, His bounty, and His returning to the wrongdoer with mercy.

﴿Will you not fight a people who broke their oaths, and resolved to expel the Messenger, and they began against you first? Do you fear them? God has more right that you fear Him, if you are believers.⟩ ("Ala") is a particle of urging, and its meaning here is to incite them to fight. They claimed that it is composed of the interrogative hamza and the negative la, so that it carries the sense of specification. Al-Zamakhshari said: the hamza entered for affirmation of the negation of fighting, and its meaning is urging to it in the manner of emphasis. When God commanded the killing of the people of disbelief, He followed it with the cause that moves one to fight them, which is three things they combined, each of which on its own is sufficient to urge fighting them. The meaning of "they broke their oaths" is that they violated the covenant. Al-Suddi, Ibn Ishaq, and al-Kalbi said: it was revealed about the disbelievers of Mecca, who broke their oaths after the treaty of al-Hudaybiyya and aided Banu Bakr against Khuza'a. Their resolution was the resolution of Quraysh to expel the Messenger from Mecca when they deliberated in the Dar al-Nadwa (the council house), so God permitted the migration, and he went out by himself. Or it was Banu Bakr's resolution to expel him from Medina because of what they undertook of consultation and gathering. Or the Jews resolved to betray the Messenger ﷺ, broke his covenant, and aided the hypocrites in expelling him from Medina. These are three opinions, the first of which is that of al-Suddi. Al-Hasan said: from Medina. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is consistent for the battle of Uhud, the confederates, and others, and they are the ones who initiated the fighting, because the Messenger of God ﷺ first came to them with the clear Book and challenged them with it, but they turned away from contesting it because they were unable to, and turned to fighting. So they were the initiators, and the initiator is the more unjust. What prevents you, then, from fighting them with the same, striking them with evil as they struck you? He rebuked them for abandoning the fight and urged them to it, then described them with what necessitates urging it. It is established that whoever has attributes like theirs, breaking covenants, expelling the Messenger, and beginning fighting without any justification, deserves that his assault not be left unanswered, and that whoever neglects it be rebuked. This was said by al-Zamakhshari, and it is an exaggeration. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "the first time" (awwal marra) has been said to mean their deeds in Mecca against the Prophet ﷺ and the believers. Mujahid said: it is what Quraysh began with, the aid they gave Banu Bakr, their allies, against Khuza'a, the allies of the Prophet, and this was the beginning of the breaking. Al-Tabari said: it means their act on the day of Badr. End of quote.

When the verb was attached to the waw of the pronoun, the ya' dropped, giving "badawkum," just as you say "ramawkum." ("Atakhshawnahum") is an affirmation of the fear of them and a rebuke for it.

Al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and Abu al-Fath said: this is an existing matter whether they were fought or not, so there is no way to include "today" in the answer of the condition in "fight them." End of quote. Zayd ibn 'Ali, al-A'raj, Ibn Abi Ishaq, 'Isa al-Thaqafi, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, 'Umar ibn Qa'id, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub, as transmitted from them, read "wa-yatuba Allahu" with nasb of the ba', making it included in the answer of the command by way of meaning. It was said: it is possible that repentance is included in the reward. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is valid in my view if it is taken that repentance is meant as: the killing of the disbelievers and jihad in the way of Allah is a repentance for you, O believers, and a perfection of your faith, so repentance on this view enters into the condition of fighting. Others said: when He commanded them to fight, that was difficult for some of them, so when they proceeded to fight, that action served as repentance from that aversion. It was said: the existence of disbelief and abundance of wealth is a pleasure sought by a forbidden way, so when a lawful way was gained for them, that was a motive for them to repent of what preceded, so repentance became connected with that fighting. End of quote. What they established about repentance entering under the answer of the command concerns the believers who were commanded to fight the disbelievers, but what appears is that it concerns the disbelievers: the meaning is "upon whom He wills of the disbelievers," because fighting the disbelievers and the Muslims' overcoming them may result in the Islam of many people, even if they had no desire for Islam and no inclination before the fighting. Do you not see how the fighting of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) against the people of Makkah was a cause of their Islam, because one who enters Islam may enter it with insight, and may enter it with reluctance and compulsion, and then his condition may become good in Islam. Do you not see how 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Sarh's condition was first in Islam, then his affair came to the best state, and he died the best death in prostration in his prayer, and he was among the best of the Companions? "And Allah is Knowing" knows what will be just as He knows what has been, and in that is an affirmation of what He arranged of those promises, and that they will certainly occur. "Wise" in directing His servants from state to state according to what His wisdom, exalted is He, requires.

﴿Or do you think that you will be left alone while Allah has not yet known those of you who strove and did not take, other than Allah and His Messenger and the believers, an intimate (walijah)﴾. The explanation of a parallel of this clause was given earlier, and the meaning is: you will not be left as you are until the sincere among you are distinguished, who are the strivers in the way of Allah, who did not take as intimates anyone other than Allah from among others.

﴿and did not take, other than Allah and His Messenger and the believers, an intimate (walijah)﴾. "And did not take" is coordinated with "strove" (jahadu), meaning: not taking an intimate. The walijah is an pattern (fa'ilah) from walaja, like al-dakhilah from dakhala, and it is the inner circle and the entrance into which one enters secretly; hypocrisy was likened to it. Qatadah said: the walijah is betrayal; al-Dahhak said: deception; 'Ata' said: the enemies; al-Hasan said: disbelief and hypocrisy. Abu 'Ubaydah said: everything you introduce into something while it is not of it is a walijah, and a man who is among a people while not of them is a walijah; it is used for the singular, dual and plural with one form. A man's walijah is the one who is specially entrusted with the secret of his affair from among the people; its plural is wala'ij and wulj, like sahifah, sahaif and suhuf. 'Ubadah ibn Safwan al-Ghanawi said:

"And their intimates in every open and gathering,
to everyone who is hoped for and everyone who is feared."

In this verse is a reproach of the hypocrites who took intimates, especially at the imposition of fighting. The meaning: you must be tested, O believers, as in His saying: ﴿Do people think that they will be left to say, "We believe," and they will not be tested?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 2]. Since a man may fight while being a hypocrite, He negated this description of him, and explained that jihad necessarily requires sincerity, free of hypocrisy, showing off, and cultivating friendship with the disbelievers.

﴿And Allah is Aware of what you do﴾. Al-Jumhur read with the ta' as address, in harmony with His saying "Or do you think," and al-Hasan, Ya'qub in one narration from Ruways, and Sallam read with the ya' as the third person by way of iltifat.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verses 17–22 (part 1 of 2):

﴿It is not for the polytheists to maintain the mosques of Allah while they testify against themselves to disbelief.﴾ Ibn al-Sumayqa recited: "an yu'imiru" (with a damma on the yā' and a kasra on the mīm), meaning "to help in its upkeep." Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and al-Jahdari recited "masjid" in the singular, while the rest of the Seven (qira'at, the canonical readings) and Mujahid, Qatada, Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj and Shayba recited it in the plural.

The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when Allah mentioned the disavowal of the polytheists and kinds of their ugly deeds that necessitate disavowing them, He mentioned that they are described with praiseworthy qualities that negate the disavowal from them, namely that they maintain the Sacred Mosque. It is related that the Emigrants and the Helpers approached the captives of Badr, rebuking them for associating partners with Allah. 'Ali began to reproach al-'Abbas, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Severing of ties of kinship!" and spoke harshly to him. Al-'Abbas said: "Do you display our bad deeds and conceal our good deeds?" He said: "Do you have good deeds?" They said: "Yes, and we are better than you in reward: we maintain the Sacred Mosque, we cover the Ka'ba, we give water to the pilgrims, and we free the captives." So Allah revealed this verse in response to them.

The meaning of "It is not for the polytheists" is: not with the due right; otherwise they had maintained it in the past and present, by way of dominance. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, it is not valid and not proper. Its maintenance (i'mara) is entering it, sitting in it and staying in it, from their saying: "So-and-so maintains the mosque," meaning he frequently visits it; or raising its building and repairing what has collapsed of it; or worshipping in it and circumambulating it. As for prayer, there are three opinions. Whoever recited it in the singular, it may be understood to mean the Sacred Mosque, due to His saying: ﴿and the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque﴾, or it may be the genus, which would include the Sacred Mosque, as it is the head of that genus, its foremost part. Whoever recited it in the plural, it may be understood to mean the Sacred Mosque, and the plural is applied to it either because every place within it is a mosque, or because it is the qibla of all mosques and their leader, so its maintainer is the maintainer of all mosques. It may also be understood to mean the plural in general, which includes the Sacred Mosque, and this is more emphatic, because its method is that of metonymy (kināya, indirect expression), as when you say: "So-and-so does not read the books of Allah," you negate his reading of the Qur'an more strongly than by stating it directly.

"Witnessing" (shāhidīn) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl, a clause describing the condition of the subject), and the meaning is: it is not right for them to combine two contradictory matters: maintaining the places of worship of Allah the Exalted together with disbelief in Him and the worship of Him.

Zayd ibn 'Ali recited "shāhidūn" (nominative), on the assumption of an implied subject: "they are witnesses." Their testimony against themselves to disbelief is their saying during circumambulation: "Here I am, O Allah, here I am; You have no partner, except a partner who is Yours, You own him and what he owns." Or their saying when asked about their religion: "We worship al-Lat and al-'Uzza." Or their denial of the Messenger. Or the saying of a polytheist: "I am a polytheist," as the Jew says "he is a Jew," the Christian says "he is a Christian," the Magian says "he is a Magian," and the Sabian says "he is a Sabian." Or the manifestation of the actions of the disbelievers, such as erecting their idols and circumambulating the House naked. These are five opinions. This is when "against themselves" is taken in its literal sense. It has been said that its meaning is: witnesses against their Messenger, and "themselves" is used for him, because there is no tribe of the Arabs but that it has kinship ties with them. This opinion is supported by the reading of whoever recited "'alā anfasihim" with a fatḥa on the fā', meaning "their most noble and most eminent."

﴿Those, their deeds have become void﴾, which are the maintenance, the custody of the Ka'ba (ḥijāba), the giving of water (siqāya), freeing the captives, and other things mentioned as praiseworthy deeds. Al-Zamakhshari said: If disbelief or a major sin destroys established and sound deeds when it follows them, what then of what accompanies them? Allah the Exalted alluded to this by His saying "witnesses," where He made it a state (ḥāl) concerning them, and it indicates that they combined maintenance and testimony to disbelief against themselves in one state, and that is impossible and not proper. End of quotation. His saying "or a major sin" is a Mu'tazili (rationalist) insertion, because major sins according to them destroy deeds.

﴿And in the Fire they will abide eternally.﴾ It mentions the end of the polytheists, which is the Fire, abiding in it forever. Zayd ibn 'Ali recited "yā'" with a fatḥa (yakhlud, in the masculine form), as a circumstantial state, and "in the Fire" is the predicate, as you say: "In the house is Zayd seated." Al-Wahidi said: The verse indicates that disbelievers are prohibited from maintaining the mosques of the Muslims; if one of them bequeaths something, his bequest is not accepted; and he is prevented from entering mosques. If he enters without permission from a Muslim, he deserves a discretionary punishment (ta'zīr); if he enters with permission, he is not punished. The better course is to honor the mosques and prevent them from entering. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) lodged the delegation of Thaqif, who were disbelievers, in the mosque, and he tied Thumama ibn Uthal al-Hanafi to one of the pillars of the mosque while he was a disbeliever.

﴿Only one who believes in Allah and the Last Day, establishes prayer, gives zakat, and fears none but Allah maintains the mosques of Allah; perhaps those will be among the guided.﴾ Al-Jahdari and Hammad ibn Abi Salama, from Ibn Kathir, recited "masjidan li-Allāh" in the singular with monotheism. The Seven and a group recited it in the plural. The meaning is: he maintains them with the due right, and this applies to whoever has these characteristics. Within this statement is a command to the believers to maintain the mosques, and their maintenance includes repairing what has collapsed of them, cleaning them, lighting them, honoring them, and making them habitual places of worship and remembrance. Among remembrance is the study of knowledge, indeed it is its greatest part, and guarding them from what they were not built for, such as discussing worldly affairs. In a hadith: "When you see a man frequenting the mosque, bear witness that he is a believer." Belief in the Messenger is not mentioned, because belief in the Last Day is only received from the reports of the Messenger, so it includes belief in the Messenger. Or it was not mentioned because it is known and well established that belief in Allah the Exalted is accompanied by belief in the Messenger (ﷺ), since the words of the testimony, the adhan and the iqama, and others include both of them together, paired, as if they were one thing that cannot be separated from each other. So belief in the Messenger (ﷺ) is included within the mention of belief in Allah the Exalted. It has been said: it indicates it by mentioning establishing prayer and giving zakat, since these are only received from him. The purpose of building mosques and maintaining them is that they be a gathering place for establishing prayers in them and acts of worship such as remembrance and seclusion (i'tikāf) and others. It is fitting that the mention of giving zakat appears alongside maintaining mosques, because since they are a gathering place for people, the affairs of the rich and the poor become evident in them, and the states of the one who pays zakat and the one who deserves it are known.

﴿And fears none but Allah.﴾ Ibn 'Aṭiyya said: He means the fear of reverence, worship and obedience. There is no doubt that a person fears others and fears worldly dangers, but he should fear in all of that the decree of Allah and His disposal. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is the fear and piety in the matters of this world, and that he does not prefer the pleasure of another over the pleasure of Allah; and if two matters confront him, one of which is the right of Allah the Exalted and the other the right of his own self, he fears Allah and prefers the right of Allah over the right of his own self. It has been said: They used to fear the idols and hope in them, so the intention is to negate that fear from them. End of quotation. "Perhaps" (ʿasā) from Allah the Exalted is obligatory wherever it occurs in the Qur'an. In this is the cutting off of the hopes of the polytheists that they might be guided, since whoever combines these four qualities is treated as one for whom guidance is hoped; how then of one who is devoid of them? In this is the preference of fear over hope, and the rejection of being deceived by good deeds, for some corrupting element may enter them while their doer is unaware of it. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿among the guided﴾, that is, among those for whom guidance has preceded; the construction did not come as "that they would be guided," but they were made a part of the guided. Their being among them is less in honor than declaring the ruling of guidance for them without qualification.

﴿Do you consider providing water for the pilgrims and maintaining the Sacred Mosque equal to one who believes in Allah and the Last Day and strives in the way of Allah? They are not equal in the sight of Allah, and Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾ In the Sahih of Muslim, from the hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, he said: "I was at the pulpit of the Messenger of Allah when a man said: 'I do not care if I do no deed after giving water to the pilgrims.' Another said: 'I do not care if I do no deed after maintaining the Sacred Mosque.' Another said: 'Striving in the way of Allah is better than what you have said.' 'Umar rebuked them and said: 'Do not raise your voices at the pulpit of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and it is Friday. But when I have prayed the Friday prayer, I will enter and ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about what you have disagreed about.' So this verse was revealed." Ibn 'Aṭiyya mentioned other opinions about the occasion of revelation, all of which indicate boasting about providing water and maintenance.

The majority recited "siqāyata" and "'imārata," and both are verbal nouns, like "ṣiyāna" and "wiqāya," and they are paired with persons (dhawāt). So an ellipsis is needed in the first: that is, "the people of providing water"; or an ellipsis in the second: that is, "like the deed of one who believes." Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Baqir and Abu Haywa recited "saqāt al-ḥājj" and "'amarat al-masjid," as plurals of sāqin and 'āmir, like kirām, ruma, ṣāni' and ṣan'a. Ibn Jubayr recited similarly, except that he put "al-masjid" in the accusative on the assumption of the nunation of "'amaratan." Al-Ḍaḥḥāk recited "suqāyata" with a damma on the sīn, and "'imrata," the plural formed on the pattern fi'āl, like rikhl and rukhāl, and ẓi'r and ẓu'ār. It would have been appropriate for it to be without the tā' marbūṭa, but he added the tā' as it is added in ḥijāra.

Providing water was in the hands of the Banu Hashim, and al-'Abbas was in charge of it. When this verse was revealed, al-'Abbas said: "I think I will leave providing water." The Prophet said: "Keep to it, for it is good for you." Maintenance of the mosque is the custody (sidāna), and it was in the Banu 'Abd al-Dar. Shayba and 'Uthman ibn Talha are the two to whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave the key of the Ka'ba on the eighth day of the conquest, after al-'Abbas and 'Ali had requested it. He said to 'Uthman and Shayba: "Take it, eternal and inherited; no one will dispute it with you except a wrongdoer," meaning the custody.

The meaning of the verse: a denial that the polytheists should be compared to the believers, or their voided deeds to established deeds. When He negated equality between them, He clarified with His saying: ﴿and Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ which of the two is superior, and that those who disbelieve in Allah are the wrongdoers. They wronged themselves by abandoning belief in Allah and what the Messenger brought, and they wronged the Sacred Mosque, for Allah made it a place of worship for them, but they made it a place of worship for their idols. Regarding the believers, He mentioned affirming guidance for them with His saying: ﴿perhaps those will be among the guided﴾, and regarding the polytheists here He negated guidance with His saying: ﴿and Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾.

﴿Those who believed, emigrated, and struggled in the way of Allah with their wealth and their selves are greater in rank with Allah, and those are the triumphant.﴾ This verse added further clarity to the preference of the believers who are described with these qualities over the polytheists who boast of providing water and maintenance. They purified their selves from the filth of polytheism through faith, and they purified their bodies by emigrating to the homeland of the Messenger and leaving their homes in which they were raised. Then they exerted themselves in striving in the way of Allah with wealth and self, which are exposed to destruction in striving. These qualities are the greatest ranks of humanity. "Greater" (a'ẓam) here may remain on its original comparative sense, and this would be on the assumption that the polytheists believed their providing water and maintenance held merit, so they were addressed according to their belief. Or the meaning is: greater in rank than those who believed but did not emigrate and did not strive. It has been said: "a'ẓam" is not on its original sense, but is like His saying: ﴿the companions of the Garden on that day are better in abode﴾ [al-Furqan: 24], and the saying of Hassan:

"So the worst of you two is the ransom for the better of you two."

And it is as if it were said: "great in rank." "With Allah" (ʿinda Allah) refers to status, not place, as in His saying: ﴿And those who are with Him do not disdain to worship Him﴾ [al-Anbiya: 19]. Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: When the pure human souls are cleansed of the defilement of bodily attributes and the filth of the physical body, they are illumined by the lights of majesty, the lights of the world of beauty rise over them, and they ascend from servanthood (ʿabdiyyah) to nearness (ʿindiyyah). Indeed, there is no perfection in servanthood except by witnessing the reality of nearness, and for this reason He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra: 1]. End of quote. This resembles the speech of the Sufis. Then He, exalted is He, mentioned that whoever possesses these attributes is the one who succeeds and attains his wish, the one saved from the Fire.

﴿Their Lord gives them good news of mercy from Him, and approval, and gardens for them wherein is lasting bliss﴾ ﴿Abiding therein forever. Indeed, with Allah is a great reward.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: This refers specifically to the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun). End of quote. The giving of good news is attributed to "their Lord" because it is a kindness to them: the One who owns their affair and oversees their interests is the One who gives them good news, and this confirms their servanthood to their Lord. Since the attributes with which they adorned themselves and by which they became true servants are three—faith, emigration, and striving with wealth and self—they are matched in the good news with three: mercy, approval, and gardens. He began with mercy, because it is the more general attribute, from which the facilitation of faith for them arises. He followed it with approval, because it is the ultimate goal of the Lord's kindness to His servant, and it corresponds to striving, which is the expenditure of self and wealth. And it is placed before the gardens, because Allah's approval of the servant is better than settling them in Paradise. In the authentic hadith: "Indeed Allah, exalted is He, says: O people of Paradise, are you content? They say: Our Lord, how could we not be content when You have removed us far from Your Fire and admitted us into Your Garden? He says: I have something better for you than that. They say: What could be better than that? He says: I shall bestow upon you My approval, so I shall never be displeased with you after it." Third, He said: ﴿and gardens for them wherein is lasting bliss﴾; that is, enduring, never cut off. This corresponds to His saying "and emigrated," because they left their homelands in which they grew up and lived in comfort, and preferred emigration to the abode of disbelief over the settled place of faith and the Message; for this they were rewarded with gardens possessing enduring bliss. Thus the ordering of their attributes follows the reality: faith, then emigration, then striving. And the ordering in the reward follows the general, then the most noble, then the completing. Al-Tabrizi said: He made "mercy" and "approval" indefinite for magnification and exaltation. (With mercy) meaning: a mercy that no describer's description can reach.

Al-Aʿmash, Talhah ibn Musarrif, and Humayd ibn Hilal read yubshiruhum with a fatha on the yaʾ and a damma on the shin, lightened. ʿAsim, in the narration of Abu Bakr, read wa-ruḍwan with a damma on the raʾ, and this was mentioned at the beginning of Al ʿImran. Al-Aʿmash read with damma on both the raʾ and the ḍad together. Abu Hatim said: This is not permissible. End of quote. It ought to be permissible, for the Arabs have said sultan with a damma on the lam, and the morphologists (al-tasrifiyyun) included it among the patterns of nouns.

Whoever recited it in the singular, it may be understood to mean the Sacred Mosque, due to His saying: ﴿and the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque﴾, or it may be the genus, which would include the Sacred Mosque, as it is the head of that genus, its foremost part. Whoever recited it in the plural, it may be understood to mean the Sacred Mosque, and the plural is applied to it either because every place within it is a mosque, or because it is the qibla of all mosques and their leader, so its maintainer is the maintainer of all mosques. It may also be understood to mean the plural in general, which includes the Sacred Mosque, and this is more emphatic, because its method is that of metonymy (kināya, indirect expression), as when you say: "So-and-so does not read the books of Allah," you negate his reading of the Qur'an more strongly than by stating it directly.

"Witnessing" (shāhidīn) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl, a clause describing the condition of the subject), and the meaning is: it is not right for them to combine two contradictory matters: maintaining the places of worship of Allah the Exalted together with disbelief in Him and the worship of Him.

Zayd ibn 'Ali recited "shāhidūn" (nominative), on the assumption of an implied subject: "they are witnesses." Their testimony against themselves to disbelief is their saying during circumambulation: "Here I am, O Allah, here I am; You have no partner, except a partner who is Yours, You own him and what he owns." Or their saying when asked about their religion: "We worship al-Lat and al-'Uzza." Or their denial of the Messenger. Or the saying of a polytheist: "I am a polytheist," as the Jew says "he is a Jew," the Christian says "he is a Christian," the Magian says "he is a Magian," and the Sabian says "he is a Sabian." Or the manifestation of the actions of the disbelievers, such as erecting their idols and circumambulating the House naked. These are five opinions. This is when "against themselves" is taken in its literal sense. It has been said that its meaning is: witnesses against their Messenger, and "themselves" is used for him, because there is no tribe of the Arabs but that it has kinship ties with them. This opinion is supported by the reading of whoever recited "'alā anfasihim" with a fatḥa on the fā', meaning "their most noble and most eminent."

﴿Those, their deeds have become void﴾, which are the maintenance, the custody of the Ka'ba (ḥijāba), the giving of water (siqāya), freeing the captives, and other things mentioned as praiseworthy deeds. Al-Zamakhshari said: If disbelief or a major sin destroys established and sound deeds when it follows them, what then of what accompanies them? Allah the Exalted alluded to this by His saying "witnesses," where He made it a state (ḥāl) concerning them, and it indicates that they combined maintenance and testimony to disbelief against themselves in one state, and that is impossible and not proper. End of quotation. His saying "or a major sin" is a Mu'tazili (rationalist) insertion, because major sins according to them destroy deeds.

﴿And in the Fire they will abide eternally.﴾ It mentions the end of the polytheists, which is the Fire, abiding in it forever. Zayd ibn 'Ali recited "yā'" with a fatḥa (yakhlud, in the masculine form), as a circumstantial state, and "in the Fire" is the predicate, as you say: "In the house is Zayd seated." Al-Wahidi said: The verse indicates that disbelievers are prohibited from maintaining the mosques of the Muslims; if one of them bequeaths something, his bequest is not accepted; and he is prevented from entering mosques. If he enters without permission from a Muslim, he deserves a discretionary punishment (ta'zīr); if he enters with permission, he is not punished. The better course is to honor the mosques and prevent them from entering. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) lodged the delegation of Thaqif, who were disbelievers, in the mosque, and he tied Thumama ibn Uthal al-Hanafi to one of the pillars of the mosque while he was a disbeliever.

﴿Only one who believes in Allah and the Last Day, establishes prayer, gives zakat, and fears none but Allah maintains the mosques of Allah; perhaps those will be among the guided.﴾ Al-Jahdari and Hammad ibn Abi Salama, from Ibn Kathir, recited "masjidan li-Allāh" in the singular with monotheism. The Seven and a group recited it in the plural. The meaning is: he maintains them with the due right, and this applies to whoever has these characteristics. Within this statement is a command to the believers to maintain the mosques, and their maintenance includes repairing what has collapsed of them, cleaning them, lighting them, honoring them, and making them habitual places of worship and remembrance. Among remembrance is the study of knowledge, indeed it is its greatest part, and guarding them from what they were not built for, such as discussing worldly affairs. In a hadith: "When you see a man frequenting the mosque, bear witness that he is a believer." Belief in the Messenger is not mentioned, because belief in the Last Day is only received from the reports of the Messenger, so it includes belief in the Messenger. Or it was not mentioned because it is known and well established that belief in Allah the Exalted is accompanied by belief in the Messenger (ﷺ), since the words of the testimony, the adhan and the iqama, and others include both of them together, paired, as if they were one thing that cannot be separated from each other. So belief in the Messenger (ﷺ) is included within the mention of belief in Allah the Exalted.
