The purpose of building mosques and maintaining them is that they be a gathering place for establishing prayers in them and acts of worship such as remembrance and seclusion (i'tikāf) and others. ﴿And fears none but Allah.﴾ Ibn 'Aṭiyya said: He means the fear of reverence, worship and obedience. There is no doubt that a person fears others and fears worldly dangers, but he should fear in all of that the decree of Allah and His disposal. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is the fear and piety in the matters of this world, and that he does not prefer the pleasure of another over the pleasure of Allah; and if two matters confront him, one of which is the right of Allah the Exalted and the other the right of his own self, he fears Allah and prefers the right of Allah over the right of his own self. It has been said: They used to fear the idols and hope in them, so the intention is to negate that fear from them. End of quotation. "Perhaps" (ʿasā) from Allah the Exalted is obligatory wherever it occurs in the Qur'an. In this is the cutting off of the hopes of the polytheists that they might be guided, since whoever combines these four qualities is treated as one for whom guidance is hoped; how then of one who is devoid of them? Their being among them is less in honor than declaring the ruling of guidance for them without qualification.

They are not equal in the sight of Allah, and Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾ In the Sahih of Muslim, from the hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, he said: "I was at the pulpit of the Messenger of Allah when a man said: 'I do not care if I do no deed after giving water to the pilgrims.' 'Umar rebuked them and said: 'Do not raise your voices at the pulpit of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and it is Friday. But when I have prayed the Friday prayer, I will enter and ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about what you have disagreed about.' So this verse was revealed." Ibn 'Aṭiyya mentioned other opinions about the occasion of revelation, all of which indicate boasting about providing water and maintenance.

The majority recited "siqāyata" and "'imārata," and both are verbal nouns, like "ṣiyāna" and "wiqāya," and they are paired with persons (dhawāt). So an ellipsis is needed in the first: that is, "the people of providing water"; or an ellipsis in the second: that is, "like the deed of one who believes." Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Baqir and Abu Haywa recited "saqāt al-ḥājj" and "'amarat al-masjid," as plurals of sāqin and 'āmir, like kirām, ruma, ṣāni' and ṣan'a. Ibn Jubayr recited similarly, except that he put "al-masjid" in the accusative on the assumption of the nunation of "'amaratan." Al-Ḍaḥḥāk recited "suqāyata" with a damma on the sīn, and "'imrata," the plural formed on the pattern fi'āl, like rikhl and rukhāl, and ẓi'r and ẓu'ār. It would have been appropriate for it to be without the tā' marbūṭa, but he added the tā' as it is added in ḥijāra.

Providing water was in the hands of the Banu Hashim, and al-'Abbas was in charge of it. When this verse was revealed, al-'Abbas said: "I think I will leave providing water." He said to 'Uthman and Shayba: "Take it, eternal and inherited; no one will dispute it with you except a wrongdoer," meaning the custody.

The meaning of the verse: a denial that the polytheists should be compared to the believers, or their voided deeds to established deeds. When He negated equality between them, He clarified with His saying: ﴿and Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ which of the two is superior, and that those who disbelieve in Allah are the wrongdoers. They wronged themselves by abandoning belief in Allah and what the Messenger brought, and they wronged the Sacred Mosque, for Allah made it a place of worship for them, but they made it a place of worship for their idols. Regarding the believers, He mentioned affirming guidance for them with His saying: ﴿perhaps those will be among the guided﴾, and regarding the polytheists here He negated guidance with His saying: ﴿and Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾.

They purified their selves from the filth of polytheism through faith, and they purified their bodies by emigrating to the homeland of the Messenger and leaving their homes in which they were raised. Then they exerted themselves in striving in the way of Allah with wealth and self, which are exposed to destruction in striving. These qualities are the greatest ranks of humanity. Or the meaning is: greater in rank than those who believed but did not emigrate and did not strive. It has been said: "a'ẓam" is not on its original sense, but is like His saying: ﴿the companions of the Garden on that day are better in abode﴾ [al-Furqan: 24], and the saying of Hassan:

"So the worst of you two is the ransom for the better of you two."

And it is as if it were said: "great in rank." "With Allah" (ʿinda Allah) refers to status, not place, as in His saying: ﴿And those who are with Him do not disdain to worship Him﴾ [al-Anbiya: 19]. Indeed, there is no perfection in servanthood except by witnessing the reality of nearness, and for this reason He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra: 1]. End of quote. This resembles the speech of the Sufis. Then He, exalted is He, mentioned that whoever possesses these attributes is the one who succeeds and attains his wish, the one saved from the Fire.

Indeed, with Allah is a great reward.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: This refers specifically to the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun). End of quote. The giving of good news is attributed to "their Lord" because it is a kindness to them: the One who owns their affair and oversees their interests is the One who gives them good news, and this confirms their servanthood to their Lord. Since the attributes with which they adorned themselves and by which they became true servants are three—faith, emigration, and striving with wealth and self—they are matched in the good news with three: mercy, approval, and gardens. He began with mercy, because it is the more general attribute, from which the facilitation of faith for them arises. He followed it with approval, because it is the ultimate goal of the Lord's kindness to His servant, and it corresponds to striving, which is the expenditure of self and wealth. And it is placed before the gardens, because Allah's approval of the servant is better than settling them in Paradise. They say: Our Lord, how could we not be content when You have removed us far from Your Fire and admitted us into Your Garden? He says: I have something better for you than that. They say: What could be better than that? He says: I shall bestow upon you My approval, so I shall never be displeased with you after it." Third, He said: ﴿and gardens for them wherein is lasting bliss﴾; that is, enduring, never cut off. This corresponds to His saying "and emigrated," because they left their homelands in which they grew up and lived in comfort, and preferred emigration to the abode of disbelief over the settled place of faith and the Message; for this they were rewarded with gardens possessing enduring bliss. Thus the ordering of their attributes follows the reality: faith, then emigration, then striving. And the ordering in the reward follows the general, then the most noble, then the completing. Al-Tabrizi said: He made "mercy" and "approval" indefinite for magnification and exaltation. (With mercy) meaning: a mercy that no describer's description can reach.

Al-Aʿmash, Talhah ibn Musarrif, and Humayd ibn Hilal read yubshiruhum with a fatha on the yaʾ and a damma on the shin, lightened. ʿAsim, in the narration of Abu Bakr, read wa-ruḍwan with a damma on the raʾ, and this was mentioned at the beginning of Al ʿImran. Al-Aʿmash read with damma on both the raʾ and the ḍad together. Abu Hatim said: This is not permissible. End of quote. It ought to be permissible, for the Arabs have said sultan with a damma on the lam, and the morphologists (al-tasrifiyyun) included it among the patterns of nouns.

"So the worst of you two is the ransom for the better of you two."

And it is as if it were said: "great in rank." "With Allah" (ʿinda Allah) refers to status, not place, as in His saying: ﴿And those who are with Him do not disdain to worship Him﴾ [al-Anbiya: 19]. Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: When the pure human souls are cleansed of the defilement of bodily attributes and the filth of the physical body, they are illumined by the lights of majesty, the lights of the world of beauty rise over them, and they ascend from servanthood (ʿabdiyyah) to nearness (ʿindiyyah). Indeed, there is no perfection in servanthood except by witnessing the reality of nearness, and for this reason He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra: 1]. End of quote. This resembles the speech of the Sufis. Then He, exalted is He, mentioned that whoever possesses these attributes is the one who succeeds and attains his wish, the one saved from the Fire.

﴿Their Lord gives them good news of mercy from Him, and approval, and gardens for them wherein is lasting bliss﴾ ﴿Abiding therein forever. Indeed, with Allah is a great reward.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: This refers specifically to the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun). End of quote. The giving of good news is attributed to "their Lord" because it is a kindness to them: the One who owns their affair and oversees their interests is the One who gives them good news, and this confirms their servanthood to their Lord. Since the attributes with which they adorned themselves and by which they became true servants are three—faith, emigration, and striving with wealth and self—they are matched in the good news with three: mercy, approval, and gardens. He began with mercy, because it is the more general attribute, from which the facilitation of faith for them arises. He followed it with approval, because it is the ultimate goal of the Lord's kindness to His servant, and it corresponds to striving, which is the expenditure of self and wealth. And it is placed before the gardens, because Allah's approval of the servant is better than settling them in Paradise. In the authentic hadith: "Indeed Allah, exalted is He, says: O people of Paradise, are you content? They say: Our Lord, how could we not be content when You have removed us far from Your Fire and admitted us into Your Garden? He says: I have something better for you than that. They say: What could be better than that? He says: I shall bestow upon you My approval, so I shall never be displeased with you after it." Third, He said: ﴿and gardens for them wherein is lasting bliss﴾; that is, enduring, never cut off. This corresponds to His saying "and emigrated," because they left their homelands in which they grew up and lived in comfort, and preferred emigration to the abode of disbelief over the settled place of faith and the Message; for this they were rewarded with gardens possessing enduring bliss. Thus the ordering of their attributes follows the reality: faith, then emigration, then striving. And the ordering in the reward follows the general, then the most noble, then the completing. Al-Tabrizi said: He made "mercy" and "approval" indefinite for magnification and exaltation. (With mercy) meaning: a mercy that no describer's description can reach.

Al-Aʿmash, Talhah ibn Musarrif, and Humayd ibn Hilal read yubshiruhum with a fatha on the yaʾ and a damma on the shin, lightened. ʿAsim, in the narration of Abu Bakr, read wa-ruḍwan with a damma on the raʾ, and this was mentioned at the beginning of Al ʿImran. Al-Aʿmash read with damma on both the raʾ and the ḍad together. Abu Hatim said: This is not permissible. End of quote. It ought to be permissible, for the Arabs have said sultan with a damma on the lam, and the morphologists (al-tasrifiyyun) included it among the patterns of nouns.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verses 17–22 (part 1 of 2):

﴿It is not for the polytheists to maintain the mosques of Allah while they testify against themselves to disbelief.﴾ Ibn al-Sumayqa recited: "an yu'imiru" (with a damma on the yā' and a kasra on the mīm), meaning "to help in its upkeep." Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and al-Jahdari recited "masjid" in the singular, while the rest of the Seven (qira'at, the canonical readings) and Mujahid, Qatada, Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj and Shayba recited it in the plural.

The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when Allah mentioned the disavowal of the polytheists and kinds of their ugly deeds that necessitate disavowing them, He mentioned that they are described with praiseworthy qualities that negate the disavowal from them, namely that they maintain the Sacred Mosque. It is related that the Emigrants and the Helpers approached the captives of Badr, rebuking them for associating partners with Allah. 'Ali began to reproach al-'Abbas, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Severing of ties of kinship!" and spoke harshly to him. Al-'Abbas said: "Do you display our bad deeds and conceal our good deeds?" He said: "Do you have good deeds?" They said: "Yes, and we are better than you in reward: we maintain the Sacred Mosque, we cover the Ka'ba, we give water to the pilgrims, and we free the captives." So Allah revealed this verse in response to them.

The meaning of "It is not for the polytheists" is: not with the due right; otherwise they had maintained it in the past and present, by way of dominance. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, it is not valid and not proper. Its maintenance (i'mara) is entering it, sitting in it and staying in it, from their saying: "So-and-so maintains the mosque," meaning he frequently visits it; or raising its building and repairing what has collapsed of it; or worshipping in it and circumambulating it. As for prayer, there are three opinions. Whoever recited it in the singular, it may be understood to mean the Sacred Mosque, due to His saying: ﴿and the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque﴾, or it may be the genus, which would include the Sacred Mosque, as it is the head of that genus, its foremost part. Whoever recited it in the plural, it may be understood to mean the Sacred Mosque, and the plural is applied to it either because every place within it is a mosque, or because it is the qibla of all mosques and their leader, so its maintainer is the maintainer of all mosques. It may also be understood to mean the plural in general, which includes the Sacred Mosque, and this is more emphatic, because its method is that of metonymy (kināya, indirect expression), as when you say: "So-and-so does not read the books of Allah," you negate his reading of the Qur'an more strongly than by stating it directly.

"Witnessing" (shāhidīn) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl, a clause describing the condition of the subject), and the meaning is: it is not right for them to combine two contradictory matters: maintaining the places of worship of Allah the Exalted together with disbelief in Him and the worship of Him.

Zayd ibn 'Ali recited "shāhidūn" (nominative), on the assumption of an implied subject: "they are witnesses." Their testimony against themselves to disbelief is their saying during circumambulation: "Here I am, O Allah, here I am; You have no partner, except a partner who is Yours, You own him and what he owns." Or their saying when asked about their religion: "We worship al-Lat and al-'Uzza." Or their denial of the Messenger. Or the saying of a polytheist: "I am a polytheist," as the Jew says "he is a Jew," the Christian says "he is a Christian," the Magian says "he is a Magian," and the Sabian says "he is a Sabian." Or the manifestation of the actions of the disbelievers, such as erecting their idols and circumambulating the House naked. These are five opinions. This is when "against themselves" is taken in its literal sense. It has been said that its meaning is: witnesses against their Messenger, and "themselves" is used for him, because there is no tribe of the Arabs but that it has kinship ties with them. This opinion is supported by the reading of whoever recited "'alā anfasihim" with a fatḥa on the fā', meaning "their most noble and most eminent."

﴿Those, their deeds have become void﴾, which are the maintenance, the custody of the Ka'ba (ḥijāba), the giving of water (siqāya), freeing the captives, and other things mentioned as praiseworthy deeds. Al-Zamakhshari said: If disbelief or a major sin destroys established and sound deeds when it follows them, what then of what accompanies them? Allah the Exalted alluded to this by His saying "witnesses," where He made it a state (ḥāl) concerning them, and it indicates that they combined maintenance and testimony to disbelief against themselves in one state, and that is impossible and not proper. End of quotation. His saying "or a major sin" is a Mu'tazili (rationalist) insertion, because major sins according to them destroy deeds.

﴿And in the Fire they will abide eternally.﴾ It mentions the end of the polytheists, which is the Fire, abiding in it forever. Zayd ibn 'Ali recited "yā'" with a fatḥa (yakhlud, in the masculine form), as a circumstantial state, and "in the Fire" is the predicate, as you say: "In the house is Zayd seated." Al-Wahidi said: The verse indicates that disbelievers are prohibited from maintaining the mosques of the Muslims; if one of them bequeaths something, his bequest is not accepted; and he is prevented from entering mosques. If he enters without permission from a Muslim, he deserves a discretionary punishment (ta'zīr); if he enters with permission, he is not punished. The better course is to honor the mosques and prevent them from entering. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) lodged the delegation of Thaqif, who were disbelievers, in the mosque, and he tied Thumama ibn Uthal al-Hanafi to one of the pillars of the mosque while he was a disbeliever.

﴿Only one who believes in Allah and the Last Day, establishes prayer, gives zakat, and fears none but Allah maintains the mosques of Allah; perhaps those will be among the guided.﴾ Al-Jahdari and Hammad ibn Abi Salama, from Ibn Kathir, recited "masjidan li-Allāh" in the singular with monotheism. The Seven and a group recited it in the plural. The meaning is: he maintains them with the due right, and this applies to whoever has these characteristics. Within this statement is a command to the believers to maintain the mosques, and their maintenance includes repairing what has collapsed of them, cleaning them, lighting them, honoring them, and making them habitual places of worship and remembrance. Among remembrance is the study of knowledge, indeed it is its greatest part, and guarding them from what they were not built for, such as discussing worldly affairs. In a hadith: "When you see a man frequenting the mosque, bear witness that he is a believer." Belief in the Messenger is not mentioned, because belief in the Last Day is only received from the reports of the Messenger, so it includes belief in the Messenger. Or it was not mentioned because it is known and well established that belief in Allah the Exalted is accompanied by belief in the Messenger (ﷺ), since the words of the testimony, the adhan and the iqama, and others include both of them together, paired, as if they were one thing that cannot be separated from each other. So belief in the Messenger (ﷺ) is included within the mention of belief in Allah the Exalted. It has been said: it indicates it by mentioning establishing prayer and giving zakat, since these are only received from him. The purpose of building mosques and maintaining them is that they be a gathering place for establishing prayers in them and acts of worship such as remembrance and seclusion (i'tikāf) and others. It is fitting that the mention of giving zakat appears alongside maintaining mosques, because since they are a gathering place for people, the affairs of the rich and the poor become evident in them, and the states of the one who pays zakat and the one who deserves it are known.

﴿And fears none but Allah.﴾ Ibn 'Aṭiyya said: He means the fear of reverence, worship and obedience. There is no doubt that a person fears others and fears worldly dangers, but he should fear in all of that the decree of Allah and His disposal. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is the fear and piety in the matters of this world, and that he does not prefer the pleasure of another over the pleasure of Allah; and if two matters confront him, one of which is the right of Allah the Exalted and the other the right of his own self, he fears Allah and prefers the right of Allah over the right of his own self. It has been said: They used to fear the idols and hope in them, so the intention is to negate that fear from them. End of quotation. "Perhaps" (ʿasā) from Allah the Exalted is obligatory wherever it occurs in the Qur'an. In this is the cutting off of the hopes of the polytheists that they might be guided, since whoever combines these four qualities is treated as one for whom guidance is hoped; how then of one who is devoid of them? In this is the preference of fear over hope, and the rejection of being deceived by good deeds, for some corrupting element may enter them while their doer is unaware of it. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿among the guided﴾, that is, among those for whom guidance has preceded; the construction did not come as "that they would be guided," but they were made a part of the guided. Their being among them is less in honor than declaring the ruling of guidance for them without qualification.

﴿Do you consider providing water for the pilgrims and maintaining the Sacred Mosque equal to one who believes in Allah and the Last Day and strives in the way of Allah? They are not equal in the sight of Allah, and Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾ In the Sahih of Muslim, from the hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, he said: "I was at the pulpit of the Messenger of Allah when a man said: 'I do not care if I do no deed after giving water to the pilgrims.' Another said: 'I do not care if I do no deed after maintaining the Sacred Mosque.' Another said: 'Striving in the way of Allah is better than what you have said.' 'Umar rebuked them and said: 'Do not raise your voices at the pulpit of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and it is Friday. But when I have prayed the Friday prayer, I will enter and ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about what you have disagreed about.' So this verse was revealed." Ibn 'Aṭiyya mentioned other opinions about the occasion of revelation, all of which indicate boasting about providing water and maintenance.

The majority recited "siqāyata" and "'imārata," and both are verbal nouns, like "ṣiyāna" and "wiqāya," and they are paired with persons (dhawāt). So an ellipsis is needed in the first: that is, "the people of providing water"; or an ellipsis in the second: that is, "like the deed of one who believes." Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Baqir and Abu Haywa recited "saqāt al-ḥājj" and "'amarat al-masjid," as plurals of sāqin and 'āmir, like kirām, ruma, ṣāni' and ṣan'a. Ibn Jubayr recited similarly, except that he put "al-masjid" in the accusative on the assumption of the nunation of "'amaratan." Al-Ḍaḥḥāk recited "suqāyata" with a damma on the sīn, and "'imrata," the plural formed on the pattern fi'āl, like rikhl and rukhāl, and ẓi'r and ẓu'ār. It would have been appropriate for it to be without the tā' marbūṭa, but he added the tā' as it is added in ḥijāra.

Providing water was in the hands of the Banu Hashim, and al-'Abbas was in charge of it. When this verse was revealed, al-'Abbas said: "I think I will leave providing water." The Prophet said: "Keep to it, for it is good for you." Maintenance of the mosque is the custody (sidāna), and it was in the Banu 'Abd al-Dar. Shayba and 'Uthman ibn Talha are the two to whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave the key of the Ka'ba on the eighth day of the conquest, after al-'Abbas and 'Ali had requested it. He said to 'Uthman and Shayba: "Take it, eternal and inherited; no one will dispute it with you except a wrongdoer," meaning the custody.

The meaning of the verse: a denial that the polytheists should be compared to the believers, or their voided deeds to established deeds. When He negated equality between them, He clarified with His saying: ﴿and Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ which of the two is superior, and that those who disbelieve in Allah are the wrongdoers. They wronged themselves by abandoning belief in Allah and what the Messenger brought, and they wronged the Sacred Mosque, for Allah made it a place of worship for them, but they made it a place of worship for their idols. Regarding the believers, He mentioned affirming guidance for them with His saying: ﴿perhaps those will be among the guided﴾, and regarding the polytheists here He negated guidance with His saying: ﴿and Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾.

﴿Those who believed, emigrated, and struggled in the way of Allah with their wealth and their selves are greater in rank with Allah, and those are the triumphant.﴾ This verse added further clarity to the preference of the believers who are described with these qualities over the polytheists who boast of providing water and maintenance. They purified their selves from the filth of polytheism through faith, and they purified their bodies by emigrating to the homeland of the Messenger and leaving their homes in which they were raised. Then they exerted themselves in striving in the way of Allah with wealth and self, which are exposed to destruction in striving. These qualities are the greatest ranks of humanity. "Greater" (a'ẓam) here may remain on its original comparative sense, and this would be on the assumption that the polytheists believed their providing water and maintenance held merit, so they were addressed according to their belief. Or the meaning is: greater in rank than those who believed but did not emigrate and did not strive. It has been said: "a'ẓam" is not on its original sense, but is like His saying: ﴿the companions of the Garden on that day are better in abode﴾ [al-Furqan: 24], and the saying of Hassan:

"So the worst of you two is the ransom for the better of you two."

And it is as if it were said: "great in rank." "With Allah" (ʿinda Allah) refers to status, not place, as in His saying: ﴿And those who are with Him do not disdain to worship Him﴾ [al-Anbiya: 19]. Indeed, there is no perfection in servanthood except by witnessing the reality of nearness, and for this reason He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra: 1]. End of quote. This resembles the speech of the Sufis. Then He, exalted is He, mentioned that whoever possesses these attributes is the one who succeeds and attains his wish, the one saved from the Fire.

﴿Their Lord gives them good news of mercy from Him, and approval, and gardens for them wherein is lasting bliss﴾ ﴿Abiding therein forever. Indeed, with Allah is a great reward.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: This refers specifically to the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun). End of quote. The giving of good news is attributed to "their Lord" because it is a kindness to them: the One who owns their affair and oversees their interests is the One who gives them good news, and this confirms their servanthood to their Lord. Third, He said: ﴿and gardens for them wherein is lasting bliss﴾; that is, enduring, never cut off. Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verses 23–24:

﴿O you who believe, do not take your fathers and your brothers as allies if they prefer disbelief over faith. Whoever among you allies with them, those are the wrongdoers.﴾ Before the conquest of Makkah, whoever believed did not complete his faith unless he emigrated (hijra) and confronted his relatives, the disbelievers (p-22), and cut off his alliance with them. They said: "O Messenger of Allah, if we separate ourselves from those who oppose us in religion, we cut off our fathers, our sons and our clans, our livelihood is gone, our wealth is lost, our homes are ruined, and we remain lost." So it was revealed, and they emigrated. A man would have his son, his father or his brother or some of his relatives come to him, and he would not turn toward him, nor let him stay, nor spend on him. Then after that they were granted a concession. Accordingly, the address is to the believers who were in Makkah and other lands of the Arabs, and they were addressed that they should not take fathers and brothers as allies, so that they would not follow them in dwelling in the lands of disbelief. It was also said: it was revealed concerning the nine who apostatized and joined Makkah, and Allah forbade the believers from allying with them. He mentioned the fathers and brothers because they are the people of opinion and counsel, and He did not mention the sons because they are, for the most part, followers of their fathers.

ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read: أنِ اسْتَحَبُّوا (an istaḥabbū) with a fatḥa on the hamza (an-), making it a causal clause (taʿlīl, "because"). Others read it with a kasra on the hamza (in), making it a conditional clause (sharṭ, "if"). The meaning of istaḥabbū is: they preferred and favored. It is from the form istafʿala, from maḥabba (love), meaning they sought the love of disbelief. It was also said that it means aḥabba (to love), and it was used with the sense of "chose" and "preferred," which is why it takes ʿalā. When He forbade them from taking them as allies, He informed that whoever allies with them is a wrongdoer. Ibn ʿAbbās said: he is a polytheist like them, because whoever is pleased with polytheism is a polytheist. Mujāhid said: all of this was before the conquest of Makkah. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: this is the wrongdoing of disobedience (ẓulm al-maʿṣiya), not the wrongdoing of disbelief (ẓulm al-kufr).

﴿Say: If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your spouses, your kinsfolk, the wealth you have acquired, the commerce you fear will slump, and the dwellings you are pleased with are more beloved to you than Allah and His Messenger and striving in His way, then wait until Allah brings His command. And Allah does not guide the defiant people.﴾ This verse calls for emigration (ḥaḍḍ ʿalā al-hijra). He mentioned the sons because He mentioned love, and they are closer to the self, unlike the verse before it, in which they were not mentioned, because its purpose is opinion and counsel. He placed the fathers first because they are the ones whose kindness, honor and love are obligatory, and He followed them with the sons because they are closer to the hearts. When He mentioned the root and the branch, He mentioned the outer circle, which is the brothers, then He mentioned the spouses, who in love and preference are like the sons, then the more distant after the nearer in kinship, saying: "your kinsfolk."

The majority read ʿashīratukum without an alif. Abū Bakr on the authority of ʿĀṣim, Abū Rajāʾ, and Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān read it with an alif, as a plural. Al-Akhfash claimed that the Arabs pluralize ʿashīra as ʿashāʾir, and they hardly say ʿashīrāt with the sound plural suffix alif-tāʾ. Then He mentioned ﴿the wealth you have acquired﴾, i.e., you earned it (iktasabtumūhā), because the love of wealth is comparable to the love of kin, rather its love is stronger, since wealth was precious at that time and most people were poor. Then He mentioned ﴿commerce you fear will slump﴾, and commerce is not possible without wealth. Allah, exalted is He, made commerce a cause for the increase and growth of wealth. Ibn al-Mubārak's interpretation, that this refers to the daughters who do not marry because of the scarcity of their suitors, is a strange interpretation that the wording rejects. The poet said:

*They slumped from poverty among their people, and my standing with them increased their slump.*

Then He mentioned ﴿dwellings you are pleased with﴾, which are the palaces and houses. The meaning of "you are pleased with them" is: you choose to reside in them. These four motives are causes for associating with the disbelievers: love of relatives, wealth, commerce, and dwellings. So Allah, exalted is He, stated that observing the religion is better than observing these matters. There is an ellipsis in the speech, meaning: "more beloved to you than complying with the command of Allah, exalted is He, and His Messenger regarding emigration from the land of disbelief to the land of Islam." The readers read aḥabba in the accusative, because it is the predicate of kāna. al-Ḥajjāj ibn Yūsuf used to read aḥabbu in the nominative, and Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar faulted him for it. His faulting him was not on grounds of Arabic grammar; rather, it was because it contradicts the consensus (ijmāʿ) of the transmitting readers. Otherwise, it is permissible in the science of Arabic grammar, provided that a pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn) is implied in kāna, and what follows it (p-23) is necessarily a subject and predicate, and the clause is in the position of the accusative as the predicate of kāna.

The command to wait includes a threat and a warning, "until Allah brings His command." Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid said: the reference is to the conquest of Makkah. al-Ḥasan said: the reference is to a punishment or retribution from Allah. The word "the defiant" (al-fāsiqīn) is general, intended to be specific regarding those who died in their defiance, or it is absolutely general, meaning that there is no guidance in terms of defiance. In al-Taḥrīr, it is stated that fisq here means disbelief, and what is opposed to it in guidance indicates this. Disbelief is misguidance, and misguidance is the opposite of guidance. And even if this applies to the believers who did not emigrate, then fisq means departure from obedience, for they did not comply with the command of Allah or the command of His Messenger regarding emigration.

It was also said that it means aḥabba (to love), and it was used with the sense of "chose" and "preferred," which is why it takes ʿalā. When He forbade them from taking them as allies, He informed that whoever allies with them is a wrongdoer. Ibn ʿAbbās said: he is a polytheist like them, because whoever is pleased with polytheism is a polytheist. Mujāhid said: all of this was before the conquest of Makkah. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: this is the wrongdoing of disobedience (ẓulm al-maʿṣiya), not the wrongdoing of disbelief (ẓulm al-kufr).

﴿Say: If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your spouses, your kinsfolk, the wealth you have acquired, the commerce you fear will slump, and the dwellings you are pleased with are more beloved to you than Allah and His Messenger and striving in His way, then wait until Allah brings His command. And Allah does not guide the defiant people.﴾ This verse calls for emigration (ḥaḍḍ ʿalā al-hijra). He mentioned the sons because He mentioned love, and they are closer to the self, unlike the verse before it, in which they were not mentioned, because its purpose is opinion and counsel. He placed the fathers first because they are the ones whose kindness, honor and love are obligatory, and He followed them with the sons because they are closer to the hearts. When He mentioned the root and the branch, He mentioned the outer circle, which is the brothers, then He mentioned the spouses, who in love and preference are like the sons, then the more distant after the nearer in kinship, saying: "your kinsfolk."

The majority read ʿashīratukum without an alif. Abū Bakr on the authority of ʿĀṣim, Abū Rajāʾ, and Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān read it with an alif, as a plural. Al-Akhfash claimed that the Arabs pluralize ʿashīra as ʿashāʾir, and they hardly say ʿashīrāt with the sound plural suffix alif-tāʾ. Then He mentioned ﴿the wealth you have acquired﴾, i.e., you earned it (iktasabtumūhā), because the love of wealth is comparable to the love of kin, rather its love is stronger, since wealth was precious at that time and most people were poor. Then He mentioned ﴿commerce you fear will slump﴾, and commerce is not possible without wealth. Allah, exalted is He, made commerce a cause for the increase and growth of wealth. Ibn al-Mubārak's interpretation, that this refers to the daughters who do not marry because of the scarcity of their suitors, is a strange interpretation that the wording rejects. The poet said:

*They slumped from poverty among their people, and my standing with them increased their slump.*

Then He mentioned ﴿dwellings you are pleased with﴾, which are the palaces and houses. The meaning of "you are pleased with them" is: you choose to reside in them. These four motives are causes for associating with the disbelievers: love of relatives, wealth, commerce, and dwellings. So Allah, exalted is He, stated that observing the religion is better than observing these matters. There is an ellipsis in the speech, meaning: "more beloved to you than complying with the command of Allah, exalted is He, and His Messenger regarding emigration from the land of disbelief to the land of Islam." The readers read aḥabba in the accusative, because it is the predicate of kāna. al-Ḥajjāj ibn Yūsuf used to read aḥabbu in the nominative, and Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar faulted him for it. His faulting him was not on grounds of Arabic grammar; rather, it was because it contradicts the consensus (ijmāʿ) of the transmitting readers. Otherwise, it is permissible in the science of Arabic grammar, provided that a pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn) is implied in kāna, and what follows it (p-23) is necessarily a subject and predicate, and the clause is in the position of the accusative as the predicate of kāna.

The command to wait includes a threat and a warning, "until Allah brings His command." Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid said: the reference is to the conquest of Makkah. al-Ḥasan said: the reference is to a punishment or retribution from Allah. The word "the defiant" (al-fāsiqīn) is general, intended to be specific regarding those who died in their defiance, or it is absolutely general, meaning that there is no guidance in terms of defiance. In al-Taḥrīr, it is stated that fisq here means disbelief, and what is opposed to it in guidance indicates this. Disbelief is misguidance, and misguidance is the opposite of guidance. And even if this applies to the believers who did not emigrate, then fisq means departure from obedience, for they did not comply with the command of Allah or the command of His Messenger regarding emigration.

[p. 23]

Allah says: ﴿Allah had already given you victory on many occasions, and on the day of Hunayn, when your large numbers made you vain, but they availed you nothing, and the earth, spacious as it is, grew too narrow for you, and then you turned back in retreat.﴾

When His words ﴿Fight them; Allah will punish them at your hands, and disgrace them, and give you victory over them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 14] had preceded, He digressed after that into what He digressed into, and reminded them of His victory for them on many occasions. The *mawatin* (sing. *mawtin*, battle positions) are the stations and situations of war. It has been said: they are the scenes of battle where you prepare yourselves (*tuwatinun*) to meet the enemy. It is the plural of *mawtin* with a kasra on the ṭāʾ, and the poet said:

"How many a position there was, had I not been with you, you would have fallen as a thing falls from the top of a steep cliff."

These *mawatin* were: the encounter of Badr, Qurayẓah, al-Naḍīr, al-Ḥudaybiyah, Khaybar, and the conquest of Makkah. They are described as many because the imams of history, the scholars, and the chroniclers of the campaigns transmitted that they were eighty positions. Ḥunayn is a valley between Makkah and al-Ṭāʾif, near Dhū al-Majāz. It is declined (ṣuriqa) as a place-name treated as a location (*madhhab al-makān*); had it been treated as an area (*madhhab al-buqʿah*), it would not have been declined, as the poet said:

"They helped their Prophet and strengthened his back at Ḥunayn, on the day when the champions were leaving one another to fend for themselves."

He coordinated the time with the place. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "The position of the day of Ḥunayn," or "in the days of many positions and the day of Ḥunayn." Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "*Yawm* is coordinated with the position of the phrase *fī mawāṭin*, or with its wording, with the implied meaning 'and in the day of,' so the preposition was omitted," end of quote. *Idh* (when) is a substitute (*badal*) for *yawm*. He attributed the vanity (*iʿjāb*) to all of them, although it came from one man who, when he saw the large crowd, was impressed by it and said: "We will not be defeated today for lack of numbers." The speaker is said by Ibn al-Musayyab to be Abu Bakr, or Salamah ibn Salamah ibn Quraysh, or Ibn ʿAbbas, or a man from Banu Bakr. It is transmitted that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was displeased by the words of this speaker, and they were left to the words of the man.

*Al-kathrah* (multitude) is with a fatḥah on the kāf; its plural is *katharāt*. The Tamim tribe pronounce the kāf with a kasrah, and its plural is *kuthur*, like *shadhrah* and *shudhur*, and *kisrah* and *kusur*. This multitude, according to Ibn ʿAbbas, was sixteen thousand; according to al-Naḥḥas, fourteen thousand; according to Qatadah, Ibn Zayd, Ibn Ishaq, and al-Waqidi, twelve thousand; and according to Muqatil from Ibn ʿAbbas, eleven thousand five hundred.

The *bāʾ* in ﴿with what it was spacious﴾ is for circumstance (*ḥāl*), and *mā* is verbal-nominal (*maṣdariyyah*). That is: the earth grew narrow for you while being wide and spacious, because of the severity of the situation upon them and its hardship, as though they could not find a place suitable for fleeing and escape, due to the extreme terror that had seized them, so it was as if it had become narrow for them. *Al-rahb* means spaciousness, and with a fatḥah on the rāʾ it means "wide." It is said: "So-and-so is broad of chest (*raḥb al-ṣadr*), a land is spacious (*balad raḥb*), and an earth is wide (*arḍ raḥbah*)," and "it became spacious, a spaciousness and an ampleness (*raḥābah*)." Zayd ibn ʿAlī recited *bi-mā raḥbat* in both places with a sukūn on the ḥāʾ, which is the dialect of Tamim, who pronounce the ḍammah of *faʿula* with a sukūn, so they say *ẓarf* for *ẓaruf*.

﴿Then you turned back in retreat﴾; that is, you turned back fleeing on your heels, routed, abandoning the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The turning back is attributed to all of them, though it occurred from most of them, since some of the champions remained steadfast with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, as will be mentioned, if Allah wills. The account is: when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ conquered Makkah, he had ten thousand of his companions, and two thousand of the *ṭulaqāʾ* (those freed at the conquest) joined him, so they became twelve thousand, in addition to the bedouins who joined them from Sulaym, Banu Kilab, ʿAbs, and Dhubyān. The disbelieving Arabs heard of this and it grieved them, so Hawazin and their allies gathered against him, under the command of Malik ibn ʿAwf al-Naḍrī, and Thaqif, under the command of ʿAbd Yalil ibn ʿAmr. Mixed groups of people joined them until they numbered thirty thousand. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out against them after appointing ʿAttab ibn Asid over Makkah, and they gathered at Ḥunayn. When the people lined up for battle, the polytheists charged from the sides of the valley, having lain in ambush there, and the Muslims were routed. Qatadah said: "It is said that the *ṭulaqāʾ* from the people of Makkah fled and intended to cast defeat upon the Muslims, and their number reached Makkah." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ remained in his position, on a grey mule called "Duldul," not moving. Al-ʿAbbas was beside him, holding its bridle, with his cousin Abu Sufyan ibn al-Ḥarith ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, and his son Jaʿfar, and ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, Rabiʿah ibn al-Ḥarith, al-Faḍl ibn al-ʿAbbas, Usamah ibn Zayd, and Ayman ibn ʿUbayd, who is Ayman the son of Umm Ayman. These members of his household fought before the Messenger ﷺ. Abu Bakr and ʿUmar also remained with him, so they were ten men. For this reason al-ʿAbbas said:

"We helped the Messenger of Allah in the battle, nine of us, while those who fled among them had fled and dispersed."

"And our tenth met death with his own soul, for what touched him for the sake of Allah he did not complain of."

Umm Sulaym also remained among those who stood firm, holding a camel belonging to Abu Talhah, with a dagger in her hand. The Prophet ﷺ dismounted from his mule to the ground, called upon Allah for help, took a handful of dust and pebbles, threw them at the faces of the disbelievers, and said: "May the faces be disfigured." Yaʿla ibn ʿAṭāʾ said: "Their sons related to me from their fathers, who said: none of us was left without some of that dust entering his eyes." He said to al-ʿAbbas, who had a loud voice: "Call out to the companions of the *samurah* (tree)." So he called out to the Ansar clan by clan, then he called: "O companions of the tree, O companions of Surat al-Baqarah!" They turned back as one, saying: "At your service, at your service!" The polytheists were routed. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ looked at the fighting of the Muslims and said: "Now the furnace has become hot," and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ rode after them on his mule. In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from the ḥadīth of al-Barāʾ: "Hawazin were archers, and they shot at them with a volley of arrows like a swarm of locusts, and they scattered. The people then came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, while Abu Sufyan was leading his mule. He dismounted, called out, and sought victory, saying:

"I am the Prophet, no lie,
I am the son of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.
O Allah, send down Your victory."

Al-Barāʾ said: "By Allah, when the battle grew fierce we took shelter behind him ﷺ, and the bravest of us was the one who stood alongside him, meaning the Prophet ﷺ." At the beginning of this ḥadīth: "Did you turn back on the day of Ḥunayn, O Abu ʿUmārah?" He said: "I bear witness that the Messenger of Allah did not turn back."

﴿Then Allah sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers﴾. *Al-sakīnah* (tranquility): the victory in which souls found rest, as said by Ibn ʿAṭiyyah. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "His mercy by which they found rest." It has been said: it is the protection and steadfastness after agitation and unease. It follows from this view that the Messenger ﷺ is included, for he never ceased to be steadfast of heart and calm. The phrase ﴿upon the believers﴾, taken apparently, includes both those who fled and those who stood firm. It has been said: they are the Ansar, since they are the ones who charged back and reversed the defeat. It has been said: those who remained with the Messenger ﷺ when people fled. Zayd ibn ʿAlī recited *sikkīnatahu* with a kasrah on the sīn and a shaddah on the kāf, for emphasis on tranquility, like *shirrīb* and *ṭibbīkh*.

﴿And He sent down hosts you did not see﴾; they are the angels, without disagreement. The verse does not specify their number. Al-Ḥasan said: sixteen thousand. Mujahid said: eight thousand. Ibn Jubayr said: five thousand. This is a contradiction among the reports. The majority hold that they did not fight at Ḥunayn. It is transmitted from Ibn al-Musayyab: "A man who was among the polytheists on the day of Ḥunayn told me: When we routed the Muslims, we began driving them, and when we reached the owner of the grey mule, men with white and handsome faces met us and said: 'Disfigured be the faces! Turn back!' So we turned back, and they mounted upon our shoulders." The apparent meaning is that the seeing is negated for the believers, since the address is to them. It has been related that a man from Banu al-Naḍīr said to the believers after the fighting: "Where are the dappled horses and the men who were upon them, white? We were among them only like a mole, and our killing was only by their hands?" They informed the Prophet ﷺ, and he said: "Those were the angels." It has been said: ﴿you did not see﴾ negates it for all of them, and whoever saw some of them did not see all of them. It has been said: none of the Muslims or the disbelievers saw them; Allah sent them only to cast firmness into the hearts of the believers and terror and cowardice into the hearts of the disbelievers. Yazid ibn ʿAmir said: "There was in our insides something like the striking of a stone in a basin, from the terror."

﴿And He punished those who disbelieved, and that is the recompense of the disbelievers﴾; that is, by the killing that raged among them, the taking captive of their offspring and women, and the plundering of their wealth. The captives were four thousand heads; it is said six thousand. Of camels there were twelve thousand, besides an uncounted number of sheep. The Messenger ﷺ divided them at al-Jiʿranah, and in that is the story of ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas and his poetry. Malik ibn ʿAwf had brought out the people for battle along with the offspring, so that they would fight for them. Durayd ibn al-Ṣimmah criticized him for this, saying: "Will anything return the one who is routed?" On that day Durayd was slain in the well-known manner; Rabiʿah ibn Rufayʿ ibn Uhban al-Sulamī killed him, and he is called Ibn al-Dighinah.

﴿Then Allah relents after that toward whom He wills, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. This is information that Allah relents toward whom He wills, guiding whom He wills among those disbelievers who remained to Islam, and He promised forgiveness and mercy, as to Malik ibn ʿAwf al-Naḍrī, chief of Hawazin, and those of his people who embraced Islam with him. It is related that some of them came, pledged allegiance upon Islam, and said: "O Messenger of Allah, you are the best and most righteous of people, and our families and children have been taken captive and our wealth seized." That day the captives numbered six thousand souls, and camels and sheep were taken in uncountable numbers. He said: "Indeed, the best speech is the truest. Choose either your offspring and women, or your wealth." They said: "We do not value lineage above anything." The complete ḥadīth is that they took back their women and offspring, except for one woman with whom Ṣafwān ibn Umayyah had intercourse; she conceived from him, and he did not return her.

Al-Qadi al-'Alim Abu 'Ali al-Husayn ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Abi al-Ahwas al-Qurashi narrated to us, by my reading to him in the city of Malaqa, saying: Abu al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Bayqa ibn Habalah al-Khazraji, at Bawu Bulah, narrated to us, saying: al-Hafiz Abu Tahir Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Silafi al-Isfahani narrated to us at Alexandria (ḥ). Our teacher, the Imam, the great scholar and hadith master (al-hafiz) Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn Ibrahim ibn al-Zubayr also narrated to us, by my reading to him at Granada, from al-Qadi Abi al-Khattab Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Khalil al-Sukuni, from Abi Tahir al-Silafi, who was the last to narrate from him in the West (ḥ). Al-Qadi al-Sa'id Safi al-Din Abu Muhammad 'Abd al-Wahhab ibn Hasan ibn al-Furat also narrated to us, by reading to him twice at the frontier town of Alexandria, from Abu al-Tahir Isma'il ibn Salih ibn Yasin al-Jabali, who was the last to narrate from him. Both of them (al-Silafi and al-Jabali) said: Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Razi narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn Baqa ibn Muhammad al-Warraq narrated to us in Egypt, saying: Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn 'Umar al-Yamani al-Tanukhi narrated to us at Intifa' Khalaf al-Wasiti al-Hafiz (ḥ). Al-Muhaddith al-'Adl Najib al-Din Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Mu'ayyad al-Hamadani, known as Ibn al-'Ajami, also narrated to us, by my reading to him in Cairo. I said to him: Abu al-Fakhr As'ad ibn Abi al-Futuh ibn Rawh and 'Afifah bint Ahmad ibn 'Abd Allah narrated to you in their two books, and they said: Fatimah bint 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn 'Aqil al-Jawzdaniyyah narrated to us, saying: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Rayzah al-Dabbi narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Qasim Sulayman ibn Ahmad ibn Ayyub al-Tabarani, the hafiz, narrated to us. Both of them (al-Tanukhi and al-Tabarani) said: 'Ubayd Allah ibn Rama'his narrated to us. Al-Tanukhi added: Muhammad ibn Khalid ibn Habib ibn Qays ibn Ramadah from al-Ramlah, two postal stages away, in Rabi' al-Akhir of the year 280 AH. Al-Tabarani said: Ibn Rama'his al-Jushami al-Qaysi of Ramadat al-Ramlah, in the year 277 AH, said: Abu 'Amr Ziyad ibn Tariq narrated to us. Al-Tanukhi added "al-Jushami." Al-Tabarani said: He had reached one hundred and twenty years of age. Al-Tanukhi said, on the authority of Ziyad: Zuhayr Abu Jandal, who was the chief of his people, and who was known by the kunyah Abu Surad, informed us, saying: "When the day of Hunayn came, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ took us captive. While he was separating the men from the women, I got up and sat before him, reminding him of where he grew up and was raised among Hawazin, and where they nursed him. Then I began to say:"

Al-Tabarani said, on the authority of Ziyad, who said: I heard Abu Jarwal Zuhayr ibn Surad al-Jushami saying: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ took us captive on the day of Hunayn, the people of Hawazin, and he went about dividing the captives and the sheep, I came to him and began to recite this poem:"

1. Show us favour, Messenger of Allah, in generosity, for you are the man whom we hope for and await.
2. Show us favour concerning an egg-shell that has been pierced by a fate which scatters its unity in the course of time.
3. The war has left us only wailing over grief, while their hearts are covered with blindness and rust.
4. If the bounty that you spread does not reach them, O most forbearing of people when forbearance is tested,
5. show favour to the women whom you once nursed, when your mouth was filled from their milk with pearls.
6. When you were a small child, you used to nurse from them, and what you did and did not do was becoming to you.
7. O best of those over whom the dark-bay horses have pranced in battle when the fire of war flares and sparks fly.
8. Do not make us like one whose ostrich has been lifted up (i.e., who has been left without their own), and spare us, for we are a people of brightness.
9. We hope for pardon from you, which we will wear, for this is the nature of mankind: to pardon and to be victorious.
10. We indeed are grateful for the favour, though it has been denied, and beyond this day we have a store laid up.
11. So clothe in pardon the one whom you once nursed from your mothers, for pardon is well known.
12. Pardon, and may Allah pardon you for what you dread on the Day of Resurrection, when victory is brought to you.

In the narration of al-Tabarani there is some transposition of lines and a change of some words. The order of the lines after his saying "When you were a small child" is: "Do not make us like," then "Indeed we are grateful," then "So clothe in pardon," then the delay of "O best of those," then "We hope for pardon," then "Pardon." The changes in wording are his saying "wa-idh yarību-ka" with the bāʾ and rāʾ in place of the zāy and nūn, his saying "li-l-nuʿmā" "idh kufirat," and his saying "idh taʿfū." In the narration of al-Tabarani, he said: When the Prophet ﷺ heard this poem, he said ﷺ: "What belongs to me and to the sons of 'Abd al-Muttalib is yours." Quraysh said: "What belongs to us is for Allah and His Messenger." The Ansar said: "What belongs to us is for Allah and His Messenger." In the narration of al-Tanukhi: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "As for what belongs to me and to the sons of 'Abd al-Muttalib, it is for Allah and for you." The Ansar said: "What belongs to us is for Allah and His Messenger," and the Ansar returned what was in their hands of the offspring and the wealth.

[p. 23]

When the people lined up for battle, the polytheists charged from the sides of the valley, having lain in ambush there, and the Muslims were routed. Qatadah said: "It is said that the *ṭulaqāʾ* from the people of Makkah fled and intended to cast defeat upon the Muslims, and their number reached Makkah." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ remained in his position, on a grey mule called "Duldul," not moving. Al-ʿAbbas was beside him, holding its bridle, with his cousin Abu Sufyan ibn al-Ḥarith ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, and his son Jaʿfar, and ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, Rabiʿah ibn al-Ḥarith, al-Faḍl ibn al-ʿAbbas, Usamah ibn Zayd, and Ayman ibn ʿUbayd, who is Ayman the son of Umm Ayman. These members of his household fought before the Messenger ﷺ. Abu Bakr and ʿUmar also remained with him, so they were ten men. For this reason al-ʿAbbas said:

"We helped the Messenger of Allah in the battle, nine of us, while those who fled among them had fled and dispersed."

"And our tenth met death with his own soul, for what touched him for the sake of Allah he did not complain of."

Umm Sulaym also remained among those who stood firm, holding a camel belonging to Abu Talhah, with a dagger in her hand. The Prophet ﷺ dismounted from his mule to the ground, called upon Allah for help, took a handful of dust and pebbles, threw them at the faces of the disbelievers, and said: "May the faces be disfigured." Yaʿla ibn ʿAṭāʾ said: "Their sons related to me from their fathers, who said: none of us was left without some of that dust entering his eyes." He said to al-ʿAbbas, who had a loud voice: "Call out to the companions of the *samurah* (tree)." So he called out to the Ansar clan by clan, then he called: "O companions of the tree, O companions of Surat al-Baqarah!" They turned back as one, saying: "At your service, at your service!" The polytheists were routed. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ looked at the fighting of the Muslims and said: "Now the furnace has become hot," and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ rode after them on his mule. In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from the ḥadīth of al-Barāʾ: "Hawazin were archers, and they shot at them with a volley of arrows like a swarm of locusts, and they scattered. The people then came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, while Abu Sufyan was leading his mule. He dismounted, called out, and sought victory, saying:

"I am the Prophet, no lie,
I am the son of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.
O Allah, send down Your victory."

Al-Barāʾ said: "By Allah, when the battle grew fierce we took shelter behind him ﷺ, and the bravest of us was the one who stood alongside him, meaning the Prophet ﷺ." At the beginning of this ḥadīth: "Did you turn back on the day of Ḥunayn, O Abu ʿUmārah?" He said: "I bear witness that the Messenger of Allah did not turn back."

﴿Then Allah sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers﴾. *Al-sakīnah* (tranquility): the victory in which souls found rest, as said by Ibn ʿAṭiyyah. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "His mercy by which they found rest." It has been said: it is the protection and steadfastness after agitation and unease. It follows from this view that the Messenger ﷺ is included, for he never ceased to be steadfast of heart and calm. The phrase ﴿upon the believers﴾, taken apparently, includes both those who fled and those who stood firm. It has been said: they are the Ansar, since they are the ones who charged back and reversed the defeat. It has been said: those who remained with the Messenger ﷺ when people fled. Zayd ibn ʿAlī recited *sikkīnatahu* with a kasrah on the sīn and a shaddah on the kāf, for emphasis on tranquility, like *shirrīb* and *ṭibbīkh*.

﴿And He sent down hosts you did not see﴾; they are the angels, without disagreement. The verse does not specify their number. Al-Ḥasan said: sixteen thousand. Mujahid said: eight thousand. Ibn Jubayr said: five thousand. This is a contradiction among the reports. The majority hold that they did not fight at Ḥunayn. It is transmitted from Ibn al-Musayyab: "A man who was among the polytheists on the day of Ḥunayn told me: When we routed the Muslims, we began driving them, and when we reached the owner of the grey mule, men with white and handsome faces met us and said: 'Disfigured be the faces! Turn back!' So we turned back, and they mounted upon our shoulders." The apparent meaning is that the seeing is negated for the believers, since the address is to them. It has been related that a man from Banu al-Naḍīr said to the believers after the fighting: "Where are the dappled horses and the men who were upon them, white? We were among them only like a mole, and our killing was only by their hands?" They informed the Prophet ﷺ, and he said: "Those were the angels." It has been said: ﴿you did not see﴾ negates it for all of them, and whoever saw some of them did not see all of them. It has been said: none of the Muslims or the disbelievers saw them; Allah sent them only to cast firmness into the hearts of the believers and terror and cowardice into the hearts of the disbelievers. Yazid ibn ʿAmir said: "There was in our insides something like the striking of a stone in a basin, from the terror."

﴿And He punished those who disbelieved, and that is the recompense of the disbelievers﴾; that is, by the killing that raged among them, the taking captive of their offspring and women, and the plundering of their wealth. The captives were four thousand heads; it is said six thousand. Of camels there were twelve thousand, besides an uncounted number of sheep. The Messenger ﷺ divided them at al-Jiʿranah, and in that is the story of ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas and his poetry. Malik ibn ʿAwf had brought out the people for battle along with the offspring, so that they would fight for them. Durayd ibn al-Ṣimmah criticized him for this, saying: "Will anything return the one who is routed?" On that day Durayd was slain in the well-known manner; Rabiʿah ibn Rufayʿ ibn Uhban al-Sulamī killed him, and he is called Ibn al-Dighinah.

﴿Then Allah relents after that toward whom He wills, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. This is information that Allah relents toward whom He wills, guiding whom He wills among those disbelievers who remained to Islam, and He promised forgiveness and mercy, as to Malik ibn ʿAwf al-Naḍrī, chief of Hawazin, and those of his people who embraced Islam with him. It is related that some of them came, pledged allegiance upon Islam, and said: "O Messenger of Allah, you are the best and most righteous of people, and our families and children have been taken captive and our wealth seized." That day the captives numbered six thousand souls, and camels and sheep were taken in uncountable numbers. He said: "Indeed, the best speech is the truest. Choose either your offspring and women, or your wealth." They said: "We do not value lineage above anything." The complete ḥadīth is that they took back their women and offspring, except for one woman with whom Ṣafwān ibn Umayyah had intercourse; she conceived from him, and he did not return her.

Al-Qadi al-'Alim Abu 'Ali al-Husayn ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Abi al-Ahwas al-Qurashi narrated to us, by my reading to him in the city of Malaqa, saying: Abu al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Bayqa ibn Habalah al-Khazraji, at Bawu Bulah, narrated to us, saying: al-Hafiz Abu Tahir Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Silafi al-Isfahani narrated to us at Alexandria (ḥ). Our teacher, the Imam, the great scholar and hadith master (al-hafiz) Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn Ibrahim ibn al-Zubayr also narrated to us, by my reading to him at Granada, from al-Qadi Abi al-Khattab Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Khalil al-Sukuni, from Abi Tahir al-Silafi, who was the last to narrate from him in the West (ḥ). Al-Qadi al-Sa'id Safi al-Din Abu Muhammad 'Abd al-Wahhab ibn Hasan ibn al-Furat also narrated to us, by reading to him twice at the frontier town of Alexandria, from Abu al-Tahir Isma'il ibn Salih ibn Yasin al-Jabali, who was the last to narrate from him. Both of them (al-Silafi and al-Jabali) said: Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Razi narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn Baqa ibn Muhammad al-Warraq narrated to us in Egypt, saying: Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn 'Umar al-Yamani al-Tanukhi narrated to us at Intifa' Khalaf al-Wasiti al-Hafiz (ḥ). Al-Muhaddith al-'Adl Najib al-Din Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Mu'ayyad al-Hamadani, known as Ibn al-'Ajami, also narrated to us, by my reading to him in Cairo. I said to him: Abu al-Fakhr As'ad ibn Abi al-Futuh ibn Rawh and 'Afifah bint Ahmad ibn 'Abd Allah narrated to you in their two books, and they said: Fatimah bint 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn 'Aqil al-Jawzdaniyyah narrated to us, saying: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Rayzah al-Dabbi narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Qasim Sulayman ibn Ahmad ibn Ayyub al-Tabarani, the hafiz, narrated to us. Both of them (al-Tanukhi and al-Tabarani) said: 'Ubayd Allah ibn Rama'his narrated to us. Al-Tanukhi added: Muhammad ibn Khalid ibn Habib ibn Qays ibn Ramadah from al-Ramlah, two postal stages away, in Rabi' al-Akhir of the year 280 AH. Al-Tabarani said: Ibn Rama'his al-Jushami al-Qaysi of Ramadat al-Ramlah, in the year 277 AH, said: Abu 'Amr Ziyad ibn Tariq narrated to us. Al-Tanukhi added "al-Jushami." Al-Tabarani said: He had reached one hundred and twenty years of age. Al-Tanukhi said, on the authority of Ziyad: Zuhayr Abu Jandal, who was the chief of his people, and who was known by the kunyah Abu Surad, informed us, saying: "When the day of Hunayn came, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ took us captive. While he was separating the men from the women, I got up and sat before him, reminding him of where he grew up and was raised among Hawazin, and where they nursed him. Then I began to say:"

Al-Tabarani said, on the authority of Ziyad, who said: I heard Abu Jarwal Zuhayr ibn Surad al-Jushami saying: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ took us captive on the day of Hunayn, the people of Hawazin, and he went about dividing the captives and the sheep, I came to him and began to recite this poem:"

1. Show us favour, Messenger of Allah, in generosity, for you are the man whom we hope for and await.
2. Show us favour concerning an egg-shell that has been pierced by a fate which scatters its unity in the course of time.
3. The war has left us only wailing over grief, while their hearts are covered with blindness and rust.
4. If the bounty that you spread does not reach them, O most forbearing of people when forbearance is tested,
5. show favour to the women whom you once nursed, when your mouth was filled from their milk with pearls.
6. When you were a small child, you used to nurse from them, and what you did and did not do was becoming to you.
7. O best of those over whom the dark-bay horses have pranced in battle when the fire of war flares and sparks fly.
8. Do not make us like one whose ostrich has been lifted up (i.e., who has been left without their own), and spare us, for we are a people of brightness.
9. We hope for pardon from you, which we will wear, for this is the nature of mankind: to pardon and to be victorious.
10. We indeed are grateful for the favour, though it has been denied, and beyond this day we have a store laid up.
11. So clothe in pardon the one whom you once nursed from your mothers, for pardon is well known.
12. Pardon, and may Allah pardon you for what you dread on the Day of Resurrection, when victory is brought to you.

In the narration of al-Tabarani there is some transposition of lines and a change of some words. The order of the lines after his saying "When you were a small child" is: "Do not make us like," then "Indeed we are grateful," then "So clothe in pardon," then the delay of "O best of those," then "We hope for pardon," then "Pardon." The changes in wording are his saying "wa-idh yarību-ka" with the bāʾ and rāʾ in place of the zāy and nūn, his saying "li-l-nuʿmā" "idh kufirat," and his saying "idh taʿfū." In the narration of al-Tabarani, he said: When the Prophet ﷺ heard this poem, he said ﷺ: "What belongs to me and to the sons of 'Abd al-Muttalib is yours." Quraysh said: "What belongs to us is for Allah and His Messenger." The Ansar said: "What belongs to us is for Allah and His Messenger." In the narration of al-Tanukhi: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "As for what belongs to me and to the sons of 'Abd al-Muttalib, it is for Allah and for you." The Ansar said: "What belongs to us is for Allah and His Messenger," and the Ansar returned what was in their hands of the offspring and the wealth.

[p. 23]

Allah says: ﴿Allah had already given you victory on many occasions, and on the day of Hunayn, when your large numbers made you vain, but they availed you nothing, and the earth, spacious as it is, grew too narrow for you, and then you turned back in retreat.﴾

When His words ﴿Fight them; Allah will punish them at your hands, and disgrace them, and give you victory over them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 14] had preceded, He digressed after that into what He digressed into, and reminded them of His victory for them on many occasions. The *mawatin* (sing. *mawtin*, battle positions) are the stations and situations of war. It has been said: they are the scenes of battle where you prepare yourselves (*tuwatinun*) to meet the enemy. It is the plural of *mawtin* with a kasra on the ṭāʾ, and the poet said:

"How many a position there was, had I not been with you, you would have fallen as a thing falls from the top of a steep cliff."

These *mawatin* were: the encounter of Badr, Qurayẓah, al-Naḍīr, al-Ḥudaybiyah, Khaybar, and the conquest of Makkah. They are described as many because the imams of history, the scholars, and the chroniclers of the campaigns transmitted that they were eighty positions. Ḥunayn is a valley between Makkah and al-Ṭāʾif, near Dhū al-Majāz. It is declined (ṣuriqa) as a place-name treated as a location (*madhhab al-makān*); had it been treated as an area (*madhhab al-buqʿah*), it would not have been declined, as the poet said:

"They helped their Prophet and strengthened his back at Ḥunayn, on the day when the champions were leaving one another to fend for themselves."

He coordinated the time with the place. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "The position of the day of Ḥunayn," or "in the days of many positions and the day of Ḥunayn." Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "*Yawm* is coordinated with the position of the phrase *fī mawāṭin*, or with its wording, with the implied meaning 'and in the day of,' so the preposition was omitted," end of quote. *Idh* (when) is a substitute (*badal*) for *yawm*. He attributed the vanity (*iʿjāb*) to all of them, although it came from one man who, when he saw the large crowd, was impressed by it and said: "We will not be defeated today for lack of numbers." The speaker is said by Ibn al-Musayyab to be Abu Bakr, or Salamah ibn Salamah ibn Quraysh, or Ibn ʿAbbas, or a man from Banu Bakr. It is transmitted that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was displeased by the words of this speaker, and they were left to the words of the man.

*Al-kathrah* (multitude) is with a fatḥah on the kāf; its plural is *katharāt*. The Tamim tribe pronounce the kāf with a kasrah, and its plural is *kuthur*, like *shadhrah* and *shudhur*, and *kisrah* and *kusur*. This multitude, according to Ibn ʿAbbas, was sixteen thousand; according to al-Naḥḥas, fourteen thousand; according to Qatadah, Ibn Zayd, Ibn Ishaq, and al-Waqidi, twelve thousand; and according to Muqatil from Ibn ʿAbbas, eleven thousand five hundred.

The *bāʾ* in ﴿with what it was spacious﴾ is for circumstance (*ḥāl*), and *mā* is verbal-nominal (*maṣdariyyah*). That is: the earth grew narrow for you while being wide and spacious, because of the severity of the situation upon them and its hardship, as though they could not find a place suitable for fleeing and escape, due to the extreme terror that had seized them, so it was as if it had become narrow for them. *Al-rahb* means spaciousness, and with a fatḥah on the rāʾ it means "wide." It is said: "So-and-so is broad of chest (*raḥb al-ṣadr*), a land is spacious (*balad raḥb*), and an earth is wide (*arḍ raḥbah*)," and "it became spacious, a spaciousness and an ampleness (*raḥābah*)." Zayd ibn ʿAlī recited *bi-mā raḥbat* in both places with a sukūn on the ḥāʾ, which is the dialect of Tamim, who pronounce the ḍammah of *faʿula* with a sukūn, so they say *ẓarf* for *ẓaruf*.

﴿Then you turned back in retreat﴾; that is, you turned back fleeing on your heels, routed, abandoning the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The turning back is attributed to all of them, though it occurred from most of them, since some of the champions remained steadfast with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, as will be mentioned, if Allah wills. The account is: when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ conquered Makkah, he had ten thousand of his companions, and two thousand of the *ṭulaqāʾ* (those freed at the conquest) joined him, so they became twelve thousand, in addition to the bedouins who joined them from Sulaym, Banu Kilab, ʿAbs, and Dhubyān. The disbelieving Arabs heard of this and it grieved them, so Hawazin and their allies gathered against him, under the command of Malik ibn ʿAwf al-Naḍrī, and Thaqif, under the command of ʿAbd Yalil ibn ʿAmr. Mixed groups of people joined them until they numbered thirty thousand. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out against them after appointing ʿAttab ibn Asid over Makkah, and they gathered at Ḥunayn. When the people lined up for battle, the polytheists charged from the sides of the valley, having lain in ambush there, and the Muslims were routed. Qatadah said: "It is said that the *ṭulaqāʾ* from the people of Makkah fled and intended to cast defeat upon the Muslims, and their number reached Makkah." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ remained in his position, on a grey mule called "Duldul," not moving. Al-ʿAbbas was beside him, holding its bridle, with his cousin Abu Sufyan ibn al-Ḥarith ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, and his son Jaʿfar, and ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, Rabiʿah ibn al-Ḥarith, al-Faḍl ibn al-ʿAbbas, Usamah ibn Zayd, and Ayman ibn ʿUbayd, who is Ayman the son of Umm Ayman. These members of his household fought before the Messenger ﷺ. Abu Bakr and ʿUmar also remained with him, so they were ten men. For this reason al-ʿAbbas said:

"We helped the Messenger of Allah in the battle, nine of us, while those who fled among them had fled and dispersed."

"And our tenth met death with his own soul, for what touched him for the sake of Allah he did not complain of."

Umm Sulaym also remained among those who stood firm, holding a camel belonging to Abu Talhah, with a dagger in her hand. The Prophet ﷺ dismounted from his mule to the ground, called upon Allah for help, took a handful of dust and pebbles, threw them at the faces of the disbelievers, and said: "May the faces be disfigured." Yaʿla ibn ʿAṭāʾ said: "Their sons related to me from their fathers, who said: none of us was left without some of that dust entering his eyes." He said to al-ʿAbbas, who had a loud voice: "Call out to the companions of the *samurah* (tree)." So he called out to the Ansar clan by clan, then he called: "O companions of the tree, O companions of Surat al-Baqarah!" They turned back as one, saying: "At your service, at your service!" The polytheists were routed. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ looked at the fighting of the Muslims and said: "Now the furnace has become hot," and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ rode after them on his mule. In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from the ḥadīth of al-Barāʾ: "Hawazin were archers, and they shot at them with a volley of arrows like a swarm of locusts, and they scattered. The people then came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, while Abu Sufyan was leading his mule. He dismounted, called out, and sought victory, saying:

"I am the Prophet, no lie,
I am the son of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.
O Allah, send down Your victory."

Al-Barāʾ said: "By Allah, when the battle grew fierce we took shelter behind him ﷺ, and the bravest of us was the one who stood alongside him, meaning the Prophet ﷺ." At the beginning of this ḥadīth: "Did you turn back on the day of Ḥunayn, O Abu ʿUmārah?" He said: "I bear witness that the Messenger of Allah did not turn back."

﴿Then Allah sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers﴾. *Al-sakīnah* (tranquility): the victory in which souls found rest, as said by Ibn ʿAṭiyyah. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "His mercy by which they found rest." It has been said: it is the protection and steadfastness after agitation and unease. It follows from this view that the Messenger ﷺ is included, for he never ceased to be steadfast of heart and calm. The phrase ﴿upon the believers﴾, taken apparently, includes both those who fled and those who stood firm.
