﴿And He sent down hosts you did not see﴾; they are the angels, without disagreement. The verse does not specify their number. Al-Ḥasan said: sixteen thousand. Mujahid said: eight thousand. Ibn Jubayr said: five thousand. This is a contradiction among the reports. The majority hold that they did not fight at Ḥunayn. It is transmitted from Ibn al-Musayyab: "A man who was among the polytheists on the day of Ḥunayn told me: When we routed the Muslims, we began driving them, and when we reached the owner of the grey mule, men with white and handsome faces met us and said: 'Disfigured be the faces! Turn back!' So we turned back, and they mounted upon our shoulders." The apparent meaning is that the seeing is negated for the believers, since the address is to them. It has been related that a man from Banu al-Naḍīr said to the believers after the fighting: "Where are the dappled horses and the men who were upon them, white? We were among them only like a mole, and our killing was only by their hands?" They informed the Prophet ﷺ, and he said: "Those were the angels." It has been said: ﴿you did not see﴾ negates it for all of them, and whoever saw some of them did not see all of them. It has been said: none of the Muslims or the disbelievers saw them; Allah sent them only to cast firmness into the hearts of the believers and terror and cowardice into the hearts of the disbelievers. Yazid ibn ʿAmir said: "There was in our insides something like the striking of a stone in a basin, from the terror."

﴿And He punished those who disbelieved, and that is the recompense of the disbelievers﴾; that is, by the killing that raged among them, the taking captive of their offspring and women, and the plundering of their wealth. The captives were four thousand heads; it is said six thousand. Of camels there were twelve thousand, besides an uncounted number of sheep. The Messenger ﷺ divided them at al-Jiʿranah, and in that is the story of ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas and his poetry. Malik ibn ʿAwf had brought out the people for battle along with the offspring, so that they would fight for them. Durayd ibn al-Ṣimmah criticized him for this, saying: "Will anything return the one who is routed?" On that day Durayd was slain in the well-known manner; Rabiʿah ibn Rufayʿ ibn Uhban al-Sulamī killed him, and he is called Ibn al-Dighinah.

﴿Then Allah relents after that toward whom He wills, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. This is information that Allah relents toward whom He wills, guiding whom He wills among those disbelievers who remained to Islam, and He promised forgiveness and mercy, as to Malik ibn ʿAwf al-Naḍrī, chief of Hawazin, and those of his people who embraced Islam with him. It is related that some of them came, pledged allegiance upon Islam, and said: "O Messenger of Allah, you are the best and most righteous of people, and our families and children have been taken captive and our wealth seized." That day the captives numbered six thousand souls, and camels and sheep were taken in uncountable numbers. He said: "Indeed, the best speech is the truest. Choose either your offspring and women, or your wealth." They said: "We do not value lineage above anything." The complete ḥadīth is that they took back their women and offspring, except for one woman with whom Ṣafwān ibn Umayyah had intercourse; she conceived from him, and he did not return her.

Al-Qadi al-'Alim Abu 'Ali al-Husayn ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Abi al-Ahwas al-Qurashi narrated to us, by my reading to him in the city of Malaqa, saying: Abu al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Bayqa ibn Habalah al-Khazraji, at Bawu Bulah, narrated to us, saying: al-Hafiz Abu Tahir Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Silafi al-Isfahani narrated to us at Alexandria (ḥ). Our teacher, the Imam, the great scholar and hadith master (al-hafiz) Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn Ibrahim ibn al-Zubayr also narrated to us, by my reading to him at Granada, from al-Qadi Abi al-Khattab Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Khalil al-Sukuni, from Abi Tahir al-Silafi, who was the last to narrate from him in the West (ḥ). Al-Qadi al-Sa'id Safi al-Din Abu Muhammad 'Abd al-Wahhab ibn Hasan ibn al-Furat also narrated to us, by reading to him twice at the frontier town of Alexandria, from Abu al-Tahir Isma'il ibn Salih ibn Yasin al-Jabali, who was the last to narrate from him. Both of them (al-Silafi and al-Jabali) said: Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Razi narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn Baqa ibn Muhammad al-Warraq narrated to us in Egypt, saying: Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn 'Umar al-Yamani al-Tanukhi narrated to us at Intifa' Khalaf al-Wasiti al-Hafiz (ḥ). Al-Muhaddith al-'Adl Najib al-Din Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Mu'ayyad al-Hamadani, known as Ibn al-'Ajami, also narrated to us, by my reading to him in Cairo. I said to him: Abu al-Fakhr As'ad ibn Abi al-Futuh ibn Rawh and 'Afifah bint Ahmad ibn 'Abd Allah narrated to you in their two books, and they said: Fatimah bint 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn 'Aqil al-Jawzdaniyyah narrated to us, saying: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Rayzah al-Dabbi narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Qasim Sulayman ibn Ahmad ibn Ayyub al-Tabarani, the hafiz, narrated to us. Both of them (al-Tanukhi and al-Tabarani) said: 'Ubayd Allah ibn Rama'his narrated to us. Al-Tanukhi added: Muhammad ibn Khalid ibn Habib ibn Qays ibn Ramadah from al-Ramlah, two postal stages away, in Rabi' al-Akhir of the year 280 AH. Al-Tabarani said: Ibn Rama'his al-Jushami al-Qaysi of Ramadat al-Ramlah, in the year 277 AH, said: Abu 'Amr Ziyad ibn Tariq narrated to us. Al-Tanukhi added "al-Jushami." Al-Tabarani said: He had reached one hundred and twenty years of age. Al-Tanukhi said, on the authority of Ziyad: Zuhayr Abu Jandal, who was the chief of his people, and who was known by the kunyah Abu Surad, informed us, saying: "When the day of Hunayn came, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ took us captive. While he was separating the men from the women, I got up and sat before him, reminding him of where he grew up and was raised among Hawazin, and where they nursed him. Then I began to say:"

Al-Tabarani said, on the authority of Ziyad, who said: I heard Abu Jarwal Zuhayr ibn Surad al-Jushami saying: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ took us captive on the day of Hunayn, the people of Hawazin, and he went about dividing the captives and the sheep, I came to him and began to recite this poem:"

1. Show us favour, Messenger of Allah, in generosity, for you are the man whom we hope for and await.
2. Show us favour concerning an egg-shell that has been pierced by a fate which scatters its unity in the course of time.
3. The war has left us only wailing over grief, while their hearts are covered with blindness and rust.
4. If the bounty that you spread does not reach them, O most forbearing of people when forbearance is tested,
5. show favour to the women whom you once nursed, when your mouth was filled from their milk with pearls.
6. When you were a small child, you used to nurse from them, and what you did and did not do was becoming to you.
7. O best of those over whom the dark-bay horses have pranced in battle when the fire of war flares and sparks fly.
8. Do not make us like one whose ostrich has been lifted up (i.e., who has been left without their own), and spare us, for we are a people of brightness.
9. We hope for pardon from you, which we will wear, for this is the nature of mankind: to pardon and to be victorious.
10. We indeed are grateful for the favour, though it has been denied, and beyond this day we have a store laid up.
11. So clothe in pardon the one whom you once nursed from your mothers, for pardon is well known.
12. Pardon, and may Allah pardon you for what you dread on the Day of Resurrection, when victory is brought to you.

In the narration of al-Tabarani there is some transposition of lines and a change of some words. The order of the lines after his saying "When you were a small child" is: "Do not make us like," then "Indeed we are grateful," then "So clothe in pardon," then the delay of "O best of those," then "We hope for pardon," then "Pardon." The changes in wording are his saying "wa-idh yarību-ka" with the bāʾ and rāʾ in place of the zāy and nūn, his saying "li-l-nuʿmā" "idh kufirat," and his saying "idh taʿfū." In the narration of al-Tabarani, he said: When the Prophet ﷺ heard this poem, he said ﷺ: "What belongs to me and to the sons of 'Abd al-Muttalib is yours." Quraysh said: "What belongs to us is for Allah and His Messenger." The Ansar said: "What belongs to us is for Allah and His Messenger." In the narration of al-Tanukhi: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "As for what belongs to me and to the sons of 'Abd al-Muttalib, it is for Allah and for you." The Ansar said: "What belongs to us is for Allah and His Messenger," and the Ansar returned what was in their hands of the offspring and the wealth.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verse 28–29 (part 1 of 2):

﴿O you who have believed, indeed the polytheists are unclean, so let them not approach al-Masjid al-Haram after this, their year. And if you fear poverty, Allah will enrich you from His bounty, if He wills. Indeed, Allah is Knowing and Wise.﴾; When the Prophet ﷺ commanded ʿAli to recite to the polytheists of Makkah the beginning of (Bara'ah) [Repudiation], and to renounce their covenant to them, and that Allah is free of the polytheists and so is His Messenger, some people said: "O people of Makkah, you will know what hardship you will suffer, the cutting off of roads and the loss of camel-loads," and so it was revealed. It was also said: When ﴿Indeed, the polytheists are unclean﴾ was revealed, it weighed heavily on the Muslims, and they said: "Who will bring us our food?" For they used to come to them with trade, so ﴿And if you fear poverty﴾ down to the end of the verse was revealed. The majority hold that the polytheist is one who takes another god alongside Allah, and that the People of the Book are not polytheists. Some scholars applied the name of association (shirk) to them, based on His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾ [al-Nisa': 48]; that is, that He be disbelieved in.

Al-Jumhur read (najas) with a fatha on the nun and the jim, and it is a verbal noun of najisa, najasan, meaning he became filthy, filth. The apparent meaning is a judgement against them that they are unclean, that is, possessors of uncleanness. Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz and others said: shirk itself is what made them unclean, so their very persons are unclean, like wine, dogs and pigs. Al-Hasan said: whoever shakes hands with a polytheist, let him perform ablution. In al-Tahrir it says: al-Hasan went to such an extreme that he said: ablution is obligatory from touching a polytheist; and no one adopted al-Hasan's view except al-Hadi of the Zaydiyyah. Qatadah, Maʿmar ibn Rashid and others said: the polytheist was described as unclean because he is in a state of major impurity (junub), since his washing from major impurity is not a valid washing; and according to this view, washing is obligatory upon those among the polytheists who embrace Islam, and this is the view of Malik. Ibn ʿAbd al-Hakam said: it is not obligatory. There is no doubt that they do not purify themselves, do not wash, and do not avoid impurities, so they were called "unclean" as an intensification in describing them with uncleanness.

Abu Haywah read (nijs) with a kasra on the nun and a sukun on the jim, on the assumption that the qualified noun is omitted, meaning: a kind that is unclean, or a sort that is unclean, and it is an active participle from najisa; they lightened it after the assimilation, as they said for kabid: kibd, and karish: kirsh. Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ read: anjas, which may be the plural of najas as a verbal noun, as they said asnaf, and it may be the plural of nijs, an active participle.

The prohibition of approaching means preventing them from entering it and circumambulating it, whether for hajj, ʿumrah or otherwise, as they used to do in the Jahiliyyah. In terms of meaning, this prohibition relates to the Muslims; that is, they should not allow them to approach al-Masjid al-Haram. The apparent meaning is that the prohibition is specific to the polytheists and to al-Masjid al-Haram, and this is the view of Abu Hanifah. He permitted the entry of Jews and Christians into al-Masjid al-Haram and other mosques, and the entry of idol-worshippers into all other mosques. Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning of His saying "so let them not approach al-Masjid al-Haram" is: let them not perform hajj or ʿumrah; and this is supported by the saying of ʿAli when he proclaimed (Bara'ah): "No polytheist shall perform hajj after this year of ours." He said: "And they are not prevented from entering the Haram, al-Masjid al-Haram, and all other mosques, according to Abu Hanifah," end. Al-Shafiʿi said: it is general concerning the disbelievers and specific to al-Masjid al-Haram, so he permitted the entry of Jews, Christians and pagans into all other mosques. Malik analogised all disbelievers, from the People of the Book and others, to the polytheists, and analogised all mosques to al-Masjid al-Haram, and forbade all of them from entering all mosques. ʿAta' said: by al-Masjid al-Haram is meant the Haram, and that the Muslims must not enable them to enter it. It was also said: by approaching is meant that they be prevented from taking charge of al-Masjid al-Haram and carrying out its affairs, and be removed from that. Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah and Qatadah said: no polytheist shall approach al-Masjid al-Haram except one who is a free person, or a slave of a Muslim. The meaning of His saying "after this their year" is: it is the year nine after the Hijrah, the year in which Abu Bakr performed hajj as commander over the season, and ʿAli was sent after him, and during it (Bara'ah) was proclaimed. Qatadah said: it is the tenth year, in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ performed hajj. And (ʿaylah) means poverty. Ibn Masʿud and ʿAlqamah, from among his companions, read: ʿa'ilah, which is a verbal noun like al-ʿaqibah, or a qualifier of an omitted noun; that is, a state of poverty. Here (in) retains its conditional function. ʿAmr ibn Qa'id said: the meaning is: "since you feared," like their saying: "if you are my son, obey me," that is, "since you are." That (in) means (idh) is an opinion that is not favoured. The occasion of revelation of this verse and His favour, exalted is He, has already been mentioned. Al-Dahhak said: it is what He opened to them through taking the jizyah from the protected people (dhimmis). ʿIkrimah said: He enriched them by abundant rain upon them, the Arabs embraced Islam, and their hajj and sacrifice continued; and Allah enriched them from His bounty through jihad and victory over nations. He tied the enrichment to His will, because it happens for some and not others, and at one time and not another. It was also said: it is to make the ruling follow wisdom, so if wisdom and benefit require enriching you, He will enrich you. Al-Qurtubi said: to inform that provision does not come by stratagem or effort, but is purely the bounty of Allah. It is related from al-Shafiʿi:
Had wealth come through stratagems, you would have found me clinging to the stars of the horizons of the sky.
But whoever is granted intellect is denied wealth: two opposites, parted by a most complete parting.
And among the proofs of destiny and its being: the misery of the intelligent and the pleasant life of the fool.

(Indeed Allah is Knowing) of your conditions, (Wise), who gives and withholds only for a wisdom. Ibn ʿAbbas said: Knowing of what sets you right, Wise in what He has judged concerning the polytheists.

﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah or the Last Day, and do not forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden, and do not adopt the religion of truth from among those who were given the Book, until they give the jizyah willingly while they are humbled.﴾ It was revealed when the Messenger ﷺ was commanded to fight the Romans, and after its revelation he campaigned to Tabuk. It was also said: it was revealed concerning Qurayzah and al-Nadir, and he made peace with them, and it was the first jizyah that the Muslims obtained. The first thing that befell the People of the Book at the hands of the Muslims was the negation of faith in Allah from them, because their path is the path of those who do not believe in Allah, since they describe Him with what does not befit Him to be described with. This was said by al-Karmani. Al-Zajjaj said: because they made for Him a son, altered their Book, forbade what was not forbidden, and permitted what was not permitted. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: because they abandoned the laws of Islam which they were obliged to enter, so all that they have concerning resurrection and concerning Allah became imaginings and beliefs without meaning, since they hold them without their proper basis. Also, their beliefs were not upright, since they associated and said: "ʿUzayr is the son of Allah," and "the third of three," and other things. They also have many opinions on resurrection concerning the abodes of Paradise, from the monks. And the Jews' saying that in Hell they will remain for some days, end. In al-Ghunyan: He negated faith from them because they are anthropomorphists (mujassimah), and the believer does not anthropomorphise, end. What is related of the Jews and Christians is their denial of bodily resurrection, so it seems they hold to a spiritual resurrection.

(What Allah has forbidden) in His Book, (and His Messenger) in the Sunnah. It was also said: in the Torah and the Gospel, because they permitted things that the Torah and the Gospel had forbidden; and the Messenger according to this view is Moses and Jesus, while according to the first view it is Muhammad ﷺ. It was also said: and they do not forbid wine and pork. It was also said: and they do not forbid lying against Allah; they said: ﴿We are the children of Allah and His beloved﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 18], and ﴿They said: None will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111]. It was also said: what Allah has forbidden of usury and the property of the unlettered. The apparent meaning is the generality of what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden in the Torah, the Gospel and the Qur'an.

﴿And do not adopt the religion of truth﴾; that is: they do not believe in the religion of Islam, which is the religion of truth, and whatever is other than it is false. It was also said: the religion of truth is the religion of Allah, and the Truth is Allah, said by Qatadah. One says: so-and-so follows a religion, that is, takes it as a religion and believes in it. Abu ʿUbaydah said: its meaning is: they do not obey the obedience of the people of Islam, and whoever is under the authority of a king is on his religion, and has submitted to him and humbled himself. Zuhayr said:
If you alight in a land among the Banu Asad, under the religion of ʿAmr, and Fadak comes between us...

﴿From those who were given the Book﴾ is an explanation of His saying "those". The apparent meaning is that the taking of the jizyah is specific to the People of the Book, namely the Children of Israel and the Romans, explicitly. And the people are in agreement on this. As for the Magians, Ibn al-Mundhir said: I know of no disagreement that the jizyah is taken from them, end. It is related that a prophet named Zoroaster was sent to the Magians, and the companions of Malik differed concerning the Magians of the Arabs. As for the Samaritans and the Sabians, the majority hold that they are among the Jews and Christians, and the jizyah is taken from them and their slaughtered animals are eaten. One group said: no jizyah is taken from them, and their slaughtered animals are not eaten. It was also said: the jizyah is taken from them, but their slaughtered animals are not eaten. Al-Awza'i said: it is taken from every worshipper of an idol, or of fire, or of a denier who is inanimate. Abu Hanifah said: nothing is accepted from the polytheists of the Arabs except Islam or the sword, while the jizyah is accepted from the People of the Book and from all disbelieving non-Arabs. Malik said: it is taken from the worshipper of fire, of idols, and other than that, whoever he may be, whether an Arab of Taghlib, or a Qurashi, or a non-Arab, except an apostate. Al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Abu Thawr said: it is accepted only from Jews, Christians and Magians alone. The apparent meaning is the inclusion of all the People of the Book in giving the jizyah. Abu Hanifah, Malik and al-Shafi'i said: it is taken only from adult, free, sane men, and is not imposed on the monks of the monasteries and churches who have withdrawn. Malik said in al-Wadihah: if it had been imposed on them and then they withdrew, it does not lapse, and it is imposed on the monks of the churches; and it was disputed concerning the aged elder.

The verse does not specify the amount due upon each head, (p-30) nor the time of its payment. As for its amount, Malik and many scholars of knowledge adopted what ʿUmar prescribed: four dinars upon the people of gold, and forty dirhams upon the people of silver; ʿUmar also imposed hospitality, provisions and clothing. Al-Thawri said: various levies are related from ʿUmar, and I think that was according to his judgement of their hardship and their ease. Al-Shafi'i and others said: one dinar per head. Abu Hanifah said: upon the poor who works, twelve dirhams; upon the moderately well-off, double that; upon the wealthy, double the double, forty-eight dirhams; and according to him nothing is taken from a poor person who has no earnings. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: all this is in the case of a period of respite. As for a settlement, it is what they are reconciled upon, whether little or much. As for its time, according to Abu Hanifah it is the beginning of each year, and according to al-Shafi'i the end of the year. It is called jizyah from jazā yajzī, when one repays what was bestowed upon him, so it is as if they gave it as recompense for the safety they were granted; and it is like the ʿuqdah and the jilsah, and from this meaning is the saying of the poet:
We shall repay you, or praise you; and whoever praises you for what you have done has indeed repaid you.

It was also said: because it is a portion of what the protected people must pay (yajzūhu), that is, they must discharge it.

(Regarding "an yadin"): Ibn ʿAbbas said: they give it with their own hands and do not send it with others. ʿUthman said: they give it in cash, not on credit (nasiʾah). Qatadah said: they give it while their hands are beneath the hand of the one who takes it, so the meaning is that they are subjugated. It was also said: "an iʿtirafin" (in acknowledgment). It was said: "an quwwatin minkum wa qahrin wa dhullin wa nafadhi amrin fihim" (from a position of strength on your part, domination, humiliation, and the enforcement of command over them), as you say: "al-yad fi hadha li-fulan" (the hand in this matter belongs to so-and-so), meaning the authority is his. It was also said: "an inʿamin ʿalayhim bi-dhalika" (as a favor bestowed upon them), because accepting it from them in exchange for their lives is a favor upon them, from the saying: "lahu ʿalayya yad" (he has a yad over me), meaning a favor (niʿmah). Al-Qutabi said: it is said "aʿtahu ʿan yadin" and "ʿan zahri yadin" when one gives him something initiating it, without repaying him. It was also said: "ʿan yadin" means "ʿan jamaʿatin" (from a group), i.e., no one among them of standing is exempted because of his standing. The yad is the group of people; it is said "al-qawmu ʿala yadin wahidatin" (the people are upon one hand), meaning they are united. It was also said: "ʿan yadin" means "ʿan ghina wa qudrah" (from wealth and ability), so it is not taken from the poor. Al-Zamakhshari summarized this, saying: If it means the hand of the one who takes, then the meaning is "until he overpowers it," from a dominating, controlling hand, and from a favor upon them, because accepting the jizyah from them and leaving them their lives is a great favor upon them. And if it means the hand of the one who gives, then the meaning is "from a willing hand, not refusing," because whoever refuses and resists does not give his hand, unlike the obedient, submissive one. For this reason they said: "aʿta bi-yadihi" when he submitted and yielded. Do you not see their saying: "naza`a yadahu ʿan al-taʿah" (he withdrew his hand from obedience)? Or "ʿan yadin ila yadin," meaning in cash, not on credit, or not sent by the hand of another, but "ʿan yadi al-muʿti al-bareedi al-akhidhi" (from the hand of the giver to the taker).

"Wa hum saghirun" is a circumstantial clause (jumlah hāliyyah), meaning: humbled and despised. They mentioned modes of taking it from them and of their humiliation, but the verse does not specify any one of them. Ibn ʿAbbas said: they walk with it while being seized by the collar (mulabbabin). Sulayman al-Farisi said: they are not praised for giving it. ʿIkrimah said: he (the payer) stands while the taker sits. Al-Kalbi said: when they hand it over, it is said to him: "Pay the jizyah," and he is struck on the nape of the neck (yusakku fi qafahu). Al-Baghawi related: he is seized by his beard and struck in his lahzimah (the area beneath the jaw).

And among the proofs of destiny and its being: the misery of the intelligent and the pleasant life of the fool.

(Indeed Allah is Knowing) of your conditions, (Wise), who gives and withholds only for a wisdom. Ibn ʿAbbas said: Knowing of what sets you right, Wise in what He has judged concerning the polytheists.

﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah or the Last Day, and do not forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden, and do not adopt the religion of truth from among those who were given the Book, until they give the jizyah willingly while they are humbled.﴾ It was revealed when the Messenger ﷺ was commanded to fight the Romans, and after its revelation he campaigned to Tabuk. It was also said: it was revealed concerning Qurayzah and al-Nadir, and he made peace with them, and it was the first jizyah that the Muslims obtained. The first thing that befell the People of the Book at the hands of the Muslims was the negation of faith in Allah from them, because their path is the path of those who do not believe in Allah, since they describe Him with what does not befit Him to be described with. This was said by al-Karmani. Al-Zajjaj said: because they made for Him a son, altered their Book, forbade what was not forbidden, and permitted what was not permitted. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: because they abandoned the laws of Islam which they were obliged to enter, so all that they have concerning resurrection and concerning Allah became imaginings and beliefs without meaning, since they hold them without their proper basis. Also, their beliefs were not upright, since they associated and said: "ʿUzayr is the son of Allah," and "the third of three," and other things. They also have many opinions on resurrection concerning the abodes of Paradise, from the monks. And the Jews' saying that in Hell they will remain for some days, end. In al-Ghunyan: He negated faith from them because they are anthropomorphists (mujassimah), and the believer does not anthropomorphise, end. What is related of the Jews and Christians is their denial of bodily resurrection, so it seems they hold to a spiritual resurrection.

(What Allah has forbidden) in His Book, (and His Messenger) in the Sunnah. It was also said: in the Torah and the Gospel, because they permitted things that the Torah and the Gospel had forbidden; and the Messenger according to this view is Moses and Jesus, while according to the first view it is Muhammad ﷺ. It was also said: and they do not forbid wine and pork. It was also said: and they do not forbid lying against Allah; they said: ﴿We are the children of Allah and His beloved﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 18], and ﴿They said: None will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111]. It was also said: what Allah has forbidden of usury and the property of the unlettered. The apparent meaning is the generality of what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden in the Torah, the Gospel and the Qur'an.

﴿And do not adopt the religion of truth﴾; that is: they do not believe in the religion of Islam, which is the religion of truth, and whatever is other than it is false. It was also said: the religion of truth is the religion of Allah, and the Truth is Allah, said by Qatadah. One says: so-and-so follows a religion, that is, takes it as a religion and believes in it. Abu ʿUbaydah said: its meaning is: they do not obey the obedience of the people of Islam, and whoever is under the authority of a king is on his religion, and has submitted to him and humbled himself. Zuhayr said:
If you alight in a land among the Banu Asad, under the religion of ʿAmr, and Fadak comes between us...

﴿From those who were given the Book﴾ is an explanation of His saying "those". The apparent meaning is that the taking of the jizyah is specific to the People of the Book, namely the Children of Israel and the Romans, explicitly. And the people are in agreement on this. As for the Magians, Ibn al-Mundhir said: I know of no disagreement that the jizyah is taken from them, end. It is related that a prophet named Zoroaster was sent to the Magians, and the companions of Malik differed concerning the Magians of the Arabs. As for the Samaritans and the Sabians, the majority hold that they are among the Jews and Christians, and the jizyah is taken from them and their slaughtered animals are eaten. One group said: no jizyah is taken from them, and their slaughtered animals are not eaten. It was also said: the jizyah is taken from them, but their slaughtered animals are not eaten. Al-Awza'i said: it is taken from every worshipper of an idol, or of fire, or of a denier who is inanimate. Abu Hanifah said: nothing is accepted from the polytheists of the Arabs except Islam or the sword, while the jizyah is accepted from the People of the Book and from all disbelieving non-Arabs. Malik said: it is taken from the worshipper of fire, of idols, and other than that, whoever he may be, whether an Arab of Taghlib, or a Qurashi, or a non-Arab, except an apostate. Al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Abu Thawr said: it is accepted only from Jews, Christians and Magians alone. The apparent meaning is the inclusion of all the People of the Book in giving the jizyah. Abu Hanifah, Malik and al-Shafi'i said: it is taken only from adult, free, sane men, and is not imposed on the monks of the monasteries and churches who have withdrawn. Malik said in al-Wadihah: if it had been imposed on them and then they withdrew, it does not lapse, and it is imposed on the monks of the churches; and it was disputed concerning the aged elder.

The verse does not specify the amount due upon each head, (p-30) nor the time of its payment. As for its amount, Malik and many scholars of knowledge adopted what ʿUmar prescribed: four dinars upon the people of gold, and forty dirhams upon the people of silver; ʿUmar also imposed hospitality, provisions and clothing. Al-Thawri said: various levies are related from ʿUmar, and I think that was according to his judgement of their hardship and their ease. Al-Shafi'i and others said: one dinar per head. Abu Hanifah said: upon the poor who works, twelve dirhams; upon the moderately well-off, double that; upon the wealthy, double the double, forty-eight dirhams; and according to him nothing is taken from a poor person who has no earnings. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: all this is in the case of a period of respite. As for a settlement, it is what they are reconciled upon, whether little or much. As for its time, according to Abu Hanifah it is the beginning of each year, and according to al-Shafi'i the end of the year. It is called jizyah from jazā yajzī, when one repays what was bestowed upon him, so it is as if they gave it as recompense for the safety they were granted; and it is like the ʿuqdah and the jilsah, and from this meaning is the saying of the poet:
We shall repay you, or praise you; and whoever praises you for what you have done has indeed repaid you.

It was also said: because it is a portion of what the protected people must pay (yajzūhu), that is, they must discharge it.

(Regarding "an yadin"): Ibn ʿAbbas said: they give it with their own hands and do not send it with others. ʿUthman said: they give it in cash, not on credit (nasiʾah). Qatadah said: they give it while their hands are beneath the hand of the one who takes it, so the meaning is that they are subjugated. It was also said: "an iʿtirafin" (in acknowledgment). It was said: "an quwwatin minkum wa qahrin wa dhullin wa nafadhi amrin fihim" (from a position of strength on your part, domination, humiliation, and the enforcement of command over them), as you say: "al-yad fi hadha li-fulan" (the hand in this matter belongs to so-and-so), meaning the authority is his. It was also said: "an inʿamin ʿalayhim bi-dhalika" (as a favor bestowed upon them), because accepting it from them in exchange for their lives is a favor upon them, from the saying: "lahu ʿalayya yad" (he has a yad over me), meaning a favor (niʿmah). Al-Qutabi said: it is said "aʿtahu ʿan yadin" and "ʿan zahri yadin" when one gives him something initiating it, without repaying him. It was also said: "ʿan yadin" means "ʿan jamaʿatin" (from a group), i.e., no one among them of standing is exempted because of his standing. The yad is the group of people; it is said "al-qawmu ʿala yadin wahidatin" (the people are upon one hand), meaning they are united. It was also said: "ʿan yadin" means "ʿan ghina wa qudrah" (from wealth and ability), so it is not taken from the poor. Al-Zamakhshari summarized this, saying: If it means the hand of the one who takes, then the meaning is "until he overpowers it," from a dominating, controlling hand, and from a favor upon them, because accepting the jizyah from them and leaving them their lives is a great favor upon them. And if it means the hand of the one who gives, then the meaning is "from a willing hand, not refusing," because whoever refuses and resists does not give his hand, unlike the obedient, submissive one. For this reason they said: "aʿta bi-yadihi" when he submitted and yielded. Do you not see their saying: "naza`a yadahu ʿan al-taʿah" (he withdrew his hand from obedience)? Or "ʿan yadin ila yadin," meaning in cash, not on credit, or not sent by the hand of another, but "ʿan yadi al-muʿti al-bareedi al-akhidhi" (from the hand of the giver to the taker).

"Wa hum saghirun" is a circumstantial clause (jumlah hāliyyah), meaning: humbled and despised. They mentioned modes of taking it from them and of their humiliation, but the verse does not specify any one of them. Ibn ʿAbbas said: they walk with it while being seized by the collar (mulabbabin). Sulayman al-Farisi said: they are not praised for giving it. ʿIkrimah said: he (the payer) stands while the taker sits. Al-Kalbi said: when they hand it over, it is said to him: "Pay the jizyah," and he is struck on the nape of the neck (yusakku fi qafahu). Al-Baghawi related: he is seized by his beard and struck in his lahzimah (the area beneath the jaw).

﴿And the Jews said, "Ezra is the son of God," and the Christians said, "The Messiah is the son of God." That is their statement from their mouths; they imitate the saying of those who disbelieved before them. May God fight them; how are they deluded?﴾

(p-31) He, exalted is He, made clear that the Jews and Christians are joined with the people of polytheism (shirk), even though the forms of polytheism differ, distinguishing between one who worships an idol and one who worships the Messiah or something else. This is because shirk is taking a deity alongside God. Rather, the worshipper of an idol is less disbelieving than the Christian, because he does not believe that the idol is the Creator of the world, whereas the Christian holds to incarnation (ḥulūl) and union (ittiḥād). Those who said this were a group of Jews who were in Medina.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: Four of their rabbis (aḥbār, scholars of the Jews) said it: Salam ibn Mishkam, Nuʿman ibn Awfa, Shas ibn Qays, and Malik ibn al-Sayf. It was also said: Finhas said it. Al-Naqqash said: No Jew remains who says it; rather, they have died out. A group may be censured or praised for the utterance of something that corresponds to this from some of its members.

It was said: The evidence that this statement was among them is that the verse was recited to them and they neither denied it nor called it false, despite their eagerness to deny. The cause of this statement is that the Jews killed the prophets after Moses, so God removed the Torah from them and erased it from their hearts. Ezra, who was a youth, went wandering in the land, and Gabriel came to him and said, "Where are you going?" He said, "I seek knowledge." So Gabriel made him memorize the Torah, and he dictated it to them from memory, without omitting a single letter. They said, "God gathered the Torah in his breast while he was a youth, only because he is His son." They related narratives about this.

The apparent meaning of the Christians' statement, "The Messiah is the son of God," is sonship of begetting, just as the Arabs said about the angels. Likewise, the statement of al-Dahhak, al-Tabari and others about them implies that the Messiah is a god and that he is the son of God. It is said that some of them believe it to be a sonship of tenderness and mercy. This statement did not appear until after the Muhammadan prophethood and the manifestation of the signs of its truthfulness, and after they mixed with the Muslims and debated with them, whereupon they returned from what they had believed about Jesus.

ʿĀṣim and al-Kisāʾī read "ʿUzayr" with tanwīn, treating it as Arabic. The rest of the seven readers read it without tanwīn, as a proper noun that is not declined (mamnūʿ al-ṣarf) because of its foreignness (ʿujma) and its status as a proper name (ʿalamiyya), like ʿĀdhir, ʿIdhār and ʿAzrāʾīl. In both readings, "ibn" is the predicate (khabar).

Abu ʿUbayd said: It is a foreign word, light in form, so it takes tanwīn like Nuh, Lut and Hud. It was said: His statement is not sound, because it has four letters and is not a diminutive (muṣaghghar). Rather, it is a foreign proper name that came in the form of a diminutive, just as Sulayman came in the form of ʿUthman, and is not a diminutive.

As for one who claims that tanwīn was dropped from "ʿUzayr" because of the meeting of two quiescent letters, like the reading of "Say: He is God, One" (Q. 112:1) and "God, the Eternal Refuge" (Q. 112:2), and the poet's verse:

"When Ghuṭayf al-Sulamī fled"

or because "ibn" is an adjective of "ʿUzayr" placed between two proper nouns so that its tanwīn was dropped, with the predicate omitted, meaning: "Our god and our object of worship" — his statement is strained, because what was denied against them is only the attribution of sonship to God, exalted is He.

The meaning of "with their mouths" is that it is a statement unsupported by proof; it is nothing but an empty utterance that they pronounce, like meaningless words that are only sounds and tones and indicate no meanings. That is because a statement that indicates the meaning of a word is spoken by the mouth, and its meaning affects the heart, whereas what has no meaning is said only by the mouth and nothing more.

It was also said: The meaning of "with their mouths" is to emphasize the saying and to bind them to it, as He said: "They write the Book with their own hands" (Q. 2:79), and "nor a bird that flies with its two wings" (Q. 6:38). There must be an omitted noun in His statement "they imitate" (yuḍāhiʾūn), meaning "the saying of those who disbelieved" (yuḍāhī qawl). "Those who disbelieved" refers to their predecessors, so it is an ancient disbelief among them; or the polytheists who said that the angels are the daughters of God, which is the statement of al-Dahhak. Or the pronoun refers to the Christians, and "those who disbelieved" refers to the Jews; that is, the Christians' statement in their claim of the sonship of Jesus imitates the Jews' statement in their claim of the sonship of Ezra. The Jews are older than the Christians. This is the statement of Qatada.

ʿĀṣim and Ibn Musarrif read "yuḍāhi'ūn" with a hamza, and the rest of the seven readers read it without a hamza.

﴿May God fight them; how are they deluded?﴾: This is a general supplication against them for all kinds of evil, and whoever God fights is one who is fought. Ibn ʿAbbas said: Its meaning is "May God curse them." Abban ibn Taghlib said:

"May God fight her; she blames me, though she knows
that I am the one who ruins and reforms myself."

Qatada said: It means "May He kill them." Ibn al-Anbari mentioned: It means "He opposes them." Al-Naqqash said: The original sense of (qātala) is supplication; then its use became so common that they said it in the sense of wonder, both for good and for evil, while they did not intend supplication. Al-Aṣmaʿī recited:

"May God fight Layla; how she pleases me,
yet I tell people that I do not care for her."

It is not of the pattern of mufāʿala (reciprocal action); rather, it is of the pattern of "ṭāraqtu al-naʿl" (I hammered the sandal) and "ʿāqabtu al-liṣṣ" (I punished the thief).

(annā yu'faku-na): how are they turned away from the truth after the proof has become clear, in the manner of amazement.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verse 31:

﴿They took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah, and the Messiah, son of Maryam.﴾ Here "ittakhadha" (took) is transitive to two objects, and the pronoun refers to the Jews and the Christians. Hudhayfah said: "They did not worship them, but they made lawful for them what was unlawful and so they made it lawful, and they made unlawful for them what was lawful and so they made it unlawful." This has also come in a marfu' (traced to the Prophet ﷺ) report in al-Tirmidhi, from the hadith of 'Adi ibn Hatim. It was also said: they used to prostrate to them as they prostrate to Allah, and prostration is only to be made to Allah, so this was applied to them figuratively. It was also said: He, glorified is He, knew that they believe in incarnation (hulul), that He, glorified is He, manifests Himself in their inner beings, so they prostrate to Him, believing that it is to Allah who has indwelt in them and manifested Himself in their hearts; these, then, took them as lords in reality. The doctrine of hulul spread widely in this community, and they spoke of ittihad (unity with God). It has spread most among the shaykhs of the Sufis and the poor in our time, and I have seen among them a group who claim that they are great ones (akabir). Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi related that it was widespread in his time, and he related it in his tafsir from some of the Marwazis who used to say to their companions: "You are my slaves," and when he was alone with some of the foolish among his followers he claimed divinity. If this is witnessed in this community, how far-fetched is its occurrence among the earlier nations? End of quotation. It is quoted from the book al-Tahrir wa'l-Tahbir. Our shaykh, the hadith scholar and Sufi Qutb al-Din Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn al-Qastallani, composed a book on this group, and he mentioned among them al-Husayn ibn Mansur al-Hallaj; Abu 'Abd Allah al-Shawdhi, who was in Tilimsan; Ibrahim ibn Yusuf ibn Muhammad ibn Dahhan, known as Ibn al-Mar'ah; Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Ahla, the one who took the title "Lurqa"; Abu 'Abd Allah ibn al-'Arabi al-Ta'i; 'Umar ibn 'Ali ibn al-Farid; 'Abd al-Haqq ibn Sab'in; Abu'l-Hasan al-Shushtari, from among his companions; Ibn Mutarrif al-A'ma, from among the companions of Ibn Ahla; al-Sufayfir, also from his companions; and al-'Afif al-Tilimsani. He mentioned in his book of their states, speech and poetry what indicates this doctrine. Sultan Abu 'Abd Allah ibn al-Ahmar, king of al-Andalus, killed al-Sufayfir in Gharnata and crucified him. I have seen al-'Afif al-Kufi, and he recited to me some of his poetry, and he used to conceal this doctrine. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Ayki, shaykh of the khanqah of Sa'id al-Su'ada', was in close association with him, a great deal of mixing, and he was accused of this doctrine. Al-Tilimsani fled from Cairo to al-Sham out of fear of being killed for zandaqah (heresy). As for the Ubaydid kings in the Maghrib and Egypt, their followers believe in their divinity; the first of them was 'Ubayd Allah, titled al-Mahdi, and the last of them was Sulayman, titled al-'Adid. The rabbis (al-ahbar) are the scholars of the Jews, and the monks (al-ruhban) are the worshippers of the Christians who renounced the world and withdrew from people into monasteries. He reported about the collective, and each returned to what suits it; that is, the Jews took their rabbis, and the Christians their monks.

﴿And the Messiah, son of Maryam﴾ is conjoined (atf) to "ruhbanahum" (their monks).

﴿Yet they were only commanded to worship one God; there is no god but He; glorified is He above what they associate﴾. The apparent reading is that the pronoun refers to whatever it referred to in "ittakhadhu" (they took); that is, they were commanded in the Torah and the Gospel through the tongues of their prophets. It was also said: in the Qur'an, through the tongue of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. It was also said: in the three books. It was also said: in the revealed books, and through the tongues of all the prophets. Al-Zamakhshari said: the proofs of reason and the texts in the Gospel and of the Messiah, peace be upon him, commanded them with this, that whoever associates others with Allah, Allah has forbidden him Paradise. It was also said: the pronoun refers to the rabbis and monks who were taken as lords; that is, they too were commanded only to worship Allah and affirm His oneness, so how could they be lords when they are commanded and made to serve? In His saying "what they associate" there is an indication that the term shirk is applied to the Jews and the Christians.

[p. 33] Their similitude, and the similitude of their condition in seeking to nullify the prophethood (*nubuwwah*) of Muhammad (ﷺ) by denying it, is like that of one who wants to blow upon a great light spread across the horizons. The light of Allah is His guidance, which proceeds from the Qur'an and the widely disseminated divine law (*sharī'ah*). Because He called it a light, He called the attempt to corrupt it "extinguishing." A group said: the light is the Qur'an, and He used "mouths" as a metaphor for their lack of means and their weakness. He informed that they attempt a grave matter with feeble effort, so the extinguishing was by blowing with the mouth. It is possible that it refers to statements without proof, which do not go beyond the mouths to reach the understanding of a listener, and the mention of extinguishing suited the mention of mouths. It was said: Allah did not mention a saying linked with mouths and tongues except that it is falsehood. The coming of *illā* (إلّا) after *wa-ya'bā* (وَيَأْبى) indicates an omitted object of exception, because it is an affirmative verb, and an affirmative verb is not followed by *illā*; you do not say, "I disliked except Zayd." The supplied object of exception is: "and Allah refuses everything except that He perfect (His light)," as said by al-Zajjāj. ʿAlī ibn Sulaymān said: this is permissible with *abā* (أبى) because it expresses prohibition and refusal, so it resembles negation. al-Kirmānī said: the meaning of *abā* here is "does not accept, except that He perfect His light by the continuance of His religion until the Hour (Resurrection) comes." al-Farrā' said: *illā* entered because there is an element of negation (*juhd*) in the speech. al-Zamakhsharī said: he treated *abā* as if it were in the position of "did not want." Do you not see how *yurīdūna an yutfi'ū* (يُرِيدُونَ أنْ يُطْفِئُوا) was paired with *wa-ya'bā Allāhu* (وَيَأْبى اللَّهُ), and how it was placed in the position of "and Allah does not want except that He perfect His light"?

﴿It is He who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, that He may make it prevail over all religion, even though the polytheists dislike it.﴾ "He" refers to Muhammad ﷺ. (Al-Huda) means: monotheism (al-tawhid), or the Qur'an, or the explanation of the obligatory duties (al-fara'id), three opinions. (Din al-haqq) means: Islam, as in ﴿Indeed, the religion in the sight of Allah is Islam﴾ [Al 'Imran: 19]. The apparent view is that the pronoun in (liyuzhirahu, "that He may make it prevail") refers to the Messenger ﷺ, because he is the one being spoken of. Here "the religion" (al-din) is a genus, meaning: that He may raise him above the followers of all religions. So there is an elided word (hadhf mudaf), i.e., "the people of all religions." Accordingly, his community (ﷺ) overcame the Jews and expelled them from the lands of the Arabs, overcame the Christians in the lands of the Levant up to the region of the Romans and the West, overcame the Magians (Majus) and took their kingdom, and overcame the idol-worshippers in many of their lands adjoining the Turks and India. The same holds for all other religions. It has also been said: the meaning is that He informs him of the laws of the religion, so that nothing of it remains hidden from him; thus "the religion" here means the Shari'ah that he brought. Al-Shafi'i said: Allah made His Messenger ﷺ prevail over the religions by making clear to everyone who heard him that it is the truth, and that whatever opposes it among the religions is falsehood. It has also been said: the pronoun refers to "the religion." Abu Hurayrah, al-Baqir and Jabir ibn Abd Allah said: the prevalence of the religion will occur at the descent of Jesus son of Mary, when all religions return to the religion of Islam. It is as if this group understood it to mean that it prevails in its most complete forms, so that no other religion remains alongside it. Another group said: it means that He makes it the highest and most manifest, and if there is any other religion alongside it, it will be beneath it. According to this view, the descent of Jesus is not needed; rather, this was in the early period of the community, and it remains so, God willing. Al-Suddi said: this will occur at the emergence of the Mahdi, when no one remains except that he enters Islam and pays the kharaj (the land tax). It has also been said: it is specific to the Arabian Peninsula, and this has been accomplished, since He left no unbeliever in it. It has also been said: it is specific to the approach of the Hour, for then people will return to the religion of their fathers. It has also been said: that He may make it prevail through proof and clear explanation. This view has been deemed weak, because that was already the case at the beginning of the matter.

It has also been said: the verse was revealed on account of a specific occasion, namely that the Quraysh had two journeys: the winter journey to Yemen and the summer journey to the Levant and the two Iraqs. When they embraced Islam, both journeys were cut off because of the difference in religion and land. They mentioned this to the Messenger ﷺ, and this verse was revealed. The meaning, then, is: that He may make it prevail over all religion in the lands of the two journeys. This has happened: the people of Yemen, the Levant and the two Iraqs embraced Islam. In a hadith: "The earth was folded up for me, so I was shown its eastern and western parts, and the dominion of my community will reach what was folded up for me of it." Some scholars said: for this reason Islam spread in the East and the West, but did not spread in the South. End of quotation. Especially in our time, the spread of Islam in the East is such that little unbelief remains there; indeed, most of the Tatars and Khitai Turks and everyone who had opposed Islam have embraced it and entered the religion of Allah in multitudes, praise be to Allah.

(p-34) The polytheists (al-mushrikun) are mentioned specifically here because the dislike in this context is specific to the manifestation of the religion of Muhammad ﷺ, whereas the unbelievers (al-kafirun) were mentioned earlier because that dislike concerns the perfecting of the light of Allah in ancient times. The remainder of it encompasses the disbelievers from the creation of the world until its end. The dislike and the perfecting have occurred many times.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verses 34–35 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿O you who believe, indeed many of the rabbis and monks devour the wealth of people in falsehood and bar [them] from the way of Allah. And those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in the way of Allah, give them tidings of a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿On the Day it will be heated in the fire of Hell, and their foreheads, their sides and their backs will be branded with it: "This is what you hoarded for yourselves, so taste what you used to hoard."﴾ ﴿Indeed the number of months with Allah is twelve months in the Book of Allah, from the day He created the heavens and the earth; of them four are sacred. That is the upright religion, so do not wrong yourselves therein. And fight the polytheists all together, as they fight you all together, and know that Allah is with the God-fearing.﴾ [At-Tawbah: 36] ﴿Indeed the postponement (al-nasi') is an increase in disbelief by which those who disbelieve are led astray. They make it lawful one year and make it unlawful another year, to match the number of what Allah has made unlawful, so they make lawful what Allah has made unlawful. The evil of their deeds has been made attractive to them. And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.﴾ [At-Tawbah: 37] ﴿O you who believe, what is the matter with you that when it is said to you, "Go forth in the way of Allah," you cling heavily to the earth? Are you content with the life of this world rather than the Hereafter? The enjoyment of the life of this world, compared with the Hereafter, is but little.﴾ [At-Tawbah: 38] ﴿If you do not go forth, He will punish you with a painful punishment and replace you with another people, and you will not harm Him at all. And Allah is competent over all things.﴾ [At-Tawbah: 39] ﴿If you do not support him, Allah has already supported him when those who disbelieved expelled him, the second of two. (p-35) The root of kanz (hoarding) in the language is gathering and accumulating, and it is not restricted to gold and silver. [A poet] said:

*"May my good fortune not be good if I feed their destitute the dregs of al-Hatti, while with me stored wheat is kept."*

They also said: "A man is mukhtanaz al-khuluq," meaning his character is gathered together (self-contained). And the rajiz (rajaz poet) said:

*"Upon a strong one whose flesh is compact, who spent the night stirring me to the journeys' stages."*

Then its use became, by custom, restricted to buried gold and silver. Al-kayy (branding) is well known; it is the application of something hot to a part of the body until the skin tears. Al-jabhah (forehead) is well known; it is the upper surface of the face. Al-ghar (cave) is well known; it is a hollow in a mountain in which one can hide. Ibn Faris said: al-ghar is a cave; al-ghar is a fragrant plant; al-ghar is a group; and al-gharan are the belly and the private parts. *Thabbatahu 'an al-amr* means he delayed him from the matter, made him slow to it; and *naqah thabtah* means a slow-moving she-camel. The origin of *tathbit* is obstruction, which is to come between a person and a matter he wants, by making him averse to it. Al-zahaq means to come out with difficulty. Al-Zajjaj said: with a kasra (zahiq), it refers to the departure of the soul. Al-Kisa'i and al-Mubarrad said: *zahaqat nafsuhu* and *zahiqat* are two dialects. Al-zahaq also means destruction, and *zahaqa al-hajar min tahti hafir al-dabbah* means the stone flew out from under the animal's hoof when it slipped. Al-zahud means distance, and al-zahud is a deep well with a wide mouth. Al-maljaʾ is a place-noun (*maf'al*) from *laja'a ila kadha*, meaning he took refuge and withdrew to it; and *alja'tuhu ila kadha* means I compelled him to it. Jamaha means he fled rapidly; from their saying, "a jamuh horse," that is, one whose bridle does not restrain it when it charges. [A poet] said:

*"Swift and galloping, and its charge is like the crackling of a blazing palm-frond."*

Muhalhil said:

*"I have charged fiercely into their blood until I saw the bodies of their owners grow stiff."*

Another said:

*"When your women are drawn to him, he is a stallion, as if he were a tightly stretched rope."*

Jamaza means he leapt; it is also said to mean the same as jamaha. Ru'bah said:

*"I brought my neck and my jumping close together."*

Al-lamz: al-Layth said it is like al-ghamz (winking) in the face. Al-Jawhari said it is fault-finding, and its origin is pointing with the eye and the like. Al-Azhari said the origin of al-lamz is pushing; *lamaztuhu* means I pushed him. Al-gharm: its origin is the obligation of what is burdensome, and al-gharam is a hard punishment; love (ʿishq) was called gharam because it is burdensome and binding.

﴿O you who believe, indeed many of the rabbis and monks devour the wealth of people in falsehood and bar [them] from the way of Allah, and those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in the way of Allah, give them tidings of a painful punishment.﴾ When He mentioned that they had taken their rabbis and monks as lords besides Allah, He mentioned what many of them do, as a belittling of their standing and a degrading of them, and that such people should not be honored, let alone taken as lords, because of what they contain of devouring people's wealth in falsehood and barring [people] from the way of Allah. They are included in the general sense of "those who hoard gold and silver," so they combined the two blameworthy traits: devouring wealth in falsehood, and hoarding wealth by refusing to spend it in the way of Allah. Their devouring of wealth in falsehood is taking from their followers' wealth taxes under the name of churches and synagogues, and other things by which they lead them to believe that spending on them is part of the Law and a drawing near to Allah. They also keep those funds locked away, like the monk whose hoard Salman (may Allah be pleased with him) uncovered. And just as they take bribes in legal rulings, such as the pretense of protecting their religion. Their barring [people] from the way of Allah is [barring them from] the religion of Islam and following the Messenger. It has been said that it means injustice in judgment. The verb *yasudduna* may be transitive, which is more emphatic in censure, and it may be intransitive.

The majority read *wa-alladhina* with a *waw*, which is general and includes Muslims who hoard. It is a subject (mubtada') that carries the meaning of a condition, and for this reason the *fa* appears in its predicate in His words *fa-bashshirhum* ("so give them tidings"). It has been said that *wa-alladhina yaknizuna* describes a number of the rabbis and monks. This view was narrated from Uthman and Mu'awiyah (may Allah be pleased with them). It has also been said that it is a new sentence intended for those among the Muslims who withhold zakat; this was narrated from al-Suddi. The apparent meaning is generality, as we have stated: it links hoarders among the Muslims with the bribe-takers among the rabbis and monks, as an intensification and an indication that they are equal in the announcement of punishment. Generality was narrated from Abu Dharr and others. Ibn Musarrif read *alladhina* without a *waw*, which apparently makes it a description of those mentioned earlier, and it allows the reading of a new sentence and generality. The apparent meaning is the censure of one who hoards and does not spend in the way of Allah. As for what has come in censure of one who leaves gold and silver (*safra'* and *bayda'*) unspent, and that he will be branded with it, and other hadiths, that was before zakat was made obligatory. The threat concerning hoarding applies only to withholding the rights due from it. For this reason many scholars said: hoarding is wealth whose zakat is not paid, even if it is on the surface of the earth. As for buried wealth whose zakat has been paid, it is not hoarding. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whatever zakat you have paid on, it is not hoarding." And it was narrated from Umar that he said to a man who had sold land: "Secure your money that you received; dig a hole for it under your wife's bed." The man said: "Is that not hoarding?" He said: "What its zakat has been paid on is not hoarding." The same was narrated from Ibn Umar, Ikrimah, al-Sha'bi, al-Suddi, Malik, and the majority of the people of knowledge.

Ali said: four thousand and what is below it is spending, and whatever exceeds it is hoarding, even if its zakat is paid. Abu Dharr and a group with him said: whatever exceeds a man's needs for himself is hoarding. These two statements imply that the censure applies to the category of wealth itself, not only to withholding zakat. Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz said: it was abrogated by His words, "Take from their wealth a charity" [At-Tawbah: 103], so the obligation of zakat came upon all of this. It is as if the verse included: "Do not gather wealth lest you be punished," and then the confirmation in His words, "Take from their wealth a charity" [At-Tawbah: 103], abrogated it. Allah the Exalted is too generous to gather wealth against His servant from a source He has permitted him, and then, having had its obligation paid from it on his behalf, punish him. Many of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them all), such as Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf and Talhah ibn Ubayd Allah, kept wealth and managed it, and no one among those who turned away from fitnah criticized them, because turning away is a choice of what is better and more conducive to piety and to asceticism in this world. Keeping wealth is permissible with wide latitude, and its possessor is not blamed. What was narrated from Ali is a statement about what is better.

I have translated this passage, though I should flag a problem with the request first: the passage contains a mix of Qur'anic quotations, hadith, and grammatical discussion, and I'm producing it as a faithful rendering of the Arabic text.

**Translation:**

And Abu al-Sammal and Yahya ibn Ya'mar read *yukanziyuna* with a *ḍamma* on the *yāʾ*. He singled out gold and silver from among all other wealth, because they are the measures (*qiyam*) of wealth and its prices (*athman*). They are hoarded only from surplus and in abundance, and whoever hoards them has not been deprived of the other kinds of wealth, and hoarding them indicates what is other than them.

The pronoun in *wa-la yunfiqūnahā* ("and do not spend it") refers to gold, because its feminine gender is more common, or to silver, and in these two opinions the coordinated term is omitted. Or it refers to both of them, taking into account that each contains varieties, so the meaning is observed, as in His saying: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight⦌ [al-Ḥujurāt: 9]. Or because they both contain a collection of dinars and dirhams. Or it refers to the things hoarded, as indicated by *yakniznūna*. Or to wealth. Or to the spending (*nafaqa*), which is the verbal noun implied by *wa-la yunfiqūnahā*. Or to the zakat, meaning: "and they do not pay the zakat of wealth." These are the opinions.

Many exegetes said: it refers to one of the two, as in His saying: ﴿And when they see a trade or a diversion⦌ [al-Jumuʿa: 11], but this is not similar, because that is coordination with *aw* (or), and the rule for *aw* is that the pronoun returns to one of the two coordinated items, unlike *wa* (and). The exception is if one claims that the *wāw* in *wa-l-fiḍḍa* ("and silver") means *aw* so that it works out, but this goes against the apparent meaning.

﴿On the Day when it will be heated in the fire of Hell, and their foreheads, sides, and backs will be branded with it. "This is what you hoarded for yourselves, so taste what you used to hoard."⦌

It is said: *ḥamaytu al-ḥadīda fī al-nār*, meaning I kindled the fire upon it so that it would be heated, and one says *aḥmaytuhā*, meaning I put it in so that it would also be heated, and it became hot. The majority read ﴿yuḥmā ʿalayhā⦌ with *yāʾ*; its original form is *yuḥmī al-nār ʿalayhā* (they will heat the fire upon it). When the object that has not been named as subject was omitted and the verb was attributed to the prepositional phrase, the *tāʾ* was not attached, as you say: *rafaʿtu al-qiṣṣa ilā al-amīr* (I raised the matter to the emir). When the matter is omitted and the prepositional phrase takes its place, you say: *ruffiʿa ilā al-amīr*. That this was originally attributed to the fire is shown by the reading of al-Ḥasan and Ibn ʿĀmir in one narration, *tuḥmā* with *tāʾ*. It was said: whoever reads with *yāʾ*, the meaning is that the fuel is heated; whoever reads with *tāʾ*, the meaning is that the fire is heated. It is the verb that governs *yawm alīm* (a painful day), or it is implied and explained by *ʿadhāb* (punishment), meaning: they will be punished on the day it is heated.

Abu Haywa read *fa-yukwā* with *yāʾ*, since what it is attributed to has a real feminine form, and a separation also occurred, which was mentioned. Some people assimilated *jibāhuhum* (their foreheads), and this is narrated from Abu ʿAmr, in the major assimilation (*idghām al-kabīr*), as *manāsikakum* and *mā salakakum* were assimilated. These places were singled out for branding. It was said: because the forehead is the most disgraceful place, and the side and back are the most painful. It was said: because they are hollow, so the heat reaches their insides, unlike the hand and foot. It was said: its meaning is that they are branded on the three directions: their fronts, their backs, and their sides. It was said: when they sought wealth and status, God disfigured their faces, and when they turned away from the poor when he sat with them, their backs were branded. Al-Zamakhshari said: because they did not seek, with their wealth, anything other than worldly aims, when they did not spend it in the way of God, except worldly purposes of prestige among people and advancement, and that the water of their faces should be preserved among them, being received with courtesy, greeted with honor, and held in awe; and from eating good things of which they fill themselves, and puffing out their sides; and from wearing soft fine garments which they throw over their backs, as you see the rich of your time: these are their aims and desires from their wealth. They do not bring to mind the saying of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "The people of wealth have gone off with the rewards." It was said: because whenever they saw the poor they frowned, and whenever a gathering brought them together with him they turned away from him, turned aside with their sides, and turned their backs.

The verb is implied in *hādhā mā kanaztum* ("this is what you hoarded"), meaning: it will be said to them at the time of branding. The reference of *hādhā* is to the hoarded wealth, or it is a reference to the branding, with an omitted modifier from *mā kanaztum*, meaning: this branding is the consequence of what you hoarded, or the fruit of what you hoarded. The meaning of *li-anfusikum* is: so that your selves might benefit from it and be pleased, and it became a punishment for you. This statement is a rebuke to them. *Fa-dhūqū mā kuntum* means: the evil consequence of the wealth which you used to hoard. It is permissible for *mā* to be a verbal (*maṣdariyya*) particle, meaning: the evil consequence of your being hoarders. It was read *yaknuzūna* with a *ḍamma* on the *nūn*.

In the hadith of Abu Dharr: "Give glad tidings to the hoarders of a heated stone in the fire of Hell, which will be placed on the nipples of their breasts, and it will shake them, and their foreheads, sides and backs will be branded, until the heat meets inside them." In the Sahih of al-Bukhari and the Sahih of Muslim: "The severe threat is for the withholder of zakat."

And just as they take bribes in legal rulings, such as the pretense of protecting their religion. Their barring [people] from the way of Allah is [barring them from] the religion of Islam and following the Messenger. It has been said that it means injustice in judgment. The verb *yasudduna* may be transitive, which is more emphatic in censure, and it may be intransitive.

The majority read *wa-alladhina* with a *waw*, which is general and includes Muslims who hoard. It is a subject (mubtada') that carries the meaning of a condition, and for this reason the *fa* appears in its predicate in His words *fa-bashshirhum* ("so give them tidings"). It has been said that *wa-alladhina yaknizuna* describes a number of the rabbis and monks. This view was narrated from Uthman and Mu'awiyah (may Allah be pleased with them). It has also been said that it is a new sentence intended for those among the Muslims who withhold zakat; this was narrated from al-Suddi. The apparent meaning is generality, as we have stated: it links hoarders among the Muslims with the bribe-takers among the rabbis and monks, as an intensification and an indication that they are equal in the announcement of punishment. Generality was narrated from Abu Dharr and others. Ibn Musarrif read *alladhina* without a *waw*, which apparently makes it a description of those mentioned earlier, and it allows the reading of a new sentence and generality. The apparent meaning is the censure of one who hoards and does not spend in the way of Allah. As for what has come in censure of one who leaves gold and silver (*safra'* and *bayda'*) unspent, and that he will be branded with it, and other hadiths, that was before zakat was made obligatory. The threat concerning hoarding applies only to withholding the rights due from it. For this reason many scholars said: hoarding is wealth whose zakat is not paid, even if it is on the surface of the earth. As for buried wealth whose zakat has been paid, it is not hoarding. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whatever zakat you have paid on, it is not hoarding." And it was narrated from Umar that he said to a man who had sold land: "Secure your money that you received; dig a hole for it under your wife's bed." The man said: "Is that not hoarding?" He said: "What its zakat has been paid on is not hoarding." The same was narrated from Ibn Umar, Ikrimah, al-Sha'bi, al-Suddi, Malik, and the majority of the people of knowledge.

Ali said: four thousand and what is below it is spending, and whatever exceeds it is hoarding, even if its zakat is paid. Abu Dharr and a group with him said: whatever exceeds a man's needs for himself is hoarding. These two statements imply that the censure applies to the category of wealth itself, not only to withholding zakat. Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz said: it was abrogated by His words, "Take from their wealth a charity" [At-Tawbah: 103], so the obligation of zakat came upon all of this. It is as if the verse included: "Do not gather wealth lest you be punished," and then the confirmation in His words, "Take from their wealth a charity" [At-Tawbah: 103], abrogated it. Allah the Exalted is too generous to gather wealth against His servant from a source He has permitted him, and then, having had its obligation paid from it on his behalf, punish him. Many of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them all), such as Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf and Talhah ibn Ubayd Allah, kept wealth and managed it, and no one among those who turned away from fitnah criticized them, because turning away is a choice of what is better and more conducive to piety and to asceticism in this world. Keeping wealth is permissible with wide latitude, and its possessor is not blamed. What was narrated from Ali is a statement about what is better.

I have translated this passage, though I should flag a problem with the request first: the passage contains a mix of Qur'anic quotations, hadith, and grammatical discussion, and I'm producing it as a faithful rendering of the Arabic text.

**Translation:**

And Abu al-Sammal and Yahya ibn Ya'mar read *yukanziyuna* with a *ḍamma* on the *yāʾ*. He singled out gold and silver from among all other wealth, because they are the measures (*qiyam*) of wealth and its prices (*athman*). They are hoarded only from surplus and in abundance, and whoever hoards them has not been deprived of the other kinds of wealth, and hoarding them indicates what is other than them.

The pronoun in *wa-la yunfiqūnahā* ("and do not spend it") refers to gold, because its feminine gender is more common, or to silver, and in these two opinions the coordinated term is omitted. Or it refers to both of them, taking into account that each contains varieties, so the meaning is observed, as in His saying: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight⦌ [al-Ḥujurāt: 9]. Or because they both contain a collection of dinars and dirhams. Or it refers to the things hoarded, as indicated by *yakniznūna*. Or to wealth. Or to the spending (*nafaqa*), which is the verbal noun implied by *wa-la yunfiqūnahā*. Or to the zakat, meaning: "and they do not pay the zakat of wealth." These are the opinions.

Many exegetes said: it refers to one of the two, as in His saying: ﴿And when they see a trade or a diversion⦌ [al-Jumuʿa: 11], but this is not similar, because that is coordination with *aw* (or), and the rule for *aw* is that the pronoun returns to one of the two coordinated items, unlike *wa* (and). The exception is if one claims that the *wāw* in *wa-l-fiḍḍa* ("and silver") means *aw* so that it works out, but this goes against the apparent meaning.

﴿On the Day when it will be heated in the fire of Hell, and their foreheads, sides, and backs will be branded with it. "This is what you hoarded for yourselves, so taste what you used to hoard."⦌

It is said: *ḥamaytu al-ḥadīda fī al-nār*, meaning I kindled the fire upon it so that it would be heated, and one says *aḥmaytuhā*, meaning I put it in so that it would also be heated, and it became hot. The majority read ﴿yuḥmā ʿalayhā⦌ with *yāʾ*; its original form is *yuḥmī al-nār ʿalayhā* (they will heat the fire upon it). When the object that has not been named as subject was omitted and the verb was attributed to the prepositional phrase, the *tāʾ* was not attached, as you say: *rafaʿtu al-qiṣṣa ilā al-amīr* (I raised the matter to the emir). When the matter is omitted and the prepositional phrase takes its place, you say: *ruffiʿa ilā al-amīr*. That this was originally attributed to the fire is shown by the reading of al-Ḥasan and Ibn ʿĀmir in one narration, *tuḥmā* with *tāʾ*. It was said: whoever reads with *yāʾ*, the meaning is that the fuel is heated; whoever reads with *tāʾ*, the meaning is that the fire is heated. It is the verb that governs *yawm alīm* (a painful day), or it is implied and explained by *ʿadhāb* (punishment), meaning: they will be punished on the day it is heated.

Abu Haywa read *fa-yukwā* with *yāʾ*, since what it is attributed to has a real feminine form, and a separation also occurred, which was mentioned. Some people assimilated *jibāhuhum* (their foreheads), and this is narrated from Abu ʿAmr, in the major assimilation (*idghām al-kabīr*), as *manāsikakum* and *mā salakakum* were assimilated. These places were singled out for branding. It was said: because the forehead is the most disgraceful place, and the side and back are the most painful. It was said: because they are hollow, so the heat reaches their insides, unlike the hand and foot. It was said: its meaning is that they are branded on the three directions: their fronts, their backs, and their sides. It was said: when they sought wealth and status, God disfigured their faces, and when they turned away from the poor when he sat with them, their backs were branded. Al-Zamakhshari said: because they did not seek, with their wealth, anything other than worldly aims, when they did not spend it in the way of God, except worldly purposes of prestige among people and advancement, and that the water of their faces should be preserved among them, being received with courtesy, greeted with honor, and held in awe; and from eating good things of which they fill themselves, and puffing out their sides; and from wearing soft fine garments which they throw over their backs, as you see the rich of your time: these are their aims and desires from their wealth. They do not bring to mind the saying of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "The people of wealth have gone off with the rewards." It was said: because whenever they saw the poor they frowned, and whenever a gathering brought them together with him they turned away from him, turned aside with their sides, and turned their backs.

The verb is implied in *hādhā mā kanaztum* ("this is what you hoarded"), meaning: it will be said to them at the time of branding. The reference of *hādhā* is to the hoarded wealth, or it is a reference to the branding, with an omitted modifier from *mā kanaztum*, meaning: this branding is the consequence of what you hoarded, or the fruit of what you hoarded. The meaning of *li-anfusikum* is: so that your selves might benefit from it and be pleased, and it became a punishment for you. This statement is a rebuke to them. *Fa-dhūqū mā kuntum* means: the evil consequence of the wealth which you used to hoard. It is permissible for *mā* to be a verbal (*maṣdariyya*) particle, meaning: the evil consequence of your being hoarders. It was read *yaknuzūna* with a *ḍamma* on the *nūn*.

In the hadith of Abu Dharr: "Give glad tidings to the hoarders of a heated stone in the fire of Hell, which will be placed on the nipples of their breasts, and it will shake them, and their foreheads, sides and backs will be branded, until the heat meets inside them." In the Sahih of al-Bukhari and the Sahih of Muslim: "The severe threat is for the withholder of zakat."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verses 36–37 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve months in the Book of Allah, from the day He created the heavens and the earth. Four of them are sacred. That is the upright religion. So do not wrong yourselves therein. Fight the polytheists all together, as they fight you all together. And know that Allah is with the God-fearing.﴾

The Arabs had no livelihood for most of them except through raids and the practice of their weapons. So when the four sacred months came in succession, it was hard for them and they became impoverished. The Banu Fuqaym of Kinanah were people of religion who adhered to the law of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). From among them, al-Qalammas, who was Hudhayfah ibn Ubayd ibn Fuqaym, was appointed, and he postponed (nasa'a) the months for the Arabs. Then he was succeeded in this by his son Abbad, then his son Qala', then his son Umayyah, then his son Awf, then his son Junadah ibn Awf, and upon this (practice) Islam came.

When the Arabs had finished their Hajj, whoever among them wished would come to him gathered together and say: "Postpone for us a month," meaning: "Shift the sanctity of the Muharram away from us and place it in Safar." So the Muharram would be made lawful for them, and they would raid in it and live. Then they would observe the sanctity of Safar so as to match the number of the four months.
