**"Until"** (*hatta*) is a limit (*ghayah*) to what the interrogative (*al-istifham*) implies. That is: it was not for you to permit them until it became clear who had the excuse. This is how al-Hawfi (*al-Hawfi*) estimated it. Abu al-Baqa' said: *hatta yatabayyana* is connected to an omitted element indicated by the context, its estimate being: "Why did you not delay them until it became clear," or "so that it might become clear." His words "Why did you permit them" indicate the omitted element. *Hatta* cannot be connected to *adhinta*, because that would require that he permitted them up to this limit, or for the purpose of clarifying, and this is not something one is blamed for. End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari's commentary on His words ﴿May God pardon you! Why did you permit them?﴾ is something that must be discarded altogether, let alone quoted and then refuted.

His words **"those who spoke the truth"** mean: in their request for permission. And "that if you had not permitted them, they would have gone out with you." **"And that you would know the liars"**: he means, in that they asked your permission, showing you that they would stop at your limit, while they were liars, and had already resolved on disobedience, whether you permitted them or not. Al-Tabari said: *hatta ta'lama al-sadiqin* means until you know those who speak the truth that they have an excuse, and *ta'lama al-kadhibin* means know the liars who have no excuse. Qatada said: after this verse, the verse of al-Nur was revealed: ﴿So when they ask your permission for some matter of theirs, give permission to whomever of them you wish﴾ [al-Nur 24:62]. This is an error, because al-Nur was revealed in the fourth year of the Hijra, at the Battle of the Trench, concerning the permission some believers sought from the Messenger for some of their affairs in their homes at certain times, and God allowed him to grant it. Thus the two verses differ in time and in meaning.

﴿Those who believe in God and the Last Day do not ask your permission to strive with their wealth and their selves. And God knows the righteous.﴾ (p-48) Ibn Abbas said: "they do not ask your permission" means after the Battle of Tabuk. Al-Jumhur said it is not so, because what comes before this verse and what follows it was revealed concerning the story of Tabuk. The apparent meaning is that the object of the asking of permission is "to strive" (*an yujahidu*). That is: it is not the custom of believers to ask you permission to strive. The sincere ones among the Emigrants and the Helpers never asked the Prophet (ﷺ) for permission, and they would say: "We will certainly strive with him with our wealth and our selves." It has also been said: the estimate is: the believers do not ask your permission to go out or to stay back out of reluctance to strive; rather, when you command something, they rush to it, and asking permission at that time would be a sign of hypocrisy. His words **"And God knows the righteous"** are a testimony to them that they are counted among the righteous, and a promise to them of the greatest reward.

﴿Only those ask your permission who do not believe in God and the Last Day, and whose hearts are in doubt, so they waver in their doubt﴾: they are the hypocrites, and they were thirty-nine men. *Irtabat* means "doubted." *Yataraddadun* means "they are bewildered," unable to find a path to guidance; at times it occurs to them that the Messenger's matter is true, and at other times the opposite occurs to them.

﴿Had they wished to go out, they would have prepared for it some provision. But God disliked their dispatch, so He held them back, and it was said: "Sit with those who sit."﴾ Ibn Abbas said: *uddatan* means provisions of food and water and a mount, since their journey was far in a time of intense heat. Their not preparing provision is evidence that they intended to stay behind. Others said they were able to obtain the provision and the equipment. Al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn Abbas: the *uddah* is the sincere intention in striving. Al-Tabari related: it is everything prepared for fighting, of provision and weapons. Muhammad ibn Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan and his son Mu'awiya read *udd* with a *damma* on the *ayn* and without a *ta'*. Al-Farra' said the *ta'* drops because of the *idafa* (construct genitive), and he took as an example *wa-iqam al-salat*, meaning *wa-iqamat al-salat*. This occurs in several verses of Arabic poetry, but one does not make it a rule; we stop at what has been heard. Sahib al-Lawami said: when he added (the noun), the pronominal suffix took the place of the *ta'* and so it was dropped, because *udd* without a *ta'* is a pimple that appears on the face (the word here being the same root as the *ta'*-less form). Abu Hatim said it is a plural of *uddah*, like *burrah* and *burr*, *durrah* and *durr*, and the proper form would be *uddad*, but it does not agree with the Qur'anic script. Zirr ibn Hubaysh and Aban from Asim read *iddah* with a *kasra* on the *ayn* and the pronominal suffix *ha'*. Ibn Atiyya said: in my view it is a noun for what is prepared, like *dhabh* (slaughter) and *qatl* (killing) for the act of counting, and it was called *qatl* because it is necessary that it be killed. It was also read *iddatan* with a *kasra* on the *ayn* and with a *ta'* without an *idafa*, meaning "a provision of food and weapons," or "something they possess," derived from *al-adad* (number).

Because the sentence includes the negation of going out and of preparing, and was followed by *lakin* (but), and *lakin* only occurs between two opposites, or two contraries, or two disagreements with a disagreement in them, not between two things in agreement, while what follows *lakin* in apparent meaning matches what precedes it...

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "What is the position of the particle of contrast (*harf al-istidrak*)?" I say: since His words "Had they wished to go out" gave the meaning of negating their going out and their preparation for the raid, it was said "But God disliked their dispatch," as if it were said: "They did not go out, but they held back from going out because God disliked their being dispatched," as you would say: "How kindly Zayd treated me, but he harmed me." End quote. But the verse is not similar to this example, because in the example *lakin* falls between two opposites, whereas in the verse *lakin* falls between two things that agree in meaning. *Al-inbi'ath* is setting out and rising. Ibn Abbas said: *fa-thabbatahum* means their laziness and the slackening of their intentions held them back. The verb *qila* (it was said) is in the passive, so it may be that the speaking refers to the Messenger's permission to them to stay behind, or the saying of some of them to others, either verbally or in meaning, or it refers to God's word in His prior decree. Al-Zamakhshari said: He made God's placing in their hearts the dislike of going out an order to stay behind. It has also been said it is from the whispering of Satan. He said: If you ask, "How is it permissible for God to place in their souls dislike of going out to the raid, when it is ugly, and God is exalted above inspiring what is ugly?" I say: their going out was a corruption, because of His words: ﴿Had they gone out with you, they would have added nothing to you but corruption﴾ (p-49), so placing dislike of that going out in their souls was good and a benefit. End quote.

This question and answer follow the Mu'tazilite approach (*al-i'tizal*) concerning corruption and benefit. This statement is a rebuke of them and a belittling, and it places them with the women, the children and the infirm, whose nature is to sit and remain in the houses. They are "those who sit" (*al-qa'idun*), "those who stay behind" (*al-khalifun*) and "the remaining ones" (*al-khawalif*). This is clarified by His words: ﴿They were content to be with the remaining ones﴾ [al-Tawba 9:87]. Sitting here is an expression for holding back and delay, as the poet said:

*Leave noble deeds, do not journey toward their pursuit;*
*sit, for you are the one who eats and is clothed.*

﴿Had they gone out with you, they would have added nothing to you but corruption, and they would have hurried between your ranks, seeking to cause you sedition. And among you are listeners to them. And God knows the wrongdoers.﴾ When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out, he pitched his army at the Thaniyyat al-Wada'. Abd Allah ibn Ubayy pitched his army below it, and it was not the smaller of the two armies. When he set out, Abd Allah stayed behind with those who stayed behind, so the verse was revealed concerning "the excuses ... of God and His Messenger" up to His words "while they are averse" [al-Tawba 9:90–91]. *Fikum* means among your army or among your whole body. It has been said *fi* here means *ma'a* (with). Ibn Abbas said: *al-khabal* is corruption and seeking to extinguish the word. Al-Dahhak said: deceit and treachery. Ibn Isa said: turmoil. Al-Kalbi said: evil, and Ibn Qutayba said the same. It has also been said: creating disagreement and rumors. The explanation of *khabal* was given earlier in Al 'Imran.

This exception (*istithna'*) is connected (*muttasil*) and is "emptied" (*mufarragh*), since the second object of *zaada* was not mentioned, and in this expedition there were many hypocrites, who undoubtedly had corruption; so if these had gone out, they would have gathered together and the corruption would have increased. Al-Zamakhshari said: the thing excepted from is not mentioned, so the exception is from the most general of the general, which is "thing," and so it is a connected exception, because *khabal* is a part of the most general of the general, as if it were said: "They added nothing to you but corruption." It has also been said it is a disconnected exception (*munqati'*), which is the view of one who said there was no corruption in the Messenger's army. The meaning then is: they added to you no strength or power, but rather corruption. Ibn Abi Abla read *ma zaadukum* without a *waw*, meaning: their going out added to you nothing but corruption. *Al-iyda'* is speeding. The poet said:

*We see ourselves hastening toward an unseen matter,*
*and we are bewitched by food and drink.*

It is said: the she-camel *wada'at* (hastens) with *wad'an* and *wuqu'an*. The poet said:

*Would that I were in it as a young camel, racing in it and hastening.*

Al-Hasan said its meaning is: they would have hastened with tale-bearing. Muhammad ibn al-Qasim read: they would have hastened with flight. The object of *awda'u* is omitted, its estimate being: they would have urged their mounts among you, because the rider is faster than the walker. Mujahid and Muhammad ibn Zayd read *la-awfadu*, meaning they would have hastened, as in His word: ﴿toward idols they rush﴾ [al-Ma'arij 70:43]. Ibn al-Zubayr read *la-arfadu* with the *ra'*, from *rafada*, meaning he hastened in his walk with a rapid gait. Hassan said:

*With a flask that gushed out what was in its belly, gushing like a she-camel with a hurried rider.*

(p-50) Another said:

*And those who hasten to Mina and then to al-Qabqab.*

*Al-khilal* is the plural of *khalal*, which is the gap between two things. Al-Asma'i said: I went through the people, I entered between their gaps and their midst; and we sat *khilal* the houses and *khilal* the dwellings, meaning between them. *Yabghunakum* is a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning seeking. Al-Farra' said: they seek it for you. Here *al-fitnah* means disbelief, according to Muqatil, Ibn Qutayba and al-Dahhak; or fault and evil, according to al-Kalbi; or the splitting of the community; or the trial of the division of the word; or tale-bearing. Al-Zamakhshari said: they try to tempt you by bringing about disagreement among you and corrupting your intentions in your campaign. **"And among you are listeners to them"**: that is, tale-bearers who listen to your talk and carry it to them, or among you are people who listen to the hypocrites and obey them. End quote. So the *lam* in the first view is for causation, and in the second it reinforces the transitivity, as in His word: ﴿a doer of what He wills﴾ [Hud 11:107]. The first view was stated by Sufyan ibn Uyayna, al-Hasan, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd, who said its meaning is spies who listen to the news and carry it to them, and al-Tabari preferred it. The second view is the view of the majority, who said its meaning is: among you are obedient listeners to them. The meaning of **"among you"** is in your midst, from them, or from you, among those whose conversion to Islam was recent. **"And God knows the wrongdoers"** encompasses every wrongdoer. Its meaning is that He will requite him for his wrongdoing. It includes whoever accepts the speech of the hypocrites, whoever conveys the news of the believers to them, and whoever among the hypocrites stayed behind from this raid.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verses 38–47 (part 1 of 3):

﴿O you who have believed, what is [the matter] with you that when you are told, "Go forth in the cause of Allah," you adhere heavily to the earth? Are you satisfied with the life of this world rather than the Hereafter? But the enjoyment of worldly life, compared to the Hereafter, is little.﴾ When Allah commanded His Messenger to the expedition of Tabuk, and it was a time of drought and intense heat, and the fruits had ripened, this weighed heavily on the people and they loved to remain. [The verse] was revealed as a reproach to those who stayed behind from this expedition. It was in the ninth year after the Hijrah, a year after the Conquest (of Makkah). In it he (ﷺ) fought the Romans with twenty thousand men, mounted and on foot. Tribes of people and many men among the believers, as well as hypocrites, stayed behind from him. He singled out the three [men] for severe reproach in accordance with their standing in companionship, since they were from among the people of Badr and were among those who are followed as examples, and their staying behind was without any excuse, as will come, if Allah wills. When [Allah] had described the reproach of the disbelievers, He desired to confront them. The phrase "What is [the matter] with you" (ma lakum) is an interrogative whose meaning is denunciation and rebuke. The verb "qila" (was said) is in the passive form, and the one who said it was the Messenger (ﷺ), who was not mentioned out of harshness and roughness toward them, and to preserve his mention, since whoever inclined to ease and comfort, and opposed his command (ﷺ), had gone to them.

Al-A'mash recited "tathaqaltum" (you were heavy), which is the original reading of the majority, "ithaqaltum" (you adhered heavily). It is a past form with the meaning of the present, and it occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and it governs "idha" (when). That is: "What is [the matter] with you, you are adhering heavily when you are told, 'Go forth'?" Abu al-Baqa' said: "The past tense here has the meaning of the present; that is, 'What is [the matter] with you, you adhere heavily,' and its position is accusative; that is, 'What is it for you in adhering heavily?' Or it is in the genitive position according to the view of al-Khalil." End of quote. This is not a good view, because it would require the deletion of "an" (that), since a verbal noun is formed only from a particle of the verbal type and the verb, and the deletion of "an" in such a construction is very rare or a poetic necessity. And if the estimate is "in adhering heavily," then it cannot govern "idha," because the complement of the connected verbal noun cannot precede it, so the governing element for "idha," and what is connected to it in "adhering heavily," would be what is known to you, which is the predicate of "ma." It was also read "ithaqaltum" as an interrogative with the meaning of denunciation and rebuke, and what follows an interrogative particle cannot govern "idha." Al-Zamakhshari said: "What governs it is what is indicated by it, or what is in 'ma lakum' of the meaning of a verb, as if he said, 'What do you do when it is said to you,' just as you govern it in a circumstantial clause when you say, 'What is with you standing?'" The more apparent is that the estimate is: "What is [the matter] with you that you adhere heavily when you are told, 'Go forth'," and it is deleted because "ithaqaltum" indicates it. The meaning of "ithaqaltum ila al-ard" (you adhered heavily to the earth) is: you inclined toward the desires of the world when the earth brought forth its fruits, as said by Mujahid, and you disliked the hardships of travel. It was said: you inclined to remain in your land, as said by al-Zajjaj. Since the meaning of inclination and adherence was implied, it took "ila" (to). In His saying "Are you satisfied (a-radhitum)," there is a kind of denunciation and wonder; that is, "Are you satisfied with the immediate pleasure of the transient world instead of the lasting pleasure?" The particle "min" (from) — the statements of the commentators agree that it has the meaning of "instead of"; that is, instead of the Hereafter, as in His saying: ﴿We would have made from among you angels﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 60], meaning "instead of you." From this is the saying of the poet:

"Would that we had from the water of Zamzam a drink, cooled, that has spent the night upon a tahyan."

That is, instead of the water of Zamzam. The tahyan is a wooden post set up at one side of the house for the air, on which water containers are hung until they cool. Our companions (the Shafi'is) do not accept that "min" may mean "instead of." The phrase "fi al-akhirah" (in the Hereafter) is connected to a deleted element; the estimate is: "so what is the enjoyment of the worldly life, reckoned in the bliss of the Hereafter?" Al-Hawfi said: "fi al-akhirah" is connected to "qalil" (little), and "qalil" is the predicate of the inceptive. It is permissible that it governs the adverbial phrase when placed first, because the scent of the verb governs the adverbial phrase. If you said, "Zayd is not 'Amran except that he strikes," it would not be permissible.

﴿If you do not go forth, He will punish you with a painful punishment and replace you with a people other than you, and you will not harm Him at all. And Allah is over all things competent.﴾ This is a great displeasure toward those who adhere heavily, in that He threatened them with an absolute painful punishment that encompasses the punishment of both abodes, and that He would destroy them and replace them with other people better than them and more obedient, and that He is free of need of them in supporting His religion, and their heaviness does not diminish it at all. It was said: He punishes you by withholding rain from you. It is related from Ibn Abbas that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) summoned a tribe to go forth, and they sat [and did not go], so Allah withheld the rain from them and punished them with it." The one replaced (al-mustabdal) who was promised: the people of Yemen, said a group. Ibn Jubayr said: the sons of Persia. Ibn Abbas said: they are the Successors (al-Tabi'un). The apparent meaning does not need specification. Al-Asamm said: its meaning is that Allah, the Exalted, brings out His Messenger from among them to Madinah. Al-Qadi said: "This is weak, because the wording has no indication that he moves from Madinah to another place, and it is not impossible that people appear in Madinah who help him in the expedition, and it is not impossible that He helps him with groups of angels also while he is there." The pronoun in "wa la tadurruhu shay'an" (and you will not harm Him at all) refers to Allah, the Exalted; that is, "you will not harm His religion at all." It was said: it refers to the Messenger, because He, the Exalted, has protected him and promised him victory, and His promise is certain without doubt. When He had made the punishment, the replacement, and the absence of harm contingent upon their not going forth, He informed that He is over all things, every thing whose will relates to it, competent — of punishment, change, and other than that.

﴿If you do not support him, then Allah has already supported him when those who disbelieved drove him out, the second of two. When they were in the cave, he said to his companion, "Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us."﴾ "If you do not support him" indicates the negation of support by any means, whether by going forth or otherwise. The response of the condition is deleted, its estimate being: "then He will support him," and "then Allah has already supported him" indicates it; that is, He supports him in the future as He supported him in the past. [p. 43] Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say, how can His saying, 'then Allah has already supported him,' be a response to the condition? I say: there are two aspects. One: 'then He will support him,' and he mentioned the meaning of what we have preceded. The second: that He, the Exalted, made support obligatory for him and made him supported at that time, so he was not forsaken afterward." End of quote. This does not clearly show the response of the condition, because making support obligatory for him is a matter that has already preceded, and the past does not follow from the future. So what is apparent is the first aspect. The meaning of "the driving out by those who disbelieved" is their doing to him what leads to departure, and the reference is to the departure of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from Makkah to Madinah. The driving out was attributed to them figuratively, as it was attributed in His saying: "[the town] which drove you out." The account of the departure of the Messenger (ﷺ) and Abu Bakr is mentioned in the biographies.

"The second of two" (thani ithnayn) is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause; that is, one of two, and they were the Messenger of Allah and Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him. It is related that when he was commanded to depart, he said to Jibril, peace be upon him: "Who will go out with me?" He said: Abu Bakr. Al-Layth said: No prophets have accompanied, peace and blessings be upon them, like Abu Bakr. Sufyan ibn Uyayna said: Abu Bakr was excluded from this verse of reproach in His saying, "If you do not support him." Ibn Atiyyah said: rather, everyone who witnessed the expedition of Tabuk was excluded from it, and the reproach was only for those who stayed behind. This verse highlights the status of Abu Bakr, his precedence, and his earliness in Islam. In this verse there is an encouragement for them toward jihad and support of Allah's religion, since He explained in it that Allah supports him as He supported him when he was in the cave, and there was no one with him in it except Abu Bakr. A group recited "thani ithnayn" with the sukun on the ya' of "thani." Ibn Jinni said: Abu Amr related it, and its basis is that he made the ya' quiescent by analogy with the alif. The "ghar" (cave) is a hollow at the top of Thawr, a mountain to the right of Makkah at a distance of one hour's travel, where he remained for three [days]. "Idh huma" (when they two) is a substitution, and "idh yaqulu" (when he said) is a second substitution. The scholars said: whoever denies the companionship of Abu Bakr has disbelieved, because he denies the speech of Allah, the Exalted, and this is not the case for the rest of the Companions. The cause of Abu Bakr's grief was his fear for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so the Messenger forbade him in order to calm his heart, and informed him with his saying, "indeed Allah is with us," meaning: with aid and victory. Abu Bakr said: "O Messenger of Allah, if I am killed, I am only one man; but if you are killed, the nation will perish and the religion of Allah will be lost." He said: "What do you think of two whom Allah is the third of?" Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

"The Prophet said, and he did not panic, reassuring me, while we were in the darkness of the cave's gloom.
'Do not fear anything, for Allah is our third, and He has guaranteed to me manifestation from Him.'
Indeed, the plot of one whose harm you fear is only the plot of the devils, which has plotted for the disbelievers.
Allah will destroy them all for what they have done, and will make their final destination the Fire."

﴿So Allah sent down His tranquility upon him and supported him with soldiers you did not see, and made the word of those who disbelieved the lowest; and the word of Allah is the highest. And Allah is Exalted in Might and Wise.﴾ Ibn Abbas said: "al-sakinah" is mercy. Qatadah and others said: dignity. Ibn Qutaybah said: reassurance. These statements are close in meaning. The pronoun in "alayhi" (upon him) refers to his companion, as said by Habib ibn Abi Thabit, or to the Messenger, as said by the majority, or to both of them, and it was made singular because of their inseparability. This is supported by the fact that in the Mushaf of Hafsah it reads: "So Allah sent down His tranquility upon both of them and supported both of them." The "junud" (soldiers) are the angels on the day of Badr, the Confederates, and Hunayn. It was said: at that time they cast good tidings into his heart and turned the faces of the disbelievers away from him. The apparent is that the pronoun "alayhi" refers to Abu Bakr, because the Prophet was steadfast of heart, and for that reason he said, "Do not grieve, indeed Allah is with us." And that the pronoun in "wa ayyadahu" (and supported him) refers to the Messenger (ﷺ), as in His saying: ﴿that you may believe in Allah and His Messenger, and support him and honor him﴾ [al-Fath: 9], meaning the Messenger, and "tusabbihuhu" (glorify Him) meaning Allah, the Exalted. Ibn Atiyyah said: "al-sakinah, in my view, is only what Allah sends down upon His prophets of protection for them and special qualities that are fitting only for them, such as His saying: ﴿In it is tranquility from your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 248]. It is possible that His saying, 'So Allah sent down His tranquility' [p. 44] to the end of the verse means by it what Allah did for His Prophet up to the time of Tabuk of manifestation and conquests, and not that this is specific to the story of the cave." The word of those who disbelieved is shirk, and it is subdued. The word of Allah is tawhid, and it is manifest. This is the saying of the majority. From Ibn Abbas: the word of the disbelievers is what they agreed upon among themselves of plotting against him to kill him, and the word of Allah is that He is his helper. It was said: the word of Allah is "There is no god but Allah," and the word of the disbelievers is their saying in war: "O clan of so-and-so, O so-and-so!" It was said: the word of Allah is His saying, "I and My messengers will surely prevail" [al-Mujadilah: 21], and the word of those who disbelieved is their saying in war: "Exalt Hubal," meaning their greatest idol. Mujahid recited "wa-ayyadahu" (without doubling the ya'). The majority recited "wa-ayyadahu" with the doubled ya'. It was read "wa-kalimatu Allah" in the accusative, meaning "and He made." The reading of the majority with the nominative is more established in the sense of the report. From Anas: I saw in the Mushaf of Ubayy: "and He made His word the highest," and the description with might fits the indication of domination and victory, and with wisdom fits the indication of what He does with His prophets and allies, and those who oppose them, by strengthening His religion and extinguishing disbelief.

﴿Go forth, light and heavy, and strive with your wealth and your lives in the cause of Allah. That is best for you, if you only knew.﴾ When Allah, the Exalted, threatened those who do not go forth with the Messenger (ﷺ), and set forth for him what examples He set forth, He followed it with this decisive command. The meaning is: "Go forth in the state in which jihad is light for you, or in the state in which it is heavy." Lightness and heaviness here are used figuratively for one who can travel with ease, and one who can travel with difficulty; as for one who cannot, such as the blind and the like, he is excluded from this. It is related that Ibn Umm Maktum came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "Is it obligatory upon me to go forth?" He said: "Yes," until the verse was revealed: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind﴾ [al-Nur: 61].

The commentators have mentioned many meanings of lightness and heaviness, not as specific restrictions to some and not others, but these are to be taken as examples rather than an exhaustive list. Al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah and Mujahid said: young and old. Abu Salih said: rich and poor, in ease and hardship. Al-Awza'i said: riding and on foot. It was also said the reverse. Zayd ibn Aslam said: unmarried and married. Juwaybir said: healthy and sick. A group said: light in weapons, meaning few of them, and heavy, meaning having many of them. Al-Hakam ibn 'Uyayna and Zayd ibn 'Ali said: light of occupations and heavy with them. Ibn 'Abbas said: light of dependents and heavy with them. Al-Tabrizi related: light of followers and retinue and heavy with them. 'Ali ibn 'Isa said: it is from the lightness of certainty and its heaviness at times of dislike. Al-Mawardi related: light toward obedience and heavy against disobedience. The author of al-Fityan related: light toward single combat and heavy in steadfastness. He also related: light in hastening and rushing, and heavy after deliberation and reflection. Ibn Zayd said: those with a trade, which is the heavy, and those without a trade, which is the light. Al-Naqqash related: brave and cowardly. It was said: emaciated and fat. It was said: swift to war like the advance guard, which is the front of the army, while the heavy is the whole army. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: the energetic and the lazy.

The majority hold that the command is restricted to collective obligation (fard al-kifaya), and was not intended as individual obligation (fard al-a'yan). Al-Hasan and 'Ikrimah said: it is an obligation upon the believers, meaning individual obligation during that period, and then it was abrogated (naskh) by His saying: ﴿And the believers should not all go forth at once﴾ [al-Tawbah: 122]. The phrase ﴿light and heavy﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). The words ﴿with your wealth and your lives﴾ are mentioned because that describes the most perfect and most beneficial form of jihad in the sight of Allah, so it urges the attainment of complete qualities. Wealth is mentioned first, as it is the first expenditure at the time of equipping. What the mujahid is engaged in is mentioned, which is the way of Allah. The goodness (khayriyyah) is in this world through overcoming the enemy and inheriting the land, and in the Hereafter through reward and the good pleasure of Allah. Abu Talhah went on campaign until he went on campaign at sea and died there. Al-Miqdad went on campaign despite his bulk and fatness. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib went on campaign when one of his eyes had been lost. Ibn Umm Maktum went on campaign despite being blind.

[p. 45] ﴿Had it been a near gain and a moderate journey, they would have followed you. But the distance seemed long to them. They will swear by Allah, "Had we been able, we would have gone out with you." They destroy themselves, and Allah knows that they are liars.﴾ Meaning: had what they were called to been a near gain, easily obtained, and a moderate journey, middling and close. This verse concerns the story of Tabuk, when he called the believers to march and they marched, and a group among them made excuses to their companions, especially from the tribes neighbouring Madinah. His saying ﴿O you who believe, what is wrong with you﴾ is not addressed to the hypocrites specifically, but is general. The hypocrites made excuses with false pretexts, so Allah, exalted is He, began by mentioning the hypocrites and exposing their inner intentions. (They would have followed you): they would have hastened to it, not for the sake of Allah, nor for the exaltation of His word. ﴿But the distance seemed long to them﴾; that is, the long distance in the campaign against the Romans. The shuqqah, with a dammah, means a garment, and shuqqah also means a long journey; it is sometimes said with a kasrah, as al-Jawhari reported. Al-Zajjaj said: al-shuqqah is the goal that is aimed at. Ibn 'Isa said: al-shuqqah is a stretch of land whose traversing causes hardship. Ibn Faris said: al-shuqqah is travelling to a distant land, and its derivation is from splitting (shaqq) or from hardship (mashaqqah). 'Isa ibn 'Umar read: ﴿ba'idat 'alayhimu al-shiqqah﴾ with a kasrah on the 'ayn and the shin, and al-A'raj agreed with him on ba'idat. Abu Hatim said: it is the dialect of the Banu Tamim in both words. End of quote. Al-Kisa'i related: shuqqatan and shiqqatan. (They will swear): that is, the hypocrites, and this is a report of the unseen. Al-Zamakhshari said regarding His saying ﴿They will swear by Allah﴾, the following: "(By Allah) is connected to 'they will swear', or it is part of their speech, and the saying is intended in both cases; that is, they will swear, seeking to be exempt when you return from the campaign of Tabuk, offering excuses, saying: by Allah, had we been able we would have gone out with you. Or: they will swear by Allah, saying: had we been able." His saying ﴿we would have gone out﴾ takes the place of the answer to the oath and of the answer to 'had', together. The report of what would happen after their oath and excuse was among the miracles. The meaning of istita'ah (ability) is ability of equipment and ability of bodies, as if they were feigning illness. End of quote. But what he held, that His saying ﴿we would have gone out﴾ takes the place of the answer to the oath and of 'had' together, is not sound. Rather, the grammarians have two positions on this. The first: that ﴿we would have gone out﴾ is the answer to the oath, and the answer to 'law' (had) is omitted, according to the rule of combining an oath and a condition when the oath precedes the condition; this is the choice of Abu al-Hasan ibn 'Usfur. The second: that ﴿we would have gone out﴾ is the answer to 'law', and the answer to the oath is 'law' and its answer. This is the view of Ibn Malik, that ﴿we would have gone out﴾ takes the place of both. I know of no one who held that. It may be interpreted that his statement means: when the answer to 'law' is omitted and is indicated by the answer to the oath, it is treated as if it took the place of the answer to the oath and the answer to 'law' together.

Al-A'mash and Zayd ibn 'Ali read: ﴿law-u istata'na﴾ with a dammah on the waw, avoiding the weight of the kasrah on the waw, and likening it to the waw of the plural when it is moved because of the meeting of two sukuns. Al-Hasan read it with a fathah, as in ﴿ishtaraw al-dalalah﴾ (they bought the error), in the three ways. (They destroy themselves): by the false oath; that is, they cast themselves into destruction by it. The apparent view is that it is a new sentence, a report from Him, exalted is He. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿they destroy themselves﴾ may be a substitute for ﴿they will swear﴾, or a circumstantial state meaning ﴿destroying﴾; the meaning is that they cast themselves into destruction by their false oath and by what they break from of staying behind. It may also be a circumstantial state of His saying ﴿we would have gone out﴾; that is, we would have gone out with you, even if we destroyed ourselves and cast ourselves into ruin by the march over that distance. He used the third-person form because they are the subject of the report. Do you not see that if it were said: ﴿They will swear by Allah, had they been able they would have gone out﴾, it would be sound? One says: he swore by Allah he would do, and I will do. So the third person is according to the report, and the first person according to the quotation. End of quote. As for ﴿they destroy themselves﴾ being a substitute for ﴿they will swear﴾, that is far-fetched, because destruction is not synonymous with swearing, nor is it a type of swearing, and one verb may not be substituted for another unless it is synonymous with it or a type of it. As for it being a circumstantial state of His saying ﴿we would have gone out﴾, what appears is that this is not permissible, because His saying ﴿we would have gone out﴾ contains a first-person pronoun, so what is predicated of it must agree with a first-person pronoun. If it were a circumstantial state of the pronoun in ﴿we would have gone out﴾, the construction would be: ﴿we destroy ourselves﴾; that is, ﴿destroyers of ourselves﴾. As for his analogy with ﴿he swore by Allah he would do, and I will do﴾, it is not correct, because if he applies it to the third-person pronoun, it does not shift from them to the first-person pronoun. If you said: "Zayd swore he would do, while I am standing", making "while I am standing" a circumstantial state of the pronoun in "he would do", it would not be permitted; and likewise the reverse, as in: "Zayd swore he would do, he is standing" meaning "standing", that would not be permitted. As for his saying "it is according to the report of the third person, because it is a report about them", this is a fallacy, since it is not a report about them by His saying "had we been able we would have gone out with you"; rather it reproduces the wording of their speech. Then he said: "Do you not see that if it were said: 'had they been able they would have gone out', it would be sound," and so on, which is a correct statement; but He, exalted is He, did not say that as a report about them, but as a quotation. The circumstantial state is part of their reported speech, so it is not permissible to differ between the one described and his state, since both share the same governing element. If you said: "Zayd said: I went out, striking Khalid," meaning "I will strike Khalid", it would not be permitted. And if you said: "Hind said: Zayd went out [p. 47] I will strike Khalid", meaning "Zayd went out striking Khalid", it would not be permitted.

﴿May Allah pardon you. Why did you grant them leave until those who were truthful became clear to you and you knew the liars?﴾ Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this verse concerns a category that went to great lengths in hypocrisy. Those who sought permission without making excuses were: 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, al-Jadd ibn Qays, Rifa'ah ibn al-Tabut, and those who followed them. Some of them said: "Grant me leave and do not tempt me." Some of them said: "Grant us leave to remain." So he granted them leave, out of sparing them and taking the easier of the matters, and relying upon Allah. Mujahid said: some of them said, "We will ask his permission; if he permits us to sit, we will sit, and if he does not permit, we will sit," so the verse was revealed concerning that. End of quote. Abu 'Abd Allah Ibrahim ibn 'Arafa al-Nahwi al-Dawudi, known as Nifawayh, who was rejected, said: some people went to the view that the Prophet ﷺ was reproached by this verse, and far be it from him. Rather, it was for him to do or not to do until revelation came down to him, as he said: "Had I known at the start of my affair what I learned at its end, I would have made it an 'umrah," because it was for him to do or not to do. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿You may postpone whom you wish of them and take to yourself whom you wish﴾ [al-Ahzab: 51], because it was for him to do whatever he wished of what had not been revealed to him concerning it. The ones left behind asked him for leave to stay behind and made excuses, and he chose the easier of the two matters, out of his generosity and graciousness, may blessings and peace be upon him. So Allah, exalted is He, made clear that had he not granted them leave, they would have stayed behind for the hypocrisy in their hearts, and that they were liars in displaying obedience and consultation. So His saying ﴿May Allah pardon you﴾ is, in his view, the opening of a speech which Allah informed him by, that there is no blame upon him for what he did in granting leave, and it is not a pardon for a sin. Rather, Allah informed him that he was not obliged to refuse them leave, just as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah has pardoned you concerning the charity of horses and slaves," and they were never obligated; its meaning is that He left off imposing that upon you. End of quote. A group agreed with him and said: the mention of pardon here did not come after a prior sin, but is an opening of speech of a kind the Arabs customarily use when addressing one they honour and elevate, intending by it a supplication for him. They say: "May Allah set right the Amir, such and such is the case." So its wording is that of a report, but its meaning is supplication. End of quote.

(p-47)

**"Why"** (*lima*) and **"for them"** (*lahum*) both depend on *adhinta* (you permitted). Yet the two lams differ in meaning: the lam in *lima* marks cause or reason (*ta'lil*), while the lam in *lahum* marks the one for whom or to whom something is done (*tabligh*). Because their meanings differ, the two can be joined to the same verb. The object of the permission is not stated. What we have already mentioned indicates that it is sitting behind (*al-qu'ud*). That is: why did you permit them to stay behind and to hold back from the expedition, so that you could know those with a valid excuse for staying behind from those who have no excuse? It has also been said that the object of the permission is going out with him to the expedition, because of the harms that resulted from their going out, since they were spies for the disbelievers against the Muslims. This is supported by His words: ﴿And among you are listeners to them﴾. They used to discourage the believers and wish that misfortune would befall them. So it was said: Why did you permit them to go out when they were in this evil state? He made clear that their going out with him was not a benefit, by His words: ﴿Had they gone out with you, they would have added nothing to you but corruption﴾.

**"Until"** (*hatta*) is a limit (*ghayah*) to what the interrogative (*al-istifham*) implies. That is: it was not for you to permit them until it became clear who had the excuse. This is how al-Hawfi (*al-Hawfi*) estimated it. Abu al-Baqa' said: *hatta yatabayyana* is connected to an omitted element indicated by the context, its estimate being: "Why did you not delay them until it became clear," or "so that it might become clear." His words "Why did you permit them" indicate the omitted element. *Hatta* cannot be connected to *adhinta*, because that would require that he permitted them up to this limit, or for the purpose of clarifying, and this is not something one is blamed for. End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari's commentary on His words ﴿May God pardon you! Why did you permit them?﴾ is something that must be discarded altogether, let alone quoted and then refuted.

His words **"those who spoke the truth"** mean: in their request for permission. And "that if you had not permitted them, they would have gone out with you." **"And that you would know the liars"**: he means, in that they asked your permission, showing you that they would stop at your limit, while they were liars, and had already resolved on disobedience, whether you permitted them or not. Al-Tabari said: *hatta ta'lama al-sadiqin* means until you know those who speak the truth that they have an excuse, and *ta'lama al-kadhibin* means know the liars who have no excuse. Qatada said: after this verse, the verse of al-Nur was revealed: ﴿So when they ask your permission for some matter of theirs, give permission to whomever of them you wish﴾ [al-Nur 24:62]. This is an error, because al-Nur was revealed in the fourth year of the Hijra, at the Battle of the Trench, concerning the permission some believers sought from the Messenger for some of their affairs in their homes at certain times, and God allowed him to grant it. Thus the two verses differ in time and in meaning.

﴿Those who believe in God and the Last Day do not ask your permission to strive with their wealth and their selves. And God knows the righteous.﴾ (p-48) Ibn Abbas said: "they do not ask your permission" means after the Battle of Tabuk. Al-Jumhur said it is not so, because what comes before this verse and what follows it was revealed concerning the story of Tabuk. The apparent meaning is that the object of the asking of permission is "to strive" (*an yujahidu*). That is: it is not the custom of believers to ask you permission to strive. The sincere ones among the Emigrants and the Helpers never asked the Prophet (ﷺ) for permission, and they would say: "We will certainly strive with him with our wealth and our selves." It has also been said: the estimate is: the believers do not ask your permission to go out or to stay back out of reluctance to strive; rather, when you command something, they rush to it, and asking permission at that time would be a sign of hypocrisy. His words **"And God knows the righteous"** are a testimony to them that they are counted among the righteous, and a promise to them of the greatest reward.

﴿Only those ask your permission who do not believe in God and the Last Day, and whose hearts are in doubt, so they waver in their doubt﴾: they are the hypocrites, and they were thirty-nine men. *Irtabat* means "doubted." *Yataraddadun* means "they are bewildered," unable to find a path to guidance; at times it occurs to them that the Messenger's matter is true, and at other times the opposite occurs to them.

﴿Had they wished to go out, they would have prepared for it some provision. But God disliked their dispatch, so He held them back, and it was said: "Sit with those who sit."﴾ Ibn Abbas said: *uddatan* means provisions of food and water and a mount, since their journey was far in a time of intense heat. Their not preparing provision is evidence that they intended to stay behind. Others said they were able to obtain the provision and the equipment. Al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn Abbas: the *uddah* is the sincere intention in striving. Al-Tabari related: it is everything prepared for fighting, of provision and weapons. Muhammad ibn Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan and his son Mu'awiya read *udd* with a *damma* on the *ayn* and without a *ta'*. Al-Farra' said the *ta'* drops because of the *idafa* (construct genitive), and he took as an example *wa-iqam al-salat*, meaning *wa-iqamat al-salat*. This occurs in several verses of Arabic poetry, but one does not make it a rule; we stop at what has been heard. Sahib al-Lawami said: when he added (the noun), the pronominal suffix took the place of the *ta'* and so it was dropped, because *udd* without a *ta'* is a pimple that appears on the face (the word here being the same root as the *ta'*-less form). Abu Hatim said it is a plural of *uddah*, like *burrah* and *burr*, *durrah* and *durr*, and the proper form would be *uddad*, but it does not agree with the Qur'anic script. Zirr ibn Hubaysh and Aban from Asim read *iddah* with a *kasra* on the *ayn* and the pronominal suffix *ha'*. Ibn Atiyya said: in my view it is a noun for what is prepared, like *dhabh* (slaughter) and *qatl* (killing) for the act of counting, and it was called *qatl* because it is necessary that it be killed. It was also read *iddatan* with a *kasra* on the *ayn* and with a *ta'* without an *idafa*, meaning "a provision of food and weapons," or "something they possess," derived from *al-adad* (number).

Because the sentence includes the negation of going out and of preparing, and was followed by *lakin* (but), and *lakin* only occurs between two opposites, or two contraries, or two disagreements with a disagreement in them, not between two things in agreement, while what follows *lakin* in apparent meaning matches what precedes it...

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "What is the position of the particle of contrast (*harf al-istidrak*)?" I say: since His words "Had they wished to go out" gave the meaning of negating their going out and their preparation for the raid, it was said "But God disliked their dispatch," as if it were said: "They did not go out, but they held back from going out because God disliked their being dispatched," as you would say: "How kindly Zayd treated me, but he harmed me." End quote. But the verse is not similar to this example, because in the example *lakin* falls between two opposites, whereas in the verse *lakin* falls between two things that agree in meaning. *Al-inbi'ath* is setting out and rising. Ibn Abbas said: *fa-thabbatahum* means their laziness and the slackening of their intentions held them back. The verb *qila* (it was said) is in the passive, so it may be that the speaking refers to the Messenger's permission to them to stay behind, or the saying of some of them to others, either verbally or in meaning, or it refers to God's word in His prior decree. Al-Zamakhshari said: He made God's placing in their hearts the dislike of going out an order to stay behind. It has also been said it is from the whispering of Satan. He said: If you ask, "How is it permissible for God to place in their souls dislike of going out to the raid, when it is ugly, and God is exalted above inspiring what is ugly?" I say: their going out was a corruption, because of His words: ﴿Had they gone out with you, they would have added nothing to you but corruption﴾ (p-49), so placing dislike of that going out in their souls was good and a benefit. End quote.

This question and answer follow the Mu'tazilite approach (*al-i'tizal*) concerning corruption and benefit. This statement is a rebuke of them and a belittling, and it places them with the women, the children and the infirm, whose nature is to sit and remain in the houses. They are "those who sit" (*al-qa'idun*), "those who stay behind" (*al-khalifun*) and "the remaining ones" (*al-khawalif*). This is clarified by His words: ﴿They were content to be with the remaining ones﴾ [al-Tawba 9:87]. Sitting here is an expression for holding back and delay, as the poet said:

*Leave noble deeds, do not journey toward their pursuit;*
*sit, for you are the one who eats and is clothed.*

﴿Had they gone out with you, they would have added nothing to you but corruption, and they would have hurried between your ranks, seeking to cause you sedition. And among you are listeners to them. And God knows the wrongdoers.﴾ When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out, he pitched his army at the Thaniyyat al-Wada'. Abd Allah ibn Ubayy pitched his army below it, and it was not the smaller of the two armies. When he set out, Abd Allah stayed behind with those who stayed behind, so the verse was revealed concerning "the excuses ... of God and His Messenger" up to His words "while they are averse" [al-Tawba 9:90–91]. *Fikum* means among your army or among your whole body. It has been said *fi* here means *ma'a* (with). Ibn Abbas said: *al-khabal* is corruption and seeking to extinguish the word. Al-Dahhak said: deceit and treachery. Ibn Isa said: turmoil. Al-Kalbi said: evil, and Ibn Qutayba said the same. It has also been said: creating disagreement and rumors. The explanation of *khabal* was given earlier in Al 'Imran.

This exception (*istithna'*) is connected (*muttasil*) and is "emptied" (*mufarragh*), since the second object of *zaada* was not mentioned, and in this expedition there were many hypocrites, who undoubtedly had corruption; so if these had gone out, they would have gathered together and the corruption would have increased. Al-Zamakhshari said: the thing excepted from is not mentioned, so the exception is from the most general of the general, which is "thing," and so it is a connected exception, because *khabal* is a part of the most general of the general, as if it were said: "They added nothing to you but corruption." It has also been said it is a disconnected exception (*munqati'*), which is the view of one who said there was no corruption in the Messenger's army. The meaning then is: they added to you no strength or power, but rather corruption. Ibn Abi Abla read *ma zaadukum* without a *waw*, meaning: their going out added to you nothing but corruption. *Al-iyda'* is speeding. The poet said:

*We see ourselves hastening toward an unseen matter,*
*and we are bewitched by food and drink.*

It is said: the she-camel *wada'at* (hastens) with *wad'an* and *wuqu'an*. The poet said:

*Would that I were in it as a young camel, racing in it and hastening.*

Al-Hasan said its meaning is: they would have hastened with tale-bearing. Muhammad ibn al-Qasim read: they would have hastened with flight. The object of *awda'u* is omitted, its estimate being: they would have urged their mounts among you, because the rider is faster than the walker. Mujahid and Muhammad ibn Zayd read *la-awfadu*, meaning they would have hastened, as in His word: ﴿toward idols they rush﴾ [al-Ma'arij 70:43]. Ibn al-Zubayr read *la-arfadu* with the *ra'*, from *rafada*, meaning he hastened in his walk with a rapid gait. Hassan said:

*With a flask that gushed out what was in its belly, gushing like a she-camel with a hurried rider.*

(p-50) Another said:

*And those who hasten to Mina and then to al-Qabqab.*

*Al-khilal* is the plural of *khalal*, which is the gap between two things. Al-Asma'i said: I went through the people, I entered between their gaps and their midst; and we sat *khilal* the houses and *khilal* the dwellings, meaning between them. *Yabghunakum* is a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning seeking. Al-Farra' said: they seek it for you. Here *al-fitnah* means disbelief, according to Muqatil, Ibn Qutayba and al-Dahhak; or fault and evil, according to al-Kalbi; or the splitting of the community; or the trial of the division of the word; or tale-bearing. Al-Zamakhshari said: they try to tempt you by bringing about disagreement among you and corrupting your intentions in your campaign. **"And among you are listeners to them"**: that is, tale-bearers who listen to your talk and carry it to them, or among you are people who listen to the hypocrites and obey them. End quote. So the *lam* in the first view is for causation, and in the second it reinforces the transitivity, as in His word: ﴿a doer of what He wills﴾ [Hud 11:107]. The first view was stated by Sufyan ibn Uyayna, al-Hasan, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd, who said its meaning is spies who listen to the news and carry it to them, and al-Tabari preferred it. The second view is the view of the majority, who said its meaning is: among you are obedient listeners to them. The meaning of **"among you"** is in your midst, from them, or from you, among those whose conversion to Islam was recent. **"And God knows the wrongdoers"** encompasses every wrongdoer. Its meaning is that He will requite him for his wrongdoing. It includes whoever accepts the speech of the hypocrites, whoever conveys the news of the believers to them, and whoever among the hypocrites stayed behind from this raid.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verses 38–47 (part 1 of 3):

﴿O you who have believed, what is [the matter] with you that when you are told, "Go forth in the cause of Allah," you adhere heavily to the earth? Are you satisfied with the life of this world rather than the Hereafter? But the enjoyment of worldly life, compared to the Hereafter, is little.﴾ When Allah commanded His Messenger to the expedition of Tabuk, and it was a time of drought and intense heat, and the fruits had ripened, this weighed heavily on the people and they loved to remain. [The verse] was revealed as a reproach to those who stayed behind from this expedition. It was in the ninth year after the Hijrah, a year after the Conquest (of Makkah). In it he (ﷺ) fought the Romans with twenty thousand men, mounted and on foot. Tribes of people and many men among the believers, as well as hypocrites, stayed behind from him. He singled out the three [men] for severe reproach in accordance with their standing in companionship, since they were from among the people of Badr and were among those who are followed as examples, and their staying behind was without any excuse, as will come, if Allah wills. When [Allah] had described the reproach of the disbelievers, He desired to confront them. The phrase "What is [the matter] with you" (ma lakum) is an interrogative whose meaning is denunciation and rebuke. The verb "qila" (was said) is in the passive form, and the one who said it was the Messenger (ﷺ), who was not mentioned out of harshness and roughness toward them, and to preserve his mention, since whoever inclined to ease and comfort, and opposed his command (ﷺ), had gone to them.

Al-A'mash recited "tathaqaltum" (you were heavy), which is the original reading of the majority, "ithaqaltum" (you adhered heavily). It is a past form with the meaning of the present, and it occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and it governs "idha" (when). That is: "What is [the matter] with you, you are adhering heavily when you are told, 'Go forth'?" Abu al-Baqa' said: "The past tense here has the meaning of the present; that is, 'What is [the matter] with you, you adhere heavily,' and its position is accusative; that is, 'What is it for you in adhering heavily?' Or it is in the genitive position according to the view of al-Khalil." End of quote. This is not a good view, because it would require the deletion of "an" (that), since a verbal noun is formed only from a particle of the verbal type and the verb, and the deletion of "an" in such a construction is very rare or a poetic necessity. And if the estimate is "in adhering heavily," then it cannot govern "idha," because the complement of the connected verbal noun cannot precede it, so the governing element for "idha," and what is connected to it in "adhering heavily," would be what is known to you, which is the predicate of "ma." It was also read "ithaqaltum" as an interrogative with the meaning of denunciation and rebuke, and what follows an interrogative particle cannot govern "idha." Al-Zamakhshari said: "What governs it is what is indicated by it, or what is in 'ma lakum' of the meaning of a verb, as if he said, 'What do you do when it is said to you,' just as you govern it in a circumstantial clause when you say, 'What is with you standing?'" The more apparent is that the estimate is: "What is [the matter] with you that you adhere heavily when you are told, 'Go forth'," and it is deleted because "ithaqaltum" indicates it. The meaning of "ithaqaltum ila al-ard" (you adhered heavily to the earth) is: you inclined toward the desires of the world when the earth brought forth its fruits, as said by Mujahid, and you disliked the hardships of travel. It was said: you inclined to remain in your land, as said by al-Zajjaj. Since the meaning of inclination and adherence was implied, it took "ila" (to). In His saying "Are you satisfied (a-radhitum)," there is a kind of denunciation and wonder; that is, "Are you satisfied with the immediate pleasure of the transient world instead of the lasting pleasure?" The particle "min" (from) — the statements of the commentators agree that it has the meaning of "instead of"; that is, instead of the Hereafter, as in His saying: ﴿We would have made from among you angels﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 60], meaning "instead of you." From this is the saying of the poet:

"Would that we had from the water of Zamzam a drink, cooled, that has spent the night upon a tahyan."

That is, instead of the water of Zamzam. The tahyan is a wooden post set up at one side of the house for the air, on which water containers are hung until they cool. Our companions (the Shafi'is) do not accept that "min" may mean "instead of." The phrase "fi al-akhirah" (in the Hereafter) is connected to a deleted element; the estimate is: "so what is the enjoyment of the worldly life, reckoned in the bliss of the Hereafter?" Al-Hawfi said: "fi al-akhirah" is connected to "qalil" (little), and "qalil" is the predicate of the inceptive. It is permissible that it governs the adverbial phrase when placed first, because the scent of the verb governs the adverbial phrase. If you said, "Zayd is not 'Amran except that he strikes," it would not be permissible.

﴿If you do not go forth, He will punish you with a painful punishment and replace you with a people other than you, and you will not harm Him at all. And Allah is over all things competent.﴾ This is a great displeasure toward those who adhere heavily, in that He threatened them with an absolute painful punishment that encompasses the punishment of both abodes, and that He would destroy them and replace them with other people better than them and more obedient, and that He is free of need of them in supporting His religion, and their heaviness does not diminish it at all. It was said: He punishes you by withholding rain from you. It is related from Ibn Abbas that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) summoned a tribe to go forth, and they sat [and did not go], so Allah withheld the rain from them and punished them with it." The one replaced (al-mustabdal) who was promised: the people of Yemen, said a group. Ibn Jubayr said: the sons of Persia. Ibn Abbas said: they are the Successors (al-Tabi'un). The apparent meaning does not need specification. Al-Asamm said: its meaning is that Allah, the Exalted, brings out His Messenger from among them to Madinah. Al-Qadi said: "This is weak, because the wording has no indication that he moves from Madinah to another place, and it is not impossible that people appear in Madinah who help him in the expedition, and it is not impossible that He helps him with groups of angels also while he is there." The pronoun in "wa la tadurruhu shay'an" (and you will not harm Him at all) refers to Allah, the Exalted; that is, "you will not harm His religion at all." It was said: it refers to the Messenger, because He, the Exalted, has protected him and promised him victory, and His promise is certain without doubt. When He had made the punishment, the replacement, and the absence of harm contingent upon their not going forth, He informed that He is over all things, every thing whose will relates to it, competent — of punishment, change, and other than that.

﴿If you do not support him, then Allah has already supported him when those who disbelieved drove him out, the second of two. When they were in the cave, he said to his companion, "Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us."﴾ "If you do not support him" indicates the negation of support by any means, whether by going forth or otherwise. The response of the condition is deleted, its estimate being: "then He will support him," and "then Allah has already supported him" indicates it; that is, He supports him in the future as He supported him in the past. [p. 43] Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say, how can His saying, 'then Allah has already supported him,' be a response to the condition? I say: there are two aspects. One: 'then He will support him,' and he mentioned the meaning of what we have preceded. The second: that He, the Exalted, made support obligatory for him and made him supported at that time, so he was not forsaken afterward." End of quote. This does not clearly show the response of the condition, because making support obligatory for him is a matter that has already preceded, and the past does not follow from the future. So what is apparent is the first aspect. The meaning of "the driving out by those who disbelieved" is their doing to him what leads to departure, and the reference is to the departure of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from Makkah to Madinah. The driving out was attributed to them figuratively, as it was attributed in His saying: "[the town] which drove you out." The account of the departure of the Messenger (ﷺ) and Abu Bakr is mentioned in the biographies.

"The second of two" (thani ithnayn) is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause; that is, one of two, and they were the Messenger of Allah and Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him. It is related that when he was commanded to depart, he said to Jibril, peace be upon him: "Who will go out with me?" He said: Abu Bakr. Al-Layth said: No prophets have accompanied, peace and blessings be upon them, like Abu Bakr. Sufyan ibn Uyayna said: Abu Bakr was excluded from this verse of reproach in His saying, "If you do not support him." Ibn Atiyyah said: rather, everyone who witnessed the expedition of Tabuk was excluded from it, and the reproach was only for those who stayed behind. This verse highlights the status of Abu Bakr, his precedence, and his earliness in Islam. In this verse there is an encouragement for them toward jihad and support of Allah's religion, since He explained in it that Allah supports him as He supported him when he was in the cave, and there was no one with him in it except Abu Bakr. A group recited "thani ithnayn" with the sukun on the ya' of "thani." Ibn Jinni said: Abu Amr related it, and its basis is that he made the ya' quiescent by analogy with the alif. The "ghar" (cave) is a hollow at the top of Thawr, a mountain to the right of Makkah at a distance of one hour's travel, where he remained for three [days]. "Idh huma" (when they two) is a substitution, and "idh yaqulu" (when he said) is a second substitution. The scholars said: whoever denies the companionship of Abu Bakr has disbelieved, because he denies the speech of Allah, the Exalted, and this is not the case for the rest of the Companions. The cause of Abu Bakr's grief was his fear for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so the Messenger forbade him in order to calm his heart, and informed him with his saying, "indeed Allah is with us," meaning: with aid and victory. Abu Bakr said: "O Messenger of Allah, if I am killed, I am only one man; but if you are killed, the nation will perish and the religion of Allah will be lost." He said: "What do you think of two whom Allah is the third of?" Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

"The Prophet said, and he did not panic, reassuring me, while we were in the darkness of the cave's gloom.
'Do not fear anything, for Allah is our third, and He has guaranteed to me manifestation from Him.'
Indeed, the plot of one whose harm you fear is only the plot of the devils, which has plotted for the disbelievers.
Allah will destroy them all for what they have done, and will make their final destination the Fire."

﴿So Allah sent down His tranquility upon him and supported him with soldiers you did not see, and made the word of those who disbelieved the lowest; and the word of Allah is the highest. And Allah is Exalted in Might and Wise.﴾ Ibn Abbas said: "al-sakinah" is mercy. Qatadah and others said: dignity. Ibn Qutaybah said: reassurance. These statements are close in meaning. The pronoun in "alayhi" (upon him) refers to his companion, as said by Habib ibn Abi Thabit, or to the Messenger, as said by the majority, or to both of them, and it was made singular because of their inseparability. This is supported by the fact that in the Mushaf of Hafsah it reads: "So Allah sent down His tranquility upon both of them and supported both of them." The "junud" (soldiers) are the angels on the day of Badr, the Confederates, and Hunayn. It was said: at that time they cast good tidings into his heart and turned the faces of the disbelievers away from him. The apparent is that the pronoun "alayhi" refers to Abu Bakr, because the Prophet was steadfast of heart, and for that reason he said, "Do not grieve, indeed Allah is with us." And that the pronoun in "wa ayyadahu" (and supported him) refers to the Messenger (ﷺ), as in His saying: ﴿that you may believe in Allah and His Messenger, and support him and honor him﴾ [al-Fath: 9], meaning the Messenger, and "tusabbihuhu" (glorify Him) meaning Allah, the Exalted. Ibn Atiyyah said: "al-sakinah, in my view, is only what Allah sends down upon His prophets of protection for them and special qualities that are fitting only for them, such as His saying: ﴿In it is tranquility from your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 248]. It is possible that His saying, 'So Allah sent down His tranquility' [p. 44] to the end of the verse means by it what Allah did for His Prophet up to the time of Tabuk of manifestation and conquests, and not that this is specific to the story of the cave." The word of those who disbelieved is shirk, and it is subdued. The word of Allah is tawhid, and it is manifest. This is the saying of the majority. From Ibn Abbas: the word of the disbelievers is what they agreed upon among themselves of plotting against him to kill him, and the word of Allah is that He is his helper. It was said: the word of Allah is "There is no god but Allah," and the word of the disbelievers is their saying in war: "O clan of so-and-so, O so-and-so!" It was said: the word of Allah is His saying, "I and My messengers will surely prevail" [al-Mujadilah: 21], and the word of those who disbelieved is their saying in war: "Exalt Hubal," meaning their greatest idol. Mujahid recited "wa-ayyadahu" (without doubling the ya'). The majority recited "wa-ayyadahu" with the doubled ya'. It was read "wa-kalimatu Allah" in the accusative, meaning "and He made." The reading of the majority with the nominative is more established in the sense of the report. From Anas: I saw in the Mushaf of Ubayy: "and He made His word the highest," and the description with might fits the indication of domination and victory, and with wisdom fits the indication of what He does with His prophets and allies, and those who oppose them, by strengthening His religion and extinguishing disbelief.

﴿Go forth, light and heavy, and strive with your wealth and your lives in the cause of Allah. That is best for you, if you only knew.﴾ When Allah, the Exalted, threatened those who do not go forth with the Messenger (ﷺ), and set forth for him what examples He set forth, He followed it with this decisive command. The meaning is: "Go forth in the state in which jihad is light for you, or in the state in which it is heavy." Lightness and heaviness here are used figuratively for one who can travel with ease, and one who can travel with difficulty; as for one who cannot, such as the blind and the like, he is excluded from this. It is related that Ibn Umm Maktum came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "Is it obligatory upon me to go forth?" He said: "Yes," until the verse was revealed: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind﴾ [al-Nur: 61].

The commentators have mentioned many meanings of lightness and heaviness, not as specific restrictions to some and not others, but these are to be taken as examples rather than an exhaustive list. Al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah and Mujahid said: young and old. Abu Salih said: rich and poor, in ease and hardship. Al-Awza'i said: riding and on foot. It was also said the reverse. Zayd ibn Aslam said: unmarried and married. Juwaybir said: healthy and sick. A group said: light in weapons, meaning few of them, and heavy, meaning having many of them. Al-Hakam ibn 'Uyayna and Zayd ibn 'Ali said: light of occupations and heavy with them. Ibn 'Abbas said: light of dependents and heavy with them. Al-Tabrizi related: light of followers and retinue and heavy with them. 'Ali ibn 'Isa said: it is from the lightness of certainty and its heaviness at times of dislike. Al-Mawardi related: light toward obedience and heavy against disobedience. The author of al-Fityan related: light toward single combat and heavy in steadfastness. He also related: light in hastening and rushing, and heavy after deliberation and reflection. Ibn Zayd said: those with a trade, which is the heavy, and those without a trade, which is the light. Al-Naqqash related: brave and cowardly. It was said: emaciated and fat. It was said: swift to war like the advance guard, which is the front of the army, while the heavy is the whole army. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: the energetic and the lazy.

The majority hold that the command is restricted to collective obligation (fard al-kifaya), and was not intended as individual obligation (fard al-a'yan). Al-Hasan and 'Ikrimah said: it is an obligation upon the believers, meaning individual obligation during that period, and then it was abrogated (naskh) by His saying: ﴿And the believers should not all go forth at once﴾ [al-Tawbah: 122]. The phrase ﴿light and heavy﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). The words ﴿with your wealth and your lives﴾ are mentioned because that describes the most perfect and most beneficial form of jihad in the sight of Allah, so it urges the attainment of complete qualities. Wealth is mentioned first, as it is the first expenditure at the time of equipping. What the mujahid is engaged in is mentioned, which is the way of Allah. The goodness (khayriyyah) is in this world through overcoming the enemy and inheriting the land, and in the Hereafter through reward and the good pleasure of Allah. Abu Talhah went on campaign until he went on campaign at sea and died there. Al-Miqdad went on campaign despite his bulk and fatness. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib went on campaign when one of his eyes had been lost. Ibn Umm Maktum went on campaign despite being blind.

[p. 45] ﴿Had it been a near gain and a moderate journey, they would have followed you. But the distance seemed long to them. They will swear by Allah, "Had we been able, we would have gone out with you." They destroy themselves, and Allah knows that they are liars.﴾ Meaning: had what they were called to been a near gain, easily obtained, and a moderate journey, middling and close. This verse concerns the story of Tabuk, when he called the believers to march and they marched, and a group among them made excuses to their companions, especially from the tribes neighbouring Madinah. His saying ﴿O you who believe, what is wrong with you﴾ is not addressed to the hypocrites specifically, but is general. The hypocrites made excuses with false pretexts, so Allah, exalted is He, began by mentioning the hypocrites and exposing their inner intentions. (They would have followed you): they would have hastened to it, not for the sake of Allah, nor for the exaltation of His word. ﴿But the distance seemed long to them﴾; that is, the long distance in the campaign against the Romans. The shuqqah, with a dammah, means a garment, and shuqqah also means a long journey; it is sometimes said with a kasrah, as al-Jawhari reported. Al-Zajjaj said: al-shuqqah is the goal that is aimed at. Ibn 'Isa said: al-shuqqah is a stretch of land whose traversing causes hardship. Ibn Faris said: al-shuqqah is travelling to a distant land, and its derivation is from splitting (shaqq) or from hardship (mashaqqah). 'Isa ibn 'Umar read: ﴿ba'idat 'alayhimu al-shiqqah﴾ with a kasrah on the 'ayn and the shin, and al-A'raj agreed with him on ba'idat. Abu Hatim said: it is the dialect of the Banu Tamim in both words. End of quote. Al-Kisa'i related: shuqqatan and shiqqatan. (They will swear): that is, the hypocrites, and this is a report of the unseen. Al-Zamakhshari said regarding His saying ﴿They will swear by Allah﴾, the following: "(By Allah) is connected to 'they will swear', or it is part of their speech, and the saying is intended in both cases; that is, they will swear, seeking to be exempt when you return from the campaign of Tabuk, offering excuses, saying: by Allah, had we been able we would have gone out with you. Or: they will swear by Allah, saying: had we been able." His saying ﴿we would have gone out﴾ takes the place of the answer to the oath and of the answer to 'had', together. The report of what would happen after their oath and excuse was among the miracles. The meaning of istita'ah (ability) is ability of equipment and ability of bodies, as if they were feigning illness. End of quote. But what he held, that His saying ﴿we would have gone out﴾ takes the place of the answer to the oath and of 'had' together, is not sound. Rather, the grammarians have two positions on this. The first: that ﴿we would have gone out﴾ is the answer to the oath, and the answer to 'law' (had) is omitted, according to the rule of combining an oath and a condition when the oath precedes the condition; this is the choice of Abu al-Hasan ibn 'Usfur. The second: that ﴿we would have gone out﴾ is the answer to 'law', and the answer to the oath is 'law' and its answer. This is the view of Ibn Malik, that ﴿we would have gone out﴾ takes the place of both. I know of no one who held that. It may be interpreted that his statement means: when the answer to 'law' is omitted and is indicated by the answer to the oath, it is treated as if it took the place of the answer to the oath and the answer to 'law' together.

Al-A'mash and Zayd ibn 'Ali read: ﴿law-u istata'na﴾ with a dammah on the waw, avoiding the weight of the kasrah on the waw, and likening it to the waw of the plural when it is moved because of the meeting of two sukuns. Al-Hasan read it with a fathah, as in ﴿ishtaraw al-dalalah﴾ (they bought the error), in the three ways. (They destroy themselves): by the false oath; that is, they cast themselves into destruction by it. The apparent view is that it is a new sentence, a report from Him, exalted is He. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿they destroy themselves﴾ may be a substitute for ﴿they will swear﴾, or a circumstantial state meaning ﴿destroying﴾; the meaning is that they cast themselves into destruction by their false oath and by what they break from of staying behind. It may also be a circumstantial state of His saying ﴿we would have gone out﴾; that is, we would have gone out with you, even if we destroyed ourselves and cast ourselves into ruin by the march over that distance. He used the third-person form because they are the subject of the report. Do you not see that if it were said: ﴿They will swear by Allah, had they been able they would have gone out﴾, it would be sound? One says: he swore by Allah he would do, and I will do. So the third person is according to the report, and the first person according to the quotation. End of quote. As for ﴿they destroy themselves﴾ being a substitute for ﴿they will swear﴾, that is far-fetched, because destruction is not synonymous with swearing, nor is it a type of swearing, and one verb may not be substituted for another unless it is synonymous with it or a type of it. As for it being a circumstantial state of His saying ﴿we would have gone out﴾, what appears is that this is not permissible, because His saying ﴿we would have gone out﴾ contains a first-person pronoun, so what is predicated of it must agree with a first-person pronoun. If it were a circumstantial state of the pronoun in ﴿we would have gone out﴾, the construction would be: ﴿we destroy ourselves﴾; that is, ﴿destroyers of ourselves﴾. As for his analogy with ﴿he swore by Allah he would do, and I will do﴾, it is not correct, because if he applies it to the third-person pronoun, it does not shift from them to the first-person pronoun. If you said: "Zayd swore he would do, while I am standing", making "while I am standing" a circumstantial state of the pronoun in "he would do", it would not be permitted; and likewise the reverse, as in: "Zayd swore he would do, he is standing" meaning "standing", that would not be permitted. As for his saying "it is according to the report of the third person, because it is a report about them", this is a fallacy, since it is not a report about them by His saying "had we been able we would have gone out with you"; rather it reproduces the wording of their speech. Then he said: "Do you not see that if it were said: 'had they been able they would have gone out', it would be sound," and so on, which is a correct statement; but He, exalted is He, did not say that as a report about them, but as a quotation.
