The basis of this reading is the assimilation of "lan" to "lā" and "lam," and this nūn of emphasis has been heard attached to "lā" and "lam"; and when "lan" shared with them in negation, the nūn of emphasis was attached with it. This is a deviant justification; that is: what befell us is neither from you nor by you, but Allah is the One who struck us, and wrote—that is, in the Preserved Tablet or in the Qur'an—the promise of victory and the multiplication of reward upon the misfortune, or what He decreed and judged; three opinions. "He is our Protector" (huwa mawlānā): that is, our helper and guardian, as the majority said. Al-Kalbi said: nearer to us than ourselves in death and life. It was said: our Master and Lord, so He disposes as He wills; therefore it is obligatory to be content with what proceeds from Him. And He said: "That is because Allah is the Protector of those who believe, and because the disbelievers have no protector" [Muhammad: 11]. So He is our Mawla who protects us, and we protect Him.

﴿Say, "Do you await for us anything but one of the two best outcomes, while we await for you that Allah will afflict you with a punishment from Himself or by our hands. So wait; indeed we are waiting with you."﴾ That is: they do not await for us except one of two consequences, each of which is the best of consequences: either victory, or martyrdom. Victory ends in dominance and seizure, and martyrdom ends in Paradise. Ibn ʿAbbas said: the two best outcomes are spoils and martyrdom. It was said: reward and spoils. It was said: martyrdom and forgiveness. In a ḥadīth: "Allah has guaranteed for whoever strives in His way, that nothing brings him out of his house except striving in His way and belief in His word, that He will admit him to Paradise, or return him to the dwelling from which he went out, with whatever reward and spoils he has gained." As for "a punishment from Allah," Ibn ʿAbbas said: here it means thunderbolts. Ibn Jurayj said: death. It was said: a calamity from the sky that destroys them as it came upon ʿĀd and Thamūd. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: it may be that it is a threat of the punishment of the Hereafter. "Or by our hands" means: by killing for disbelief. "So wait" for the promises of Satan; "indeed we are waiting with you" for the manifestation of His religion and the uprooting of whoever opposes it, as al-Ḥasan said. Al-Zamakhshari said: "so wait for us" for what we have mentioned of our outcomes; "indeed we are waiting with you" for what your outcome will be; so we will all certainly meet what we await, and we will not pass beyond it. End. This is a command which includes threat and warning. Ibn Muḥaysin read "illā ḥdā" with the hamzah dropped. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: he joined the alif of "iḥdā," and this is a dialect but not by analogy; this is like the statement of the poet:

"O Abu al-Mughirah, many a perplexing matter..."

and like the statement of the other:

"If I do not fight, then clothe me in a veil."

End.

﴿Say, "Spend willingly or unwillingly; it will never be accepted from you. Indeed you have been a defiantly disobedient people."﴾ Al-Aʿmash and Ibn Wathhab read "kurhan" with a ḍammah on the kāf, and it means: in the way of Allah and the paths of righteousness. It was said: this is a command whose meaning is threat and rebuke. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is a command in the sense of a statement, like His saying: "Say, whoever is in error, let the Most Merciful extend for him an extension" [Maryam: 75], and its meaning: "it will never be accepted from you whether you spend willingly or unwillingly." Similar to it is His saying: "Ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them" [al-Tawbah: 80], and the poet's saying: "Treat us badly or treat us well, there is no blame," meaning: Allah will never forgive them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them, and we will not blame you whether you did ill to us or did well. End. Some of them said other than this, that its meaning is condition and conditional: that is, if you spend willingly or unwillingly, it will not be accepted from you, and he mentioned the verse; and Kathir composed poetry on this meaning. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "spend" is a command which contains a condition, and this continues in every command which carries a condition; the estimate is: if you spend, it will never be accepted from you. As for when the command is stripped of an answer, it does not carry the implication of the condition. End. What weakens this explanation is that when the command contains the meaning of the condition, the answer is like the answer of the condition, so on this basis the construction should be "fa-lan yutaqabbal" with the fāʾ, since "lan" does not occur as an answer to a condition except with the fāʾ, and likewise what is implied in meaning. Do you not see how he apocopates the answer in such as: "aim at Zayd, he will treat you well" (uqṣid Zaydan yuḥsin ilaykā). "Willingly" means without compulsion from Allah and His Messenger, and "unwillingly" means with compulsion. Compulsion is called "unwillingly" because they were hypocrites, so compulsion became burdensome for them like coercion. Or it may be without compulsion from your leaders, or compulsion from them, because they used to urge them to spend on account of the benefit they saw in it.

It was said: martyrdom and forgiveness. In a ḥadīth: "Allah has guaranteed for whoever strives in His way, that nothing brings him out of his house except striving in His way and belief in His word, that He will admit him to Paradise, or return him to the dwelling from which he went out, with whatever reward and spoils he has gained." End.

The majority of scholars hold that these verses were revealed concerning al-Jadd ibn Qays, when he asked for exemption from going out (to the battle) and said: "This is my wealth; I will help you with it." Ibn 'Abbas said: it is then an instance of the plural being used for the singular, at first, and for whoever does his deed.

Al-Bayhaqi and other imams narrated that they were eighty-three men, from whom he excepted the three who were left behind, and the rest were destroyed. The negation of acceptance (of their expenditure) is either because the Messenger did not accept it from them and rejected it, or because Allah does not reward it. Its absence was attributed to wickedness (fisq). Al-Zamakhshari said: it means rebelliousness and insolence, and it is better to interpret it as disbelief (kufr). Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: this is an indication that the non-acceptance is conditioned upon their being wicked (fasiqin), so it shows that wickedness has an effect in removing this meaning. Al-Jubba'i confirmed that with his well-known proof on this question, namely that wickedness necessitates the everlasting blame and punishment, and obedience necessitates the everlasting praise and reward, and combining the two is impossible. So combining the deserving of both is impossible. Allah removed this doubt by His saying: (And nothing prevented them...) the verse, and that the explicit statement of this wording does not affect acceptance except disbelief. This shows that mere wickedness does not nullify acts of obedience. Thus the Exalted negated that the non-acceptance is conditioned by the general fact that it is wickedness, but rather by the specific attribute of it, which is that this wickedness is disbelief. Therefore it is established that al-Jubba'i's argument is invalid. End of quotation. There is some abridgment in it.

﴿And nothing prevented their expenditures from being accepted from them except that they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger, and they do not come to the prayer except while they are lazy, and they do not spend except while they are unwilling.﴾ He mentioned the cause which by itself prevents the acceptance of their expenditures, which is disbelief, and followed it with what arises from disbelief, necessitates it, and is evidence of it. That is coming to prayer while lazy, and giving expenditure while unwilling. Laziness in prayer, neglecting eagerness for it, and taking it up with reluctance are fruits of disbelief; so performing it, for them, is not done with hope of reward, nor with fear of punishment for neglecting it. Likewise, spending wealth, they do not do it except while they do not hope for reward from it. He mentioned these two great acts of righteousness, prayer and expenditure, and sufficed with them, even though they were in a worse state in the rest of the acts of righteousness, because prayer is the most noble of the physical acts, and spending in the way of Allah is the most noble of the financial acts, and these are two attributes whose manifestation is desired in Islam and by which faith is inferred; and enumerating the vices increases the one described by them in blame and ugliness.

Al-Akhawan, Zayd ibn 'Ali read "an yuqbala" with the yaʾ, and the rest of the seven read with the tāʾ; "nafaqatuhum" is read in the plural by all, and Zayd ibn 'Ali in the singular. Al-A'raj, with a variant from him, read "an tuqbala" with the tāʾ from above, "nafaqatihim" in the singular. In these readings the verb is in the passive voice. A group read: "an naqbala minhum nafaqatahum" with the nūn and the accusative on "nafaqah." Al-Zamakhshari said: the reading of al-Sulami "an naqbala minhum nafaqatihim" is on the basis that the verb belongs to God, the Exalted. End of quotation. "An tuqbala" is a second object, either because "mana'a" reaches it directly, or on the assumption that the preposition has been dropped, so the verb reaches it.

It was said: it means seeking deceit, from their saying: "He is a ḥawwal qallab" (a man who turns things about). Maslamah ibn Muharib read "wa-qallabū" with the lām lightened. "Until the truth came" means: the Qur'an and the Shariʿah of the Messenger ﷺ. The word "came" (jāʾa) implies that it had gone away. "And the command of Allah prevailed" — He described it with prevalence because it had been as if hidden; that is, the religion of Allah overcame and rose high, while they were averse to the coming of the truth and the prevalence of the religion of Allah. In this there is an alert that their plotting and scheming, and their exertion in stirring up evil, have no effect, for whenever they aimed at that, Allah turned it back upon their own necks, reversed their intention, and brought about the opposite of their aim. Just as this happened in the past, so it will happen in the future.

﴿And among them is one who says, "Grant me leave and do not tempt me. Have they not already fallen into temptation? Indeed, Hell encompasses the disbelievers."﴾ It was revealed concerning al-Jadd ibn Qays. It is mentioned that "when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded the expedition to the lands of the Romans, he urged the people. He said to al-Jadd ibn Qays: 'Would you, this year, take part in the fighting against the Banu al-Asfar?' and he said to him and to the people: 'Fight, and you will gain the daughters of al-Asfar as spoils.' Al-Jadd said: 'Grant me leave to stay behind and do not tempt me with mention of the daughters of al-Asfar, for my people know that I cannot restrain myself from women when I see them, and they will tempt me; so do not tempt me with women.'" This is the statement of Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd. It was said: "and do not tempt me" means: do not make it hard for me so that I would need to commit your disobedience; so make it easy for me and leave me untroubled. Al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Zajjaj said something close to this; they said: do not make me bear sin by your command to me to go out, which is not feasible for me, so that I would sin by opposing you. Al-Dahhak said: do not declare me a disbeliever by obliging me to go out with you. Ibn Bahr said: do not divert me from my occupations, so that you cause my interests to be lost and most of my produce to go. It was said: "and tempt me into ruin," for if I go out with you my wealth and my family will perish. It was also said that he said: "But I will help you with my wealth." Al-Naḥḥas said, in substance: when the wāw or the fāʾ enters upon "ādhan" (i.e., "wa-idhan", "fa-idhan"), its spelling in the script is with an alif, dhāl and nūn without a yāʾ; but with "thumma" the spelling is with an alif, yāʾ, dhāl and nūn, and the difference is that "thumma" is pausable upon, whereas the others are not separated. ʿĪsā ibn ʿAmr read: "lā tufntinnī" with a ḍammah on the first tāʾ, from afnata. Abu Hatim said: this is the dialect of Tamim, and it is also the reading of Ibn al-Sumayqaʿ, and Ibn Mujahid attributed it to Ismaʿil al-Makki. The poet combined the two dialects, saying:

"If she tempted me, yesterday she tempted Saʿid, and he has become weary of every Muslim."

The temptation into which they fell is the temptation of staying behind, and the manifestation of their disbelief and hypocrisy. The word "fallen" (saqaṭū) indicates the firm establishment of their falling into it. Qatadah said: the sin is in their opposing the Messenger in his command. The encompassing of Hell around them is either on the Day of Resurrection, or now in a figurative sense, because the causes of encompassment are with them, so it is as if they were within it; or because their final destination is toward it.

﴿If good befalls you, it distresses them; and if a misfortune strikes you, they say, "We had already taken our precaution before," and they turn away while rejoicing.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: "the good" is on the day of Badr, and "the misfortune" is the day of Uhud. It is proper to take his statement as an example, and the wording is general for every desired and disliked thing; the context of the passage requires that this be about the expedition, and for this reason they said: "the good" is victory and spoils, and "the misfortune" is defeat and rout, like what happened at the beginning of the battle of Uhud. The meaning of "our affair" (amrunā), which we are characterized by, is caution, vigilance and acting with prudence in staying behind from the expedition, before the misfortune that befell them. It was said: they turned away from faith. It was said: from the Messenger, so "turning away" would be figurative.

They said: "ṣawwaba raʾyahu" when he formed it on faʿʿala, because it is from the roots with waw. They also said: ṣāba yaṣūbu, and maṣāwib is the plural of muṣībah; and some Arabs say: ṣāba al-sahmu yuṣību, making it from the roots with yāʾ. Victory ends in dominance and seizure, and martyrdom ends in Paradise. Ibn ʿAbbas said: the two best outcomes are spoils and martyrdom. It was said: reward and spoils. It was said: martyrdom and forgiveness. In a ḥadīth: "Allah has guaranteed for whoever strives in His way, that nothing brings him out of his house except striving in His way and belief in His word, that He will admit him to Paradise, or return him to the dwelling from which he went out, with whatever reward and spoils he has gained." Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: it may be that it is a threat of the punishment of the Hereafter. "Or by our hands" means: by killing for disbelief. "So wait" for the promises of Satan; "indeed we are waiting with you" for the manifestation of His religion and the uprooting of whoever opposes it, as al-Ḥasan said. Al-Zamakhshari said: "so wait for us" for what we have mentioned of our outcomes; "indeed we are waiting with you" for what your outcome will be; so we will all certainly meet what we await, and we will not pass beyond it. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: he joined the alif of "iḥdā," and this is a dialect but not by analogy; this is like the statement of the poet:

"O Abu al-Mughirah, many a perplexing matter..."

and like the statement of the other:

"If I do not fight, then clothe me in a veil."

End.

﴿Say, "Spend willingly or unwillingly; it will never be accepted from you. It was said: this is a command whose meaning is threat and rebuke. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is a command in the sense of a statement, like His saying: "Say, whoever is in error, let the Most Merciful extend for him an extension" [Maryam: 75], and its meaning: "it will never be accepted from you whether you spend willingly or unwillingly." End. As for when the command is stripped of an answer, it does not carry the implication of the condition. End. What weakens this explanation is that when the command contains the meaning of the condition, the answer is like the answer of the condition, so on this basis the construction should be "fa-lan yutaqabbal" with the fāʾ, since "lan" does not occur as an answer to a condition except with the fāʾ, and likewise what is implied in meaning. Do you not see how he apocopates the answer in such as: "aim at Zayd, he will treat you well" (uqṣid Zaydan yuḥsin ilaykā). "Willingly or unwillingly" (ṭawʿan aw karhan) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. "Willingly" means without compulsion from Allah and His Messenger, and "unwillingly" means with compulsion. Compulsion is called "unwillingly" because they were hypocrites, so compulsion became burdensome for them like coercion. Or it may be without compulsion from your leaders, or compulsion from them, because they used to urge them to spend on account of the benefit they saw in it.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 9, verses 48–54 (part 2 of 2):

The majority of scholars hold that these verses were revealed concerning al-Jadd ibn Qays, when he asked for exemption from going out (to the battle) and said: "This is my wealth; I will help you with it." Ibn 'Abbas said: it is then an instance of the plural being used for the singular, at first, and for whoever does his deed.

Al-Bayhaqi and other imams narrated that they were eighty-three men, from whom he excepted the three who were left behind, and the rest were destroyed. The negation of acceptance (of their expenditure) is either because the Messenger did not accept it from them and rejected it, or because Allah does not reward it. Its absence was attributed to wickedness (fisq). Al-Zamakhshari said: it means rebelliousness and insolence, and it is better to interpret it as disbelief (kufr). Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: this is an indication that the non-acceptance is conditioned upon their being wicked (fasiqin), so it shows that wickedness has an effect in removing this meaning. Al-Jubba'i confirmed that with his well-known proof on this question, namely that wickedness necessitates the everlasting blame and punishment, and obedience necessitates the everlasting praise and reward, and combining the two is impossible. So combining the deserving of both is impossible. Allah removed this doubt by His saying: (And nothing prevented them...) the verse, and that the explicit statement of this wording does not affect acceptance except disbelief. This shows that mere wickedness does not nullify acts of obedience. Thus the Exalted negated that the non-acceptance is conditioned by the general fact that it is wickedness, but rather by the specific attribute of it, which is that this wickedness is disbelief. Therefore it is established that al-Jubba'i's argument is invalid. End of quotation. There is some abridgment in it.

﴿And nothing prevented their expenditures from being accepted from them except that they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger, and they do not come to the prayer except while they are lazy, and they do not spend except while they are unwilling.﴾ He mentioned the cause which by itself prevents the acceptance of their expenditures, which is disbelief, and followed it with what arises from disbelief, necessitates it, and is evidence of it. That is coming to prayer while lazy, and giving expenditure while unwilling. Laziness in prayer, neglecting eagerness for it, and taking it up with reluctance are fruits of disbelief; so performing it, for them, is not done with hope of reward, nor with fear of punishment for neglecting it. Likewise, spending wealth, they do not do it except while they do not hope for reward from it. He mentioned these two great acts of righteousness, prayer and expenditure, and sufficed with them, even though they were in a worse state in the rest of the acts of righteousness, because prayer is the most noble of the physical acts, and spending in the way of Allah is the most noble of the financial acts, and these are two attributes whose manifestation is desired in Islam and by which faith is inferred; and enumerating the vices increases the one described by them in blame and ugliness.

Al-Akhawan, Zayd ibn 'Ali read "an yuqbala" with the yaʾ, and the rest of the seven read with the tāʾ; "nafaqatuhum" is read in the plural by all, and Zayd ibn 'Ali in the singular. Al-A'raj, with a variant from him, read "an tuqbala" with the tāʾ from above, "nafaqatihim" in the singular. In these readings the verb is in the passive voice. A group read: "an naqbala minhum nafaqatahum" with the nūn and the accusative on "nafaqah." Al-Zamakhshari said: the reading of al-Sulami "an naqbala minhum nafaqatihim" is on the basis that the verb belongs to God, the Exalted. End of quotation. The better view is that the subject of "mana'a" is the phrase "illa annahum," that is, their disbelief; it is possible that it is the name of Allah, i.e., "and Allah did not prevent them," and "illa annahum" would be, in its estimate, "only because they disbelieved." "An tuqbala" is a second object, either because "mana'a" reaches it directly, or on the assumption that the preposition has been dropped, so the verb reaches it.

What weakens this explanation is that when the command contains the meaning of the condition, the answer is like the answer of the condition, so on this basis the construction should be "fa-lan yutaqabbal" with the fāʾ, since "lan" does not occur as an answer to a condition except with the fāʾ, and likewise what is implied in meaning. Do you not see how he apocopates the answer in such as: "aim at Zayd, he will treat you well" (uqṣid Zaydan yuḥsin ilaykā). "Willingly or unwillingly" (ṭawʿan aw karhan) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. "Willingly" means without compulsion from Allah and His Messenger, and "unwillingly" means with compulsion. Compulsion is called "unwillingly" because they were hypocrites, so compulsion became burdensome for them like coercion. Or it may be without compulsion from your leaders, or compulsion from them, because they used to urge them to spend on account of the benefit they saw in it.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 9, verses 48–54 (part 2 of 2):

The majority of scholars hold that these verses were revealed concerning al-Jadd ibn Qays, when he asked for exemption from going out (to the battle) and said: "This is my wealth; I will help you with it." Ibn 'Abbas said: it is then an instance of the plural being used for the singular, at first, and for whoever does his deed.

Al-Bayhaqi and other imams narrated that they were eighty-three men, from whom he excepted the three who were left behind, and the rest were destroyed. The negation of acceptance (of their expenditure) is either because the Messenger did not accept it from them and rejected it, or because Allah does not reward it. Its absence was attributed to wickedness (fisq). Al-Zamakhshari said: it means rebelliousness and insolence, and it is better to interpret it as disbelief (kufr). Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: this is an indication that the non-acceptance is conditioned upon their being wicked (fasiqin), so it shows that wickedness has an effect in removing this meaning. Al-Jubba'i confirmed that with his well-known proof on this question, namely that wickedness necessitates the everlasting blame and punishment, and obedience necessitates the everlasting praise and reward, and combining the two is impossible. So combining the deserving of both is impossible. Allah removed this doubt by His saying: (And nothing prevented them...) the verse, and that the explicit statement of this wording does not affect acceptance except disbelief. This shows that mere wickedness does not nullify acts of obedience. Thus the Exalted negated that the non-acceptance is conditioned by the general fact that it is wickedness, but rather by the specific attribute of it, which is that this wickedness is disbelief. Therefore it is established that al-Jubba'i's argument is invalid. End of quotation. There is some abridgment in it.

﴿And nothing prevented their expenditures from being accepted from them except that they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger, and they do not come to the prayer except while they are lazy, and they do not spend except while they are unwilling.﴾ He mentioned the cause which by itself prevents the acceptance of their expenditures, which is disbelief, and followed it with what arises from disbelief, necessitates it, and is evidence of it. That is coming to prayer while lazy, and giving expenditure while unwilling. Laziness in prayer, neglecting eagerness for it, and taking it up with reluctance are fruits of disbelief; so performing it, for them, is not done with hope of reward, nor with fear of punishment for neglecting it. Likewise, spending wealth, they do not do it except while they do not hope for reward from it. He mentioned these two great acts of righteousness, prayer and expenditure, and sufficed with them, even though they were in a worse state in the rest of the acts of righteousness, because prayer is the most noble of the physical acts, and spending in the way of Allah is the most noble of the financial acts, and these are two attributes whose manifestation is desired in Islam and by which faith is inferred; and enumerating the vices increases the one described by them in blame and ugliness.

Al-Akhawan, Zayd ibn 'Ali read "an yuqbala" with the yaʾ, and the rest of the seven read with the tāʾ; "nafaqatuhum" is read in the plural by all, and Zayd ibn 'Ali in the singular. Al-A'raj, with a variant from him, read "an tuqbala" with the tāʾ from above, "nafaqatihim" in the singular. In these readings the verb is in the passive voice. A group read: "an naqbala minhum nafaqatahum" with the nūn and the accusative on "nafaqah." Al-Zamakhshari said: the reading of al-Sulami "an naqbala minhum nafaqatihim" is on the basis that the verb belongs to God, the Exalted. End of quotation. The better view is that the subject of "mana'a" is the phrase "illa annahum," that is, their disbelief; it is possible that it is the name of Allah, i.e., "and Allah did not prevent them," and "illa annahum" would be, in its estimate, "only because they disbelieved." "An tuqbala" is a second object, either because "mana'a" reaches it directly, or on the assumption that the preposition has been dropped, so the verb reaches it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verse 55:

﴿So let not their wealth nor their children impress you. Allah intends only to punish them thereby in the worldly life, and that their souls depart while they are disbelievers.﴾

When he had cut off the hope of the hypocrites from all the benefits of the Hereafter, he clarified that the things they think to be among the benefits of this world, Allah the Exalted has made them means by which He punishes them in this world. That is: "Let them not impress you, O listener, in a sense that is not approved, nor let you be seduced by what they have been given of (p-54) the adornment of the worldly life," as in His saying: ﴿And do not extend your eyes﴾ [Ta-Ha: 131]. In this there is a belittling of the status of the hypocrites.

Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Mujahid, al-Suddi and Ibn Qutaybah said: there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the speech, and the meaning is: "So let not their wealth nor their children impress you in the worldly life; indeed Allah intends only to punish them thereby in the Hereafter." End of quote. And the clause "Allah intends only to punish them thereby" would be a parenthetical clause (jumlah i'tiradiyyah) in which there is an intensification of the speech and a strengthening of the negation of being impressed; because whoever's eventual outcome of being given wealth and children is punishment, his condition should not be approved of nor should one be seduced by it. However, the restriction of the prohibited impressiveness, which arises from their wealth and children, is known to occur only in the worldly life; so the negation of that is, as it were, an added emphasis, unlike punishment, which may occur in this world as it occurs in the Hereafter. Although the inversion, our companions summarised it as a necessity (bi'l-darurah).

Al-Hasan said: the aspect of the punishment is that by what He obligated upon them concerning them, of paying zakat and spending in the way of Allah. So the pronoun in His saying "thereby" refers, in this view, to the wealth alone.

Ibn Zayd and others said: the punishment is the calamities of the world and its afflictions, which are a punishment for them, since they are not rewarded for them. End of quote. This view is strengthened by the fact that punishing them through the imposition of the Shariah is greater than punishing them with all the other afflictions; this is because of the combination of humiliation and defeat with the command of the Shariah upon them, as Ibn 'Atiyyah said. Al-Zamakhshari gathered all of this and said: He gave them what He gave them only for punishment, by exposing them to the spoils and captivity, and testing them therein with calamities and misfortunes, and obligating them to spend from it in the avenues of good while they dislike it against their will, and making them taste kinds of burdens and hardships in gathering and acquiring it and in raising their children.

It was said: their wealth which they spend, for it is not accepted from them; nor are their children who are Muslims, like Abdullah ibn Abdullah ibn Ubayy and others, for they do not benefit their hypocrite fathers. This was related by al-Qushayri.

It was said: the love of wealth becomes firmly established in their hearts, and the toil in gathering it, and the anxiety in guarding it, and the regret over its loss in the presence of one who does not praise it; then they come before a King who does not excuse them.

He placed the wealth before the children because it was more attached to their hearts, and their souls were more inclined toward it, for they used to kill their children for fear of the loss of their wealth. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty﴾ [al-Isra: 31].

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: if the punishment is linked to the will of Allah the Exalted, then what about the departure of their souls while they are disbelievers? I say: what is meant is the gradual leading on through blessings, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿We only give them respite so that they may increase in sin﴾ [Al 'Imran: 178]. As if it were said: "and He wills to continue His blessing upon them until they die while they are disbelievers, distracted by enjoyment from considering the outcome." End of quote. This is an elaboration of the speech of Ibn 'Isa, who is al-Rummani, and both of them are Mu'tazilites. Ibn 'Isa said: the meaning is: Allah intends only to grant them respite and lead them on gradually, so that He punishes them. End of quote. And this is a Mu'tazilite tendency. What appears, from the fact that He conjoined "and their souls depart" to "to punish", is that the meaning is: "to punish them thereby in the worldly life and in the Hereafter," and He drew attention to the punishment of the Hereafter through its cause, which is the departure of their souls upon disbelief; for whoever dies a disbeliever will certainly be punished in the Hereafter. The apparent meaning is that the departure of the soul here is a metaphor for death. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is also possible that he intends "and their souls depart" from the severity of the punishment that reaches them.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 9, verses 56–57:**

﴿And they swear by God that they are truly of you, but they are not of you; rather, they are a people who are afraid.﴾ That is, they are among the body of the Muslims. God refuted them with His words: "but they are not of you." The meaning of "they are afraid" is that they fear being killed and what is done to the polytheists, so they outwardly display Islam out of *taqiyya* (dissimulation, concealing one's true belief under threat), while inwardly harboring hypocrisy. Or they fear that God will inform the believers of their inner states, so that what befalls the disbelievers will befall them. When the Exalted lowered the status of the hypocrites, their wealth and their children, He returned to mention their interests and what they were upon of corrupt inner dispositions, and so He said: "And they swear by God" in general terms, not by specific identification, and this is God's custom in concealing the persons of the disobedient.

﴿If they found a refuge, or caves, or a place to enter, they would turn toward it while rushing headlong.﴾ When He mentioned the hypocrites' fear of the believers, He informed of what they were upon with them, of what the fear entails: that if it were possible for them to flee from them, they would flee; but their companionship with them is companionship out of compulsion, not choice. Ibn Abbas said: "*al-malja'*" is a shelter. Qatada said: a fortress. Al-Suddi said: a place of escape. Al-Asma'i said: a place in which one takes refuge. Ibn Kaysan said: a people from whom one feels safe.

*Al-maghārāt* is the plural of *maghāra*, which is *al-ghār* (a cave), and it is pluralized as *ghīrān*. It is formed from *ghāra yaghūru*, meaning "entered," on the pattern *maf'ala* for a place, like their saying *mazra'a* (a field). It was also said: *al-maghāra* is a tunnel beneath the earth like the burrow of the jerboa.

Sa'd ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf recited *mughārāt* with a *ḍamma* on the *mīm*, so that it is from *aghāra*. It was said: the Arabs say *ghāra al-rajul* and *aghāra* with the meaning of "entered," so according to this, *maghārāt* would be from the intransitive *aghāra*. It is also permissible that it be from the causative *aghāra* derived by the hamza from *ghāra*, meaning places in the mountains in which they make themselves go astray. Al-Zajjaj said: It is also valid that it be from their saying *jabal maghār*, meaning "twisted," and then this is used metaphorically for a firm, tightly bound matter, so the interpretation according to this is: "if they found support, or firmly bound and fastened affairs that would protect them from you, or a place to enter, they would turn toward it." Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that it be from *aghāra al-tha'lab*, when the fox hastens, with the meaning of places of flight and places of escape. End of quote.

*Al-mudkhal*: Mujahid said: a stronghold that protects them from the believers. Qatada said: a tunnel in which they move in concealment. Al-Kalbi said: a tunnel like the burrow of the jerboa. Al-Hasan said: a way in which they enter contrary to the Messenger. It was said: a tribe into which they enter, which protects them from the Messenger and from the believers.

Most scholars said: *mudkhalan*, and its origin is *mudtakhal*, a *muftaʿal* form from *idtakhala*, and it is a form of emphasis and intensification. Its meaning is a tunnel and a burrow in the earth, as Ibn Abbas stated. It begins first with the more general term, which is *malja'*, since it applies to everything a person takes refuge in; then it mentions *maghārāt*, which are the caves in the mountains; then it comes third with *mudkhal*, which is the tunnel, the inner part of the earth. Al-Zajjaj said: *al-mudkhal* is a people whom they let enter into their group.

Al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Maslama ibn Muharib, Ibn Muhaysin, Ya'qub, and Ibn Kathir in one of his transmissions recited *madkhalan* with a *fatḥa* on the *mīm*, from *dakhala*. Mahbub on the authority of al-Hasan recited *mudkhalan* with a *ḍamma* on the *mīm*, from *adkhala*. This is also reported from al-A'mash and Isa ibn Umar. Qatada, Isa ibn Umar and al-A'mash recited *mudaḵḵalan* with *tashdīd* (doubling) on both the *dāl* and the *khā'*, its origin being *mutadakhkhil*, and the *tā'* was assimilated into the *dāl*. Ubayy recited *mundakhalan* with a *nūn*, from *indakhala*. He said: "And my hand does not slip into the heated handle of the knife." Abu Hatim said: Ubayy's recitation is *mutdakhalan* with a *tā'*. Al-Ash'hab al-Uqayli recited *lawālaw ilayhi*, meaning they would follow and hasten toward it. Ibn Abi Ubayda ibn Mu'awiya ibn Nawfal, on the authority of his father, on the authority of his grandfather, who had companionship (with the Prophet, ﷺ), reported that he recited *lawālaw ilayhi* from *al-muwālāh* (alliance). Sa'id ibn Muslim denied this and said: I think it is *lawa'alu*, with the meaning of *la-laja'u* (they would take refuge). Abu al-Fadl Abd al-Rahman ibn Ahmad al-Razi said: This is among what came with *fā'ala* and *fa'ala* with one meaning, and similar to it is *ḍā'afa* and *ḍa'ufa*. End of quote. Al-Zamakhshari said: Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited *mutdakhalan*, *lawālaw ilayhi*, meaning *lal-tajā'ū ilayhi* (they would have sought refuge in it). End of quote. It is also reported from Ubayy: *lawallaw wujūhahum ilayhi* (they would have turned their faces toward it).

Since the connective was *aw* (or), the pronoun returned in the singular *ilayhi* according to the grammatical rule for *aw*, so from the standpoint of syntax it could refer to *al-malja'* or to *al-mudkhal*. It cannot refer outwardly to *al-maghārāt* because of its masculine grammatical gender, but by interpretation (*ta'wīl*) it is permissible for it to refer to them.

﴿And they would rush headlong﴾: they hasten with a speed that nothing can turn back. Anas ibn Malik and al-A'mash recited *wa-hum yajmazūn*. It was said: *yajmaḥūn*, *yajmazūn*, and *yashtaddūn* are one in meaning. Ibn Atiyya said: *yajmazūn* means they run quickly (*yuharwilūn*), and from it is their saying in the hadith about stoning: "When the stones made him suffer, he *jamaza*" (ran off).
