Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verses 58–59:

﴿And among them are those who find fault with you concerning the charities. If they are given from them, they are pleased; but if they are not given from them, behold, they become angry.﴾ The one who finds fault is Hurqus ibn Zuhayr al-Tamimi, and he is the son of Dhu al-Khuwaysira, the head of the Kharijites (al-Khawarij, the seceders). The Messenger of God (ﷺ) (p-56) was dividing the spoils of Hunayn, and he said: "Be just, O Messenger of God." The hadith continues. It is also said that he was Ibn al-Jawwaz the hypocrite, who said: "Do you not see your companion? He only divides your charities among the shepherds of the goats." It is also said that it was Tha'laba ibn Hatib, who used to say: "Muhammad only gives to Quraysh." It is also said that it was a man from the Ansar who came to the Messenger with a charity he was distributing, and said: "Is this not just?" This is the remark of a hypocrite.

The meaning is: whoever criticizes you regarding the distribution of the charities. The pronoun in "among them" refers to the hypocrites, and the kaf (you) refers to the Messenger. This alternation between the two conditions indicates the baseness of their natures and the impurity of their characters, and that their faulting of the Messenger is only due to their greed in acquiring worldly things and their love of wealth, and that their pleasure and anger are only connected to the giving. The apparent meaning is the occurrence of giving in general or its negation. It has also been said that the implied meaning is: "If they are given a great deal from it, they are pleased; and if they are not given a great deal from it, but only a little, they become angry." How excellent is the coming of the answer to these two conditions: the first does not necessarily require that it be accompanied by its consequence, nor that it immediately follow it, but it may be delayed, as in the example: "If you embrace Islam, you will enter Paradise," for it only implies the general sequence. As for the answer to the second condition, it came with idha al-fujaiyya (the sudden "idha"), indicating that when they are not given, their anger suddenly appears, and its delay was not possible because of what they were created with of love of the world and greed to obtain it. The object of "radu" (they were pleased) is omitted; that is, they were pleased with what they were given. The meaning is not that they were pleased with the Messenger, because they are hypocrites, and because their pleasure and anger were not for the sake of religion, but for the sake of this world. Al-Jumhur (the majority) read "yalmizuka" with a kasra on the mim. Ya'qub and Hammad ibn Salama, from Ibn Kathir, al-Hasan, Abu Raja' and others read it with a damma, and this is the reading of the Meccans, and it is also transmitted from Abu 'Amr. Al-A'mash read "yalmazuka." Hammad ibn Salama also transmitted from Ibn Kathir: "yulamizuka," which is a form of mufa'ala from one party. It has been said that the Messenger (ﷺ) generously gave the share of the people of Mecca from the spoils in order to win their hearts, so the hypocrites protested.

﴿And if they had been pleased with what God and His Messenger gave them, and had said: "God is sufficient for us; God will give us of His bounty, and so will His Messenger; indeed, we turn to God in desire,"﴾ this is a description of the state of those who are upright in their religion. That is, they were pleased with the division of God and His Messenger, and said: "The bounty of God suffices us," and they hung their hopes on what God would give them, and their desire was directed to God and not to anyone else. The answer to "law" (if) is omitted, and its estimate is: "it would have been better for them in their religion and their worldly life." That action indicates their transition from hypocrisy to pure faith, because it included contentment with God's distribution and the acknowledgment of God and His Messenger, since they used to say: "God will give us of His bounty, and so will His Messenger." It has been said that the answer to "law" is His saying "and they said," with the addition of the waw, and this is the view of the Kufan grammarians. Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning is: "If they had been pleased with what the Messenger gave them from the spoils, and their souls were content with it even if their share was small, and they had said: 'The bounty and provision of God the Exalted suffices us, and what He has apportioned to us is enough; He will provide us with another spoil, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) will give us more than what he has given us today; indeed, we are desirous of God that He may grant us spoils and bestow upon us His bounty.'" End of quotation. Ibn 'Abbas said: "We are desirous of what He grants us of reward and turns away from us of punishment." Al-Tabrizi said: "We are desirous that He will widen His bounty upon us, and make us independent of charity and other things that are in the hands of people." It has been said: "What God gave them" refers to the decree, and "His Messenger" refers to the distribution. End of quotation. He first mentioned the station of contentment, which is an inward act arising from one who knows that God is exalted above blame and error, all-knowing of outcomes, so all His decree is right and true, with no objection to it. Then he followed with the manifestation of the effects of the inward quality, which is the acknowledgment with the tongue: "God is sufficient for us," which is what He has been pleased with. Then He mentioned, third, that as long as they are in this worldly life, He extends His blessings and kindness to them, and this is a good report, since there is no believer except that God's blessings continually accrue to him, both in state and in outcome, either in this world or in the Hereafter. Then He mentioned, fourth, the sentence that requires seeking refuge in God and not in anyone else, and turning desire toward Him, so faith does not seek the taking of wealth and leadership in this world. Since the two sentences are different, one including inward contentment and the other including outward acknowledgment with the tongue, they are conjoined by "and" (waw). And since the last two sentences are effects of their saying "God is sufficient for us," they are not conjoined, as they are like an explanation (p-57) of their saying "God is sufficient for us," so there is no difference between them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verses 58–59:

﴿And among them are those who find fault with you concerning the charities. If they are given from them, they are pleased; but if they are not given from them, behold, they become angry.﴾ The one who finds fault is Hurqus ibn Zuhayr al-Tamimi, and he is the son of Dhu al-Khuwaysira, the head of the Kharijites (al-Khawarij, the seceders). The Messenger of God (ﷺ) (p-56) was dividing the spoils of Hunayn, and he said: "Be just, O Messenger of God." The hadith continues. It is also said that he was Ibn al-Jawwaz the hypocrite, who said: "Do you not see your companion? He only divides your charities among the shepherds of the goats." It is also said that it was Tha'laba ibn Hatib, who used to say: "Muhammad only gives to Quraysh." It is also said that it was a man from the Ansar who came to the Messenger with a charity he was distributing, and said: "Is this not just?" This is the remark of a hypocrite.

The meaning is: whoever criticizes you regarding the distribution of the charities. The pronoun in "among them" refers to the hypocrites, and the kaf (you) refers to the Messenger. This alternation between the two conditions indicates the baseness of their natures and the impurity of their characters, and that their faulting of the Messenger is only due to their greed in acquiring worldly things and their love of wealth, and that their pleasure and anger are only connected to the giving. The apparent meaning is the occurrence of giving in general or its negation. It has also been said that the implied meaning is: "If they are given a great deal from it, they are pleased; and if they are not given a great deal from it, but only a little, they become angry." How excellent is the coming of the answer to these two conditions: the first does not necessarily require that it be accompanied by its consequence, nor that it immediately follow it, but it may be delayed, as in the example: "If you embrace Islam, you will enter Paradise," for it only implies the general sequence. As for the answer to the second condition, it came with idha al-fujaiyya (the sudden "idha"), indicating that when they are not given, their anger suddenly appears, and its delay was not possible because of what they were created with of love of the world and greed to obtain it. The object of "radu" (they were pleased) is omitted; that is, they were pleased with what they were given. The meaning is not that they were pleased with the Messenger, because they are hypocrites, and because their pleasure and anger were not for the sake of religion, but for the sake of this world. Al-Jumhur (the majority) read "yalmizuka" with a kasra on the mim. Ya'qub and Hammad ibn Salama, from Ibn Kathir, al-Hasan, Abu Raja' and others read it with a damma, and this is the reading of the Meccans, and it is also transmitted from Abu 'Amr. Al-A'mash read "yalmazuka." Hammad ibn Salama also transmitted from Ibn Kathir: "yulamizuka," which is a form of mufa'ala from one party. It has been said that the Messenger (ﷺ) generously gave the share of the people of Mecca from the spoils in order to win their hearts, so the hypocrites protested.

﴿And if they had been pleased with what God and His Messenger gave them, and had said: "God is sufficient for us; God will give us of His bounty, and so will His Messenger; indeed, we turn to God in desire,"﴾ this is a description of the state of those who are upright in their religion. That is, they were pleased with the division of God and His Messenger, and said: "The bounty of God suffices us," and they hung their hopes on what God would give them, and their desire was directed to God and not to anyone else. The answer to "law" (if) is omitted, and its estimate is: "it would have been better for them in their religion and their worldly life." That action indicates their transition from hypocrisy to pure faith, because it included contentment with God's distribution and the acknowledgment of God and His Messenger, since they used to say: "God will give us of His bounty, and so will His Messenger." It has been said that the answer to "law" is His saying "and they said," with the addition of the waw, and this is the view of the Kufan grammarians. Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning is: "If they had been pleased with what the Messenger gave them from the spoils, and their souls were content with it even if their share was small, and they had said: 'The bounty and provision of God the Exalted suffices us, and what He has apportioned to us is enough; He will provide us with another spoil, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) will give us more than what he has given us today; indeed, we are desirous of God that He may grant us spoils and bestow upon us His bounty.'" End of quotation. Ibn 'Abbas said: "We are desirous of what He grants us of reward and turns away from us of punishment." Al-Tabrizi said: "We are desirous that He will widen His bounty upon us, and make us independent of charity and other things that are in the hands of people." It has been said: "What God gave them" refers to the decree, and "His Messenger" refers to the distribution. End of quotation. He first mentioned the station of contentment, which is an inward act arising from one who knows that God is exalted above blame and error, all-knowing of outcomes, so all His decree is right and true, with no objection to it. Then he followed with the manifestation of the effects of the inward quality, which is the acknowledgment with the tongue: "God is sufficient for us," which is what He has been pleased with. Then He mentioned, third, that as long as they are in this worldly life, He extends His blessings and kindness to them, and this is a good report, since there is no believer except that God's blessings continually accrue to him, both in state and in outcome, either in this world or in the Hereafter. Then He mentioned, fourth, the sentence that requires seeking refuge in God and not in anyone else, and turning desire toward Him, so faith does not seek the taking of wealth and leadership in this world. Since the two sentences are different, one including inward contentment and the other including outward acknowledgment with the tongue, they are conjoined by "and" (waw). And since the last two sentences are effects of their saying "God is sufficient for us," they are not conjoined, as they are like an explanation (p-57) of their saying "God is sufficient for us," so there is no difference between them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verse 60 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Charity is only for the poor and the needy, and those employed to collect it, and those whose hearts are to be reconciled, and for freeing captives, and for those in debt, and for the cause of God, and for the wayfarer; an obligation from God. And God is Knowing and Wise.﴾: When God mentioned those who criticized the Messenger (ﷺ) in the distribution of charity, saying that he gives to whom he wills and withholds from whom he wills, or that he favors his relatives, or that he takes the remainder for himself, and they were asking for more than they deserved, God explained the allocation of charity and that he distributed it according to what God had prescribed. If the particle "innama" (only) was coined for restriction, then restriction is derived from its wording; and if it was not coined for restriction, then restriction is derived from the attributes, since the link of a ruling to an attribute requires that the attribute be the cause, and causation by a thing requires limiting it to that thing. The apparent meaning is that the recipients of charity are these categories. The apparent meaning is also that the conjunction implies difference, so the poor (fuqara') are other than the needy (masakin). The apparent meaning is that this ruling remains in force for the eight categories permanently, since no text has come concerning the abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by a later text) of any of them. The apparent meaning is that for each category, what its wording indicates is taken into account, if it exists. The disagreement concerns each of these apparent meanings.

As for the claim that the recipients of charity are these categories, a group of the Companions and the Successors held that it is permissible to restrict it to some of these categories, and permissible to spend it on all of them. From the Companions: Umar, Ali, Mu'adh, Hudhayfah, and Ibn Abbas. From the Successors: al-Nakha'i, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, Abu al-Aliyah, and Ibn Jubayr. They said: "Wherever you place it among them, it suffices you." Ibn Jubayr said: "If you looked at a household of Muslims who are poor and abstain from asking, and you gave them the choice of it, that would be more beloved to me." Al-Zamakhshari said: "This is the position of Abu Hanifah." Others said: "And of Abu Yusuf, Muhammad, Zufar, and Malik." A group of Successors said: it is not permissible to restrict it to one of these categories, among them Zayn al-Abidin Ali ibn al-Husayn, Ikrimah, and al-Zuhri; rather it is spent on the eight categories. Al-Zuhri wrote to Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz: "Distribute it among the eight categories." This is the position of al-Shafi'i, who said: "Except the mu'allafah (those whose hearts are to be reconciled, i.e., people given charity to incline their hearts toward Islam), for they have ceased."

As for the claim that the poor are other than the needy, a group of the early scholars held that the poor and the needy are the same, with no difference in meaning, even if they differ in name, and that they are one category named with two names so that they receive two shares, out of consideration and mercy for them. Al-Tahrir (by al-Kamal ibn al-Humam) said: "This is one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i." The majority held that they are two categories united by lack and need, and they differed about what distinguishes them. Al-Asma'i and others, including Ahmad ibn Hanbal and Ahmad ibn Ubayd, said: "The poor (faqir) is more destitute." Others, including Abu Hanifah, Yunus ibn Habib, Ibn al-Sikkit, and Ibn Qutaybah, said: "The needy (miskin) is more destitute, because he has nothing." The faqir is one who has a sufficiency (bulghah) of something. Al-Dahhak said: "The poor are among the emigrants (muhajirun), and the needy are those who did not emigrate." Al-Nakha'i said something similar. Ikrimah said: "The poor are among the Muslims, and the needy are among the People of the Covenant (dhimmis). We do not call poor Muslims 'needy.'" It is also reported from him the reverse, related by Makki. Al-Shafi'i said in the book of Ibn al-Mundhir: "The faqir is one who has no property and no trade, whether he asks or abstains from asking. The miskin is one who has a trade or property but it does not suffice him, whether he asks or does not ask." Qatadah said: "The faqir is the disabled needy person, and the miskin is the able-bodied needy person." Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Zuhri, Ibn Zayd, Jabir ibn Zayd, al-Hakam, Muqatil, and Muhammad ibn Maslamah said: "The masakin are those who go about and ask, and the fuqara' are those who restrain themselves."

As for the continuation of the ruling for the eight categories, Umar ibn al-Khattab, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, and a group held that the category of the mu'allafah ended with the strengthening and dominance of Islam. This is the well-known position of Malik and Abu Hanifah. Some Hanafis said: "The Companions agreed on the cancellation of their share in the caliphate of Abu Bakr, when God strengthened Islam and cut off the root of the disbelievers." Al-Qadi Abd al-Wahhab said: "If they are needed at some times, they are given from the charity." Many people of knowledge said: "The mu'allafah exist until the Day of Resurrection." Ibn Atiyyah said: "When you consider the frontier regions, you find in them the need for conciliation." End. Yunus said: "I asked al-Zuhri about them, and he said: 'I know of no abrogation regarding that.'" Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: "On this basis the ruling concerning them is established. If someone is needed to be won over, or it is feared that a calamity would befall the Muslims from him, or his good Islam is hoped for, then he is given after the payment to him." Al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi said: "What I hold is that if Islam becomes strong, they cease, and if they are needed, they are given their share, just as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to give them." For in the Sahih: "Islam began as a stranger and will return as it began." In the book al-Tahrir, al-Shafi'i said: "The collectors and the mu'allafah are absent in this time. The other six categories remain, and it is better to spend it on the six."

As for the claim that for each category, what its wording indicates is taken into account if it exists, this is the position of al-Shafi'i, who held that each category must have at least three, since the minimum plural is three. If he gives the share of the poor to two poor people, he is liable for the share of the third, which is one third of a share. The companions of Abu Hanifah said: "It is permissible to give all of one's zakat to one needy person." Malik said: "There is no harm in a man giving the zakat al-fitr for himself and his dependents to one person." The lam in "lil-fuqara'" (for the poor) is said to indicate ownership, and it is said to indicate specification.

The apparent meaning is the generality of the poor and the needy, so it includes relatives and strangers and everyone who is characterized by poverty and need. As for the close relatives of the Messenger (ﷺ), the companions of Abu Hanifah said: "Charity is forbidden for them," among them the family of al-Abbas, the family of Ali, the family of Ja'far, the family of Aqil, and the family of al-Harith ibn Abd al-Muttalib. It is reported from Abu Hanifah, though it is not the well-known view, that the poor of the Banu Hashim enter into the verse on charity. Abu Yusuf said: "They do not enter." Abu Bakr al-Razi said: "The well-known position of our companions is that they are those mentioned before, from the family of al-Abbas and those mentioned with them, and the prohibition applies to the obligatory charity, not to voluntary charity." Malik said: "Zakat is not lawful for the family of Muhammad, but voluntary charity is lawful." Al-Thawri said: "It is not lawful for the Banu Hashim," and he did not distinguish between the voluntary and the obligatory. Al-Shafi'i said: "Obligatory charity is forbidden for the Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib, and voluntary charity is permissible for everyone except the Messenger of God (ﷺ), for he did not accept it." Ibn al-Majishun, Mutarrif, Asbagh, and Ibn Habib said: "The Banu Hashim are not given from charity, whether obligatory or voluntary." Malik said in al-Wadiha: "The family of Muhammad are not given from voluntary charity."

As for the relatives of the one paying zakat, the companions of Abu Hanifah said: "A parent, however far up, is not given from it, nor a child, however far down, nor a spouse." Malik, al-Thawri, al-Hasan ibn Salih, and al-Layth said: "One does not give to whomever one is obligated to maintain." Ibn Shubrumah said: "One does not give his zakat to relatives who inherit from him; he gives only to someone who does not inherit from him and is not among his dependents." Al-Awza'i said: "One should not pass over the poor among his relatives with his zakat if they are not among his dependents, but he may give charity to his clients from other than his zakat." Malik, al-Thawri, Ibn Shubrumah, al-Shafi'i, and the companions of Abu Hanifah said: "The obligatory portion of zakat is not given" (to them). Ubayd Allah ibn al-Hasan said: "If he does not find a Muslim, he gives to a dhimmi," meaning the dhimmi who is among them. Malik and Abu Hanifah said: "A wife does not give her husband from zakat." Al-Thawri, al-Shafi'i, Abu Yusuf, and Muhammad said: "She gives him."

They differed about the amount that, when a person owns it, enters him into the limit of wealth and takes him out of the limit of poverty, so that charity becomes forbidden to him. Some said: "If he has with his family what feeds them at lunch and dinner, charity is forbidden to him, and whoever has less than that, it is lawful for him." Some said: "Until he owns forty dirhams, or its equivalent in gold." Some said: "Until he owns fifty dirhams, or its equivalent in gold," and this is reported from Ali, Abd Allah, and al-Sha'bi. Malik said: "Until he owns two hundred dirhams, or its equivalent in goods or otherwise, beyond what he needs of a dwelling, servant, furniture, and bedding," and this is the position of the companions of Abu Hanifah. If one gives it to someone he thought was poor, and it became clear that he was rich, or it became clear that the recipient was his father or a dhimmi, and he did not know this at the time of giving, Abu Hanifah and Muhammad said: "It suffices him." Abu Yusuf said: "It does not suffice him."

The 'amil (collector) is the one whom the imam appoints to work on all the charities, and anyone who works on them and is needed for them is among the collectors. He is called the jabi of the charity and the sai. It was said:

*"Indeed the collectors disobeyed you when you sent them; they did not do, of what you commanded, even a sliver."*

And it was said:

*"One collector collected the 'iqal from us and left us no lord; so how would it be if 'Amr collected two 'iqals!"*

By 'iqal here he meant the zakat of a year, and he used "ala" (upon) and did not say "fiha" (in it), because "ala" indicates elevation, which implies authority. The majority hold that the collector receives the amount of his work and his expenses from the charity money. This is the position of Malik, al-Shafi'i in the book of Ibn al-Mundhir, and Abu Hanifah and his companions. If that exceeds the charity, it is said: it is completed for him from the other shares. It is said: from one-fifth of the spoils. Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and al-Shafi'i said: it is an eighth, according to the division of the Qur'an. Malik, in a narration from Ibn Abi Uways, and Dawud ibn Sa'id from him, said: they are given from the public treasury (bayt al-mal).

It is disputed whether the imam has a right in the charities. Some said: he is in reality the collector. Others said: he has no right in them. The majority hold that taking them is entrusted to the imam and to whomever he appoints. So if the payer distributes it himself without the imam's permission, the imam takes it from him again. Abu Hanifah said: it is not permissible for anyone from the Banu Hashim to work on charity and take his wage from it. If he volunteers, there is no disagreement among the people of knowledge about its permissibility. Others said: there is no harm for them in taking a wage from charity. It is said: if one works, he is given it from the fifth.

The mu'allafah are the nobles of the Arabs. They are either Muslims whose faith had not yet settled in their hearts, to whom he gives so that faith settles in their hearts; or disbelievers who have followers, to whom he gives so that he wins them and their followers over to Islam. Al-Zuhri said: "The mu'allafah are whoever has become Muslim from a Jew or a Christian, even if he is rich." Among the mu'allafah were Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, Suhayl ibn Amr, al-Harith ibn Hisham, Huwaytib ibn Abd al-Uzza, Safwan ibn Umayyah, Malik ibn Awf al-Nadri, and al-Ala' ibn Harithah al-Thaqafi. The Messenger (ﷺ) gave each of these a hundred camels. Makhramah ibn Nawfal al-Zuhri, Umayr ibn Wahb al-Jumahi, and Hisham ibn Amr al-Amiri gave less than a hundred. Among the mu'allafah were Sa'id ibn Yarbu', al-Abbas ibn Mirdas, Zayd al-Khayl, Alqamah ibn Ulathah, Abu Sufyan al-Harith ibn Abd al-Muttalib, Hakim ibn Hizam, Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl, Sa'id ibn Amr, and Uyaynah ibn Hisn. The Islam of the mu'allafah was good, except Uyaynah, who remained suspected.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verse 60 (part 2 of 2):

As for His saying ﴿and for the freeing of slaves﴾, the implied meaning is: "and for the freeing (fakk) of slaves," so it is given to whatever achieves the freeing of slaves, from the outset of manumission, by which one buys a slave and then frees him, or by liberating a mukatab (a slave contracted to buy his own freedom) or a captive. Al-Nakha'i, al-Sha'bi, Ibn Jubayr and Ibn Sirin said: it is not valid to free a whole slave (raqabah kamilah) from zakat, and this is the view of the companions of Abu Hanifa, al-Layth and al-Shafi'i. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn 'Umar said: free (a slave) from your zakat. Ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan, Ahmad and Ishaq said: one may free (a slave) from zakat, and his walaʾ (the right of inheritance and patronage) belongs to the community of Muslims, not to the one who frees him. It is reported from Malik and al-Awza'i: a mukatab is not given anything from zakat, nor is a slave whose master is wealthy or poor. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Malik: it refers to the beginning of manumission and to helping the mukatab with what will bring about his freedom. The majority hold that mukatabin are assisted in freeing their necks from zakat. The position of Abu Hanifa and Ibn Habib is that the freeing of captives enters into His saying ﴿and for the freeing of slaves﴾, so zakat is spent on their release. al-Zuhri said: the share for slaves is in two halves: a half for mukatabin, and a half by which Muslim slaves among those who pray are freed.

Al-gharim (the debtor): he is the one upon whom there is a debt, as said by Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid and Qatada added: provided it is not in sin or extravagance. The majority hold that the debts of the deceased are paid from it, since he is a gharim. Abu Hanifa and Ibn al-Mawwaz said: it is not used to pay them. Abu Hanifa said: nor is expiation (kaffarah) or the like of the various kinds of what God Most High has enjoined paid from it; the gharim is only one who has a debt for which he is imprisoned. It has been said: among the gharimin enters one who undertakes liabilities (hamalat) for the sake of reconciliation and righteousness, even if he is wealthy, when that depletes his wealth; this is the view of al-Shafi'i, his companions and Ahmad.

﴿and in the way of God﴾: this is the mujahid, who is given from it if he is poor. The majority hold that he is given from it even if he is wealthy, what he spends on his campaign. al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, 'Isa ibn Dinar and a group said: the wealthy is not given except if he is in need during his campaign and his provision is absent from him. Abu Hanifa and his two companions said: he is not given except if he is poor or cut off from his means, and once he is given, he owns it, even if he does not spend it on his campaign. Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam said: it is spent from the charity on horses, weapons, and whatever instruments of war are needed, and on repelling the enemy from the territory, since all of this is part of the path of the campaign and its benefit. The majority hold that it is permissible to spend from it on pilgrims and those performing 'umrah, even if they are wealthy. al-Zamakhshari said: "in the way of God" means the poor among the fighters and the pilgrims who are cut off, end quote. What the enumeration of these attributes requires is that they do not overlap; and making poverty a condition for some of them implies overlap. If the fighter or the pilgrim has poverty as a condition for his receiving, there is no need to mention it, since he is included in the general category of the poor; rather, whoever has one of these attributes may be given to, in any state, whether poor or rich, because the attribute that warrants the giving has been realized in him. Ibn 'Atiyya said: nothing from it is given for building a mosque, a bridge, or buying a copy of the Qur'an, end quote.

Ibn al-Sabil: Ibn 'Abbas said: he is the wayfarer (abir al-sabil). Qatada and others said: he is the guest. A group said: he is the traveller who is cut off from his means, even if he has wealth in his own land. Another group said: he is the pilgrim who is cut off. al-Zajjaj said: he is the one whose road has been cut by highwaymen. In the book of Sahnun it is said: Malik said: if a traveller who has been cut off finds someone who will lend to him, it is not permissible for him to take from the charity, and the apparent ruling is that it is given to him even if he has what suffices him on his way, since he is ibn al-sabil; but the well-known view is that if he has this description he is not given.

al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): why did he shift from the preposition al-lam to fi in the last four? (I say): to indicate that they are more firmly deserving of being given charity than those previously mentioned, because fi denotes a container, so he draws attention to the fact that they are worthy of having charities placed in them and of being made their recipient and destination. This is because in freeing necks there is writing (of freedom), slavery, or captivity, and in releasing the debtors from debt there is deliverance and rescue; and the poor fighter or the one cut off in the pilgrimage combines poverty with worship; likewise the ibn al-sabil combines poverty with estrangement from family and wealth. The repetition of fi in His saying, Most High: ﴿and in the way of God and the wayfarer﴾, contains a preference for these two over the slaves and debtors. (If you ask): how then does this verse come in the midst of the mention of the hypocrites and their schemes? (I say): by making these attributes the sole recipients of charities, to the exclusion of others, it indicates that they are not among them, as a cutting off of their greed and a signal that they deserve deprivation, and that they are distant from it and from its recipients, so what have they to do with it, and what has given them power to speak about it and about those who share it. ﴿Obligation﴾ (fariḍatan) is in the accusative because it has the sense of an emphatic verbal noun, since His saying, Most High: ﴿Charities are only for the poor﴾ means: a obligation from God that charities are for them. It has been read fariḍatun in the nominative, as in: "that is an obligation," end quote. Al-Kirmani and Abu al-Baqa' said: fariḍatan is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the pronoun in (lil-fuqara'), i.e., obligated (mafrūḍatan). Al-Kirmani said: as you say, "it is yours freely (ṭalaqan)," end quote. It is mentioned from Sibawayh that it is a verbal noun, the implied meaning being: God obligated the charities as an obligation. al-Farra' said: it is accusative by way of cutting off (al-qaṭʿ).

﴿And God is All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾: because whatever proceeds from Him proceeds from knowledge of His creation and from wisdom in the distribution; or He is All-Knowing of the measures of the interests, All-Wise, who legislates only what is most beneficial.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verses 61–63 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And among them are those who harm the Prophet and say, "He is all ears." Say, "An ear of good for you: he believes in Allah, and believes the believers, and is a mercy for those of you who believe. And those who harm the Messenger of Allah will have a painful punishment."﴾ ﴿They swear to you by Allah to please you, but Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him, if they are believers.﴾ ﴿Do they not know that whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger, for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever? That is the great disgrace.﴾ ﴿The hypocrites fear that a surah will be sent down about them, informing them of what is in their hearts. Say, "Mock, for Allah will surely bring out what you fear."﴾ [al-Tawbah: 64] ﴿And if you ask them, they will surely say, "We were only conversing and playing." Say, "Was it Allah, His signs, and His Messenger that you were mocking?"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 65] ﴿Make no excuses; you have disbelieved after your belief. If We pardon a group among you, We will punish another group because they were criminals.﴾ [al-Tawbah: 66] ﴿The hypocrite men and women are of one another. They enjoin what is evil, forbid what is good, and withhold their hands. They have forgotten Allah, so He has forgotten them. Indeed, the hypocrites are the defiantly disobedient.﴾ [al-Tawbah: 67] ﴿Allah has promised the hypocrite men and women and the disbelievers the fire of Hell, abiding therein. It is sufficient for them. Allah has cursed them, and for them is a lasting punishment.﴾ [al-Tawbah: 68] ﴿Like those before you, who were stronger than you in power and greater in wealth and children, and they enjoyed their share, and you have enjoyed your share as those before you enjoyed their share, and you have engaged in vain talk as they engaged. Those are the ones whose deeds became worthless in this world and the Hereafter, and those are the losers.﴾ [al-Tawbah: 69] ﴿Has there not come to them the news of those before them: the people of Noah, ʿĀd, Thamūd, the people of Abraham, the companions of Madyan, and the overturned cities? Their messengers came to them with clear proofs. Allah did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves.﴾ [al-Tawbah: 70] ﴿The believing men and women are allies of one another. They enjoin what is good, forbid what is evil, establish prayer, give zakat, and obey Allah and His Messenger. Those, Allah will have mercy upon. Indeed, Allah is Mighty and Wise.﴾ [al-Tawbah: 71] ﴿Allah has promised the believing men and women gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein, and pleasant dwellings in gardens of perpetual residence. But approval from Allah is greater. That is the great achievement.﴾ [al-Tawbah: 72]

Al-iʿtidhār (making an excuse, i.e. disclaiming one's fault): it is said that its origin is erasure, from the saying of the Arabs, "the campsites made an excuse and were effaced" (iʿtadharat al-manāzil wa-darasat), so the one who makes an excuse seeks to remove his fault. Ibn Aḥmar said:

*You knew the signs; yet they have made the traces of your beloved in the sandy tract an excuse (taʿtadhir).*

It is related from Ibn al-Aʿrābī that iʿtidhār means cutting off. From it comes ʿudhrat al-jāriya, because she is cut (tuʿdhar, i.e. her hymen is severed), and iʿtadharat al-miyāh means the waters stopped flowing. An excuse (ʿudhr) is a cause for cutting off blame. ʿAdana bi-l-makān yaʿdinu ʿudūnan means he settled, as said by Abū Zayd and Ibn al-Aʿrābī. Al-Aʿshā said:

*If they seek hospitality in his forbearance, they will be hosted by a noble one who has settled (ʿadan).*

The Arabs say: "The camels of so-and-so were left as ʿawādin in such-and-such a place," meaning the camels stay in the place, become accustomed to it, and do not leave it. The mine (maʿdin) was so named because God causes the jewel to grow in it and establishes it in the earth until it settles (ʿadana) there, i.e. becomes firm. ʿAdan is a city in Yemen, because it is the most populous of the cities of Yemen in inhabitants and houses.

﴿And among them are those who harm the Prophet and say, "He is all ears." Say, "An ear of good for you: he believes in Allah, and believes the believers, and is a mercy for those of you who believe. And those who harm the Messenger of Allah will have a painful punishment."﴾: Qudām ibn Khālid, ʿUbayd ibn Hilāl, and al-Julās ibn Suwayd, along with others, were harming the Messenger. Some of them said, "Do not do this, for we fear that it will reach him and he will strike us." Al-Julās said, "Rather, we will say whatever we wish, for Muhammad is an ear that hears; then we will come to him and he will believe us." Then this was revealed.

It was also said: it was revealed about Nabtal ibn al-Ḥārith, who used to convey the Messenger's words to the hypocrites. He was told, "Do not do this," but he said that statement.

It was also said: it was revealed about al-Julās and Zamʿa ibn Thābit, along with others, who wanted to disparage the Messenger. With them was a young man from the Anṣār named ʿĀmir ibn Qays, whom they belittled. They said, "If what Muhammad says is true, then we are worse than donkeys." The young man became angry and said, "By Allah, what Muhammad says is true, and you are worse than donkeys." Then he went to the Messenger of Allah and informed him. He summoned them and asked them, and they swore that ʿĀmir was lying. ʿĀmir swore that they were liars and said, "O Allah, do not separate us until the truthful one's truthfulness and the liar's lie become clear." Then this verse was revealed: ﴿They swear to you by Allah to please you.﴾

A man is called *udhun* (an ear) when he listens to everyone's speech; the word applies to one and to many alike, as said by al-Jawharī. Al-Zamakhsharī said: *udhun* is the man who believes everything he hears and accepts everyone's word. It is named after the organ that is the instrument of hearing, as if his whole being were a listening ear. Its parallel is the saying of people about a spy: "an eye" (ʿayn). A poet said:

*I have become an ear for slanderers, listening, through which they reach my honour; yet had I wished, they would not have reached it.*

This is from them a disparagement of the Messenger, for they described him with a lack of prudence and with being easily deceived. It was also said: the meaning is "one who has an ear" (dhū udhun), so it is an elision of a modifier, as related from Ibn ʿAbbās. It was also said: *udhun* means one with sharp hearing, who perhaps heard our saying. It was also said: *udhun* is an adjective formed on the pattern *faʿal* from *adhina yaʾdhanu udhunan*, meaning "he listened," like *anaf*, *shalal*, and *irtafaʿa* (patterns of adjectives). *Udhun* is by ellipsis of a subject: i.e., "Say: he is an ear of good for you." This construct is like the saying "a man of truth" (rajul ṣidq), meaning excellence and righteousness. It is as if it were said: "Yes, he is an ear, but what an excellent ear." It is also permissible that the meaning be: he is an ear in matters of good, truth, and what must be heard and accepted, and not an ear for anything else. This is indicated by (*khayr*) and (*raḥma*) in the reading of one who put them in the genitive as a conjunction to (*khayr*), i.e., "he is an ear of good and mercy; he hears nothing else and accepts nothing else," as said by al-Zamakhsharī.

Al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, and Abū Bakr (through ʿĀṣim, in one transmission) read (*qul udhunun*) with tanwīn and (*khayrun*) with the nominative. Scholars permitted that (*udhunun*) be the predicate of an elided subject, and "khayrun" a second predicate of that elided subject, meaning: "he is an ear, he is good for you," because he (ﷺ) accepts your excuses and does not repay you for your bad conduct. Or that (*khayrun*) be an adjective of (*udhunun*), meaning "an ear possessing good for you." Or that (*khayran*) be a comparative (*afʿal al-tafḍīl*), meaning "more beneficial for you." Or that (*udhunun*) be the subject with (*khayrun*) as its predicate. It is permissible for an indefinite to be predicated of an indefinite with a benefit obtained, as said by the author of al-Lawāmiḥ, and it is valid on the assumption of an elided modifier, i.e., "an ear that does not hold you to account is good for you." Then Allah described him as one who believes in Allah, and whoever believes in Allah is fearful of Him and does not proceed to harm with falsehood. ﴿And believes the believers﴾, i.e., he listens to the believers and accepts from them what they say, and confirms them because they are believers, so they are truthful. And ﴿a mercy for those of you who believe﴾. He specified the believers, even though he is a mercy to all the worlds, because what was obtained by them through faith by means of the Messenger was not obtained by others; and they are specified here by mention, even though they are included among "the worlds," because of the distinction they have. These three attributes explain the aspect of goodness and make manifest his being an ear of good.

The verb (*yuʾminu*) is transitive first with (*bi*) and second with (*li*). Ibn Qutayba said: both prepositions are superfluous, and the meaning is: he confirms Allah and confirms the believers.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: he intended belief in Allah, which is the opposite of disbelief, so it takes (*bi*); and he intended listening to the believers and accepting from them what they say, so it takes (*li*). Do you not see the saying of the Exalted: ﴿You are not one who believes us, even if we were truthful﴾ [Yūsuf: 17]; how sufficient it is without (*bi*). Similar is ﴿None believed in Moses except some youth among his people﴾ [Yūnus: 83]; ﴿Shall we believe you when the lowest have followed you?﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 111]; ﴿You believed in him before I gave you permission﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 71]. End of his words.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: ﴿yu'minu bi-llāh﴾ means "confirms Allah," and ﴿yu'minu lil-mu'minīn﴾: it is said that its meaning is "and confirms the believers," and the *lām* is superfluous, as it is in ﴿radifa lakum﴾ [al-Naml: 72]. Al-Mubarrad said: it is connected to a verbal noun implied from the verb, as if he said: "and his belief for the believers," i.e., his confirmation. It was also said: one says "I believed you" (āmantu laka) meaning "I confirmed you" (ṣaddaqtuka), and from it is His saying ﴿You are not one who believes us﴾. In my view, the one with (*lām*) contains within it the sense of (*bā*). So the meaning is: he confirms for the believers in what they tell him; and likewise ﴿You are not one who believes us﴾ means "in what we say to you."

Ubayy, ʿAbdullāh, al-Aʿmash, and Ḥamza read (*wa-raḥmatin*) in the genitive as a conjunction to (*khayrin*), so the clause "yu'minu" is a parenthetical between the two conjoined terms. The rest of the seven read it in the nominative as a conjunction to (*yu'minu*), and (*yu'minu*) is an adjective of ﴿udhunu khayrin﴾. Ibn Abī ʿAbla read it in the accusative as an object of purpose, its governed element elided, the meaning being: "and mercy, he permits you," which is elided because of the indication of ﴿udhunu khayrin lakum﴾.

He stated the name of the Messenger explicitly and did not use a pronoun, following the pattern of (*yu'minu*), using the word "the Messenger" to glorify his station, and to combine for him in the verse the two great ranks of prophethood and messengership. Attaching him to Allah is an increase in his honour. He decreed a painful punishment upon whoever harms him, and that is rightly theirs. ﴿And those who harm﴾ is general, including those who committed this specific harm and others.

﴿They swear to you by Allah to please you, but Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him, if they are believers.﴾: The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in (*yaḥlifūna*) refers to those who said (*huwa udhun*); they denied it and swore they had not said it. It was also said that it refers to those who said, "If what Muhammad says is true, we are worse than donkeys," and this has already been mentioned. It was also said that it refers to those who stayed behind from the expedition of Tabūk. When the Messenger and the believers returned, they made excuses, swore oaths, and offered pretexts; this was said by Ibn al-Sāʾib and chosen by al-Bayhaqī. They were eighty-three; eighty of them swore oaths, so the Messenger accepted their excuses, while three of them admitted the truth. Allah informed His Messenger of their lies and hypocrisy, and they all perished through calamities, while those who were truthful were saved. It was also said that it refers to ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy and those with him, who swore that they would not stay behind from the Messenger of Allah and would be with him against his enemy. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: the intended meaning is all the hypocrites who swear to the Messenger and the believers that they are with them in religion and in every matter and war, while they conceal hypocrisy and await misfortunes for the believers. This is the view of a group of exegetes.

The *lām* in (*li-yurḍūkum*) is the *lām* of purpose (*lām kay*). Whoever claimed it is the answer to the oath has erred. The pronoun in (*an yurḍūhu*) is singular because the two (Allah and His Messenger) are in the ruling of one object of pleasure, since Allah's pleasure is the Messenger's pleasure; or there is an elision in the sentence. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: the school of Sībawayh is that they are two sentences, the first elided because the second indicates it, and the estimate in his view is: "and Allah has more right that they should please Him, and His Messenger has more right that they should please Him." This is like the saying of the poet:

*We are content with what we have, and you are content with what you have, and the opinions differ.*

The school of al-Mubarrad is that there is anteposition and postposition in the sentence, and its estimate is: "and Allah has more right that they should please Him and His Messenger." It was also said that the pronoun refers to what was mentioned, as Ruʾba said:

*In them are lines of blackness and white, as if on the skin they were the mottling of vitiligo.*

[p. 62] … [p. 63] … [p. 64]

End of quotation. The view of Sibawayh is that they are two clauses, the first of which is omitted because the second indicates it. If the pronoun in "annahuma" refers to each of the two clauses, how can you say "the first was omitted," when it is not the first that was omitted but only its predicate? If the pronoun refers to the predicate, which is ﴿ahaqqu an yurdhuhu﴾ (more worthy that they please Him), then it is not a clause unless one holds that "an yurdhuhu" is the subject and the preceding "ahaqqu" is its predicate. However, this view is not binding, since the predicate may be singular, with the sense "ahaqqu bi-an yurdhuhu" (more worthy of pleasing Him). On the first estimate the sense is: "and the pleasing of Allah is more worthy." Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: "and Allah is more worthy that they please Him, and likewise His Messenger."

﴿If they are believers﴾ as they claim. Then the one most worthy to be pleased is Allah and His Messenger, through obedience and agreement.

﴿Do they not know that whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger, for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein. That is the great disgrace.﴾ That is, "Do the hypocrites not know?" This is an interrogative whose meaning is rebuke and denunciation. Al-Hasan and al-A'raj read it with the "ta'" (ﺗ), as a second-person address. The apparent reading is then an iltifat (shift of grammatical person) addressed to the hypocrites. It has been said that it may also be an address to the believers, in which case the interrogative means confirmation. If it is an address to the Messenger (ﷺ), it is an address of honour, and the interrogative in it expresses wonder, with the sense: "Are you not astonished at their ignorance regarding opposition to Allah the Exalted?" In the codex of Ubayy it reads: "Does he not know?" Ibn Atiyya said: "addressed to the Prophet, peace be upon him." It ended. The better view is that it is an address to the listener. The scholars of semantics (ahl al-ma'ani) said: "Have you not known?" is an address to one who has tried for a period to teach a person something and has made great effort in that teaching, yet he has not learned it, so it is said to him: "Do you not know, after the clear discussions and the long period?" This is appropriate because the Prophet (ﷺ) remained with him for a long time, and he frequently warned him against disobedience to Allah and encouraged obedience to Allah.

Some said: al-muhadda (opposition) is opposing, as in "I opposed him" (haddadtuhu, khalaftuhu), and its derivation is from the limit (hadd), i.e., he was on a limit other than the limit, like your saying "shaqqahu," he was on a side other than his side. Abu Muslim said: al-muhadda is derived from iron (al-hadid), the iron of weapons. Here, according to Ibn Abbas, al-muhadda means opposition. It has been said: warfare. It has been said: enmity. It has been said: hostility. It has been said: going beyond the limit in opposition. These sayings are close in meaning.

The majority read ﴿fa-anna lahu﴾ with a fatha on the hamza, and the fa is the response of the condition, so it requires a clause, and "anna lahu" is a singular in a position of nominative (raf') as a subject (mubtada'), its predicate omitted. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as preceded and indefinite: "then it is necessary that there be." Another estimated it as delayed: "then that for him is the fire of Hell is obligatory," which al-Akhfash said, and this was refuted on the ground that "anna" may not begin a sentence with its predicate preceding it, and this is the view of Sibawayh and the majority. Al-Akhfash, al-Farra' and Abu Hatim permitted beginning with it with its predicate preceding. Al-Akhfash drew this on his own principle. Or it is in a position of nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "then what is obligatory is that for him is the fire." Ali ibn Sulayman said: al-Jarmi and al-Mubarrad said: the second "anna" is repeated for emphasis, as if the estimate were "then for him is the fire of Hell," and "anna" was repeated for emphasis. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also possible that ﴿fa-anna lahu﴾ is conjoined to "annahu," on the basis that the response of "man" is omitted, its estimate being: "Do they not know that whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger will perish, then for him is the fire of Hell." It ended. Then ﴿fa-anna lahu nara jahannam﴾ is in a position of accusative (nasb). This which he estimated is not valid, because they stated that when the response is omitted because the speech indicates it, the verb of the condition is either past in form, or present jussive preceded by "lam." So in their speech one says, "You are wrong if you did," and it is not permitted to say, "if you do." Here the response of the condition is omitted, and the verb of the condition is neither past in form nor present with "lam." If that occurs in their speech, it is restricted to poetic necessity. Also, you find the speech complete without estimating this response. They related from Sibawayh that "anna" is a badal (substitute/apposition) of "annahu." Ibn Atiyya said: This is objected to on the ground that a thing may not be substituted for until it is complete. The better view in this place is: its predicate did not come after the response of the condition was not complete, and that clause is the predicate. Also, the fa prevents the badal, and also it is another meaning from the first, so the badal is unsettled; and if it is softened to be a badal, it is a badal of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal). It ended. Abu al-Baqa' said: This, meaning the badal, is weak for two reasons: first, the fa that accompanies it prevents that, and judging its being an extra element is weak. Second, making it a badal entails dropping the response of the speech. It ended. It has been said: it is with the omission of the lam, i.e., ﴿fa-li-anna lahu nara jahannam﴾, so the fa is the response of the condition, and one needs to supply what completes the response as a clause, i.e., "then its opposition is because for him is the fire of Hell." Ibn Abi Ablah read ﴿fa-inna lahu﴾ with a kasra on the hamza. Abu Amr al-Dani transmitted this from him, and it is the reading of Mahbub from al-Hasan, and the narration of Abu Ubayda from Abu Amr. Its grammatical basis is strong, because the fa calls for resumption (isti'naf), and the kasra is preferred because it does not need an estimate, unlike the fatha. A poet said:

*Whoever would ask about me, then indeed I*
*and Jirwa are not ones who turn back, nor are lent.*

On this, two possibilities are permitted for "inna" after the fa of the response: fatha and kasra. The reason is that the being of the fire for him, abiding therein, is the great humiliation, as our Lord said: ﴿Indeed, whoever You admit to the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him﴾ [Aal 'Imran: 192].

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verses 61–63 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And among them are those who harm the Prophet and say, "He is all ears." Say, "An ear of good for you: he believes in Allah, and believes the believers, and is a mercy for those of you who believe. And those who harm the Messenger of Allah will have a painful punishment."﴾ ﴿They swear to you by Allah to please you, but Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him, if they are believers.﴾ ﴿Do they not know that whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger, for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever? That is the great disgrace.﴾ ﴿The hypocrites fear that a surah will be sent down about them, informing them of what is in their hearts. Say, "Mock, for Allah will surely bring out what you fear."﴾ [al-Tawbah: 64] ﴿And if you ask them, they will surely say, "We were only conversing and playing." Say, "Was it Allah, His signs, and His Messenger that you were mocking?"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 65] ﴿Make no excuses; you have disbelieved after your belief. If We pardon a group among you, We will punish another group because they were criminals.﴾ [al-Tawbah: 66] ﴿The hypocrite men and women are of one another. They enjoin what is evil, forbid what is good, and withhold their hands. They have forgotten Allah, so He has forgotten them. Indeed, the hypocrites are the defiantly disobedient.﴾ [al-Tawbah: 67] ﴿Allah has promised the hypocrite men and women and the disbelievers the fire of Hell, abiding therein. It is sufficient for them. Allah has cursed them, and for them is a lasting punishment.﴾ [al-Tawbah: 68] ﴿Like those before you, who were stronger than you in power and greater in wealth and children, and they enjoyed their share, and you have enjoyed your share as those before you enjoyed their share, and you have engaged in vain talk as they engaged. Those are the ones whose deeds became worthless in this world and the Hereafter, and those are the losers.﴾ [al-Tawbah: 69] ﴿Has there not come to them the news of those before them: the people of Noah, ʿĀd, Thamūd, the people of Abraham, the companions of Madyan, and the overturned cities? Then Allah described him as one who believes in Allah, and whoever believes in Allah is fearful of Him and does not proceed to harm with falsehood. ﴿And believes the believers﴾, i.e., he listens to the believers and accepts from them what they say, and confirms them because they are believers, so they are truthful. And ﴿a mercy for those of you who believe﴾. He specified the believers, even though he is a mercy to all the worlds, because what was obtained by them through faith by means of the Messenger was not obtained by others; and they are specified here by mention, even though they are included among "the worlds," because of the distinction they have. These three attributes explain the aspect of goodness and make manifest his being an ear of good.

The verb (*yuʾminu*) is transitive first with (*bi*) and second with (*li*). Ibn Qutayba said: both prepositions are superfluous, and the meaning is: he confirms Allah and confirms the believers.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: he intended belief in Allah, which is the opposite of disbelief, so it takes (*bi*); and he intended listening to the believers and accepting from them what they say, so it takes (*li*). Do you not see the saying of the Exalted: ﴿You are not one who believes us, even if we were truthful﴾ [Yūsuf: 17]; how sufficient it is without (*bi*). Similar is ﴿None believed in Moses except some youth among his people﴾ [Yūnus: 83]; ﴿Shall we believe you when the lowest have followed you?﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 111]; ﴿You believed in him before I gave you permission﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 71]. End of his words.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: ﴿yu'minu bi-llāh﴾ means "confirms Allah," and ﴿yu'minu lil-mu'minīn﴾: it is said that its meaning is "and confirms the believers," and the *lām* is superfluous, as it is in ﴿radifa lakum﴾ [al-Naml: 72]. Al-Mubarrad said: it is connected to a verbal noun implied from the verb, as if he said: "and his belief for the believers," i.e., his confirmation. It was also said: one says "I believed you" (āmantu laka) meaning "I confirmed you" (ṣaddaqtuka), and from it is His saying ﴿You are not one who believes us﴾. In my view, the one with (*lām*) contains within it the sense of (*bā*). So the meaning is: he confirms for the believers in what they tell him; and likewise ﴿You are not one who believes us﴾ means "in what we say to you."

Ubayy, ʿAbdullāh, al-Aʿmash, and Ḥamza read (*wa-raḥmatin*) in the genitive as a conjunction to (*khayrin*), so the clause "yu'minu" is a parenthetical between the two conjoined terms. The rest of the seven read it in the nominative as a conjunction to (*yu'minu*), and (*yu'minu*) is an adjective of ﴿udhunu khayrin﴾. Ibn Abī ʿAbla read it in the accusative as an object of purpose, its governed element elided, the meaning being: "and mercy, he permits you," which is elided because of the indication of ﴿udhunu khayrin lakum﴾.

He stated the name of the Messenger explicitly and did not use a pronoun, following the pattern of (*yu'minu*), using the word "the Messenger" to glorify his station, and to combine for him in the verse the two great ranks of prophethood and messengership. Attaching him to Allah is an increase in his honour. He decreed a painful punishment upon whoever harms him, and that is rightly theirs. ﴿And those who harm﴾ is general, including those who committed this specific harm and others.

﴿They swear to you by Allah to please you, but Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him, if they are believers.﴾: The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in (*yaḥlifūna*) refers to those who said (*huwa udhun*); they denied it and swore they had not said it. It was also said that it refers to those who said, "If what Muhammad says is true, we are worse than donkeys," and this has already been mentioned. It was also said that it refers to those who stayed behind from the expedition of Tabūk. When the Messenger and the believers returned, they made excuses, swore oaths, and offered pretexts; this was said by Ibn al-Sāʾib and chosen by al-Bayhaqī. They were eighty-three; eighty of them swore oaths, so the Messenger accepted their excuses, while three of them admitted the truth. Allah informed His Messenger of their lies and hypocrisy, and they all perished through calamities, while those who were truthful were saved. It was also said that it refers to ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy and those with him, who swore that they would not stay behind from the Messenger of Allah and would be with him against his enemy. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: the intended meaning is all the hypocrites who swear to the Messenger and the believers that they are with them in religion and in every matter and war, while they conceal hypocrisy and await misfortunes for the believers. This is the view of a group of exegetes.

The *lām* in (*li-yurḍūkum*) is the *lām* of purpose (*lām kay*). Whoever claimed it is the answer to the oath has erred. The pronoun in (*an yurḍūhu*) is singular because the two (Allah and His Messenger) are in the ruling of one object of pleasure, since Allah's pleasure is the Messenger's pleasure; or there is an elision in the sentence. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: the school of Sībawayh is that they are two sentences, the first elided because the second indicates it, and the estimate in his view is: "and Allah has more right that they should please Him, and His Messenger has more right that they should please Him." This is like the saying of the poet:

*We are content with what we have, and you are content with what you have, and the opinions differ.*

The school of al-Mubarrad is that there is anteposition and postposition in the sentence, and its estimate is: "and Allah has more right that they should please Him and His Messenger." It was also said that the pronoun refers to what was mentioned, as Ruʾba said:

*In them are lines of blackness and white, as if on the skin they were the mottling of vitiligo.*

[p. 62] … [p. 63] … [p. 64]

End of quotation. The view of Sibawayh is that they are two clauses, the first of which is omitted because the second indicates it. If the pronoun in "annahuma" refers to each of the two clauses, how can you say "the first was omitted," when it is not the first that was omitted but only its predicate? If the pronoun refers to the predicate, which is ﴿ahaqqu an yurdhuhu﴾ (more worthy that they please Him), then it is not a clause unless one holds that "an yurdhuhu" is the subject and the preceding "ahaqqu" is its predicate. However, this view is not binding, since the predicate may be singular, with the sense "ahaqqu bi-an yurdhuhu" (more worthy of pleasing Him). On the first estimate the sense is: "and the pleasing of Allah is more worthy." Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: "and Allah is more worthy that they please Him, and likewise His Messenger."

﴿If they are believers﴾ as they claim. Then the one most worthy to be pleased is Allah and His Messenger, through obedience and agreement.

﴿Do they not know that whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger, for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein. That is the great disgrace.﴾ That is, "Do the hypocrites not know?" This is an interrogative whose meaning is rebuke and denunciation. Al-Hasan and al-A'raj read it with the "ta'" (ﺗ), as a second-person address. The apparent reading is then an iltifat (shift of grammatical person) addressed to the hypocrites. It has been said that it may also be an address to the believers, in which case the interrogative means confirmation. If it is an address to the Messenger (ﷺ), it is an address of honour, and the interrogative in it expresses wonder, with the sense: "Are you not astonished at their ignorance regarding opposition to Allah the Exalted?" In the codex of Ubayy it reads: "Does he not know?" Ibn Atiyya said: "addressed to the Prophet, peace be upon him." It ended. The better view is that it is an address to the listener. The scholars of semantics (ahl al-ma'ani) said: "Have you not known?" is an address to one who has tried for a period to teach a person something and has made great effort in that teaching, yet he has not learned it, so it is said to him: "Do you not know, after the clear discussions and the long period?" This is appropriate because the Prophet (ﷺ) remained with him for a long time, and he frequently warned him against disobedience to Allah and encouraged obedience to Allah.

Some said: al-muhadda (opposition) is opposing, as in "I opposed him" (haddadtuhu, khalaftuhu), and its derivation is from the limit (hadd), i.e., he was on a limit other than the limit, like your saying "shaqqahu," he was on a side other than his side. Abu Muslim said: al-muhadda is derived from iron (al-hadid), the iron of weapons. Here, according to Ibn Abbas, al-muhadda means opposition. It has been said: warfare. It has been said: enmity. It has been said: hostility. It has been said: going beyond the limit in opposition. These sayings are close in meaning.

The majority read ﴿fa-anna lahu﴾ with a fatha on the hamza, and the fa is the response of the condition, so it requires a clause, and "anna lahu" is a singular in a position of nominative (raf') as a subject (mubtada'), its predicate omitted. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as preceded and indefinite: "then it is necessary that there be." Another estimated it as delayed: "then that for him is the fire of Hell is obligatory," which al-Akhfash said, and this was refuted on the ground that "anna" may not begin a sentence with its predicate preceding it, and this is the view of Sibawayh and the majority. Al-Akhfash, al-Farra' and Abu Hatim permitted beginning with it with its predicate preceding. Al-Akhfash drew this on his own principle. Or it is in a position of nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "then what is obligatory is that for him is the fire." Ali ibn Sulayman said: al-Jarmi and al-Mubarrad said: the second "anna" is repeated for emphasis, as if the estimate were "then for him is the fire of Hell," and "anna" was repeated for emphasis. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also possible that ﴿fa-anna lahu﴾ is conjoined to "annahu," on the basis that the response of "man" is omitted, its estimate being: "Do they not know that whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger will perish, then for him is the fire of Hell." It ended. Then ﴿fa-anna lahu nara jahannam﴾ is in a position of accusative (nasb). This which he estimated is not valid, because they stated that when the response is omitted because the speech indicates it, the verb of the condition is either past in form, or present jussive preceded by "lam." So in their speech one says, "You are wrong if you did," and it is not permitted to say, "if you do." Here the response of the condition is omitted, and the verb of the condition is neither past in form nor present with "lam." If that occurs in their speech, it is restricted to poetic necessity. Also, you find the speech complete without estimating this response. They related from Sibawayh that "anna" is a badal (substitute/apposition) of "annahu." Ibn Atiyya said: This is objected to on the ground that a thing may not be substituted for until it is complete. The better view in this place is: its predicate did not come after the response of the condition was not complete, and that clause is the predicate. Also, the fa prevents the badal, and also it is another meaning from the first, so the badal is unsettled; and if it is softened to be a badal, it is a badal of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal). It ended. Abu al-Baqa' said: This, meaning the badal, is weak for two reasons: first, the fa that accompanies it prevents that, and judging its being an extra element is weak. Second, making it a badal entails dropping the response of the speech. It ended. It has been said: it is with the omission of the lam, i.e., ﴿fa-li-anna lahu nara jahannam﴾, so the fa is the response of the condition, and one needs to supply what completes the response as a clause, i.e., "then its opposition is because for him is the fire of Hell." Ibn Abi Ablah read ﴿fa-inna lahu﴾ with a kasra on the hamza. Abu Amr al-Dani transmitted this from him, and it is the reading of Mahbub from al-Hasan, and the narration of Abu Ubayda from Abu Amr. Its grammatical basis is strong, because the fa calls for resumption (isti'naf), and the kasra is preferred because it does not need an estimate, unlike the fatha. A poet said:

*Whoever would ask about me, then indeed I*
*and Jirwa are not ones who turn back, nor are lent.*

On this, two possibilities are permitted for "inna" after the fa of the response: fatha and kasra. The reason is that the being of the fire for him, abiding therein, is the great humiliation, as our Lord said: ﴿Indeed, whoever You admit to the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him﴾ [Aal 'Imran: 192].

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verses 61–63 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And among them are those who harm the Prophet and say, "He is all ears." Say, "An ear of good for you: he believes in Allah, and believes the believers, and is a mercy for those of you who believe. And those who harm the Messenger of Allah will have a painful punishment."﴾ ﴿They swear to you by Allah to please you, but Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him, if they are believers.﴾ ﴿Do they not know that whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger, for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever? That is the great disgrace.﴾ ﴿The hypocrites fear that a surah will be sent down about them, informing them of what is in their hearts. Say, "Mock, for Allah will surely bring out what you fear."﴾ [al-Tawbah: 64] ﴿And if you ask them, they will surely say, "We were only conversing and playing." Say, "Was it Allah, His signs, and His Messenger that you were mocking?"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 65] ﴿Make no excuses; you have disbelieved after your belief. If We pardon a group among you, We will punish another group because they were criminals.﴾ [al-Tawbah: 66] ﴿The hypocrite men and women are of one another. They enjoin what is evil, forbid what is good, and withhold their hands. They have forgotten Allah, so He has forgotten them. Indeed, the hypocrites are the defiantly disobedient.﴾ [al-Tawbah: 67] ﴿Allah has promised the hypocrite men and women and the disbelievers the fire of Hell, abiding therein. It is sufficient for them. Allah has cursed them, and for them is a lasting punishment.﴾ [al-Tawbah: 68] ﴿Like those before you, who were stronger than you in power and greater in wealth and children, and they enjoyed their share, and you have enjoyed your share as those before you enjoyed their share, and you have engaged in vain talk as they engaged. Those are the ones whose deeds became worthless in this world and the Hereafter, and those are the losers.﴾ [al-Tawbah: 69] ﴿Has there not come to them the news of those before them: the people of Noah, ʿĀd, Thamūd, the people of Abraham, the companions of Madyan, and the overturned cities? Their messengers came to them with clear proofs. Allah did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves.﴾ [al-Tawbah: 70] ﴿The believing men and women are allies of one another. They enjoin what is good, forbid what is evil, establish prayer, give zakat, and obey Allah and His Messenger. Those, Allah will have mercy upon. Indeed, Allah is Mighty and Wise.﴾ [al-Tawbah: 71] ﴿Allah has promised the believing men and women gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein, and pleasant dwellings in gardens of perpetual residence. But approval from Allah is greater. That is the great achievement.﴾ [al-Tawbah: 72]

Al-iʿtidhār (making an excuse, i.e. disclaiming one's fault): it is said that its origin is erasure, from the saying of the Arabs, "the campsites made an excuse and were effaced" (iʿtadharat al-manāzil wa-darasat), so the one who makes an excuse seeks to remove his fault. Ibn Aḥmar said:

*You knew the signs; yet they have made the traces of your beloved in the sandy tract an excuse (taʿtadhir).*

It is related from Ibn al-Aʿrābī that iʿtidhār means cutting off. From it comes ʿudhrat al-jāriya, because she is cut (tuʿdhar, i.e. her hymen is severed), and iʿtadharat al-miyāh means the waters stopped flowing. An excuse (ʿudhr) is a cause for cutting off blame. ʿAdana bi-l-makān yaʿdinu ʿudūnan means he settled, as said by Abū Zayd and Ibn al-Aʿrābī. Al-Aʿshā said:

*If they seek hospitality in his forbearance, they will be hosted by a noble one who has settled (ʿadan).*

The Arabs say: "The camels of so-and-so were left as ʿawādin in such-and-such a place," meaning the camels stay in the place, become accustomed to it, and do not leave it. The mine (maʿdin) was so named because God causes the jewel to grow in it and establishes it in the earth until it settles (ʿadana) there, i.e. becomes firm. ʿAdan is a city in Yemen, because it is the most populous of the cities of Yemen in inhabitants and houses.

﴿And among them are those who harm the Prophet and say, "He is all ears." Say, "An ear of good for you: he believes in Allah, and believes the believers, and is a mercy for those of you who believe. And those who harm the Messenger of Allah will have a painful punishment."﴾: Qudām ibn Khālid, ʿUbayd ibn Hilāl, and al-Julās ibn Suwayd, along with others, were harming the Messenger. Some of them said, "Do not do this, for we fear that it will reach him and he will strike us." Al-Julās said, "Rather, we will say whatever we wish, for Muhammad is an ear that hears; then we will come to him and he will believe us." Then this was revealed.

It was also said: it was revealed about Nabtal ibn al-Ḥārith, who used to convey the Messenger's words to the hypocrites. He was told, "Do not do this," but he said that statement.

It was also said: it was revealed about al-Julās and Zamʿa ibn Thābit, along with others, who wanted to disparage the Messenger. With them was a young man from the Anṣār named ʿĀmir ibn Qays, whom they belittled. They said, "If what Muhammad says is true, then we are worse than donkeys." The young man became angry and said, "By Allah, what Muhammad says is true, and you are worse than donkeys." Then he went to the Messenger of Allah and informed him. He summoned them and asked them, and they swore that ʿĀmir was lying. ʿĀmir swore that they were liars and said, "O Allah, do not separate us until the truthful one's truthfulness and the liar's lie become clear." Then this verse was revealed: ﴿They swear to you by Allah to please you.﴾

A man is called *udhun* (an ear) when he listens to everyone's speech; the word applies to one and to many alike, as said by al-Jawharī. Al-Zamakhsharī said: *udhun* is the man who believes everything he hears and accepts everyone's word. It is named after the organ that is the instrument of hearing, as if his whole being were a listening ear. Its parallel is the saying of people about a spy: "an eye" (ʿayn). A poet said:

*I have become an ear for slanderers, listening, through which they reach my honour; yet had I wished, they would not have reached it.*

This is from them a disparagement of the Messenger, for they described him with a lack of prudence and with being easily deceived. It was also said: the meaning is "one who has an ear" (dhū udhun), so it is an elision of a modifier, as related from Ibn ʿAbbās. It was also said: *udhun* means one with sharp hearing, who perhaps heard our saying. It was also said: *udhun* is an adjective formed on the pattern *faʿal* from *adhina yaʾdhanu udhunan*, meaning "he listened," like *anaf*, *shalal*, and *irtafaʿa* (patterns of adjectives). *Udhun* is by ellipsis of a subject: i.e., "Say: he is an ear of good for you." This construct is like the saying "a man of truth" (rajul ṣidq), meaning excellence and righteousness. It is as if it were said: "Yes, he is an ear, but what an excellent ear." It is also permissible that the meaning be: he is an ear in matters of good, truth, and what must be heard and accepted, and not an ear for anything else. This is indicated by (*khayr*) and (*raḥma*) in the reading of one who put them in the genitive as a conjunction to (*khayr*), i.e., "he is an ear of good and mercy; he hears nothing else and accepts nothing else," as said by al-Zamakhsharī.

Al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, and Abū Bakr (through ʿĀṣim, in one transmission) read (*qul udhunun*) with tanwīn and (*khayrun*) with the nominative. Scholars permitted that (*udhunun*) be the predicate of an elided subject, and "khayrun" a second predicate of that elided subject, meaning: "he is an ear, he is good for you," because he (ﷺ) accepts your excuses and does not repay you for your bad conduct. Or that (*khayrun*) be an adjective of (*udhunun*), meaning "an ear possessing good for you." Or that (*khayran*) be a comparative (*afʿal al-tafḍīl*), meaning "more beneficial for you." Or that (*udhunun*) be the subject with (*khayrun*) as its predicate. It is permissible for an indefinite to be predicated of an indefinite with a benefit obtained, as said by the author of al-Lawāmiḥ, and it is valid on the assumption of an elided modifier, i.e., "an ear that does not hold you to account is good for you." Then Allah described him as one who believes in Allah, and whoever believes in Allah is fearful of Him and does not proceed to harm with falsehood. ﴿And believes the believers﴾, i.e., he listens to the believers and accepts from them what they say, and confirms them because they are believers, so they are truthful. Al-Zamakhsharī said: he intended belief in Allah, which is the opposite of disbelief, so it takes (*bi*); and he intended listening to the believers and accepting from them what they say, so it takes (*li*). Do you not see the saying of the Exalted: ﴿You are not one who believes us, even if we were truthful﴾ [Yūsuf: 17]; how sufficient it is without (*bi*). ﴿Do they not know that whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger, for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein. That is the great disgrace.﴾ That is, "Do the hypocrites not know?"
