The apparent reading is then an iltifat (shift of grammatical person) addressed to the hypocrites. It has been said that it may also be an address to the believers, in which case the interrogative means confirmation. If it is an address to the Messenger (ﷺ), it is an address of honour, and the interrogative in it expresses wonder, with the sense: "Are you not astonished at their ignorance regarding opposition to Allah the Exalted?" In the codex of Ubayy it reads: "Does he not know?" Ibn Atiyya said: "addressed to the Prophet, peace be upon him." It ended. The better view is that it is an address to the listener. The scholars of semantics (ahl al-ma'ani) said: "Have you not known?" is an address to one who has tried for a period to teach a person something and has made great effort in that teaching, yet he has not learned it, so it is said to him: "Do you not know, after the clear discussions and the long period?" This is appropriate because the Prophet (ﷺ) remained with him for a long time, and he frequently warned him against disobedience to Allah and encouraged obedience to Allah.

Some said: al-muhadda (opposition) is opposing, as in "I opposed him" (haddadtuhu, khalaftuhu), and its derivation is from the limit (hadd), i.e., he was on a limit other than the limit, like your saying "shaqqahu," he was on a side other than his side. Abu Muslim said: al-muhadda is derived from iron (al-hadid), the iron of weapons. Here, according to Ibn Abbas, al-muhadda means opposition. It has been said: warfare. It has been said: enmity. It has been said: hostility. It has been said: going beyond the limit in opposition. These sayings are close in meaning.

The majority read ﴿fa-anna lahu﴾ with a fatha on the hamza, and the fa is the response of the condition, so it requires a clause, and "anna lahu" is a singular in a position of nominative (raf') as a subject (mubtada'), its predicate omitted. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as preceded and indefinite: "then it is necessary that there be." Another estimated it as delayed: "then that for him is the fire of Hell is obligatory," which al-Akhfash said, and this was refuted on the ground that "anna" may not begin a sentence with its predicate preceding it, and this is the view of Sibawayh and the majority. Al-Akhfash, al-Farra' and Abu Hatim permitted beginning with it with its predicate preceding. Al-Akhfash drew this on his own principle. Or it is in a position of nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "then what is obligatory is that for him is the fire." Ali ibn Sulayman said: al-Jarmi and al-Mubarrad said: the second "anna" is repeated for emphasis, as if the estimate were "then for him is the fire of Hell," and "anna" was repeated for emphasis. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also possible that ﴿fa-anna lahu﴾ is conjoined to "annahu," on the basis that the response of "man" is omitted, its estimate being: "Do they not know that whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger will perish, then for him is the fire of Hell." It ended. Then ﴿fa-anna lahu nara jahannam﴾ is in a position of accusative (nasb). This which he estimated is not valid, because they stated that when the response is omitted because the speech indicates it, the verb of the condition is either past in form, or present jussive preceded by "lam." So in their speech one says, "You are wrong if you did," and it is not permitted to say, "if you do." Here the response of the condition is omitted, and the verb of the condition is neither past in form nor present with "lam." If that occurs in their speech, it is restricted to poetic necessity. Also, you find the speech complete without estimating this response. They related from Sibawayh that "anna" is a badal (substitute/apposition) of "annahu." Ibn Atiyya said: This is objected to on the ground that a thing may not be substituted for until it is complete. The better view in this place is: its predicate did not come after the response of the condition was not complete, and that clause is the predicate. Also, the fa prevents the badal, and also it is another meaning from the first, so the badal is unsettled; and if it is softened to be a badal, it is a badal of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal). It ended. Abu al-Baqa' said: This, meaning the badal, is weak for two reasons: first, the fa that accompanies it prevents that, and judging its being an extra element is weak. Second, making it a badal entails dropping the response of the speech. It ended. It has been said: it is with the omission of the lam, i.e., ﴿fa-li-anna lahu nara jahannam﴾, so the fa is the response of the condition, and one needs to supply what completes the response as a clause, i.e., "then its opposition is because for him is the fire of Hell." Ibn Abi Ablah read ﴿fa-inna lahu﴾ with a kasra on the hamza. Abu Amr al-Dani transmitted this from him, and it is the reading of Mahbub from al-Hasan, and the narration of Abu Ubayda from Abu Amr. Its grammatical basis is strong, because the fa calls for resumption (isti'naf), and the kasra is preferred because it does not need an estimate, unlike the fatha. A poet said:

*Whoever would ask about me, then indeed I*
*and Jirwa are not ones who turn back, nor are lent.*

On this, two possibilities are permitted for "inna" after the fa of the response: fatha and kasra. The reason is that the being of the fire for him, abiding therein, is the great humiliation, as our Lord said: ﴿Indeed, whoever You admit to the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him﴾ [Aal 'Imran: 192].

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verses 64–66:

﴿The hypocrites are wary lest a surah should be sent down against them, informing them of what is in their hearts. Say: "Mock on! Indeed, Allah will bring out what you are wary of."﴾: The hypocrites used to disparage the Messenger and say: "Perhaps Allah will not disclose our secret." So this was revealed. This is related by Mujahid. Al-Suddi said: Some of them said: "I would rather be flogged a hundred times than have something revealed about us that exposes us." So this was revealed. Ibn Kaysan said: A group of them stood in wait for the Messenger (ﷺ) on a dark night as he was returning from Tabuk, intending to assassinate him, so Jibril (peace be upon him) informed him, and this was revealed. It is also said that they said during the expedition of Tabuk: "Does this man expect to be granted the palaces and fortresses of Syria? Far-fetched, far-fetched!" So Allah revealed: ﴿Say: "Mock on!"﴾. The apparent reading is that "yahdharu" (is wary) is a report (khabar), and this is indicated by ﴿Indeed, Allah will bring out what you are wary of.﴾ It is said: it is an actual occurrence on their part, for when they witnessed the Messenger informing them of what they were concealing, fear and dread entered their hearts. Al-Asamm said: They knew him to be a messenger from Allah, but they disbelieved out of envy. Al-Qadi considered it unlikely that one who knows Allah, His Messenger and the soundness of his religion would oppose them, but it is not improbable, for when envy becomes firmly established, the envious person disputes even what is perceptible. It is also said: it is a wariness they displayed in the manner of mockery, when they saw the Messenger mention things and that they were from revelation, and they would deny that. So Allah informed His Messenger of this and made known that He would expose their secret; and this is indicated by His saying: ﴿Say: "Mock on!"﴾. Al-Zajjaj and others who held that their disbelief was not obstinate said: it is a present-tense verb with the meaning of a command, i.e., "let the hypocrites be wary," and this is weakened by ﴿will bring out what you are wary of﴾. And "an tunazzala" (that a surah be sent down) is the object of "yahdhar," which is transitive. A poet said:

*He was wary of matters that do no harm, and felt secure from what would not save him from the decrees.*

And the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah warns you of Himself﴾ [Al 'Imran: 28]; since it was transitive to one object before the intensive form, it was made transitive to two by the intensive form. Al-Mubarrad said: "hadhara" is among the states of the soul that are not transitive, like "faza'a" (to be frightened), and the sense is: the hypocrites are wary of lest it be sent down; but this does not necessarily follow, for do you not see that "khafa" (to fear) is among the states of the soul and yet is transitive? The apparent view is that the two pronouns in His saying "'alayhim" and "tunabbi'uhum" both refer back to the hypocrites. "'Alayhim" is used because when a surah is sent down concerning their situation, it is sent down upon them; this is stated by al-Kirmani and al-Zamakhshari. Al-Kirmani said: It may also be from your saying: "This is against you, not for you."

The meaning of ﴿tunabbi'uhum bima fi qulubihim﴾ ("informs them of what is in their hearts") is: it spreads their secrets so widely that they hear them made public and circulated, so it is as though it informs them of them. Al-Zamakhshari said: The pronoun in "'alayhim" and "tunabbi'uhum" refers to the believers, and "fi qulubihim" refers to the hypocrites, and this is correct because the meaning returns to it. End of quote. The command to mock is a command of threat and warning, like His saying: ﴿Do what you will﴾ [Fussilat: 40]. The meaning of ﴿mukhrijun ma tahdharun﴾ ("will bring out what you are wary of") is: will bring into the realm of existence what you are wary of, namely the sending down of the surah; or will manifest what you were wary of, namely the exposure of your hypocrisy. Allah did this in this surah, and so it is called "al-Fadiha" (the Disgracer), because it disgraced the hypocrites. It is said: they were seventy men, whose names and the names of their fathers Allah sent down in the Qur'an; then this was lifted and abrogated, out of His mercy and compassion towards His creation, because their sons were Muslims.

﴿And if you ask them, they will surely say: "We were only engaging in idle talk and play." Say: "Was it Allah, His signs and His Messenger that you were mocking?"﴾; i.e., if you ask them about the foul things they said concerning you and your companions, such as some of them saying: "Look at this man, who wants to conquer the palaces of Syria," and some saying: "It is as if you will be tomorrow in the mountains, captives of the Banu al-Asfar," and some saying: "I have never seen the like of these: none more desirous of food, none more lying, and none more cowardly at the meeting of the enemy." So Allah informed His Prophet of this and he rebuked them, and they said: "O Prophet of Allah, we were not in anything concerning your affair or the affair of your companions; we were only in something of what (p-67) the riders talk about, we were not serious." Say: "Was it Allah?" is a rebuke for their mockery, and it carries a threat within it, and He did not heed their excuse because they were lying in it. They were treated as though they acknowledged their mockery and that it had occurred from them, so they were reproached for their faults at the point of mockery, where the one mocked at is placed in the form of a rebuke. This is only correct after the mockery has occurred and been established; this is stated by al-Zamakhshari, and it is good. The fronting of "billah" (by Allah), which is the complement of the predicate of "kana" (was), indicates the permissibility of fronting it before "kana." It is related from Ibn Umar: "I saw the one who said this statement - meaning: 'We were only engaging in idle talk and play' - Wadi'ah ibn Thabit, clinging to the rear strap of the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) she-camel, walking alongside it while the stones were striking him, and he was saying: 'We were only engaging in idle talk and play,' while the Prophet (ﷺ) was saying: 'Was it Allah, His signs and His Messenger that you were mocking?'" It is mentioned that this clinging man was Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, but that is an error, because he did not witness Tabuk.

﴿Make no excuses; you have disbelieved after your belief. If We pardon a group among you, We will punish another group, because they were criminals.﴾: They were forbidden to make excuses, because they were false excuses and therefore of no benefit. "Qad kafartum" (you have disbelieved) means: you have manifested disbelief after your belief, i.e., after displaying your belief, for they used to conceal disbelief, and then they manifested it through their mockery. The division by pardoning one group and punishing another is mentioned. The hypocrites were of two kinds: one kind was commanded to be fought against: ﴿Strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ [al-Tawbah: 73], and they were their leaders who openly spread rumours; they were punished by being expelled from the mosque and by the exposure of most of their conditions. The other kind were weak people who displayed belief even though they concealed disbelief, and they did not harm the Messenger, so he pardoned them; this punishment and pardon are in this world. It is also said: those pardoned are those whom Allah knew would sincerely renounce hypocrisy and perfect their faith, and those punished are those among them who died in their hypocrisy. It is also said: the one pardoned was a single man named Makhshi ibn Humayr, with a damma on the ha', a fatha on the mim, and a sukun on the ya'. He was among those who said: ﴿We were only engaging in idle talk and play﴾. It is said he was a hypocrite who then repented sincerely. It is also said he was a sincere Muslim, except that he heard the words of the hypocrites and laughed with them and did not object to them, so Allah pardoned him; he was martyred at Yamamah, having repented, and he was called Abd al-Rahman. He prayed to Allah that he be martyred and that his affair be unknown, and so it happened at Yamamah, and his body was never found.

Zayd ibn Thabit, Abu Abd al-Rahman, Zayd ibn Ali, and Asim, from among the Seven, read: "in na'fu" with a nun, "nu'adhdhib" with a nun, "ta'ifatan" (accusative). Our shaykh, the man of letters Abu al-Hakam Malik ibn al-Murahhal al-Maliqi, met me in Granada and asked me: "Whose recitation are you reciting today, according to Shaykh Abu Ja'far ibn al-Tabba'?" I said: "The recitation of Asim." He then recited to me:

*For Asim there is a recitation, differing from all others,*
*"In na'fu 'an ta'ifatin minkum nu'adhdhib ta'ifatan."*

The rest of the Seven read: "in ta'fu tu'adhdhab ta'ifatun," in the passive voice. Al-Jahdari read: "in ya'fu yu'adhdhibu," in the active voice in both, meaning: if Allah pardons. Mujahid read: "in tu'fa" with a ta', in the passive, and "tu'adhdhab" in the passive with a ta' as well. Ibn Atiyyah said: on the assumption: if these sins are pardoned. Al-Zamakhshari said: The correct form is the masculine, because the subject of the passive is the adverbial phrase, as you say: "sira bi-l-dabbah" (the animal was ridden), and you do not say "sirat bi-l-dabbah," but he considered the meaning, as if it were said: "in turhama ta'ifatun" (if a group is shown mercy), so he made it feminine on that basis, and this is strange. The good reading is the common reading: "in ya'fu 'an ta'ifatin" with the masculine, and "tu'adhdhab ta'ifatun" with the feminine. End of quote. (Mujrimin): persisting in hypocrisy, not repentant.

End of quote. The command to mock is a command of threat and warning, like His saying: ﴿Do what you will﴾ [Fussilat: 40]. The meaning of ﴿mukhrijun ma tahdharun﴾ ("will bring out what you are wary of") is: will bring into the realm of existence what you are wary of, namely the sending down of the surah; or will manifest what you were wary of, namely the exposure of your hypocrisy. Allah did this in this surah, and so it is called "al-Fadiha" (the Disgracer), because it disgraced the hypocrites. It is said: they were seventy men, whose names and the names of their fathers Allah sent down in the Qur'an; then this was lifted and abrogated, out of His mercy and compassion towards His creation, because their sons were Muslims.

﴿And if you ask them, they will surely say: "We were only engaging in idle talk and play." Say: "Was it Allah, His signs and His Messenger that you were mocking?"﴾; i.e., if you ask them about the foul things they said concerning you and your companions, such as some of them saying: "Look at this man, who wants to conquer the palaces of Syria," and some saying: "It is as if you will be tomorrow in the mountains, captives of the Banu al-Asfar," and some saying: "I have never seen the like of these: none more desirous of food, none more lying, and none more cowardly at the meeting of the enemy." So Allah informed His Prophet of this and he rebuked them, and they said: "O Prophet of Allah, we were not in anything concerning your affair or the affair of your companions; we were only in something of what (p-67) the riders talk about, we were not serious." Say: "Was it Allah?" is a rebuke for their mockery, and it carries a threat within it, and He did not heed their excuse because they were lying in it. They were treated as though they acknowledged their mockery and that it had occurred from them, so they were reproached for their faults at the point of mockery, where the one mocked at is placed in the form of a rebuke. This is only correct after the mockery has occurred and been established; this is stated by al-Zamakhshari, and it is good. The fronting of "billah" (by Allah), which is the complement of the predicate of "kana" (was), indicates the permissibility of fronting it before "kana." It is related from Ibn Umar: "I saw the one who said this statement - meaning: 'We were only engaging in idle talk and play' - Wadi'ah ibn Thabit, clinging to the rear strap of the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) she-camel, walking alongside it while the stones were striking him, and he was saying: 'We were only engaging in idle talk and play,' while the Prophet (ﷺ) was saying: 'Was it Allah, His signs and His Messenger that you were mocking?'" It is mentioned that this clinging man was Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, but that is an error, because he did not witness Tabuk.

﴿Make no excuses; you have disbelieved after your belief. If We pardon a group among you, We will punish another group, because they were criminals.﴾: They were forbidden to make excuses, because they were false excuses and therefore of no benefit. "Qad kafartum" (you have disbelieved) means: you have manifested disbelief after your belief, i.e., after displaying your belief, for they used to conceal disbelief, and then they manifested it through their mockery. The division by pardoning one group and punishing another is mentioned. The hypocrites were of two kinds: one kind was commanded to be fought against: ﴿Strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ [al-Tawbah: 73], and they were their leaders who openly spread rumours; they were punished by being expelled from the mosque and by the exposure of most of their conditions. The other kind were weak people who displayed belief even though they concealed disbelief, and they did not harm the Messenger, so he pardoned them; this punishment and pardon are in this world. It is also said: those pardoned are those whom Allah knew would sincerely renounce hypocrisy and perfect their faith, and those punished are those among them who died in their hypocrisy. It is also said: the one pardoned was a single man named Makhshi ibn Humayr, with a damma on the ha', a fatha on the mim, and a sukun on the ya'. He was among those who said: ﴿We were only engaging in idle talk and play﴾. It is said he was a hypocrite who then repented sincerely. It is also said he was a sincere Muslim, except that he heard the words of the hypocrites and laughed with them and did not object to them, so Allah pardoned him; he was martyred at Yamamah, having repented, and he was called Abd al-Rahman. He prayed to Allah that he be martyred and that his affair be unknown, and so it happened at Yamamah, and his body was never found.

Zayd ibn Thabit, Abu Abd al-Rahman, Zayd ibn Ali, and Asim, from among the Seven, read: "in na'fu" with a nun, "nu'adhdhib" with a nun, "ta'ifatan" (accusative). Our shaykh, the man of letters Abu al-Hakam Malik ibn al-Murahhal al-Maliqi, met me in Granada and asked me: "Whose recitation are you reciting today, according to Shaykh Abu Ja'far ibn al-Tabba'?" I said: "The recitation of Asim." He then recited to me:

*For Asim there is a recitation, differing from all others,*
*"In na'fu 'an ta'ifatin minkum nu'adhdhib ta'ifatan."*

The rest of the Seven read: "in ta'fu tu'adhdhab ta'ifatun," in the passive voice. Al-Jahdari read: "in ya'fu yu'adhdhibu," in the active voice in both, meaning: if Allah pardons. Mujahid read: "in tu'fa" with a ta', in the passive, and "tu'adhdhab" in the passive with a ta' as well. Ibn Atiyyah said: on the assumption: if these sins are pardoned. Al-Zamakhshari said: The correct form is the masculine, because the subject of the passive is the adverbial phrase, as you say: "sira bi-l-dabbah" (the animal was ridden), and you do not say "sirat bi-l-dabbah," but he considered the meaning, as if it were said: "in turhama ta'ifatun" (if a group is shown mercy), so he made it feminine on that basis, and this is strange. The good reading is the common reading: "in ya'fu 'an ta'ifatin" with the masculine, and "tu'adhdhab ta'ifatun" with the feminine. End of quote. (Mujrimin): persisting in hypocrisy, not repentant.

(p. 68) ﴿The hypocrite men and the hypocrite women are of one another. They enjoin what is evil and forbid what is good, and they withhold their hands. They have forgotten Allah, so He has forgotten them. Indeed, the hypocrites are the defiantly disobedient.﴾ He, may He be exalted, made clear that their males and females are not among the believers, as He said: ﴿And they swear by Allah that they are indeed of you, but they are not of you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 56]. Rather, "some of them are of others" in ruling, in standing, and in hypocrisy; they are upon one religion. The meaning is not partition in the literal sense, because that is well known. He described them by the opposite of what the believers are upon: that they enjoin "al-munkar" (the evil), which is disbelief, the worship of other than Allah, and acts of disobedience, and that they forbid "al-ma'ruf" (the good). This is because those about whom it was revealed did not have power or visible deeds, and that was due to the manifestation of Islam and its might. "Withholding the hands" is an expression for not spending in the way of Allah; this is what al-Hasan said. Qatadah said: "from every good." Ibn Zayd said: "from jihad and bearing arms in fighting the enemies of the religion." Sufyan said: "from raising the hands in supplication." It was also said that it is a metaphor (kinayah) for stinginess in expenditure on virtuous and obligatory matters. "Forgetting" here means abandonment. Qatadah said: "They abandoned obedience to Allah and obedience to His Messenger, so He forgot them," meaning He abandoned them from goodness; as for evil, He did not forget them. Al-Zamakhshari said: "They neglected His remembrance, so He forgot them," meaning He abandoned them from His mercy and bounty. Forgetting is used to express abandonment as an intensification, in that it does not occur to the mind at all. ﴿They are the defiantly disobedient﴾, meaning: they are the complete ones in defiant disobedience, which is persistent rebellion in disbelief and withdrawal from every good. It is sufficient a deterrent for the Muslim that he should not engage in anything that earns this foul designation with which Allah described the hypocrites.

﴿Allah has promised the hypocrite men and the hypocrite women and the disbelievers the fire of Hell, abiding therein. It is sufficient for them. And Allah has cursed them, and for them is a lasting punishment.﴾ "The disbelievers" here are those who openly declare disbelief. "Abiding therein" is a circumstantial clause anticipated (hal muqaddarah), because abiding did not coincide with the promise. "Hasbuhum" means sufficient for them, and this is an intensification of their punishment, since their punishment is something that cannot be increased upon. "Laʿanahum" (cursed them) means He humiliated them along with the punishment and made them blameworthy, joined to the accursed devils, just as He exalted the people of Paradise and joined them to the near angels. "Muqim" (lasting) means everlasting, without any transfer therein. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also possible that it means: and for them is a lasting punishment accompanying them in the immediate life, from which they never part, and it is what they suffer from the hardship of hypocrisy, and the outward appearance contrary to the inward out of fear of the Muslims, and what they fear always of disgrace and the descent of punishment if their secrets are discovered."

﴿Like those before you, who were stronger than you in might and more abundant in wealth and children. They enjoyed their share, and you enjoyed your share, as those before you enjoyed their share, and you engaged in vain talk as they engaged. Those — their deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter, and those are the losers.﴾ This is an iltifat (shift) from the pronoun of absence to the pronoun of address. Al-Farra' said: the comparison is in respect of the action, meaning: you did the deeds like the deeds of those before you, so the kaf (ka-, "like") is in the position of an accusative. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: He promised as He promised those before you, so it is connected to "wa'ada" (promised). Ibn Attiyah said: "In this there is some difficulty." Abu al-Baqa' said: it is possible that it is connected to "yastahziʾun" (they mock), but this is remote. It was also said: it is in the position of nominative, the estimate being: you are like those. The comparison occurred in enjoyment and in engaging in vain talk. His saying "they were stronger" is an explanation of their resemblance to them, and a representation of your action by their action. "Khalaq" means share, that is, what was decreed for them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: what is the benefit of His saying ﴿they enjoyed their share﴾ and His saying ﴿as those before you enjoyed their share﴾, is one not sufficient without the other, as ﴿like those who engaged in vain talk﴾ suffices? I say: its benefit is that by mentioning the first group with enjoyment, [He mentions] what they were given of worldly portions and their contentment with them and their distraction, so they are compared to those absorbed in worldly pleasure, heedless of consideration of the outcome and of seeking success in the Hereafter; and that the matter of enjoyment be debased and the one who is content with it be disparaged. Then, after that, He compared the state of those addressed to their state, just as one who wishes to alert some oppressor to the ugliness of his act says: "You are like Pharaoh, who used to kill without crime, torture, and oppress, and you do the same as his action." As for ﴿and you engaged in vain talk as they engaged﴾, it is coordinated with what precedes it, depending on it and needing no preliminary sentence because of its attachment to it. End of quotation. That is, it dispenses with the structure being: "and they engaged, so you engaged as those who engaged."

Ibn Attiyah said: "They were stronger than you and greater, and they disobeyed and perished. So you are more deserving of destruction for your disobedience and weakness. The meaning is: they hastened their share in their worldly life and abandoned the door of the Hereafter, and you followed them." End of quotation. When He mentioned their resemblance to those before them, and mentioned what they had of great strength and abundance of children, and their enjoyment of the portions decreed for them, He compared the enjoyment of the hypocrites with the enjoyment of those before them, and made them manifest by the noun (rather than a pronoun), saying: ﴿as those before you enjoyed their share﴾. The construction was not "as they enjoyed their share," so as to indicate debasement; for just as the repetition of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun indicates magnification and exaltation, so also its repetition indicates belittling and diminishing the status of the one mentioned, like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O my father, do not worship Satan. Indeed, Satan has been disobedient to the Most Merciful﴾ [Maryam: 44], and like His saying: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites are the defiantly disobedient﴾. The construction did not come as "indeed he was" nor "indeed they are they."

"Khudtum" means you entered into idle talk and falsehood. It is a metaphor taken from wading into water, and it is used only for falsehood, because dealing with truth is done in order and system, whereas the affairs of falsehood are only wading. From this comes the saying: "Many one who wades into the wealth of Allah, for him is the Fire on the Day of Resurrection."

﴿Like those who engaged﴾: that is, like the wading that they engaged in; this is said by al-Farra'. It was also said: like the wading of those who waded. It was said: the nun is omitted, meaning: like those who waded, that is, like the wading of those who. It was said: "alladhi" together with what follows it forms a verbal noun, meaning: like their wading. The apparent meaning is that "ulaʾika" (those) refers to those whom He described with strength and abundance of wealth and children, and the meaning is: you too, thus their deeds are made worthless. Ibn Attiyah said: "It is possible that by 'those' He means the hypocrites contemporary with Muhammad (ﷺ), and the address would be to Muhammad (ﷺ), and in that there is a shift from one address to another, other than the first." And His saying "in this world" refers to what befalls them in this world of hardship and corruption of their deeds, and in the Hereafter is a fire which benefits not, and upon which no reward falls. The reference by "those" to the hypocrites is strengthened by His saying in the following verse "Has there not come to them" — so reflect upon it. End of quotation. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Their deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter﴾ is the opposite of His saying: ﴿And We gave him his reward in this world, and indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 27].

﴿Has there not come to them the news of those before them: the people of Noah, ʿAd, Thamud, the people of Abraham, the companions of Madyan, and the overturned cities? Their messengers came to them with clear proofs. Allah would not have wronged them, but they were wronging themselves.﴾ When He compared the hypocrites to the earlier disbelievers in their desire for the world and their denial of the prophets, and since the expression "those before you" contained vagueness, He specified by name six groups, because they had some knowledge of their history, their lands were near the lands of the Arabs, they were the most numerous nations, and their prophets were the greatest prophets: Noah, the first of the messengers, and Abraham, the nearest father to the Arabs; and the nations next to them were close to them in strength and abundance of wealth and children. The people of Noah were destroyed by drowning, ʿAd by wind, Thamud by the Blast, the people of Abraham by the removal of blessing from them, until the gnat was given power over Nimrod, their king; the companions of Madyan by the punishment of the Day of the Canopy; and the overturned cities by making their upper parts lower and raining stones upon them.

Al-Wahidi said: The meaning of "al-iftikak" is overturning. "Afakatuhu fa-iftafak" means: I overturned it and it overturned. "Al-Mu'tafikat" is an attribute of the towns which were overturned along with their people, so their upper part was made their lower part. The overturned cities are the cities of the people of Lot. (p. 70) It was also said: they are the towns of the people of Lot, Hud, and Salih. Their overturning means the change of their conditions from good to evil. Ibn Attiyah said: "The overturned ones are the people of the four towns." It was also said: the nine towns to which Lot, peace be upon him, was sent. The word has come in the Qur'an in singular form indicating plurality. From this word is the saying of Imran ibn Hittan:

*For clear speech, unconfused, in which the tongue is sound, and an opinion not overturned.*

That is, not turned about, not changing, not unsettled. From it the wind is called "mu'tafikah," because of its shifting. From it comes His saying: ﴿How are they deluded?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 30]. And "ifk" is turning speech from truth to falsehood. End of quotation.

In His saying "Has there not come to them" is a reminder of the news of those who passed away and a warning that the like of what befell them might befall them. Most of them knew the conditions of these nations, and some of it was mentioned in the poetry of their pre-Islamic age, such as al-Afwah al-Azdi, ʿAlqamah ibn ʿAbdah, and others. It is possible that His saying "Has there not come to them" is a reminder of what Allah related to them in the Qur'an of the conditions of these people and their details. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿their messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾ refers to the six nations mentioned, and the clause is an explanation of "the news." It was said: it refers to the overturned cities specifically, and He used the word "messengers" although their prophet was one, because he used to send to every town a messenger calling to the truth, so they were messengers of the Messenger of Allah; this was mentioned by al-Tabari. Al-Karmani said: it was said that it refers to the overturned cities, meaning a messenger came to them after a messenger. "Al-bayyinat" are the miracles, and they are "and the companions [of Madyan]" with respect to the truth, not with respect to the deniers. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "[Allah would not have] wronged them" means would not have destroyed them until He sent among them a prophet to warn them. The meaning is that they were destroyed by their own deserving. Makki said: Allah would not have placed His punishment in other than its deserving place, since wronging is placing a thing in other than its place; but they were wronging themselves, in that they disobeyed Allah and denied His messengers until they angered their Lord and merited punishment, thereby wronging themselves. Al-Karmani said: [Allah would not have] wronged them by destroying them; they wronged themselves through disbelief and denial. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is not proper for Him to wrong them, for He is Wise, and what is ugly is not permissible for Him, nor that He should punish them without crime; but they wronged themselves in that they disbelieved in Him, so they deserved His punishment. End of quotation. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school). It appears that between His saying "with clear proofs" and His saying "Allah would not have" there is an omitted clause, whose estimate, and Allah knows best, is: so they denied, and Allah destroyed them; Allah would not have wronged them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verses 71–72:

﴿The believing men and the believing women are allies of one another. They enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, establish the prayer, give the zakat (obligatory alms), and obey Allah and His Messenger. Those—Allah will surely have mercy on them. Indeed, Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.﴾ When He mentioned the hypocrite men and hypocrite women, and the repugnant attributes and corrupt deeds they had, He mentioned the believing men and believing women. He said of the hypocrites: ﴿some of them are from others﴾ [al-Tawbah: 67], and of these: ﴿some of them are allies of others﴾. Ibn Atiyya said: because there is no alliance (wilaya) among the hypocrites, nor intercession for them, and they do not call upon one another; so the meaning here is alliance in Allah specifically. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: ﴿some of them are from others﴾ [al-Tawbah: 67] indicates that the hypocrisy and disbelief of the followers came about through imitation of those great leaders, and through the demands of natural disposition and habit. As for the agreement that exists among the believers, it came about not through inclination and habit, but through sharing in reasoning, success, and guidance; and alliance (wilaya) is the opposite of enmity. When He described the believers as being allies of one another, He mentioned after it what serves as an elaboration and explanation of it, namely the five marks by which the believer is distinguished from the hypocrite. The hypocrite enjoins what is wrong, forbids what is right, does not stand to the prayer except while lazy, is stingy with zakat, holds himself back from jihad, and when Allah commands him he hesitates and makes others hesitate. The believer, by contrast, is the opposite of all that: enjoining what is right, forbidding what is wrong, establishing the prayer, giving zakat, and jihad. This is what is meant in this verse by His words: ﴿and obey Allah and His Messenger﴾. End of quotation, and there is some abridgement in it. Abu al-Aliya said: everything Allah mentions in the Qur'an of enjoining what is right is a call from polytheism to Islam, and what is mentioned of forbidding what is wrong is the forbidding of worshipping idols and devils. Ibn Abbas said: ﴿and establish the prayer﴾ refers to the five daily prayers. Ibn Atiyya said: in accordance with this, the zakat is the obligatory zakat; but the praise, in my view, through voluntary acts is more eloquent, since one who maintains voluntary acts is more worthy of maintaining obligatory ones; and ﴿and obey Allah and His Messenger﴾ encompasses the recommended acts (mandubat). End of quotation.

﴿Allah will surely have mercy on them.﴾ Ibn Atiyya said: the sin (sa) introduces a delay into the promise, so that souls may find delight in hoping for His grace and bounty, exalted is He. Al-Zamakhshari said: the sin conveys that mercy is certainly obligatory, so it emphasizes the promise just as it emphasizes a threat in your saying: "I will take revenge on you someday," meaning: you will not escape me, though it be delayed. Similar to it are: ﴿the Most Merciful will appoint for them affection﴾ [Maryam: 96]; ﴿and your Lord will surely give you﴾ [al-Duha: 5]; ﴿He will surely give them their rewards﴾ [al-Nisa: 152]. End of quotation. In this there is a hidden, concealed trace of Mu'tazilism (the rationalist school holding that God is bound by justice and reason), in his saying: "the sin conveys that mercy is certainly obligatory," pointing to the view that it is obligatory upon Allah, exalted is He, to reward the obedient, just as it is obligatory to punish the disobedient. The meaning of the sin is not the emphasis of what it enters upon; it only indicates the restriction of the present tense to the future. Since mercy here is an expression for what follows from those righteous deeds of reward and punishment in the Hereafter, He used the sin, which indicates the futurity of the action. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Almighty﴾, dominant over everything, capable of it; ﴿All-Wise﴾, placing each thing in its proper place.

﴿Allah has promised the believing men and believing women gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein, and pleasant dwellings in the Gardens of Eden; and approval from Allah is greater. That is the great triumph.﴾ When He followed the hypocrites with the mention of what He had promised them of the Fire of Hell, He followed the believers with the mention of what He had promised them of the bliss of the Gardens. Since His words ﴿Allah will surely have mercy on them﴾ were a general promise, He detailed it here, to draw attention to the fact that that mercy is these things.

﴿And pleasant dwellings﴾: Ibn Abbas said: these are the dwellings of those brought near (to Allah). It was said: dwellings within the Gardens of Eden, differing in their qualities according to the differing states of those who dwell in them. It was said: palaces of emerald, pearl, and ruby, whose fragrance spreads from a distance of five hundred years' journey, in the places where they dwell. In a hadith: "A palace in Paradise of pearl, in which are seventy houses of red ruby, and in each house seventy chambers of green emerald, and in each chamber seventy couches." Other things are mentioned at the end of this hadith; and if this report from the Messenger is authentic, it is obligatory to adopt it.

﴿In the Gardens of Eden﴾, that is, of abiding residence. Ka'b al-Ahbar said: it is in Persian the vineyards and grapevines. Ibn Atiyya said: I think this is what became mixed with (the word) Firdaws. Ibn Mas'ud said: Eden is the innermost part and eastern part of Paradise, and he also said: its middle. Ata said: a river in Paradise, whose gardens are on its banks. Al-Dahhak and Abu 'Ubayda said: it is the city of Paradise and its greatest part, in which are the prophets, scholars, martyrs, and the leaders of justice, and the people are around them afterwards, and the gardens are around it. Al-Hasan said: a palace in Paradise that no one enters except a prophet, a truthful one (siddiq), a martyr, or a just judge; and he prolonged his voice with it. Also from him: palaces of pearl, red ruby, and emerald. Abu al-Darda' related from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Eden is the abode of Allah which no eye has seen and which has not occurred to the heart of any human; none dwells in it except three: the prophets, the truthful ones, and the martyrs. Allah, exalted is He, says: Blessed is he who enters you." If this is authentic from the Messenger, it is obligatory to adopt it. Muqatil said: it is the highest rank in Paradise. Abd Allah ibn Amr said: a palace around which are towers and meadows, having five thousand doors, at each door a chosen one; none enters it except a prophet, a truthful one, or a martyr. It was said: its foundation is Paradise, in which is a river with gardens on both its banks. It was said: it is Tasnim, in which are palaces of pearl, ruby, and gold, and couches, upon which are virtuous, beautiful maidens; its ceiling is the Throne of the Most Merciful; none descends into it except the prophets, the truthful ones, the martyrs, and the righteous; its fragrance spreads from a distance of five hundred years. These are reports from the early predecessors (al-salaf), very varied and inconsistent, and some of them indicate restriction, which contradicts the apparent meaning of the verse, since Allah promised them to the believing men and believing women. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Eden" is a proper name, for His words: ﴿Gardens of Eden, which the Most Merciful has promised His servants﴾ [Maryam: 61], and what Abu al-Darda' related supports it. He only inferred from the verse that Eden is a proper name because the noun it is attached to (gardens) is described by "which," and that is definite; for if "gardens" were not attached to a definite noun, it could not be described by a definite word. This is not necessarily so, since "which" may be the predicate of an omitted subject, or in the accusative by implying "I mean" or "I praise," or a substitute for "gardens." It is unlikely that it is an adjective to His words "the Garden" (al-Jannah), because of the separation by the substitute which is "gardens," and the rule is that when the adjective and the substitute are combined, the adjective is placed first and the substitute comes after it.

Al-A'mash read "wa-ridwanun" with two damma vowels. The author of al-Lawami' said: it is a dialect, and "ridwanun" is the subject of a nominal sentence. The beginning with it (as an indefinite) is permitted because it is qualified by His words "from Allah," and it is given in indefinite form to indicate a general sense: that is, some of His approval is greater than everything mentioned. When the servant knows that his Master is pleased with him, it is greater in his own soul than the bliss beyond it, and the bliss is only made ready for him by his knowledge of His pleasure with him. Just as, when he knows of His displeasure, his condition is embittered and he finds no pleasure in it. The meaning of this sentence agrees with what is related in the hadith: "Allah, exalted is He, says to His servants when they settle in Paradise: Are you content? They say: How could we not be content, O our Lord? He says: I will give you something better than all this—My approval. I am pleased with you, so I shall never be displeased with you again." Al-Hasan said: there reached their hearts, through the good pleasure of Allah, delight and joy that are more pleasant to them and more comforting to their eyes than everything they had obtained of the delights of Paradise. Ibn Atiyya said: it appears that His words, exalted is He, ﴿and approval from Allah is greater﴾ may be an allusion to the stations of those brought near, who drink from Tasnim, and who are seen as a faded star is seen on the horizon; and all who are in Paradise are content, though the stations differ, and Allah's grace is vast. End of quotation. Al-Zamakhshari said: His approval, exalted is He, is the cause of every triumph and happiness. End of quotation. The demonstrative "that" refers either to all that preceded, or to the approval; there are two opinions, and the first is more apparent.

O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be harsh with them. Their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination.

When he mentioned the threat against those who are not believers, and since the surah was revealed concerning the hypocrites, he began with them in this matter by saying: ﴿Allah has promised the hypocrite men and women and the disbelievers the fire of Hell﴾ [al-Tawbah: 68]. When the matter of jihad was mentioned, and the disbelievers, being other than the hypocrites, were more stubborn, stronger in means for fighting, and more damaging in confronting them in battle, he said: ﴿Strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾, so he began with them. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: strive against the disbelievers with the sword, and against the hypocrites with the tongue. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: and against the hypocrites by enforcing the hudud (prescribed punishments) upon them when they engage in their causes. Ibn Mas'ud said: strive against them with the hand; if you are not able, then with the tongue; if you are not able, then with the heart, and by frowning in their faces, and be harsh with them in both forms of jihad. Harshness (al-ghilaz) is the opposite of gentleness (al-riqqah), and what is meant is roughness of speech and hastening retribution, contrary to what he was commanded regarding the believers: ﴿And lower your wing to the believers﴾ [al-Hijr: 88]. Whoever is found to be corrupt in beliefs, his ruling is that he is to be struggled against with proof, and harshness is to be employed with him as far as possible.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verse 74:

﴿They swear by Allah that they did not say [it]. But they certainly uttered the word of disbelief, and disbelieved after their Islam, and aspired to what they could not attain. And they resented nothing except that Allah and His Messenger had enriched them from His bounty. So if they repent, it will be better for them; but if they turn away, Allah will punish them with a painful punishment in this world and the Hereafter, and they will have no protector or helper on earth.﴾

The pronoun refers to the hypocrites (al-munafiqun). It is said that this is the oath of al-Jullas, and his story with ʿĀmir ibn Qays has already been mentioned. It is also said that it is the oath of ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy that he did not say ﴿If we return to Madinah...﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8], to the end of the verse. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: their oath was when Ḥudhayfah conveyed to the Messenger ﷺ that they had reviled his companions and him in their private gathering.

As for ﴿and they aspired to what they could not attain﴾, it was revealed concerning Ibn Ubayy in his saying "He will surely expel [the weaker]," as Qatadah said, and it is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. It is also said [it refers] to killing the Messenger. The one who resolved on it was a man called al-Aswad from Quraysh, as Mujahid narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. Mujahid said: it was revealed concerning fifteen men (p-73) who resolved to kill him and agreed to push him from his riding-beast into the valley when he climbed the ʿAqabah. ʿAmmar ibn Yasir took hold of the halter of his mount, leading it, and Ḥudhayfah was behind it, driving it. While they were thus, Ḥudhayfah heard the sound of camels' hooves and the clinking of weapons. He turned and saw a people wearing face-coverings. He said: "Upon you, O enemies of Allah!" and they fled. Among them were ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy, ʿAbd Allah ibn Saʿd ibn Abi Sarh, Ṭuʿaymah ibn Ubayriq, al-Jullas ibn Suwayd, Abu ʿĀmir ibn Nuʿman, and Abu al-Aḥwaṣ.

It is also said that their resolve "to what they could not attain" was to crown ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy when they returned from the expedition of Tabuk, boasting over the Messenger ﷺ with him; but they did not attain what they had resolved, and so it was revealed.

From Ibn ʿAbbas: the Messenger ﷺ was sitting in the shade of a tree and said: "There will come to you a man, and a devil will look at you through him. When he comes, do not speak to him." Not long after, a blue-eyed man appeared, and he called him and said: "Why do you and your companions revile me?" The man left and brought his companions, and they swore by Allah that they had not said it. So Allah revealed this verse.

As for "the word of disbelief": it was the saying of Ibn Ubayy when he consulted al-Jahjah al-Ghifari and Sinan ibn Waburah al-Juhani, one of whom had struck the other's foot during the expedition of al-Muraysiʿ. Al-Jahjah shouted, "O Ansar!" and Sinan shouted, "O Muhajirun!" The people were stirred up, and the Messenger calmed them. Ibn Ubayy said: "I see these people have only gathered against us. Our example and theirs is only as the first one said: 'Fatten your dog and it will devour you.'" Other views are: the mockery; or the saying of al-Jullas mentioned earlier; or their saying "We will place the crown"; or their saying "He is not a Prophet"; or the statement "If we return to Madinah." These are sayings.

(And they disbelieved): that is, they openly displayed disbelief after their Islam, i.e., after displaying their Islam. The construction did not say "after their faith" because that [faith] had not gone beyond their tongues. Al-Hamm (resolve) is less than firm determination (al-ʿazm), and the disagreement regarding the one who resolves and what he resolves on has already been mentioned. It is said that it was the resolve of the hypocrites, or of al-Jullas, to kill the one who conveyed al-Jullas's words to the Messenger. There is disagreement over the name of the conveyer: it is said ʿĀṣim ibn ʿAdiyy; it is said Ḥudhayfah; it is said the stepson of al-Jullas, ʿUmayr ibn Saʿd; and it is said his name was Musʿab. It is also said that they resolved against the Messenger and the believers on things they did not attain.

﴿And they resented nothing except that Allah and His Messenger had enriched them from His bounty.﴾ This is like His saying: ﴿Do you resent us for nothing except that we believed?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 59] and ﴿They resented them only because they believed﴾ [al-Buruj: 8]. The right response of the rich toward Allah and His Messenger was to give thanks, not to resent; they made wealth a cause for resentment. This is like the saying of the poet:

"There is no fault in them, except that their swords are notched from the clashing of the battalions."

The Messenger had given ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy a blood-money (diyah) which had become heavy upon him. ʿIkrimah said: twelve thousand [dirhams]. It is also said that it was for al-Jullas. When the Messenger ﷺ came to Madinah, the Ansar were in hardship of life: they did not ride horses and did not acquire spoils, so they were given preference. The Messenger said to the Ansar: "You were poor, and Allah enriched you through me." It is also said that al-Jullas had a great debt, which the Messenger paid, and a great amount of wealth from the spoils came to him.

His saying ﴿And they resented nothing﴾ is a sentence used in the manner of mockery toward them, as you say: "I have no fault with you except that I have been good to you," for their conduct indicates that they were base. The poet said:

"They resented nothing of the Banu Umayyah except that they are forbearing when they are angered,
And that they are the lords of kings, and none is fit to rule except the Arabs over them."

Another poet, parallel to the previous verse, said:

"There is no fault in us except the lineage of a noble people, and that we do not trample upon the ant."

(So if they repent): this is a kindness from Him, exalted is He, and gentleness and grace toward them, in that He opened for them the door of repentance (tawbah) after committing those grave crimes. Al-Jullas, after his oath and denial that he had said what was reported from him, confessed, affirmed the one who reported it, repented, and his repentance was good. It is not reported that anyone else among them had his repentance accepted except al-Jullas. It is said: in this there is evidence for the acceptance of the repentance of the zindiq (one who conceals disbelief while displaying faith) (p-74), and this is the view of Abu Hanifah and al-Shafiʿi. Malik said: it is not accepted. But if he comes repenting of his own accord before he is discovered, his repentance is accepted without disagreement.

(And if they turn away): that is, from repentance, or from faith, or from sincerity, or from the Messenger. The meaning: and if they persist in turning away, since they are turning away in this world by aligning themselves with the belligerents, having openly displayed disbelief; so fighting them, killing them, taking their children and wives captive, and seizing their property becomes lawful. It is said: [the punishment is] what befalls them at death and in witnessing the angels of punishment. It is said: it is the punishment of the grave. It is said: it is weariness, fear, and shame before the believers, and in the Hereafter, the Fire.

Among them are those who made a covenant with God: "If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity and we will surely be among the righteous." But when He gave them of His bounty, they became stingy with it and turned away, refusing. So He caused hypocrisy to follow in their hearts until the Day they meet Him, because they broke to God what they had promised Him and because they used to lie. Do they not know that God knows their secret and their private talk, and that God is the Knower of the unseen?

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: They were Tha'labah ibn al-Ḥārith, Jadd ibn Qays, Mu'attib ibn Qushayr, and Tha'labah ibn Ḥāṭib, and the verse was revealed about them. Al-Ḥasan and Mujāhid said: It was about Mu'attib and Tha'labah, who went out before a gathering and said that. Ibn al-Sā'ib said: It was about a man from the clan of Banū 'Amr ibn 'Awf who had wealth in Syria, but it was slow to reach him, so he suffered greatly because of this. He swore by God, "If He gives us of His bounty," meaning of that wealth, "we will surely give charity from it and surely maintain the ties of kinship," but when it reached him, he did not do so. Most scholars hold that the verse was revealed about Tha'labah, and they mentioned a long narration about him, of which I have summarized the following: He asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to pray to God to grant him wealth. He was told: "A little that you can render thanks for is better than a lot that you cannot bear." He insisted, so he prayed to God, and he acquired sheep which multiplied until Medina could no longer contain them. He settled in a valley, and they continued to grow, and he became occupied with them until he abandoned the prayers. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent the collector to him, and he said: "This is nothing but jizyah (poll-tax), this is nothing but the sister of jizyah." Then this verse was revealed. A relative of his informed him of it, so he brought his charity to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), but he did not accept it. When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) passed away, he came to Abu Bakr, but he did not accept it; then to 'Umar, but he did not accept it; then to 'Uthman, but he did not accept it, and he died during the days of 'Uthman.

Al-A'mash recited "la-ntaṣṣaddaqanna wa-la-nakūnanna" with the light nun in both. The apparent and widely transmitted view among the occasions of revelation (asbab al-nuzul, the circumstances in which verses were revealed) is that they uttered this and spoke it aloud.
