Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verse 79:

﴿Those who find fault with those among the believers who give charity voluntarily, and [who find fault with] those who find nothing to give except their effort, so they mock them—Allah mocks them, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾ It was revealed concerning those who reproached the almsgivers. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had urged charity, so ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf gave four thousand and kept back the same amount, and the Messenger (ﷺ) blessed him for what he kept and what he gave. ʿUmar gave half of his wealth, ʿAsim ibn ʿAdi gave a hundred wasq, ʿUthman gave a great charity, and Abu ʿAqil al-Arlashi gave a sa' of dates and left his dependents one sa', for he had hired himself out to water palm trees for two measures of dates. A man gave a great she-camel and said: "It and its young one are charity, O Messenger of Allah," and he cast its halter before the Messenger. The hypocrites said: "These people gave only for show and reputation, and Abu ʿAqil gave only so that he would be mentioned among the notables, or to draw attention to himself so that he would be given from the charities, while Allah has no need of his sa'." Some said: "He gave the camel, and it is better than him." The man was the shortest of people in stature and the darkest of them in complexion, so the Messenger (ﷺ) looked at him and said: "Say: 'It is better than you and it,'" repeating it three times. The original form of (al-muttawwiʿin) is al-mutatawwiʿin, so the taʾ was assimilated into the ṭaʾ; they are those who seek blessing, such as ʿAbd al-Rahman and others.

﴿And those who find nothing except their effort﴾ are included among the al-muttawwiʿin; they were mentioned separately to honor them, since charity had not escaped them, rather they gave of what they had, even though they were the neediest of people for it, and the most exhausted in obtaining what they gave, such as Abu ʿAqil and Abu Khaythama. Abu Khaythama had been reproached for giving a small amount, and it was examined which of the two was [more deserving]. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi held that the conjoined element in this and similar cases is not included in what it is conjoined to; he said: "For it is not permissible to conjoin a thing to its like." He said the same regarding: ﴿and His angels and His messengers and Jibril and Mikal﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98], and regarding His saying: ﴿therein are fruit and palm trees and pomegranates﴾ [al-Rahman: 68]. His student Ibn Jinni also held this view, but most people disagree with both of them. Some call this (al-tajrid) (isolation), as they are singled out by mention as a mark of honor, and the discussion of this has already been presented regarding His saying: ﴿and His angels and His messengers and Jibril and Mikal﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98].

Ibn Hurmuz and a group read (jahdahum) with a fatha. It is said: these are two dialects with one meaning. Al-Qutabi said: with a damma it means capacity, and with a fatha (p-76) it means hardship. Al-Sha'bi said: with a damma it means sustenance, and with a fatha it means work. It is also said: with a damma it means a small amount by which one sustains oneself.

As for the best grammatical analysis: ﴿Those who find fault﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), ﴿in the charities﴾ is related to (yalmizun), and ﴿those who find nothing﴾ is conjoined to (al-muttawwiʿin), as if it were said: they find fault with the wealthy and others. (Fa-yaskhurun) is conjoined to (yalmizun), and ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ and what follows it is the predicate of ﴿those who find fault﴾.

Abu al-Baqa' mentioned that His saying ﴿and those who find nothing﴾ is conjoined to ﴿those who find fault﴾, and this is not possible, because what is conjoined to the subject shares in the predicate, and it is not possible for ﴿and those who find nothing except their effort﴾ to share the predicate with ﴿those who find fault﴾ unless they are likewise hypocrites. He said: It is also said that ﴿those who find nothing﴾ is conjoined to (al-mu'minin), but this is very far-fetched. He said: The predicate of the first, according to these views, has two possibilities. One: (fa-yaskhurun). The fa' entered because of the resemblance of ﴿alladhina﴾ to a conditional. End of this view. This is far-fetched, for then the predicate would be understood as if implied by the subject, since whoever reproaches and disparages someone is mocking him, so it approaches being like "the master of the slave-girl is her owner," and that is not permissible. He said: The second: that the predicate is ﴿Allah mocks them﴾. He said: On this meaning, ﴿those who find fault﴾ may be in a position of accusative governed by a verb omitted, which is explained by (sakhira): its estimate being: He condemned those who find fault. It is also said: the predicate is omitted, its estimate being: among them are those who find fault. Abu al-Baqa' also said: (min al-mu'minin) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in (al-muttawwiʿin), and (fi al-sadaqat) is related to (yalmizun), and it is not related to (al-muttawwiʿin) lest a foreign element separate them. End of quote. It is not a foreign element, because it is a circumstantial clause as established, and when it is a circumstantial clause, it is permissible for it to separate the governing element from the governed, even if that governing element is delayed, as in: "The one who passes by riding with Zayd came to me."

Al-sukhriyya is mockery. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ is a predicate both in wording and meaning, and the conjunction of the predicate to it supports this. It is also said: its form is a predicate, but its meaning is supplication. When He said ﴿they mock them﴾, He said ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ by way of reciprocity, and its meaning is: He gave them respite until they thought He had neglected them. Ibn ʿAbbas said: This occurred at the time of departure for the expedition to Tabuk. It is also said that the meaning of ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ is: He requited them for their mockery, and the requital of a thing may be named by the name of the thing, as in His saying: ﴿and the requital for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40]. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: it is a naming of the punishment by the name of the sin, and it is an expression of what befell them of disdain and humiliation in their souls. End of quote. This is close to the view before it. Al-Asamm said: Allah commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to accept their false excuses outwardly, while the consequence of their deed falls upon them as it is; so it is as if He mocked them, and for this reason He said: ﴿and for them is a painful punishment﴾, which is the lasting punishment of the Hereafter. End of quote. In this verse is an indication that finding fault with a believer and mocking him are among the grave sins, because of the threat that follows them.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 9, verse 80:**

﴿Ask forgiveness for them, or do not ask forgiveness for them. Even if you ask forgiveness for them seventy times, Allah will not forgive them. That is because they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger, and Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.﴾: "ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he was a righteous man, that he ask forgiveness for his father during his illness, and he did so. Then the verse was revealed, and he said: 'I have been given leave, so I will exceed the seventy.' Then this was revealed: ﴿It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾ [Al-Munafiqun 63:6]." It was also said: when ﴿Allah has mocked them, and for them is a painful punishment﴾ [At-Tawbah 9:79] was revealed, they asked the Messenger to ask forgiveness for them, and then this verse was revealed. On this view, the pronouns refer either to those previously mentioned or to all the hypocrites; there are two opinions. The address in the imperative is to the Messenger. The apparent meaning of this statement is that it is an option (takhyir), and this is what has been narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ʿUmar said to him: "How can you ask forgiveness for the enemy of Allah when Allah has forbidden you from asking forgiveness for them?" He (ﷺ) said: "He did not forbid me, but He gave me a choice." It is as if he (peace be upon him) were told: If you wish, ask forgiveness, and if you wish, do not ask forgiveness. Then He informed him that they would not be forgiven even if he asked forgiveness seventy times. It was also said: its wording is an imperative but its meaning is a condition, in the sense of "whether you ask forgiveness or not, Allah will not forgive them," so it is like His words: ﴿Say: Spend willingly or unwillingly; it will not be accepted from you﴾ [At-Tawbah 9:53], and like the saying of the poet:

Treat us ill or treat us well, we will not blame you, nor will we be estranged from you if you turn away.

The discussion of this has already passed in His words: ﴿Say: Spend willingly or unwillingly﴾ [At-Tawbah 9:53]. This meaning was adopted by al-Tabari and others, and it is the view chosen by al-Zamakhshari, who said: "We have mentioned that this imperative has the meaning of a statement, as if it were said: Allah will not forgive them whether you ask forgiveness for them or not, and that it contains the meaning of a condition. We have also mentioned the subtle point in using the imperative form." He means in his commentary on the words of Allah, the Exalted: "Say: Spend." He had said there: "If you ask: how did He command them to spend and then say: ﴿it will not be accepted from you﴾? I say: it is an imperative with the meaning of a statement, like His words: ﴿Say: whoever is in error, the Most Merciful will extend him an extension﴾ [Maryam 19:75]. Its meaning is: it will not be accepted from you whether you spend willingly or unwillingly. Similar to this is His words: ﴿Ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾, and the words of the poet: 'Treat us ill...' meaning: Allah will not forgive them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them, and we will not blame you whether you treat us well or badly." If it is asked: when is such a construction permissible? I say: when the context indicates it, as in your saying: "May Allah forgive Zayd and have mercy on him." If you ask: why did he do that? I say: for a subtle purpose, which is that a man may be saying to ʿAzza: "Test the gentleness of my regard for you, the strength of my love for you, and deal with me by ill-treatment and kindness, and see whether my condition changes toward you whether you treat me badly or well." Its meaning is also found in the words of the one who said:

I turn away from the one who, if you raise the sword intending to strike him, will not doubt your affection.

Similarly the meaning is: spend and see whether it will be accepted from you; ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them, and see whether you find any difference between the two states of asking forgiveness and leaving it. End of quotation. It was also said: it is an imperative of emphasis in despair, and its meaning is: even if you sought forgiveness for them as one who is commanded, or abandoned it as one who is forbidden, they would not be forgiven. It was also said: its meaning is equality (istiwa'), i.e., your asking forgiveness for them and your not asking forgiveness are equal. If you ask: how is it permissible for him to ask forgiveness for them when He has informed that they disbelieved? The answer, as they have said, comes in several aspects. The first: this was by way of reconciliation (ta'lif) so that the faith of many of them might be made sincere. It has been narrated that when he asked forgiveness for Ibn Salul, clothed him with his garment, and prayed over him, a thousand men of the Khazraj embraced Islam, seeing that he sought healing through the garment of the Messenger; and he was the leader and chief of the hypocrites. It was also said: he did this to console the heart of his son and of those among them who had embraced Islam, and this is close to the previous view. It was also said: the believers used to ask the Messenger (ﷺ) to ask forgiveness for their hypocrite kinsmen during their lives, hoping that they would become sincere in their faith, and after their deaths, hoping for forgiveness. So Allah forbade him from that and made them despair of it. ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbd Allah asked the Messenger to ask forgiveness for his father, hoping that his punishment would be lightened. It was also said: he asked forgiveness only for some of them on the basis of their outward Islam, without verifying their having left Islam. This view was rejected on the ground that Allah, the Exalted, informed that they disbelieved, so it is not valid to say that he did not know of their disbelief. Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: the closest view regarding the connection of this verse with what precedes it is what Ibn ʿAbbas mentioned: that those who used to slander were the ones who asked for forgiveness. It is not permissible that the Messenger (ﷺ) would have occupied himself with asking forgiveness and then been forbidden from it, for several reasons. The first: the hypocrite is an unbeliever, and it has become clear in his (peace be upon him) law that asking forgiveness for an unbeliever is not permissible; for this reason Allah commanded him to follow Ibrahim (peace be upon them both), except in His words: ﴿I will surely ask forgiveness for you﴾ [Al-Mumtahanah 60:4]. And if this is well known in the law, how is it permissible to undertake it? The second: one person's asking forgiveness for another does not benefit that other if he persists in ugliness and disobedience. The third: his undertaking to ask forgiveness for hypocrites is like encouraging them to commit sin. The fourth: if he were not answered, the Messenger's supplication would remain rejected before Allah, and this would entail a diminishment of his station (ﷺ). The fifth: if this supplication were accepted from the Messenger, then a little of it would be equal to much of it in obtaining an answer. Thus it is established that the purpose of this statement is that when the people asked him to ask forgiveness for them, Allah prevented him from it. The purpose of mentioning this number is not to set a limit on the prohibition; rather, it is like one who says to a person who asks him for a need: "Even if you ask me seventy times, I will not grant it to you," (not meaning that if he asked more he would grant it). Likewise here. What confirms this is His words in the verse: ﴿That is because they disbelieved﴾. He made clear that the cause for which the Messenger's asking forgiveness for them would not benefit them, even if it reached seventy times, is their disbelief and their defiance. This meaning applies to any increase above seventy, so this small number is evidence that the purpose is to remove hope that the Messenger's asking forgiveness would benefit them while they persist in their disbelief. It is confirmed by: ﴿And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people﴾. The meaning: their defiance prevents them from guidance. Thus it is established that the truth is what we have mentioned. Al-Azhari, with a group of the people of lexicography, said: "The seventy here is the plural of seven used for abundance, not the seven that comes after six." End of quotation. The Arabs use seven to express abundance in units, seventy in tens, and seven hundred in hundreds. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Seventy functions as a proverbial expression in their speech for abundance." ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

"I will surely attack al-Asi and the son of al-Asi with seventy thousand, their forelocks tied."

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: as for his using seventy specifically rather than other numbers, it is because it is a number that often serves as a limit and a convincing measure of abundance. Do you not see the people whom Musa chose, and the companions of the ʿAqabah? Some linguists have said: the root formed from sin, ba' and ʿayn (s-b-ʿ) indicates intensity of matter in this regard, namely the seven, for it is a convincing number: it is found in the heavens and the earth, in the creation of man, in his body, in his limbs by which he obeys Allah and by which he disobeys Him, and in the arrangement of the gates of Hell as some people have mentioned; these are: his eyes, his ears, his teeth, his belly, his private parts, his hands, and his feet. It is also found in the arrows of the game of chance, in the climes, and elsewhere. From this root comes "the seven" (al-sabʿ), "the gloomy" (al-ʿubus), "the lion" (al-ʿanbas), and similar expressions. End of quotation.

Those who argue from implication (dalil al-khitab), and that specifying a number indicates that the ruling beyond it is contrary to it, use as evidence what has been narrated: that he said: "By Allah, I will surely exceed the seventy," and he did not stop until this was revealed: ﴿It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them; Allah will not forgive them﴾ [Al-Munafiqun 63:6], and so he refrained. It has been said: one may argue that this reasoning is better in reverse, because when He, the Exalted, made clear that He would absolutely not forgive them, it became established that the situation beyond the number is equal to the situation at the number, and this indicates that restricting to a number does not require that the ruling beyond it be contrary to it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: how was it hidden from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), though he was the most eloquent of the Arabs and the most knowledgeable of them in the methods and figures of speech, while what is understood from mentioning this number is the abundance of asking forgiveness, and how, when it was followed by His words, ﴿That is because they disbelieved﴾, which clarified what prevents forgiveness for them, so that he said: 'My Lord has given me leave, so I will exceed the seventy'?" I say: it was not hidden from him, but he was led to imagine by what he said, to display the extent of his mercy and compassion toward those he was sent to, as Ibrahim (peace be upon him) said: ﴿And whoever disobeys me, indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [Ibrahim 14:36]. In the Prophet's (ﷺ) display of compassion and mercy is a kindness to his community and an invitation for them to show mercy to one another. End of quotation.

In this question and answer there is a diminishing of the station of prophethood, a lack of proper manners toward the prophets, and an attribution to them of what is not fitting for them. If the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It is not for a prophet to have the treachery of the eyes" or as he said, which is a gesture, how then could he speak something by way of imagining (tahyil)? Far be the station of the prophets from that. But this man is loose in his wording regarding the prophets in ways that do not befit their condition. He spoke, in his commentary on the words of Allah, ﴿May Allah pardon you; why did you grant them permission?﴾ [At-Tawbah 9:43], with words about the Messenger that I have deemed my book too pure to transmit in it. And Allah, the Exalted, protects us from slips in speech and in action.

That (ذَلِكَ) is a reference to the negation of forgiveness and the clarification of the cause that necessitates it. And the negation of Allah's guidance for the defiantly disobedient applies to those for whom He has decreed it by this (cause); so it is a general statement that is specified.

(p-79) When God, exalted is He, mentioned the hypocrisy and mockery that had appeared among those who went out with him on the expedition to Tabuk from among the hypocrites, He mentioned the condition of the hypocrites who did not go out with him and stayed behind from the struggle, offering excuses and false pretexts, until he granted them permission. God then revealed to the Messenger (ﷺ) their true condition and informed him of their evil conduct. God revealed to him: ﴿Those who stayed behind rejoiced in their sitting behind the Messenger of God﴾, i.e., concerning the expedition to Tabuk. The Messenger had left them in Medina when they offered their excuses, and he granted them permission. This verse implies rebuke and warning. The word (al-mukhallafun, "those who stayed behind") implies blame and contempt, and for this reason the Qur'an says ﴿They were content to be with those who remain behind﴾ [al-Tawbah: 93]. This word is more apt than al-mutakhallifin (those who deliberately stay behind), since they are the ones who were made to stay behind, and only a hypocrite would rejoice at this. Thus the three who were excused and the people with valid excuses are excluded from this.

The noun (al-maq'ad) can denote time, place, or the verbal noun (masdar, the infinitive). Here it denotes the verbal noun, meaning "by their sitting," which is an expression for remaining in Medina. (Khilaf) is in the accusative as an adverb of place (zarf), meaning "after the Messenger of God (ﷺ)." It is said: "So-and-so stayed behind (aqama khilaf al-hayy)," meaning after them, when they departed and he did not depart with them. This is the statement of Abu Ubayda, al-Akhfash, and Isa ibn Amr. A poet said:

"The spring came after them (ʿaqaba al-rabiʿu khilafahum), so it was as if the palm-leaf weavers had spread a mat among them."

From the same usage is the saying of another poet:

"So say to the one who seeks what has passed: prepare for another like it, as if it had already come."

This interpretation is supported by the recitation (qira'a) of Ibn Abbas, Abu Haywa, and Amr ibn Maymun: "khalfa rasul Allah" (behind the Messenger of God). Qutrub, Mu'arrij, al-Zajjaj, and al-Tabari said that (khilaf) is in the accusative as a object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi, a noun of cause), meaning "out of opposition to the Messenger of God," because they opposed him when he rose for the struggle and they sat down. This interpretation is supported by the recitation of the one who read (khulf) with a dammah on the kha', and by what the reports widely agree upon: that he commanded them to go forth, and they became angry and opposed him and sat down, some seeking permission and others not seeking it. Their aversion to the struggle was because they did not hope for reward from it, nor did they believe it would ward off punishment from them. In His saying (rejoiced) and (they disliked) there is a semantic contrast, because joy is one of the fruits of love. In His saying ﴿that they should strive with their wealth and their lives﴾ there is an allusion to the believers and their bearing of great hardships, meaning: like the believers who spent their wealth and lives in the struggle in the way of God and preferred that over ease and comfort. The hypocrites disliked this, and how could they not dislike it, since they did not have the motive of faith that the believers had? Rejoicing in sitting implies disliking departure. It seems that rejoicing in sitting is for the likes of staying in one's own land for the sake of familiarity and comfort with family and children, while disliking going out to the expedition is because it exposes oneself and one's wealth to death and destruction.

They pleaded the severity of the heat as an excuse, so God answered what they mentioned as a reason for abandoning the expedition. It is said that some of them said to others, and they were eighty-four men. It was also said: they said to the believers, "Their hypocrisy and laziness were not enough for them, so they wanted to recruit others and alert them to the cause that requires abandoning the expedition." Ibn Abbas, Abu Razin, and al-Rabi' said: a man said, "O Messenger of God, the heat is severe, so do not go forth in the heat." Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: he was a man from Banu Salama. End of quotation. That is, he said this on their behalf, which is why (they said) is in the plural.

The expedition to Tabuk took place at the height of the heat, when the fruits had ripened and the shade was pleasant. So God commanded His Prophet to say to them: ﴿Say: the fire of Hell is more intense in heat﴾. He established the proof against them by saying to them: if you dread the heat of the summer, then the fire of Hell, which is more intense, is more deserving that you should dread it, if you had understanding. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Say: the fire of Hell is more intense in heat﴾ is a rebuke to them, because whoever protects himself from the hardship of an hour and by that falls into the hardship of eternity is more ignorant than every ignorant person. And one of them said:

"A pleasure of grudges, after which I met a sorrow of a day, through which I see something like aloes."

"How then will you meet the pleasure of an hour, behind which is the sorrow of ages?" End of quotation.

(p-80) Ubayd Allah recited (ya'lamun, "they know") in place of "yafqahun" (they understand). This reading should be taken in the sense of an explanation (tafsir), because it contradicts the consensus of the Muslims and what the imams have transmitted from him. The command to laugh and weep is in the sense of a statement of fact. The meaning is: they will laugh little and weep much, but it was expressed in the form of a command to show that it is decreed and cannot be otherwise. It is reported that the people of hypocrisy will be in the Fire for the lifetime of the world, their tears will not dry up, and they will not be granted sleep. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿So let them laugh little﴾ refers to the duration of life in this world, and ﴿and let them weep much﴾ refers to the eternity of everlasting abode. Thus it came in the form of a command but its meaning is a report about their condition. Ibn Atiyya said: it is also possible that it describes their state, meaning: because of what they are in, of danger before God and evil condition, it is fitting that their laughter be little and their weeping much on account of that. This implies that the time of laughing and weeping is in this world, like the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him) to his community: "If you knew what I know, you would weep much and laugh little."

(Qalilan, "little") and (kathiran, "much") are in the accusative as adverbs of the verbal noun (masdar), since they are qualifiers of the verbal noun, meaning: little laughter and much weeping. This is one of the places where the modified noun is omitted and its qualifier takes its place, because the verb indicates it. Abu al-Baqa said: they may also be qualifiers of an omitted adverb of time (zarf), meaning: a little time and a long time. End of quotation. The first is better, because the verb indicates the verbal noun by its root letters and indicates time by its form, so its indication of the verbal noun is stronger.

(Jaza'an, "as a recompense") is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), and it is connected to His saying: ﴿and let them weep much﴾.

The first is better, because the verb indicates the verbal noun by its root letters and indicates time by its form, so its indication of the verbal noun is stronger.

(Jaza'an, "as a recompense") is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), and it is connected to His saying: ﴿and let them weep much﴾.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verse 83:

﴿So if Allah returns you to a faction of them, and they ask your permission to go out, then say: "You will never go out with me, nor will you fight an enemy with me. Indeed, you were content with sitting [at home] the first time, so sit with those who stay behind."﴾: The address is to the Messenger, and the meaning is: if Allah returns you from this journey of yours, which is the expedition of Tabuk. It has been said: the use of "in" (in) here, which is used for what is likely to occur, indicates that he (ﷺ) does not know the future of his affairs, including the appointed term and other things, except when Allah informs him. He stated this explicitly in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: "I am not a novelty among the Messengers, and I do not know what will be done with me or with you"﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 9], and ﴿Had I known the unseen, I would have acquired much good, and harm would not have touched me﴾ [al-A'raf: 188]. Ibn 'Atiyyah and others said similarly.

﴿to a faction of them﴾, because among them were those who died, and among them were those who repented and regretted, and among them were those who stayed behind for a valid excuse. So the "faction" here refers to those who were thoroughly steeped in hypocrisy and remained firm upon it, so it has been said. If the pronoun in (minhum, "of them") refers to those who stayed behind who went out and disliked to fight, then what appears is that mention of the "faction" is for the sake of the fact that some of them died. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It seems that this faction had been destined to die upon hypocrisy, and they were identified to the Prophet (ﷺ); otherwise, how would the prohibition of praying over their dead be consequential if he had not identified them? His saying: ﴿and they die while they are defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Tawbah: 84] is a text on their dying in this state. What supports this is that the Prophet (ﷺ) identified them to Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, and when the Companions saw Hudhayfah hold back from praying over the funeral of a man, they would hold back from it as well. It is related from Hudhayfah that he said one day: "There remain of the hypocrites so-and-so many." 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said to him: "I adjure you by Allah, am I among them?" He said: "No, by Allah, I will not declare anyone safe from them after you." Allah commanded His Prophet to say to them: ﴿You will never go out with me﴾; this is a punishment for them and a display of the baseness of their station and the evil of their condition. This is what is intended in the story of Tha'labah ibn Hatib, which was mentioned earlier regarding the refusal to accept his charity, and there is no greater disgrace than for a person to be rejected by the Law and cast off like a mangy camel.

al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Then they ask your permission to go out﴾ means to a campaign after the campaign of Tabuk. The removal of their names from the register of fighters was a punishment for them for their staying behind, which Allah, Exalted is He, knew was prompted only by hypocrisy, unlike the other who stayed behind. End. He moved the negation from what is hard for them, which is going out to the campaigns, to what is harder, which is fighting the enemy, because it is the greatest of jihad, the fruit of going out, and the place of the glint of swords beneath which is Paradise. Then (p-81) he gave as the reason for the negation of going out and fighting that they were content with sitting the first time, and their contentment arose from their hypocrisy, disbelief, deceit and disobedience to Allah's command in His saying: ﴿Go forth, light and heavy﴾ [al-Tawbah: 41], and they themselves said: ﴿Do not go forth in the heat﴾ [al-Tawbah: 81]. So he gave as the cause the effect, which is the contentment arising from the cause, which is hypocrisy. And ﴿the first time﴾ is the first going out to the expedition of Tabuk. And "marrah" (time) is a verbal noun; it is as if it were said: the first departure to which you were called; for it was not the first departure the Messenger made for a campaign, so it must be restricted, since "first" implies precedence. It has been said: the estimate is: the first departure the Messenger made for the campaign against the Romans himself. It has been said: ﴿the first time﴾ means before the seeking of permission. Abu al-Baqa' said: ﴿the first time﴾ is an adverbial phrase, meaning an adverb of time, and this is remote.

al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: "marrah" is indefinite, placed in the position of the plural "marrat" for the superlative, then why is the superlative mentioned with the noun it is joined to, when it indicates one of the times? I say: the most common of the two usages is "Hind is the greatest of women," and she is the greatest of them. Then, your saying: "she is the greatest [kubra] of women" is hardly to be found, but rather "she is the greatest woman," and "first time" and "last time." End.

﴿So sit with those who stay behind﴾, that is: remain; it is not a command to sitting which is the equivalent of sitting down, rather what is meant is preventing them from going out with him. Abu 'Ubaydah said: the "khalif" is the one who remained behind after one who went out, and sat in his tent, and he is the one who lags behind the people. It has been said: "al-khalifin" means "al-mukhalifin" (the opponents), from their saying: "a khalif slave," meaning one who opposes his master. It has been said: it means the lowly and base, from their saying: "so-and-so is the khalifah of his people," for the most despicable and vile of them. This verse indicates the avoidance of the companionship of one who shows deceit, treachery and guile, severing the bond between them, and guarding against him. From Qatadah: it was mentioned to us that they were twelve men. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the "khalifun" are all who stayed behind, including women, children and those with excuses; the masculine was given precedence, so it is made plural with the masculine sound plural, even though there were women among them, and it is the plural of "khalif." Qatadah said: the "khalifun" are the women, and this is rejected. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are the men. al-Tabari said: his saying in both cases may intend the corrupt ones, and this would be taken from "khalafa al-shay'" when it spoils, and from it "khulufu fam al-sa'im" (the odor of the fasting person's mouth). Malik ibn Dinar and 'Ikrimah read: ﴿ma'a al-khalifin﴾, and it is a shortened form of "al-khalifin," as one says "'iddan" and "biddan," meaning "'adidan" and "badidan," and as the other said:

Like the dew-moisture, which the striking of the shades has matted down.

meaning "al-zilal" (the shades).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verse 84:

﴿And do not pray over any of them who has died, ever, nor stand at his grave. Indeed, they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger, and died while they were defiantly disobedient.﴾: The prohibition against praying over the hypocrites when they die is a second punishment and a perpetual disgrace upon them. It is reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to pray over the hypocrites when they died, and stand at their graves, because of what they displayed of Islam, for they would pronounce the two testimonies of faith, pray, and fast. So he based the matter on what appeared of their statements and actions, and left their inner states to Allah. He continued to do so until the incident of Abdullah ibn Ubayy occurred. Al-Zamakhshari and others elaborated on his story, and the reports converge that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed over him, and this verse was revealed after that. Anas reported that when he (ﷺ) moved forward to pray over him, Jibril came to him, pulled him by his garment, and recited to him: ﴿And do not pray over any of them who has died, ever﴾, so he turned away and did not pray. They also mentioned the exchange between Umar and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he came to pray over him. The word (died) is an attribute of (any one), so the descriptive phrase with the preposition was placed first, then the clause, and it is in the past tense with the meaning of the future, because death is certain to occur. Allah forbade him from praying over him and from standing at his grave, which is remaining by his grave until his burial is finished. It was said: the meaning is: do not take charge of his burial and his grave, so "the grave" is a verbal noun. When the deceased was buried, the Prophet (ﷺ) would stand at his grave and supplicate for him, so he was forbidden from doing so with regard to the hypocrites, and thereafter he did not pray over any hypocrite, nor did he stand at his grave.

﴿Indeed, they disbelieved﴾ is a reason for the prohibition of praying and standing, with what requires abstention from that, namely disbelief and dying upon it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verse 85:

﴿Let not their wealth nor their children impress you. Allah only intends to punish them thereby in this world, and that their souls should depart while they are disbelievers.﴾: The like of this verse has already come before, and it is repeated because the renewal of the revelation has a significance (p-82) in confirming and emphasizing what it was sent down for, and in intending that it be in the mind of the addressee, so that he does not forget it or neglect it, and that he believes that acting upon it is important and requires special care, especially when the interval between the two revelations is long. It thus resembles a matter that concerns its owner, so he returns to it in the course of his speech and turns to it. This meaning was repeated because of its strength in regard to what must be guarded against, as al-Zamakhshari said. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The purpose of its repetition is to emphasize this meaning. Abu 'Ali said: Its outward form indicates that it is a repetition, but it is not a repetition, because the two verses concern two groups of the hypocrites; and if it were a repetition, then, given the distance between the two verses, it would serve the benefit of emphasis and reminder. It has been said: By the first he meant, do not venerate them during their lifetime because of the abundance of wealth and children, and by the second, do not venerate them after their death, due to the barrier of disbelief and hypocrisy. The two verses differ in wording: here "wa" (and), and there "fa" (so); the suitability of the fa is that it comes right after His saying: ﴿And they do not spend except while they are unwilling﴾ [al-Tawbah: 54], i.e., for spending, so they are impressed by the abundance of wealth and children, and so He forbade him from being impressed, with the fa of consequence. The suitability of the wa is that it is a prohibition conjoined to a prohibition before it: (Do not pray), (Do not stand), (Let not impress you), so the wa is appropriate. Here (wa awladuhum), and there (wa la awladuhum); the mention of "la" indicates the prohibition of being impressed by each one individually. That includes the prohibition of the whole collectively. Here it has been dropped, so it was a prohibition of being impressed by the whole collectively. That includes the prohibition of being impressed by each one individually. Thus the two verses, by their explicit and implicit meanings, indicate the prohibition of being impressed by wealth and children together and separately. Here "an yu'adhdhibahum" (that He punish them), and there (li-yu'adhdhibahum) (in order to punish them); so he used the lam, which indicates causation. The object of (yurid) is omitted, i.e., Allah only intends to test them with wealth and children in order to punish them. He used "an" because the target of the intention is the punishment, i.e., Allah only intends to punish them. Thus the object of the verb differs between the two verses; this is the apparent meaning, although it is possible that the lam is additional and the causation is expressed by "an." There (al-dunya), and here (fi al-hayat al-dunya); so "fi al-hayah" was affirmed in its original form, and it was omitted here to draw attention to the baseness of this world and that it does not deserve to be called life, especially since the mention of the death of the hypocrites precedes it, so it was fitting that it not be called life.

﴿When a surah was sent down, saying, "Believe in Allah and strive alongside His Messenger," the men of wealth among them asked your permission, and said, "Leave us, that we may be with those who sit back."﴾ ﴿They were content to be with those left behind, and a seal was set upon their hearts, so they do not comprehend.﴾

The majority hold that "surah" here means every surah in which there was a command to believe and to strive. It was said that it refers to Bara'ah (Surah al-Tawbah), because it contains the command to both. It was also said that it means part of a surah, and so the term "surah" is applied to it, just as "Qur'an" and "Kitab" are applied to part of the Qur'an.

Although it has already been mentioned that they had asked the Messenger for permission to remain behind, this verse indicates that whenever a surah was revealed containing the command to believe and to strive, they would ask for permission. Here, *idha* (إذا) does not only convey conditionality, but also carries the sense of repetition, whether that is by its original lexical imposition or by its predominant usage rather than its original imposition. This is a point of disagreement among the grammarians. Among the examples in which repetition is found with *idha* is the poet's verse:

"When I find the heat of fire in my liver, I come toward the water-skins of the people, seeking coolness."

Do you not see that the meaning is "whenever I find"?

*An amanu* (أنْ آمِنُوا) may be explanatory (*tafsiriyyah*), since before it there is a clause that carries the sense of that command; and it may be verbal-noun-introducing (*masdariyyah*), meaning "by believing," i.e., "by faith." The apparent sense is that the address is to the hypocrites, meaning: "Believe with your hearts as you have believed with your tongues." It was said that it may also be an address to the believers, and its meaning would be continuance (*al-istidamah*).

As for *al-tawl* (الطَّوْلِ), Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan said it means wealth. It was also said it means strength and capability. Al-Asamm said: "Ulu al-tawl" are the nobles and leaders. "Ulu al-amr minhum" (أُولُو الأمْرِ مِنهم) means "among them," i.e., among the hypocrites, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, al-Jadd ibn Qays, Mu'attib ibn Qushayr, and their likes. I specify "ulu al-tawl" because they are the ones capable of deterring others and of striving; whoever has no wealth and no capability does not need to ask permission, and asking permission while one is able to move is more ugly and more shameful. The meaning is: "The men of wealth among them asked your permission to remain behind." In (p-٨٣) *(istadhanaka)* (اسْتَأْذَنَكَ) there is an *iltifat* (shift of grammatical person), since it moves from the third-person form, which is His saying *(rasulihi)* (رَسُولِهِ), to the second-person address.

﴿And they said, "Leave us, that we may be with those who sit back."﴾ The "those who sit back" are the disabled, the people with valid excuses, and those left to guard Madinah, since that is an excuse. In His saying: ﴿They were content to be with those left behind﴾ there is a disparagement of them and an exaggeration in blame. *Al-khawalif* (الخَوالِفُ) means the women, as the majority said, such as Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, Shamir ibn 'Atiyyah, Ibn Zayd, and al-Farra'. This is more eloquent in blame, as the poet said:

"I do not know, and I think I will come to know, whether the people of Hisn are men or women.
If women are kept hidden away, then every chaste woman deserves a lament."

Another said:

"Killing and fighting have been prescribed for us,
and for the pampered women, the trailing of skirts."

So their being content to sit with the women in Madinah is the most eloquent blame and disparagement of them, because they placed themselves in the position of feeble women who have no means of defense and no means of sufficiency. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: *al-khawalif* are those in whom there is no good. Al-Nahhas said: a man in whom there is no good is called *khalifah*, and this is its plural by the form of the word; the meaning is the lowest of people and their worst. A group said: *al-khawalif* is the plural of *khalif*, and it follows the pattern of *fawaris*, *nawakis*, and *hawalik*.

The apparent sense is that His saying *(wa-tuba'a)* (وطُبِعَ) is a statement from Allah about what He did to them. It was said it is an interrogative, meaning: "Was a seal set upon their hearts?" So, because of the seal, they do not comprehend, nor reflect, nor understand what there is in striving of success and happiness, and what there is in staying behind of misery and misguidance?

﴿But the Messenger and those who believed with him strove with their wealth and their selves. For them are the good things, and they are the successful.﴾ ﴿Allah has prepared for them gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein; that is the great triumph.﴾

When He mentioned that those hypocrites chose ease, disliked striving, fled from fighting, and mentioned what that had effected in them of a seal upon their hearts, He mentioned the condition of the Messenger and the believers in persevering in striving, and what reward they have. The particle *lakin* (لَكِنِ) is normally placed between two opposites. Since the hypocrites' saying "Leave us" and their asking permission to remain behind included the explicit negation of striving, it is as if it was said: "They were content with such-and-such and did not strive, but the Messenger and those who believed with him strove." The meaning is: if these hypocrites stay behind, then one better than them and sincerer in intention has turned to striving.

Like His Exalted saying: ﴿If these disbelieve in it, We have indeed entrusted it to a people who are not disbelievers in it﴾ (Al-An'am 6:89), and ﴿If they are arrogant, then those who are with your Lord glorify Him night and day﴾ (Fussilat 41:38).

*Al-khayrat* (الخَيْراتُ) is the plural of *khayrah*, which is the most admirable of everything, so it encompasses the goods of this world and the Hereafter due to the generality of the wording, and its frequent use for women. From this is: ﴿Therein are good and beautiful ones﴾ (Al-Rahman 55:70). The poet said:

"I have certainly struck the joints of the lines of Hind's armies,
the lines of Hind, the best of the sovereign queens."

It was said that what is meant here by *al-khayrat* is the wide-eyed maidens of Paradise (*al-hur al-'in*). It was said that what is meant by them is the spoils of war, in wealth and captives. It was also said: "Allah has prepared for them gardens" is an explanation of *al-khayrat*, since it is an ambiguous word.

In His saying: ﴿They were content to be with those left behind﴾ there is a disparagement of them and an exaggeration in blame. *Al-khawalif* (الخَوالِفُ) means the women, as the majority said, such as Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, Shamir ibn 'Atiyyah, Ibn Zayd, and al-Farra'. This is more eloquent in blame, as the poet said:

"I do not know, and I think I will come to know, whether the people of Hisn are men or women.
If women are kept hidden away, then every chaste woman deserves a lament."

Another said:

"Killing and fighting have been prescribed for us,
and for the pampered women, the trailing of skirts."

So their being content to sit with the women in Madinah is the most eloquent blame and disparagement of them, because they placed themselves in the position of feeble women who have no means of defense and no means of sufficiency. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: *al-khawalif* are those in whom there is no good. Al-Nahhas said: a man in whom there is no good is called *khalifah*, and this is its plural by the form of the word; the meaning is the lowest of people and their worst. A group said: *al-khawalif* is the plural of *khalif*, and it follows the pattern of *fawaris*, *nawakis*, and *hawalik*.

The apparent sense is that His saying *(wa-tuba'a)* (وطُبِعَ) is a statement from Allah about what He did to them. It was said it is an interrogative, meaning: "Was a seal set upon their hearts?" So, because of the seal, they do not comprehend, nor reflect, nor understand what there is in striving of success and happiness, and what there is in staying behind of misery and misguidance?

﴿But the Messenger and those who believed with him strove with their wealth and their selves. For them are the good things, and they are the successful.﴾ ﴿Allah has prepared for them gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein; that is the great triumph.﴾

When He mentioned that those hypocrites chose ease, disliked striving, fled from fighting, and mentioned what that had effected in them of a seal upon their hearts, He mentioned the condition of the Messenger and the believers in persevering in striving, and what reward they have. The particle *lakin* (لَكِنِ) is normally placed between two opposites. Since the hypocrites' saying "Leave us" and their asking permission to remain behind included the explicit negation of striving, it is as if it was said: "They were content with such-and-such and did not strive, but the Messenger and those who believed with him strove." The meaning is: if these hypocrites stay behind, then one better than them and sincerer in intention has turned to striving.

Like His Exalted saying: ﴿If these disbelieve in it, We have indeed entrusted it to a people who are not disbelievers in it﴾ (Al-An'am 6:89), and ﴿If they are arrogant, then those who are with your Lord glorify Him night and day﴾ (Fussilat 41:38).

*Al-khayrat* (الخَيْراتُ) is the plural of *khayrah*, which is the most admirable of everything, so it encompasses the goods of this world and the Hereafter due to the generality of the wording, and its frequent use for women. From this is: ﴿Therein are good and beautiful ones﴾ (Al-Rahman 55:70). The poet said:

"I have certainly struck the joints of the lines of Hind's armies,
the lines of Hind, the best of the sovereign queens."

It was said that what is meant here by *al-khayrat* is the wide-eyed maidens of Paradise (*al-hur al-'in*). It was said that what is meant by them is the spoils of war, in wealth and captives. It was also said: "Allah has prepared for them gardens" is an explanation of *al-khayrat*, since it is an ambiguous word.

﴿When a surah was sent down, saying, "Believe in Allah and strive alongside His Messenger," the men of wealth among them asked your permission, and said, "Leave us, that we may be with those who sit back."﴾ ﴿They were content to be with those left behind, and a seal was set upon their hearts, so they do not comprehend.﴾

The majority hold that "surah" here means every surah in which there was a command to believe and to strive. It was said that it refers to Bara'ah (Surah al-Tawbah), because it contains the command to both. It was also said that it means part of a surah, and so the term "surah" is applied to it, just as "Qur'an" and "Kitab" are applied to part of the Qur'an.

Although it has already been mentioned that they had asked the Messenger for permission to remain behind, this verse indicates that whenever a surah was revealed containing the command to believe and to strive, they would ask for permission. Here, *idha* (إذا) does not only convey conditionality, but also carries the sense of repetition, whether that is by its original lexical imposition or by its predominant usage rather than its original imposition. This is a point of disagreement among the grammarians. Among the examples in which repetition is found with *idha* is the poet's verse:

"When I find the heat of fire in my liver, I come toward the water-skins of the people, seeking coolness."

Do you not see that the meaning is "whenever I find"?

*An amanu* (أنْ آمِنُوا) may be explanatory (*tafsiriyyah*), since before it there is a clause that carries the sense of that command; and it may be verbal-noun-introducing (*masdariyyah*), meaning "by believing," i.e., "by faith." The apparent sense is that the address is to the hypocrites, meaning: "Believe with your hearts as you have believed with your tongues." It was said that it may also be an address to the believers, and its meaning would be continuance (*al-istidamah*).

As for *al-tawl* (الطَّوْلِ), Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan said it means wealth. It was also said it means strength and capability. Al-Asamm said: "Ulu al-tawl" are the nobles and leaders. "Ulu al-amr minhum" (أُولُو الأمْرِ مِنهم) means "among them," i.e., among the hypocrites, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, al-Jadd ibn Qays, Mu'attib ibn Qushayr, and their likes. I specify "ulu al-tawl" because they are the ones capable of deterring others and of striving; whoever has no wealth and no capability does not need to ask permission, and asking permission while one is able to move is more ugly and more shameful. The meaning is: "The men of wealth among them asked your permission to remain behind." Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verse 90:

﴿And those who made excuses among the Bedouins came to be given permission, and those who lied to Allah and His Messenger sat back. There will afflict those of them who disbelieved a painful punishment.﴾: When he had mentioned the circumstances of the hypocrites who were in Madinah, he explained the circumstances of the hypocrites among the Bedouins (al-A'rab). The majority (al-Jumhur) read (al-Mu'adhdhirun) with a fatha on the ʿayn and a shaddah on the dhal, so it admits of two morphological patterns. The first: that it is fa''ala with the doubling of the ʿayn, and its meaning is: he burdened himself with an excuse when he has no excuse; it is said ʿadhdhara fi al-amr, meaning he fell short in it and was negligent. Its essential meaning is that he gives the impression that he has an excuse in what he does, while he has no excuse. The second: that its pattern is ifta'ala, and its origin is i'tadhara, like ikhtasama, so the taʾ was assimilated into the dhal, and its vowel was transferred to the ʿayn, and the alif of wasl was dropped. It is supported by the reading of Saʿid ibn Jubayr: (al-Mu'taadhirun) with a taʾ, from i'tadhara. Among those who held that its pattern is ifta'ala are al-Akhfash, al-Farra', Abu ʿUbayd, Abu Hatim, al-Zajjaj, and Ibn al-Anbari. Ibn ʿAbbas, Zayd ibn ʿAli, (p-84) al-Dahhak, al-Aʿraj, Abu Salih, Isa ibn Hilal, Yaʿqub, and al-Kisai, in one narration, read: (al-Mu'dhirun) from aʿdhara. Maslama read: (al-Mu'ʿadhdhirun) with shaddah on the ʿayn and the dhal, from taʿadhdhara in the sense of i'tadhara. Abu Hatim said: he intended al-mutaʿadhdhirin, and the taʾ is not assimilated into the ʿayn because of the distance of their articulation points, and this is an error on his part or against him.

It is differed concerning these excusers: are they believers or disbelievers? Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, and a group said: they are believers, and their excuses are true. Qatadah and a group said: they are disbelievers and their excuses are lies. Ibn ʿAbbas used to say: May Allah have mercy on the excusers (al-Mu'dhirin) and curse the excusers-falsely (al-Mu'adhdhirin). It was said: they were of Asad and Ghatafan, who said: "Indeed we have dependents, and indeed we are in hardship," so he permitted them to stay behind. It was said: they were the kinsmen of ʿAmir ibn al-Tufayl, who said: "If we join you in the campaign, the Bedouins of Tayy will raid our families and our livestock," so the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah will suffice you against them." Mujahid said: they were a group from Ghifar, who made excuses, and Allah did not accept their excuse. Ibn Ishaq said: a group from Ghifar, among them Khafaf ibn Ima'. This indicates that they were believers, and the apparent meaning is that these who came were believers, as Ibn ʿAbbas said, because the division (taqsim) requires that. Do you not see His saying: ﴿And those who lied to Allah and His Messenger sat back. There will afflict those of them who disbelieved a painful punishment.﴾ For if all of them were disbelievers, there would be no specificity in describing those who sat back as liars, and the construction would have been: "There will afflict them a painful punishment." It is possible that they were disbelievers, as Qatadah said, so they were divided into those who came making excuses and those who sat back, and a report about what afflicts the disbelievers was resumed. The pronoun in "minhum" (of them) would refer to the Bedouins, or the meaning would be: there will afflict those of these who die upon disbelief a painful punishment in this world by killing and captivity, and in the Hereafter by the Fire.

The majority read: (kadhabu) with lightening (al-takhfif), i.e. in their faith, so they displayed the opposite of what they concealed. Ubayy, al-Hasan in the well-known report from him, Nuh, and Isma'il read: (kadhdhabu) with shaddah, i.e. they did not believe Him, the Exalted, nor His Messenger, and they rejected his command; and the shaddah is more emphatic in censure.

(p. 85) When he mentioned the condition of those who stayed behind from jihad although they were able to go, he mentioned the condition of those who have an excuse for leaving it. *Al-Du'afa'* (the weak) is the plural of *da'if*, which means the aged, and also one who was created with a frail constitution and extreme weakness, such that jihad is not possible for him. *Al-mari*d (the sick) is one who has become ill, or one who is chronically disabled, and this includes the blind and the lame. *Alladhina la yajiduna ma yunfiquna* (those who do not find what they may spend) are the poor. It has been said that they were the Muzaynah, the Juhaynah and the Banu 'Udhrah. He removed blame from them for staying behind from the raid. Removing blame does not imply a prohibition on going out to the raid. So if one of these people went out to assist the fighters with whatever he is able to do, such as guarding their goods or increasing their numbers without being a burden on them, he would have a great reward for that. 

It is narrated that 'Amr ibn al-Jamuh was lame, and he was one of the pious Ansar. He was at the front of the army, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "Allah has excused you." He said: "By Allah, I will surely hop about with this limp of mine in Paradise." 

Ibn Umm Maktum was blind. He went out to Uhud and asked to be given the standard, so he took it. His hand that held the standard was struck, so he held it with the other hand. That was struck, so he held it to his chest. And he recited: "Muhammad is but a messenger; messengers have passed away before him" (Al 'Imran 144). 

He made the condition for the removal of blame to be sincere counsel (*nusḥ*) to Allah and His Messenger, which means that their intentions and their words, secret and public, are sincerely for Allah, free of deceit, striving to bring good to the believers, and invoking victory and empowerment for them. In the Sunan of Abi Dawud: "You have left behind after you a people. You have not traversed any route, nor spent any expenditure, nor crossed any valley, except that they were with you in it." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, how can they be with us when they are in Madinah?" He said: "The excuse has held them back." 

Abu Haywah recited: "*idha nasahu Allaha wa rasulahu*" with the accusative case on the divine name and on what is conjoined to it.

﴿ما عَلى المُحْسِنِينَ مِن سَبِيلٍ﴾ means: there is no blame or punishment that can be attributed to them. The word *al-muhsinin* (the good-doers) is general, and these excused people who give sincere counsel are included in it along with others. It has been said that *al-muhsinin* here refers specifically to the excused who give sincere counsel. Using this clause as evidence to deny analogical reasoning (*qiyas*), and to argue that the good-doer is the Muslim, is far-fetched, because the complete absence of any way (blame) means that no obligation is directed at him except by a separate proof, so it would restrict this general statement which indicates the clearing of his responsibility. 

Al-Karmani said: "*Al-muhsinin*" are those who obeyed Allah and His Messenger in their words. Then he emphasised the hope, saying: ﴿واللَّهُ غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾ (And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful). The reading of Ibn 'Abbas was "*wa Allahu li-ahl al-isa'ah ghafurun rahim*" (And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful to the people of wrongdoing), as an explanation and not as Qur'an, because it contradicts the consonantal text of the Mushaf.

It has been said that His saying ﴿ما عَلى المُحْسِنِينَ مِن سَبِيلٍ﴾ contains a type of rhetorical ornamentation (*al-badi'*, embellishment), called *al-tamlih* (allusion), which is when, within the sense of the speech, a well-known proverb, a rare line of poetry, a famous story, or something that functions like a proverb is alluded to. From it is the saying of Yasar ibn 'Adi when news of the killing of his brother reached him while he was drinking wine:

*Today is wine, and tomorrow news will appear,*
*and time alternates between favour and despair.*

﴿ولا عَلى الَّذِينَ إذا ما أتَوْكَ لِتَحْمِلَهُمْ﴾ is conjoined to what precedes it, and they are included in His saying ﴿ولا عَلى الَّذِينَ لا يَجِدُونَ ما يُنْفِقُونَ﴾ (nor upon those who find nothing to spend). They are mentioned in the manner of removing blame from them, and that they exerted themselves to obtain what would enable them to go out to jihad, until the situation led them to asking and to the need to humble their faces in seeking what would carry them to jihad, and to seeking help with it, so that they could fight alongside the Messenger (ﷺ) and not miss the reward of jihad. It is possible that they are not included in His saying ﴿ولا عَلى الَّذِينَ لا يَجِدُونَ ما يُنْفِقُونَ﴾, by taking them to be those who found what to spend but did not find a mount. In that case "nafaqah" (expenditure) means provisions for the journey, not what the fighter needs of provisions, mount, weapons and other things. 

This verse was revealed concerning al-'Irbad ibn Sariyah. It has been said that it was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Mughaffal. It has been said that it was revealed concerning 'A'idh ibn 'Amr. It has been said that it was revealed concerning Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and his people. It has been said that it was revealed concerning nine men from various clans, and they are the "weepers" (*al-bakka'un*): Salim ibn 'Umayr from Banu 'Awf, Huramiy ibn 'Amr from Banu Waqif, Abu Layla 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ka'b from Banu Mazin ibn al-Najjar, Salman ibn Sakhr from Banu al-Mu'alla, (p. 86) Abu Ru'aylah 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd from Banu Harithah, 'Amr ibn Ghanamah from Banu Salamah, and 'A'idh ibn 'Amr al-Muzani. It has also been said: 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr al-Muzani. Mujahid said: the *bakka'un* (weepers) are the Banu Bakr from Muzaynah. The majority said: it was revealed concerning the Banu Muqrin, who were six brothers who accompanied the Prophet (ﷺ), and there were no other six brothers among the Companions.

The meaning of *li-tahmilahum* (that you might carry them) is: upon the back of a mount, on which the belongings of the fighter may be carried. Ibn 'Abbas said this. Anas ibn Malik said: "that you might carry them with provisions." Al-Hasan ibn Salih said: "with mules." It is narrated that seven men from various tribes said: "O Messenger of Allah, you have called us to go out with you. Carry us, then, on the worn-out leather shoes and the patched sandals, so that we may fight with you." He said: ﴿لا أجِدُ ما أحْمِلُكُمْ عَلَيْهِ﴾ (I cannot find anything to carry you on), so they turned away weeping.

Ma'qil ibn Harun read "*li-nahmilahum*" with the plural "nun". 

*Idha* (when) requires an answer. The better view is that its answer is the nearest word to it, which is "*qulta*" (you said), and His saying "*tawallaw*" (they turned away) is an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "What was their condition when the Messenger answered them?" It is said: "They turned away while their eyes overflowed." It has been said that the answer to *idha* is "*tawallaw*", and "*qulta*" is a clause in the position of a circumstantial state (*hal*) relative to the *kaf* (the pronoun "you"), meaning: when they came to you saying "I cannot find." Before it, a *qad* is implied, as has been said regarding His saying ﴿حَصِرَتْ صُدُورُهُمْ﴾ (their breasts are constricted) (al-Nisa 90). This was said by al-Zamakhshari. Or it is by deleting the conjunctive particle, meaning "wa qulta" (and you said). This was said by al-Jurjani, and by Ibn 'Atiyyah, who estimated it as "fa-qulta" with the particle *fa* (so you said).

﴿وأعْيُنُهم تَفِيضُ﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*jumlah haliyyah*). Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, is it permissible for His saying "*qulta la ajidu*" to be a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*) like His saying ﴿رَضُوا بِأنْ يَكُونُوا مَعَ الخَوالِفِ﴾ (they were content to be with those who stay behind) (al-Tawbah 93), as if it were said: "When they came to you to be carried, they turned away." Then it is asked: "Why did they turn away weeping?" I say: "I cannot find what to carry them upon." Except that it stands between the condition and the answer like a parenthetical interjection. I say: Yes, and it is good. End of quote. But it is not permissible, nor is it good, in the speech of the Arabs, so how could it be in the speech of Allah, which is a non-Arabic (*a'jami*) understanding? The discussion of the like of ﴿وأعْيُنُهم تَفِيضُ مِنَ الدَّمْعِ﴾ has already been given at the beginning of the section beginning "you will surely find" (*latajidanna*) in Surah al-Ma'idah. Al-Zamakhshari said here: ﴿وأعْيُنُهم تَفِيضُ مِنَ الدَّمْعِ﴾ is like your saying "tafidu damʿan" (it overflows with tears), and it is more eloquent than "yafidu damʿuha" (its tears overflow), because the eye is made as though all of it were overflowing tears. The *min* (from) is for specification (*bayan*), like your saying "I ransom you from a man" (*afdika min rajul*), and the place of the preposition and its object is in the accusative as a specification (*tamyiz*). End of quote. But that is not permissible, because a specification whose original form is a subject cannot be marked with *min*. Moreover it is definite, and that is only permissible according to the view of the Kufans, who allow a specification to be definite. 

*Hazanan* (in sorrow) is in the accusative as an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*, object of purpose), and its governing verb is "*tafidu*" (overflows). Abu al-Baqa' said: or it is an infinitive in the position of a circumstantial state. *Allā yajidū* (that they might not find) is also an object of purpose, and its governing verb is *hazanan*. Abu al-Baqa' said: it may also be connected to "*tafidu*". End of quote. But that is not permissible on the reading that *hazanan* is an object of purpose governed by "*tafidu*", because the governing element cannot govern two objects of purpose except through conjunction or apposition. His saying ﴿ألّا يَجِدُوا ما يُنْفِقُونَ﴾ (that they do not find what to spend) indicates that they are included under His saying ﴿ولا عَلى الَّذِينَ لا يَجِدُونَ ما يُنْفِقُونَ حَرَجٌ﴾ (nor upon those who find nothing to spend, there is no blame).
