In the Sunan of Abi Dawud: "You have left behind after you a people. You have not traversed any route, nor spent any expenditure, nor crossed any valley, except that they were with you in it." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, how can they be with us when they are in Madinah?" He said: "The excuse has held them back." 

Abu Haywah recited: "*idha nasahu Allaha wa rasulahu*" with the accusative case on the divine name and on what is conjoined to it.

﴿ما عَلى المُحْسِنِينَ مِن سَبِيلٍ﴾ means: there is no blame or punishment that can be attributed to them. The word *al-muhsinin* (the good-doers) is general, and these excused people who give sincere counsel are included in it along with others. It has been said that *al-muhsinin* here refers specifically to the excused who give sincere counsel. Using this clause as evidence to deny analogical reasoning (*qiyas*), and to argue that the good-doer is the Muslim, is far-fetched, because the complete absence of any way (blame) means that no obligation is directed at him except by a separate proof, so it would restrict this general statement which indicates the clearing of his responsibility. 

Al-Karmani said: "*Al-muhsinin*" are those who obeyed Allah and His Messenger in their words. Then he emphasised the hope, saying: ﴿واللَّهُ غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾ (And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful). The reading of Ibn 'Abbas was "*wa Allahu li-ahl al-isa'ah ghafurun rahim*" (And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful to the people of wrongdoing), as an explanation and not as Qur'an, because it contradicts the consonantal text of the Mushaf.

It has been said that His saying ﴿ما عَلى المُحْسِنِينَ مِن سَبِيلٍ﴾ contains a type of rhetorical ornamentation (*al-badi'*, embellishment), called *al-tamlih* (allusion), which is when, within the sense of the speech, a well-known proverb, a rare line of poetry, a famous story, or something that functions like a proverb is alluded to. From it is the saying of Yasar ibn 'Adi when news of the killing of his brother reached him while he was drinking wine:

*Today is wine, and tomorrow news will appear,*
*and time alternates between favour and despair.*

﴿ولا عَلى الَّذِينَ إذا ما أتَوْكَ لِتَحْمِلَهُمْ﴾ is conjoined to what precedes it, and they are included in His saying ﴿ولا عَلى الَّذِينَ لا يَجِدُونَ ما يُنْفِقُونَ﴾ (nor upon those who find nothing to spend). They are mentioned in the manner of removing blame from them, and that they exerted themselves to obtain what would enable them to go out to jihad, until the situation led them to asking and to the need to humble their faces in seeking what would carry them to jihad, and to seeking help with it, so that they could fight alongside the Messenger (ﷺ) and not miss the reward of jihad. It is possible that they are not included in His saying ﴿ولا عَلى الَّذِينَ لا يَجِدُونَ ما يُنْفِقُونَ﴾, by taking them to be those who found what to spend but did not find a mount. In that case "nafaqah" (expenditure) means provisions for the journey, not what the fighter needs of provisions, mount, weapons and other things. 

This verse was revealed concerning al-'Irbad ibn Sariyah. It has been said that it was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Mughaffal. It has been said that it was revealed concerning 'A'idh ibn 'Amr. It has been said that it was revealed concerning Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and his people. It has been said that it was revealed concerning nine men from various clans, and they are the "weepers" (*al-bakka'un*): Salim ibn 'Umayr from Banu 'Awf, Huramiy ibn 'Amr from Banu Waqif, Abu Layla 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ka'b from Banu Mazin ibn al-Najjar, Salman ibn Sakhr from Banu al-Mu'alla, (p. 86) Abu Ru'aylah 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd from Banu Harithah, 'Amr ibn Ghanamah from Banu Salamah, and 'A'idh ibn 'Amr al-Muzani. It has also been said: 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr al-Muzani. Mujahid said: the *bakka'un* (weepers) are the Banu Bakr from Muzaynah. The majority said: it was revealed concerning the Banu Muqrin, who were six brothers who accompanied the Prophet (ﷺ), and there were no other six brothers among the Companions.

The meaning of *li-tahmilahum* (that you might carry them) is: upon the back of a mount, on which the belongings of the fighter may be carried. Ibn 'Abbas said this. Anas ibn Malik said: "that you might carry them with provisions." Al-Hasan ibn Salih said: "with mules." It is narrated that seven men from various tribes said: "O Messenger of Allah, you have called us to go out with you. Carry us, then, on the worn-out leather shoes and the patched sandals, so that we may fight with you." He said: ﴿لا أجِدُ ما أحْمِلُكُمْ عَلَيْهِ﴾ (I cannot find anything to carry you on), so they turned away weeping.

Ma'qil ibn Harun read "*li-nahmilahum*" with the plural "nun". 

*Idha* (when) requires an answer. The better view is that its answer is the nearest word to it, which is "*qulta*" (you said), and His saying "*tawallaw*" (they turned away) is an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "What was their condition when the Messenger answered them?" It is said: "They turned away while their eyes overflowed." It has been said that the answer to *idha* is "*tawallaw*", and "*qulta*" is a clause in the position of a circumstantial state (*hal*) relative to the *kaf* (the pronoun "you"), meaning: when they came to you saying "I cannot find." Before it, a *qad* is implied, as has been said regarding His saying ﴿حَصِرَتْ صُدُورُهُمْ﴾ (their breasts are constricted) (al-Nisa 90). This was said by al-Zamakhshari. Or it is by deleting the conjunctive particle, meaning "wa qulta" (and you said). This was said by al-Jurjani, and by Ibn 'Atiyyah, who estimated it as "fa-qulta" with the particle *fa* (so you said).

﴿وأعْيُنُهم تَفِيضُ﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*jumlah haliyyah*). Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, is it permissible for His saying "*qulta la ajidu*" to be a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*) like His saying ﴿رَضُوا بِأنْ يَكُونُوا مَعَ الخَوالِفِ﴾ (they were content to be with those who stay behind) (al-Tawbah 93), as if it were said: "When they came to you to be carried, they turned away." Then it is asked: "Why did they turn away weeping?" I say: "I cannot find what to carry them upon." Except that it stands between the condition and the answer like a parenthetical interjection. I say: Yes, and it is good. End of quote. But it is not permissible, nor is it good, in the speech of the Arabs, so how could it be in the speech of Allah, which is a non-Arabic (*a'jami*) understanding? The discussion of the like of ﴿وأعْيُنُهم تَفِيضُ مِنَ الدَّمْعِ﴾ has already been given at the beginning of the section beginning "you will surely find" (*latajidanna*) in Surah al-Ma'idah. Al-Zamakhshari said here: ﴿وأعْيُنُهم تَفِيضُ مِنَ الدَّمْعِ﴾ is like your saying "tafidu damʿan" (it overflows with tears), and it is more eloquent than "yafidu damʿuha" (its tears overflow), because the eye is made as though all of it were overflowing tears. The *min* (from) is for specification (*bayan*), like your saying "I ransom you from a man" (*afdika min rajul*), and the place of the preposition and its object is in the accusative as a specification (*tamyiz*). End of quote. But that is not permissible, because a specification whose original form is a subject cannot be marked with *min*. Moreover it is definite, and that is only permissible according to the view of the Kufans, who allow a specification to be definite. 

*Hazanan* (in sorrow) is in the accusative as an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*, object of purpose), and its governing verb is "*tafidu*" (overflows). Abu al-Baqa' said: or it is an infinitive in the position of a circumstantial state. *Allā yajidū* (that they might not find) is also an object of purpose, and its governing verb is *hazanan*. Abu al-Baqa' said: it may also be connected to "*tafidu*". End of quote. But that is not permissible on the reading that *hazanan* is an object of purpose governed by "*tafidu*", because the governing element cannot govern two objects of purpose except through conjunction or apposition. His saying ﴿ألّا يَجِدُوا ما يُنْفِقُونَ﴾ (that they do not find what to spend) indicates that they are included under His saying ﴿ولا عَلى الَّذِينَ لا يَجِدُونَ ما يُنْفِقُونَ حَرَجٌ﴾ (nor upon those who find nothing to spend, there is no blame).

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 9, verses 93–94:**

(p-87) ﴿The blame is only upon those who ask your permission while they are wealthy. They are content to be with those who stay behind (al-khawalif), and Allah has sealed their hearts, so they do not know.﴾ ﴿They will make excuses to you when you return to them. Say: Do not make excuses; we will never believe you. Allah has already informed us of your news. Allah will see your deeds, and so will His Messenger, and then you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He will inform you of what you used to do.﴾ ﴿They will swear to you by Allah when you return to them, so that you may turn away from them. So turn away from them. Indeed they are filth, and their refuge is Hell, as recompense for what they used to earn.﴾ [At-Tawba: 95] ﴿They swear to you that you may be pleased with them. But if you are pleased with them, indeed Allah is not pleased with the defiant people.﴾ [At-Tawba: 96] ﴿The Bedouins are the strongest in disbelief and hypocrisy, and the most likely not to know the limits of what Allah has sent down to His Messenger. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾ [At-Tawba: 97] ﴿Among the Bedouins is one who regards what he spends as a loss and waits for misfortunes to befall you. Upon them is the evil turn of fortune. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾ [At-Tawba: 98] ﴿Among the Bedouins is one who believes in Allah and the Last Day and regards what he spends as means of nearness to Allah and as prayers of the Messenger. Indeed, it is a means of nearness for them. Allah will admit them into His mercy. Indeed Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.﴾ [At-Tawba: 99] ﴿The foremost, the first of the Emigrants and the Helpers, and those who followed them in excellence: Allah is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him, and He has prepared for them gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the great triumph.﴾ [At-Tawba: 100] ﴿Among those around you of the Bedouins are hypocrites, and among the people of Medina are those who persisted in hypocrisy. You do not know them; We know them. We will punish them twice, and then they will be returned to a great punishment.﴾ [At-Tawba: 101] ﴿And others have acknowledged their sins. They mixed a righteous deed with another that was bad. Perhaps Allah will accept their repentance. Indeed Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.﴾ [At-Tawba: 102] ﴿Take from their wealth a charity to purify them and cause them to grow, and pray for them. Indeed your prayer is a comfort for them. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾ [At-Tawba: 103] ﴿Do they not know that Allah is He who accepts repentance from His servants and takes charities, and that Allah is the Accepter of Repentance, the Merciful?﴾ [At-Tawba: 104] ﴿And say: Work, and Allah will see your deeds, and so will His Messenger and the believers, and you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He will inform you of what you used to do.﴾ [At-Tawba: 105] ﴿And others are deferred to Allah's command: either He will punish them or He will accept their repentance. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾ [At-Tawba: 106] ﴿And those who took a mosque for harm, disbelief, and division among the believers, and as a station for one who had warred against Allah and His Messenger before. They will surely swear, "We intended only good." And Allah testifies that they are indeed liars.﴾ [At-Tawba: 107] ﴿Never stand in it. A mosque founded on piety from the first day is more worthy that you stand in it. In it are men who love to purify themselves, and Allah loves those who purify themselves.﴾ [At-Tawba: 108] ﴿Is one who founded his building on fear of Allah and His pleasure better, or one who founded his building on the edge of a crumbling bank that collapsed with him into the fire of Hell? And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾ [At-Tawba: 109] ﴿Their building which they built will not cease to be a doubt in their hearts, unless their hearts are cut to pieces. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾ [At-Tawba: 110] ﴿Indeed Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their wealth, in exchange for Paradise. They fight in the way of Allah, so they kill and are killed. This is a promise binding upon Him in the Torah, the Gospel, and the Qur'an. And who is truer to his covenant than Allah? So rejoice in the bargain you have made. That is the great triumph.﴾ [At-Tawba: 111] ﴿The repentant, the worshippers, the praisers, the travellers, the bowers, the prostrators, those who enjoin right and forbid wrong, and those who keep the limits of Allah. So give good tidings to the believers.﴾ [At-Tawba: 112] ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they were near relatives, after it has become clear to them that they are companions of Hellfire.﴾ [At-Tawba: 113] ﴿The plea for forgiveness by Abraham for his father was only due to a promise he had made to him. But when it became clear to him that he was an enemy of Allah, he disassociated himself from him. Indeed Abraham was tender-hearted and forbearing.﴾ [At-Tawba: 114] ﴿Allah would not misguide a people after He had guided them until He makes clear to them what they should beware. Indeed Allah is Knower of all things.﴾ [At-Tawba: 115] ﴿Indeed, to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He gives life and causes death. And you have, besides Allah, no protector or helper.﴾ [At-Tawba: 116] ﴿Allah has certainly turned in forgiveness to the Prophet and the Emigrants and the Helpers who followed him in the hour of hardship, after the hearts of a faction of them had nearly inclined away. Then He turned to them in forgiveness. Indeed He is Kind and Merciful to them.﴾ [At-Tawba: 117] ﴿And to the three who were left behind, until, when the earth closed in on them despite its vastness, and their souls confined them, and they thought there was no refuge from Allah except in Him. Then He turned to them so that they might repent. Indeed Allah is the Accepter of Repentance, the Merciful.﴾ [At-Tawba: 118] ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and be with the truthful.﴾ [At-Tawba: 119] ﴿It was not for the people of Medina and those around them of the Bedouins to remain behind from the Messenger of Allah, nor to prefer themselves over his self. That is because they are not afflicted by thirst or fatigue or hunger in the way of Allah, nor do they tread upon a place that enrages the disbelievers, nor do they inflict upon an enemy any harm except that a righteous deed is written for them thereby. Indeed Allah does not allow the reward of the good-doers to be lost.﴾ [At-Tawba: 120] ﴿Nor do they spend an expenditure small or large, nor do they cross a valley except that it is written for them, so that Allah may reward them with the best of what they used to do.﴾ [At-Tawba: 121]

"Al-A'rab" (the Bedouins) is a plural form, and it is distinguished from "al-'Arab" (the Arabs). The 'Arabi is one who has lineage among the Arabs. The A'rabi is the desert dweller who seeks rain and pasture, whether he is of the Arabs or of their clients (mawali). For this distinction, the word was given a relative form based on its own pronunciation, so it is said: a'rabi. The plural al-A'rab was made into al-A'arib, the plural of the plural (jam' al-jam').

"Ajdar" means more worthy and more deserving. Al-Layth said: jadara jadarah, so he is jadir and ajdar; it takes the feminine, dual and plural forms. The poet said:

*A palm grove around which is a jannah of 'abqariyya,*
*Deserving one day to attain and to rise above.*

"Assasa" is on the pattern of fa''ala with a doubled middle radical, and "a'assa" is on the pattern of fa'ala; it means he laid the foundation (al-asas), which is well known, and it is also said: (p-88) ussun. "Al-jurf" is a well that has not been lined with stone. Abu 'Ubayda said: it is a chasm, and what the torrent tears away from the valleys. "Hari" means fallen and collapsing, falling down part after part. Its verb is haara, yahuru, yahar, and yahir. The 'ayn of hari may be either a waw or a ya', so its root is hayir or hawir, which then underwent change, and it was treated as in qadin and ghazin, and became defective like shaki al-silah and la'th, as the poet said:

*Wrapped around with the acacia and the 'Ubri (tree).*

It is also said: hari is one whose middle radical is elided because of a letter related to it, so the ra' takes the various i'rab (grammatical case endings). Al-Kisa'i reported: tahawwara and tahayyara.

"Awwah" is one who says "awwah" often. It is an ism al-fi'l (a noun functioning as a verb) meaning "I am in pain." Its pattern is fa''al, for intensification. The regular verbal form would be trilateral, and Qutrub reported it: aha yau'uhu awhan, like qala yaqulu qawlan. It is reported from the grammarians that they rejected this and said: there is no trilateral verb from the word awwah; rather it is said: awwaha ta'wihan and ta'awwaha ta'awwuhan. The rajiz (rhymster) said:

*So the caller cried out, and his dog barked.*

Al-Muthaqqab al-'Abdi said:

*When I rise to saddle her in the night,*
*She groans the groan of a grieving man.*

There are several dialects regarding the ism al-fi'l "awwah," mentioned in the science of grammar. "Al-zama'" is intense thirst, and it is the verbal noun of zami'a yazma'u, so he is zam'an and she is zam'a; it is lengthened to become zima'. "Al-wadi" is what is lower than the surface, extending like the channels of torrents and the like. The Arabs made its plural awdiya, though this is not its regular pattern. God, Most High, said: ﴿So the torrents flowed according to their measure﴾ [Ar-Ra'd: 17]. Its regular pattern would be fawa'il, but they found it heavy because it would bring together two waws. Al-Nahhas said: I know of no fa'il and af'ila other than this. Others mentioned nadin and andiya. The poet said:

*Among them are fine gatherings whose faces,*
*And assemblies where speech and action are exchanged.*

"Al-nadi" is the assembly. Al-Farra' reported its plural as awda', like sahib and as'hab. Jarir said:

*I recognised at the Barqat al-Awda' a trace,*
*Effaced, your time there has been long, of its traces.*

Al-Zamakhshari said: al-wadi is every winding passage between mountains and hillocks that serves as an outlet for the torrent. It is originally fa'il from wadiya, meaning it flowed, and from it comes al-wadi (the discharge). It has become widespread in Arabic usage in the sense of land. You say: do not pray in the valley of another than you.

﴿The blame is only upon those who ask your permission while they are wealthy...﴾: He affirmed for the hypocrites what He negated for the good-doers, so by way of contrast it shows that these are wrongdoers. What wrongdoing is greater than hypocrisy, remaining behind from jihad, and preferring themselves over the Messenger of Allah? "Innama" here is not for restriction (hasr); it is for emphasis and intensification of assertion. The meaning is: the blame, the punishment and the sin are only upon those who ask your permission to remain behind from jihad while they are able to do it because of their wealth. The predicate of "al-sabil" is "ala," even though it has been separated by "ila," as the poet said:

*Is there any way to wine so I may drink it,*
*Or is there any way to the victory of Nasr ibn Hajjaj?*

Because "ala" indicates elevation and the weakness of the protection of the one it governs, there is a difference between: "I have no way over Zayd" (la sabila li 'ala Zayd) and "I have no way to Zayd" (la sabila li ila Zayd). This verse concerns the hypocrites mentioned earlier: 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, al-Jadd ibn Qays, Mu'attib ibn Qushayr, and others. "Radu" (they were content) is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), as if it were said: what is their state that they asked permission to sit in Medina while they are able to fight? So it was said: they were content with baseness and with being counted among the remainers (al-khawalif). "Wa-tabaa" is conjoined to draw attention to the fact that the cause of their remaining behind was their contentment with baseness.

﴿And Allah has sealed their hearts, so they do not know﴾: they do not know the benefits of religion and of this world that result from jihad.

﴿They will make excuses to you when you return to them. Say: Do not make excuses; we will never believe you. Allah has already informed us of your news...﴾: "Lan nu'mina lakum" is the cause of the prohibition on making excuses, because the aim of one who makes an excuse is to be believed regarding what he offers as excuse. So when it is known that he is lying in his excuse, he is restrained from it. "Qad naba'ana Allah min akhbarikum" is the cause for the negation of belief, because when God informs the Messenger and the believers of what their secret hearts contain of evil and corruption, it is not possible to believe them in their excuses. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the reference in His words "Qad naba'ana Allah min akhbarikum" is to His words "They would have only added to your confusion and would have hurried about among you" [At-Tawba: 47], and the like. Here "naba'a" takes two objects, like "arrafa," as in His words: "Who informed you of this?" The second object is "min akhbarikum," meaning a clause "min akhbarikum." According to the opinion of Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash, "min" is superfluous, meaning "akhbarakum" (your news). It has also been said: "naba'a" means "a'lama" (to inform), which takes three objects, and the third is omitted for brevity, the context indicating it: "min akhbarikum kadhiban aw nahwahu" (from your news, [that which is] false or the like).

"Wa-sayara Allah" is a threat, meaning: He will see it in its existence, so that recompense will be given for it, if good then good, and if evil then evil. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Wa-sayara Allah 'amalakum" [And Allah will see your deeds]: will you repent or will you remain upon disbelief? "Thumma turaddun" [then you will be returned] refers to resurrection from the graves, and the informing about their deeds is a metaphor for requiting them for them. Ibn 'Isa said: "Wa-sayara" is because He has made it a matter of manifestation as if it were seen, and then He recompenses for it. It has also been said: they used to show the Messenger, when presenting their excuses, love and compassion, so it was said: "And Allah will see your deeds": will they remain upon that or not? The unseen and the witnessed are two comprehensive categories of a servant's deeds, and there is no deed outside of them. This indicates that He is aware of their inner thoughts just as He is aware of their outward conduct, with no difference in that regard before Him.

In it are men who love to purify themselves, and Allah loves those who purify themselves.﴾ [At-Tawba: 108] ﴿Is one who founded his building on fear of Allah and His pleasure better, or one who founded his building on the edge of a crumbling bank that collapsed with him into the fire of Hell? And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾ [At-Tawba: 109] ﴿Their building which they built will not cease to be a doubt in their hearts, unless their hearts are cut to pieces. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾ [At-Tawba: 110] ﴿Indeed Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their wealth, in exchange for Paradise. They fight in the way of Allah, so they kill and are killed. This is a promise binding upon Him in the Torah, the Gospel, and the Qur'an. And who is truer to his covenant than Allah? So rejoice in the bargain you have made. That is the great triumph.﴾ [At-Tawba: 111] ﴿The repentant, the worshippers, the praisers, the travellers, the bowers, the prostrators, those who enjoin right and forbid wrong, and those who keep the limits of Allah. So give good tidings to the believers.﴾ [At-Tawba: 112] ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they were near relatives, after it has become clear to them that they are companions of Hellfire.﴾ [At-Tawba: 113] ﴿The plea for forgiveness by Abraham for his father was only due to a promise he had made to him. But when it became clear to him that he was an enemy of Allah, he disassociated himself from him. Indeed Abraham was tender-hearted and forbearing.﴾ [At-Tawba: 114] ﴿Allah would not misguide a people after He had guided them until He makes clear to them what they should beware. Indeed Allah is Knower of all things.﴾ [At-Tawba: 115] ﴿Indeed, to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He gives life and causes death. And you have, besides Allah, no protector or helper.﴾ [At-Tawba: 116] ﴿Allah has certainly turned in forgiveness to the Prophet and the Emigrants and the Helpers who followed him in the hour of hardship, after the hearts of a faction of them had nearly inclined away. Then He turned to them in forgiveness. Indeed He is Kind and Merciful to them.﴾ [At-Tawba: 117] ﴿And to the three who were left behind, until, when the earth closed in on them despite its vastness, and their souls confined them, and they thought there was no refuge from Allah except in Him. Then He turned to them so that they might repent. Indeed Allah is the Accepter of Repentance, the Merciful.﴾ [At-Tawba: 118] ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and be with the truthful.﴾ [At-Tawba: 119] ﴿It was not for the people of Medina and those around them of the Bedouins to remain behind from the Messenger of Allah, nor to prefer themselves over his self. That is because they are not afflicted by thirst or fatigue or hunger in the way of Allah, nor do they tread upon a place that enrages the disbelievers, nor do they inflict upon an enemy any harm except that a righteous deed is written for them thereby. Indeed Allah does not allow the reward of the good-doers to be lost.﴾ [At-Tawba: 120] ﴿Nor do they spend an expenditure small or large, nor do they cross a valley except that it is written for them, so that Allah may reward them with the best of what they used to do.﴾ [At-Tawba: 121]

"Al-A'rab" (the Bedouins) is a plural form, and it is distinguished from "al-'Arab" (the Arabs). The 'Arabi is one who has lineage among the Arabs. The A'rabi is the desert dweller who seeks rain and pasture, whether he is of the Arabs or of their clients (mawali). For this distinction, the word was given a relative form based on its own pronunciation, so it is said: a'rabi. The plural al-A'rab was made into al-A'arib, the plural of the plural (jam' al-jam').

"Ajdar" means more worthy and more deserving. Al-Layth said: jadara jadarah, so he is jadir and ajdar; it takes the feminine, dual and plural forms. The poet said:

*A palm grove around which is a jannah of 'abqariyya,*
*Deserving one day to attain and to rise above.*

"Assasa" is on the pattern of fa''ala with a doubled middle radical, and "a'assa" is on the pattern of fa'ala; it means he laid the foundation (al-asas), which is well known, and it is also said: (p-88) ussun. "Al-jurf" is a well that has not been lined with stone. Abu 'Ubayda said: it is a chasm, and what the torrent tears away from the valleys. "Hari" means fallen and collapsing, falling down part after part. Its verb is haara, yahuru, yahar, and yahir. The 'ayn of hari may be either a waw or a ya', so its root is hayir or hawir, which then underwent change, and it was treated as in qadin and ghazin, and became defective like shaki al-silah and la'th, as the poet said:

*Wrapped around with the acacia and the 'Ubri (tree).*

It is also said: hari is one whose middle radical is elided because of a letter related to it, so the ra' takes the various i'rab (grammatical case endings). Al-Kisa'i reported: tahawwara and tahayyara.

"Awwah" is one who says "awwah" often. It is an ism al-fi'l (a noun functioning as a verb) meaning "I am in pain." Its pattern is fa''al, for intensification. The regular verbal form would be trilateral, and Qutrub reported it: aha yau'uhu awhan, like qala yaqulu qawlan. It is reported from the grammarians that they rejected this and said: there is no trilateral verb from the word awwah; rather it is said: awwaha ta'wihan and ta'awwaha ta'awwuhan. The rajiz (rhymster) said:

*So the caller cried out, and his dog barked.*

Al-Muthaqqab al-'Abdi said:

*When I rise to saddle her in the night,*
*She groans the groan of a grieving man.*

There are several dialects regarding the ism al-fi'l "awwah," mentioned in the science of grammar. "Al-zama'" is intense thirst, and it is the verbal noun of zami'a yazma'u, so he is zam'an and she is zam'a; it is lengthened to become zima'. "Al-wadi" is what is lower than the surface, extending like the channels of torrents and the like. The Arabs made its plural awdiya, though this is not its regular pattern. God, Most High, said: ﴿So the torrents flowed according to their measure﴾ [Ar-Ra'd: 17]. Its regular pattern would be fawa'il, but they found it heavy because it would bring together two waws. Al-Nahhas said: I know of no fa'il and af'ila other than this. Others mentioned nadin and andiya. The poet said:

*Among them are fine gatherings whose faces,*
*And assemblies where speech and action are exchanged.*

"Al-nadi" is the assembly. Al-Farra' reported its plural as awda', like sahib and as'hab. Jarir said:

*I recognised at the Barqat al-Awda' a trace,*
*Effaced, your time there has been long, of its traces.*

Al-Zamakhshari said: al-wadi is every winding passage between mountains and hillocks that serves as an outlet for the torrent. It is originally fa'il from wadiya, meaning it flowed, and from it comes al-wadi (the discharge). It has become widespread in Arabic usage in the sense of land. You say: do not pray in the valley of another than you.

﴿The blame is only upon those who ask your permission while they are wealthy...﴾: He affirmed for the hypocrites what He negated for the good-doers, so by way of contrast it shows that these are wrongdoers. What wrongdoing is greater than hypocrisy, remaining behind from jihad, and preferring themselves over the Messenger of Allah? "Innama" here is not for restriction (hasr); it is for emphasis and intensification of assertion. The meaning is: the blame, the punishment and the sin are only upon those who ask your permission to remain behind from jihad while they are able to do it because of their wealth. The predicate of "al-sabil" is "ala," even though it has been separated by "ila," as the poet said:

*Is there any way to wine so I may drink it,*
*Or is there any way to the victory of Nasr ibn Hajjaj?*

Because "ala" indicates elevation and the weakness of the protection of the one it governs, there is a difference between: "I have no way over Zayd" (la sabila li 'ala Zayd) and "I have no way to Zayd" (la sabila li ila Zayd). This verse concerns the hypocrites mentioned earlier: 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, al-Jadd ibn Qays, Mu'attib ibn Qushayr, and others. "Radu" (they were content) is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), as if it were said: what is their state that they asked permission to sit in Medina while they are able to fight? So it was said: they were content with baseness and with being counted among the remainers (al-khawalif). "Wa-tabaa" is conjoined to draw attention to the fact that the cause of their remaining behind was their contentment with baseness.

﴿And Allah has sealed their hearts, so they do not know﴾: they do not know the benefits of religion and of this world that result from jihad.

﴿They will make excuses to you when you return to them. Say: Do not make excuses; we will never believe you. Allah has already informed us of your news...﴾: "Lan nu'mina lakum" is the cause of the prohibition on making excuses, because the aim of one who makes an excuse is to be believed regarding what he offers as excuse. So when it is known that he is lying in his excuse, he is restrained from it. "Qad naba'ana Allah min akhbarikum" is the cause for the negation of belief, because when God informs the Messenger and the believers of what their secret hearts contain of evil and corruption, it is not possible to believe them in their excuses. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the reference in His words "Qad naba'ana Allah min akhbarikum" is to His words "They would have only added to your confusion and would have hurried about among you" [At-Tawba: 47], and the like. Here "naba'a" takes two objects, like "arrafa," as in His words: "Who informed you of this?" The second object is "min akhbarikum," meaning a clause "min akhbarikum." According to the opinion of Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash, "min" is superfluous, meaning "akhbarakum" (your news). It has also been said: "naba'a" means "a'lama" (to inform), which takes three objects, and the third is omitted for brevity, the context indicating it: "min akhbarikum kadhiban aw nahwahu" (from your news, [that which is] false or the like).

"Wa-sayara Allah" is a threat, meaning: He will see it in its existence, so that recompense will be given for it, if good then good, and if evil then evil. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Wa-sayara Allah 'amalakum" [And Allah will see your deeds]: will you repent or will you remain upon disbelief? "Thumma turaddun" [then you will be returned] refers to resurrection from the graves, and the informing about their deeds is a metaphor for requiting them for them. Ibn 'Isa said: "Wa-sayara" is because He has made it a matter of manifestation as if it were seen, and then He recompenses for it. It has also been said: they used to show the Messenger, when presenting their excuses, love and compassion, so it was said: "And Allah will see your deeds": will they remain upon that or not? The unseen and the witnessed are two comprehensive categories of a servant's deeds, and there is no deed outside of them. This indicates that He is aware of their inner thoughts just as He is aware of their outward conduct, with no difference in that regard before Him.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verses 95–99:

﴿They will swear to you by Allah when you return to them, so that you may turn away from them. So turn away from them. Indeed, they are impure (rijs), and their refuge is Hell, as recompense for what they used to earn.﴾: When he mentioned that they would offer excuses, he informed that they would confirm that false excuse with oaths. The reason for the oaths is their request that the believers turn away from them, so that they would not blame or reproach them. ﴿So turn away from them﴾, meaning: respond to their request. He gave the reason for turning away from them: they are impure (rijs), meaning they are loathsome because of the hypocrisy they harbour, so keeping away from them and avoiding them is obligatory, as He said: ﴿It is an impurity from the work of Satan, so avoid it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 90]. Whoever is an impurity, reproach does not benefit him, and impurity cannot be purified. It is also possible that the reason for the oaths is their fear that the believers would turn away from them, not come near them, and not show them affection. So Allah, exalted is He, commanded turning away from them and not turning toward them, and He explained the cause of that by their impurity, and that the end of their affair is the Fire. Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿So turn away from them﴾ means: do not speak to them. And it is related in a report that when the Prophet (ﷺ) returned from Tabuk, he said: "Do not sit with them, and do not speak to them."

It has been said: this verse is among the first that was revealed concerning the hypocrites in the expedition of Tabuk. Some of the hypocrites had made excuses and asked his permission to remain behind before his march, and he granted it, so they stayed behind. One of them said: "It is nothing but a fat morsel for the first eater." When the Messenger went out, the Qur'an was revealed concerning them. A man from the people returned and said to the hypocrites in a gathering of theirs: "A Qur'an has been revealed about you." They said to him: "And what is that?" He said: "I do not remember, except that I heard your description in it as impure." Makhshi said to them: "I would wish to be flogged a hundred times and not be with you." So he went out until he caught up with the Messenger (ﷺ), who said to him: "What brought you?" He said: "The face of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) being struck by the wind while I am under shelter." It was related that he was among those who repented.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: ﴿So turn away from them﴾ is a command to rebuke them and punish them by turning away and branding them with hypocrisy. This is in general terms, not with a clear specification from Allah or from His Messenger; rather, each one of them had a wide field for speech. His saying (rijs) means: filth and defilement. This description is sufficient as a worldly stopping point, and then He turned to the stopping point of the Hereafter. From the hadith of Ka'b ibn Malik: they came making excuses and swearing oaths when he (ﷺ) arrived at Madinah, and they were some eighty-odd men. He accepted their outward profession, gave them the pledge, asked forgiveness for them, and left their inner states to Allah.

﴿They swear to you so that you may be pleased with them. But if you are pleased with them, indeed Allah is not pleased with the defiantly disobedient people (al-qawm al-fasiqin).﴾: Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy, who swore by Allah, besides whom there is no god, that he would never lag behind him after this, (p. 90) and Ibn Abi Sarh swore: "We will certainly be with him against his enemy." And he asked the Messenger to be pleased with him, so it was revealed. Here the object of the oath (al-mahluf bihi) is omitted, while in His saying ﴿They swear by Allah﴾ it is mentioned, like His saying: ﴿when they swore that they would surely cut off its fruit﴾ [al-Qalam: 17], and His saying: "and they swore by Allah." So there is no difference between its omission and its mention in establishing it as an oath. Their purpose in the oath was the pleasure of the Messenger and the believers, for their benefit in this world, not that their aim was the countenance of Allah, exalted is He. What is meant: these are false oaths and fabricated excuses with no reality behind them.

In the verse before it, when He mentioned their oath for the purpose of turning away, the command to turn away came explicitly, because turning away is among the matters that appear to people. Here He mentioned the oath for the purpose of pleasure, so He made the prohibition against being pleased appear in the form of a conditional, because pleasure is among the inward matters that are hidden. It came in the manner of one who is uncertain about it, and He made its answer the negation of Allah's pleasure with them. So the believers' pleasure with them became the most remote thing from occurring, because it is known about them that they do not become pleased with one with whom Allah is not pleased. He specified the attribute that necessitates the negation of pleasure, which is defiant disobedience (fisq). The wording came in general terms, so it may be understood as specific, as if it were said: "Indeed Allah is not pleased with them." And it may remain general, so they are included in it and are more deserving of entry, since when a general statement is revealed concerning a specific cause, that cause cannot be removed from the generality by specification or otherwise.

﴿The Bedouins (al-a'rab) are more severe in disbelief and hypocrisy, and more likely not to know the limits of what Allah has sent down to His Messenger. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾: It was revealed concerning Bedouins from Asad, Tamim, and Ghatafan, and from the Bedouins of the people of Madinah's surroundings, meaning: they are more severe in disbelief than the settled people (ahl al-hadar). When disbelief relates to the heart alone, the estimate is: "the most intense of the causes of disbelief." When actions of the limbs enter into it, severity is realised in it. They were more severe in disbelief and hypocrisy because of their wildness, the dominance of the hot wind over them, which increases their arrogance, pride, boastfulness, recklessness, and their upbringing without a guide, without a teacher, and without a restraint, so they grew up as they wished, because of their distance from witnessing scholars, from knowing the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, and because of their distance from the place of the descent of revelation. They were more outspoken in disbelief and hypocrisy than the hypocrites of Madinah, since those were overcome by fear of the believers, so their disbelief was secret, and they did not display it except by allusion.

(And more likely), meaning: more deserving (ahaqq), (not to know), meaning: that they should not know. The limits (hudud) here are the obligations (fara'id). It has been said: the threat against opposing the Messenger and lagging behind from jihad. It has been said: the measures of obligations and rulings. Qatadah said: they have the least knowledge of the Sunan. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Coarseness and hardness are in the faddadin." (And Allah is All-Knowing) knows every individual among the people of the wabar and the madar, (All-Wise) in what He bestows on their evildoer and their doer of good, of reward and punishment.

﴿Among the Bedouins are those who consider what they spend a burden (maghram), and they wait for misfortunes to befall you. Upon them is the circle of evil. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾: It was revealed concerning the Bedouins of Asad, Ghatafan, and Tamim, who used to consider what was taken from them as sadaqat (obligatory alms). It has been said: it refers to zakat (obligatory almsgiving), and for this reason some of them said: "It is nothing but a jizyah (poll tax), or something close to a jizyah." It has also been said: it is every expenditure that their souls do not desire, while it is legally required, which is what a man spends though it is not obligatory upon him, because he spends only out of dissimulation before the Muslims and for show, not for the countenance of Allah, exalted is He, and seeking reward with Him. Maghram: imposing what is not obligatory. It has been said: maghram means a penalty and a loss, which is the view of Ibn Qutaybah, and close to the previous one. Ibn Faris said: maghram is what binds its companions, and gharam is the binding debt, and from it comes gharim (creditor) because of its persistence and insistence. Tarabbus means waiting. Dawa'ir (circles) are the calamities from which there is no escape, encompassing a person as a circle encompasses. It has been said: "waiting for the circles" here means the death of the Messenger (ﷺ) and the spread of polytheism. A poet said:

"Wait for her the vicissitudes of fate, perhaps she will one day be divorced, or her husband will die."

Waiting for the circles is so that they may be rid of the exhaustion of spending. His saying ﴿upon them is the circle of evil﴾ is an intervening supplication, a supplication against them by attributing to them what He reported about them, like His saying: ﴿And the Jews say: "Allah's hand is chained." Their own hands are chained﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64]. Supplication from Allah means bringing about the thing; (p. 91) because He, exalted is He, does not supplicate against His creatures while they are in His grip. Al-Karmani said: upon them revolve the calamities and wars which they anticipate against the Muslims, and here is a promise to the Muslims and an announcement. It has been said: it is a supplication, meaning: say "upon them is the circle of evil," that is, the disliked thing. The reality of the circle is what the days revolve with. It has been said: it is what the sphere revolves with in its course, and the circles are the reversal of blessing into its opposite. In al-Hujjah: the circle may be a verbal noun like "the consequence," and it may be an attribute. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read (al-saw') here. In Surah al-Fath the second occurrence is with a damma, and the rest of the seven read with a fatha, so fatha is the verbal noun. Al-Farra' said: I did evil to him (sau'tuhu saw'an wa masa'atan wa sawa'iyatan), and the damma form is the noun, which is evil and punishment, while the fatha form is the disparagement of the circle, and it is from the construction of the qualified being attributed to its qualifier: the circle is described by the verbal noun, just as they say "a man of evil" (raj ul-saw') in contrast to "a man of truth" (raj ul-sidq), meaning in this respect corruption, not truthfulness of speech. And from it: ﴿Your father was not a man of evil﴾ [Maryam: 28], meaning a corrupt man. Al-Mubarrad said: al-saw' with a fatha is badness, and it is not permissible to use a damma on the sin in "raj ul-saw'," as most of them said. It has been reported with a damma, and a poet said:

"You were like the liar of evil (kadhib al-su') when he saw blood on his companion one day and attributed it to the blood."

And Allah is All-Hearing of their words, All-Knowing of their intentions.

﴿Among the Bedouins are those who believe in Allah and the Last Day, and who take what they spend as means of nearness (qurubat) to Allah and as the prayers of the Messenger. Indeed, it is a means of nearness for them. Allah will admit them into His mercy. Indeed, Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.﴾: It was revealed concerning the Banu Muqarrin of Muzaynah, as Mujahid said. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mughaffal ibn Muqarrin said: We were ten sons of Muqarrin, and ﴿Among the Bedouins are those who believe﴾ was revealed, meaning six or seven brothers, according to the disagreement over their number and their sons. Al-Dahhak said: it was revealed concerning 'Abdullah dhu al-Najadayn and his kin. Al-Kalbi said: it was revealed concerning Aslam, Ghifar, and Juhaynah.

When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned ﴿those who consider what they spend a burden﴾, He mentioned its counterpart, which is those who consider what they spend a gain (maghnam). He mentioned here the root upon which the spending of wealth in acts of nearness is based, which is faith in Allah and the Last Day, since the reward of what is spent appears in its lasting form only in the Hereafter. In the account of those (the previous group), He suffices with mentioning the result of disbelief and lack of faith, which is their taking what they spend as a burden and their waiting for the circles against the believers. The better view is to generalise the acts of nearness, including jihad and charity. The meaning is: they take it as a means of connection with Allah and as the supplications of the Messenger. He used to supplicate for those who gave charity with good and blessing, and ask forgiveness for them, as in his saying: "O Allah, send prayers upon the family of Abi Awfa." And Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿and pray for them﴾. The apparent reading is that ("and the prayers of the Messenger") is conjoined to ("nearness"). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is possible that ﴿and the prayers of the Messenger﴾ is conjoined to ("what they spend"), meaning: and they take, through righteous deeds, the prayers of the Messenger as nearness. Ibn 'Abbas said: the prayers of the Messenger are his asking forgiveness for them. Qatadah said: his supplications for good and blessing; he called them prayers following the linguistic literal meaning, or because supplication is in them. When Ibn Abi Awfa came with his charity, he (ﷺ) said: "May Allah reward you for what you have given, and make it a purification for you."

The pronoun in ("indeed it") is said to refer to the prayers. It has been said: it refers to the expenditures. The precise statement of this view is that it refers to what has the same meaning: the meaning is "a means of nearness for them with Allah." This is a testimony from Allah to the giver of charity that what he believed is correct, that his spending is acts of nearness and prayers, and a confirmation of his hope by way of a new sentence, with the particle of alerting, which is "alā" (indeed), and the particle of emphasis, which is "inna" (indeed). Al-Zamakhshari said: what the sin (sa-) contains of the realisation of the promise, and how indicative this statement is of Allah's pleasure with those who give charity, and that charity from Him, exalted is He, has a place when the intention of its owner is pure. End. The discussion with him about his claim that the sin (sa-) indicates the certainty of the promise has already been mentioned.

Warsh read (qurbah) with a damma on the ra', and the rest of the seven with a sukun, and both are dialects. They did not differ over (qurubat) that it is with a damma. If it is the plural of qurbah, then the damma comes in accordance with the original form; and if it is the plural of qurbah with a sukun, then the damma comes by assimilation to what precedes it, as they said: zulumat as the plural of zulmah.

What is meant: these are false oaths and fabricated excuses with no reality behind them.

Here He mentioned the oath for the purpose of pleasure, so He made the prohibition against being pleased appear in the form of a conditional, because pleasure is among the inward matters that are hidden. It came in the manner of one who is uncertain about it, and He made its answer the negation of Allah's pleasure with them. So the believers' pleasure with them became the most remote thing from occurring, because it is known about them that they do not become pleased with one with whom Allah is not pleased. He specified the attribute that necessitates the negation of pleasure, which is defiant disobedience (fisq). The wording came in general terms, so it may be understood as specific, as if it were said: "Indeed Allah is not pleased with them." And it may remain general, so they are included in it and are more deserving of entry, since when a general statement is revealed concerning a specific cause, that cause cannot be removed from the generality by specification or otherwise.

It has been said: the threat against opposing the Messenger and lagging behind from jihad. It has been said: the measures of obligations and rulings. **Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 9, verses 100–101:**

﴿The foremost, the first of the Emigrants and the Helpers, and those who followed them in goodness: Allah is well pleased with them, and they are well pleased with Him. He has prepared for them gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the supreme triumph.﴾ [p. 92] Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Ibn al-Musayyib, Ibn Sirin and Qatadah said: "The foremost, the first" are those who prayed facing both qiblahs. 'Ata' said: those who witnessed Badr. He said: the qiblah was changed two months before Badr. Al-Sha'bi said: those who attended the Pledge of al-Ridwan, the Pledge of al-Hudaybiyah, between the two emigrations. As for those who interpret "the foremost" as a single individual, such as Abu Bakr, or 'Ali, or Zayd ibn Harithah, or Khadijah bint Khuwaylid, their view is far from the wording of the plural, and it only fits the first to accept Islam. The apparent meaning is that the precedence is in Islam and faith. Ibn Bahr said: they are the foremost to death or to martyrdom among the Emigrants and the Helpers; they preceded others to the reward of Allah and His good recompense. The phrase ﴿of the Emigrants and the Helpers﴾ means: "and of the Helpers." They are the people of the first Pledge of al-'Aqabah, who were seven men, and the people of the second 'Aqabah, who were seventy, and those who believed when Abu Zurarah Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr came to them and taught them the Qur'an. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: If someone were to say that "the foremost, the first" are all who emigrated until the emigration ended, that would be a view the wording requires, and "min" [of] would be for explaining the category.

﴿And those who followed them in goodness﴾ are the rest of the Companions, and the Successors (al-tabi'un) and the rest of the Ummah enter this wording, but on condition of goodness. This title, which is the Successors, has come to apply to whoever saw the Prophet ﷺ. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: "My view, which is correct, is that they are the foremost in emigration and in support, because the expression 'the foremost' is general, and describing them as 'the Emigrants and the Helpers' requires directing it to what they are characterized by, namely emigration and support. Precedence in emigration is a great quality, since it is hard on the soul and contrary to natural inclination; whoever comes first becomes an example for others in it. Likewise, precedence in support: they attained a great station." End of the summary.

When Allah the Exalted had explained the virtues of the faithful, charitable Bedouin Arabs and what He had prepared for them of delight, He explained the state of these foremost ones and what He had prepared for them. How vast is the difference between the two preparations and the two praises! There He said: ﴿Behold, it is indeed a means of nearness for them﴾ [At-Tawbah 9:99], and here: ﴿Allah is well pleased with them﴾. There: ﴿Allah will admit them into His mercy﴾ [At-Tawbah 9:99], and here: ﴿He has prepared for them gardens﴾. There He concluded: ﴿Indeed Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ [At-Tawbah 9:102], and here: ﴿That is the supreme triumph﴾.

'Umar ibn al-Khattab, al-Hasan, Qatadah, 'Isa al-Kufi, Salam, Sa'id ibn Abi Sa'id, Talhah and Ya'qub read (wal-ansaru) with the letter ra' in the nominative case, as a conjunction with (wal-sabiqun), so that all the Helpers are included in this wording. In the reading of the majority, which is the genitive, they become two categories: a foremost first group and a non-first group. The predicate about whom approval is given is "those who preceded them." The pronoun in ﴿those who followed them﴾ in both readings refers to the Emigrants and the Helpers. The apparent view is that (al-sabiqun) is the subject and (radiya Allah) is the predicate. They also allowed that the predicate could be (al-awwalun), meaning: they are the first of the Emigrants. They also allowed that in His saying (wal-sabiqun) it could be conjoined to His saying (man yu'minu), meaning: and among them are the foremost. They also allowed that (wal-ansar) could be a subject, and in the reading with the nominative its predicate would be (radiya Allah 'anhum), and this on two grounds: (wal-sabiqun) being a conjunction, and the predicate not being (radiya Allah). These are contrived grammatical analyses (a'arib) that do not suit the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of the Qur'an.

Ibn Kathir read (min tahtiha) with the particle "min" retained, and it is attested in the Meccan codices. The rest of the seven readers omitted it, following what was written in their codices. It is reported from 'Umar that he used to read ﴿and those who followed them in goodness﴾ without the conjunction wa, as a qualifier of the Helpers, until Zayd ibn Thabit said to him: "It is with the wa." He said: "Bring me Ubayy." Ubayy said: "The confirmation of that is in the Book of Allah: at the beginning of al-Jumu'ah, ﴿and others among them who have not yet joined them﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 62:3], and in the middle of al-Hashr: ﴿and those who came after them﴾ [al-Hashr 59:10], and at the end of al-Anfal: (and those who believed afterward)." It is also narrated that he heard a man reading it with the wa, and said: "Who taught you?" He said: "Ubayy." He summoned him and said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ taught it to me." And for this reason 'Umar said: "I used to think we had reached a station that no one after us would reach."

﴿And among those around you of the Bedouin are hypocrites, and among the people of Madinah are those who have become adept at hypocrisy. You do not know them; We know them. We will punish them twice; then they will be returned to a great punishment.﴾ [p. 93] When he had explained the situation of the hypocrites of Madinah, then the situation of the hypocrites among the Bedouin, then he explained that among the Bedouin there is one who is sincere and righteous, then he identified who the leaders of the believers are, he mentioned in this verse that there are hypocrites around you among the Bedouin, and among the people of Madinah whom you do not know, meaning: you do not know their persons, or you do not know them to be hypocrites. The meaning of (around you) is: around your town, which is Madinah. Those who were around Madinah were Juhaynah, Aslam, Ashja', Ghifar, Muzaynah, 'Usayyah, Lihyan, and others who bordered Madinah. (And among the people of Madinah) may be a conjunction of single terms, so that it is conjoined to "min" in His saying (wa-mimman), and the two genitive phrases share the subject which is (munafiqun). Then (marradu) is a resumptive statement, informing that they are well practiced in hypocrisy. It is remote for (marradu) to be a qualifier of the subject (munafiqun), because of the separation between the qualifier and the qualified by a conjunction on (wa-mimman hawlakum), making it like: "in the house is Zayd, and in the palace the intelligent one." Al-Zamakhshari allowed it, following al-Zajjaj. It may also be a conjunction of sentences, with an omitted qualified noun as subject, meaning: "and among the people of Madinah are people who have become adept," or "hypocrites who have become adept." Al-Zamakhshari said: "Like his saying: 'I am the son of Jala.'" End. If he means it in general, the qualified noun is omitted; if he means it in its specific character, it is not good, because omitting the qualified noun with "min" and placing its qualifier in its place, which is in the sense of a noun, is analogical especially in the case of distribution, as in the saying: "Among us is one who departed, and among us one who stayed." *He shoots with two hands, one of the best of mankind at shooting*

meaning: with the two hands of a man. Likewise "I am the son of Jala," its sense being: "I am the son of a man who uncovered (jala) matters and made them clear." The explanation of (marradu) has already been given in His saying: ﴿a rebellious devil, cursed by Allah﴾. Here Ibn 'Abbas said: (marradu) means they became accustomed and persisted. Abu 'Ubaydah said: they became stubborn, from the saying "tamarrada." Ibn Zayd said: they persisted in it and did not repent. (You do not know them): meaning, until We inform you about them, or you do not know the outcome of their affair, as related by Ibn al-Jawzi. Or you do not know them as hypocrites, because hypocrisy is specific to the heart. The word "hypocrites" has been mentioned before, which indicates the omitted object, so it governs two objects, as al-Karmani said. Al-Zamakhshari said: They conceal it from you despite your acuteness, your nobility, and the truth of your insight, because of their great caution about anything that might cast doubt on their affair. Al-Tabari reported from Qatadah on His saying: ﴿You do not know them; We know them﴾, he said: "Then what about people who burden themselves with knowing the people's affairs: so-and-so is in Paradise, so-and-so is in Hell? The Prophet of Allah Shu'ayb said: ﴿The remainder from Allah is better for you, if you are believers. And I am not a watcher over you﴾ [Hud 11:86]. And Allah the Exalted said to His Prophet: ﴿You do not know them; We know them﴾." End. If Qatadah had lived to this age, which is the century of eight hundred, and had heard what those attributed to the Sufis have invented of claims and of showy speech that does not refer back to the Book of Allah or the Sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ, and of audacity in false reports about the unseen, he would have been astonished at it. I did not think that something like what Qatadah related would occur in that age, given its closeness to the Companions and the abundance of good, but the devils among mankind are unlikely to be free of them in any era.

(We know them): Al-Zamakhshari said: We have insight into their secret, because they conceal disbelief deep in the blackness of their hearts, and show you outwardly what appears to be the sincere believers, so that you have no doubt about their faith. That is because they became well practiced in hypocrisy and its varieties, and they have the highest hand in it. End. In His saying (We know them) there is a threat, and it is followed by His saying: (We will punish them twice). The apparent intention is the dual, though it may be that the dual is not meant as a count of two, but rather as a multiplicity, like His saying: ﴿Then return the gaze twice﴾ [al-Mulk 67:4], meaning: a glance after a glance. Likewise the meaning here is: We will punish them time after time. If the dual is intended, most people hold that the second punishment is the punishment of the grave. It is reported in this interpretation that on a Friday of Badr the Prophet, peace be upon him, delivered a sermon, naming the hypocrites openly and declaring them, and said: "Go out, O so-and-so, from the mosque, for you are a hypocrite. 'Umar saw them leaving the mosque while he was coming to the Friday prayer, and thought the people had dispersed and that the Friday prayer had passed him, so he hid from them out of shame. Then he reached the mosque and saw that the prayer had not been concluded, and understood the matter. So it is not a case of expelling sinners; rather, these are disbelievers in his view, even if they showed Islam.

Qatadah and others said: the first punishment consists of ailments and diseases which Allah informed His Prophet would strike them. It is reported that he confided to Hudhayfah about twelve of them and said: "Six of them will be sufficed by the boil, a flame of the fire of Hell that seizes the shoulder of one of them until it reaches his chest, and six will die a natural death." Ibn 'Abbas also said: it is their humiliation through the enforcement of the legal punishments of the Shari'ah upon them, while they disliked it. Ibn Ishaq said: it is their grief over the manifestation of Islam and the elevation of its word. It was also said: it is the angels striking their faces and backs at the taking of their souls. Al-Hasan said: the first is what is taken from their wealth by force, and the second is the jihad they are commanded to undertake under compulsion, because they regard that as a punishment. Ibn Zayd said: the two times are the punishments of this world through their wealth and children, each kind being a punishment, so there are two; and he recited: ﴿So do not let their wealth and their children impress you﴾ [at-Tawbah 9:55], and the verse. It was also said: the burning of the mosque of harm (masjid al-dirar) is one, and the other is their burning in the fire of Hell. There is no disagreement that His saying (to a great punishment) is the punishment of the Hereafter. In the codex of Anas, the reading is (sa-yu'adhdhibuhum) with the letter ya', and 'Ayyash, from Abu 'Amr, read the ya' with a sukun.

The apparent meaning is that the precedence is in Islam and faith. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: If someone were to say that "the foremost, the first" are all who emigrated until the emigration ended, that would be a view the wording requires, and "min" [of] would be for explaining the category.

When Allah the Exalted had explained the virtues of the faithful, charitable Bedouin Arabs and what He had prepared for them of delight, He explained the state of these foremost ones and what He had prepared for them. Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verses 102–106 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And others who have acknowledged their sins: they mixed a righteous deed with another that was evil. Perhaps Allah will accept their repentance. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ It was revealed concerning ten men who stayed behind from the expedition to Tabuk. When the Messenger (ﷺ) drew near to Madinah, they tied up seven of them. It is said that they were eight, among them Kardam, Mirdas, Abu Qays, and Abu Lubaba. It is also said that they were seven. It is said that they were six, and three of them tied themselves to the pillars of the mosque, among them Abu Lubaba. It is said that they were five. It is said that they were three: Abu Lubaba ibn Abd al-Mundhir, Aws ibn Tha'laba, and Wadi'a ibn Khidham al-Ansari. It is also said that it was revealed concerning Abu Lubaba alone. But this is unlikely from the wording "and others" (wa-akharun), since it is plural. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) arrived, he entered the mosque and prayed two rak'ahs in it, as was his custom whenever he returned from a journey. He saw them tied up and asked about them. They mentioned that they had sworn not to free themselves until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was the one who freed them. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "And I swear that I will not free them until I am commanded concerning them. They turned away from me and stayed behind from the campaign with the Muslims." Then it was revealed, and he released them and excused them. Mujahid said: It was revealed concerning Abu Lubaba regarding his affair with the Banu Qurayza, when they consulted him about coming down under the judgment of Allah and His Messenger. He gestured to them toward his throat, meaning that the Messenger (ﷺ) would slaughter them if they came down. When he was exposed, he repented and regretted it, and he bound himself to a pillar in the mosque, and swore that he would neither eat nor drink until Allah pardoned him or he died. He remained so until Allah pardoned him.

Al-i'tiraf (acknowledgment) is the affirmation of a sin. (A righteous deed) means repentance and regret. (And another evil) (p. 95) means: their staying behind from this campaign, as al-Tabari said; or going out to jihad before this and staying behind from this one, as al-Hasan and others said; or repentance and sin, as al-Kalbi said. The conjoining of one of the two with the other is evidence that each of them is mixed and is mixed with the other, like your saying: "I mixed the water and the milk," which is different from "I mixed the water with the milk," where there is only the meaning that the water was mixed into the milk. Al-Zamakhshari stated this meaning: Whenever you mix one thing with another, it is true of each of them that it is mixed and that it is mixed with (the other), in terms of the signification of mixing, since it is a relational matter. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also possible that it is from their saying: "I sold the sheep for a sheep and a dirham," meaning a sheep for a dirham.

Acknowledgment of sin is a sign of repentance, which is why it is said: "Perhaps Allah will accept their repentance." Ibn Abbas said: "Perhaps" (asa) from Allah is obligatory. End of quote. The word "perhaps" was used so that the believer would remain in a state of fear and hope, since the word "asa" expresses hope and apprehension. Thus repentance was presented in the form of this word. Then it was concluded with what indicates the acceptance of repentance, namely the attributes of forgiveness and mercy. Although this verse was revealed concerning specific people, it is general for the community until the Day of Resurrection. Abu Uthman said: In the Qur'an there is no verse more hopeful to me for this community than His saying: "And others who have acknowledged their sins."

In the hadith of the Night Journey and the Ascension, transmitted by al-Bayhaqi: those who mixed a righteous deed with another that was evil and then repented, the Messenger (ﷺ) saw them around Ibrahim, and there was something in their colors, and their colors were mixed after they bathed in three rivers, and they sat with their companions who had bright faces.

﴿Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them to grow, and pray for them. Indeed, your prayer is a comfort for them. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾ The address is to the Messenger (ﷺ), and the pronoun refers to "those who mixed." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, this is our wealth that kept us away from you, so give charity from it and purify us." He said: "I have not been commanded to take anything from your wealth." Then it was revealed. It is narrated that he took a third of their wealth, observing His saying: "Take from their wealth." What the interpreters' statements have most consistently attested, including Ibn Abbas and others, is that it concerns these ones who stayed behind. A group of jurists said: What is meant by this verse is the obligatory zakat. Then His saying, on this view, "from their wealth" applies to all wealth and people, a general term intended in a specific sense regarding wealth, since it excludes wealth on which there is no zakat, such as real estate and clothing, and from among those from whom it is taken, such as slaves. And "charity" (sadaqa) is unrestricted, so it is fulfilled by the least thing. Ibn Atiyya's characterization of it as mujmal (unspecified, requiring explanation) is not sound. In His saying "Take," there is evidence that the imam is the one who undertakes the collection of charities and oversees them. "From their wealth" is connected to "take," and "you purify them" and "you cause them to grow" are a hal (circumstantial clause) from the pronoun in "take," so the subject is the pronoun in "take." They permitted that "from their wealth" be in the position of a hal, because if it were postponed it would be a sifa (qualifier), and since it was placed first it is a hal. They also permitted that "you purify them" be a sifa, or a resumptive clause (isti'naf), and that the pronoun in "you purify them" refer back to "charity."
