﴿Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them to grow, and pray for them. Indeed, your prayer is a comfort for them. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾ The address is to the Messenger (ﷺ), and the pronoun refers to "those who mixed." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, this is our wealth that kept us away from you, so give charity from it and purify us." He said: "I have not been commanded to take anything from your wealth." Then it was revealed. It is narrated that he took a third of their wealth, observing His saying: "Take from their wealth." What the interpreters' statements have most consistently attested, including Ibn Abbas and others, is that it concerns these ones who stayed behind. A group of jurists said: What is meant by this verse is the obligatory zakat. Then His saying, on this view, "from their wealth" applies to all wealth and people, a general term intended in a specific sense regarding wealth, since it excludes wealth on which there is no zakat, such as real estate and clothing, and from among those from whom it is taken, such as slaves. And "charity" (sadaqa) is unrestricted, so it is fulfilled by the least thing. Ibn Atiyya's characterization of it as mujmal (unspecified, requiring explanation) is not sound. In His saying "Take," there is evidence that the imam is the one who undertakes the collection of charities and oversees them. "From their wealth" is connected to "take," and "you purify them" and "you cause them to grow" are a hal (circumstantial clause) from the pronoun in "take," so the subject is the pronoun in "take." They permitted that "from their wealth" be in the position of a hal, because if it were postponed it would be a sifa (qualifier), and since it was placed first it is a hal. They also permitted that "you purify them" be a sifa, or a resumptive clause (isti'naf), and that the pronoun in "you purify them" refer back to "charity." But this is unlikely because of the conjunction of "and you cause them to grow," so that the two pronouns differ. As for what Makki reported, that "you purify them" is a sifa of "charity" and "you cause them to grow" is a hal from the subject of "take," it has been rejected on the ground that the waw is for conjunction, so the sense would be: a charity that purifies and a growing by it, and this is corrupt in meaning; but if it were without the waw it would be permissible. End of quote. It is valid on the assumption of an omitted subject, with the waw for the hal, meaning: "while you cause them to grow." But this analysis is weak because such a construction is rare in the speech of the Arabs. Tazkiya is an intensification of purification and an addition to it, or it means growth and blessing in the wealth. Al-Hasan read: tuṭahhiruhum, from atbara, and iṭṭahhara, and tahhara for the transitive form of tahura (to be pure). "And pray for them": that is, invoke for them, or ask forgiveness for them, or pray over them when they die; these are the opinions. The meaning of "comfort" (sakan) is reassurance for them that Allah has accepted their charity, as Ibn Abbas said; or mercy for them, as he also said; or nearness, as he also said; or an increase of dignity for them, as Qatada said; or steadying of their hearts, as Abu Ubayda said; or security for them. He said:

"O neighbor of the tribe, if you are not a comfort (sakan) to me, since no one among the neighbors has given me rest."

These opinions are close in meaning. Abu Abd Allah al-Razi said: It was only a comfort for them because his spirit (ﷺ) was a strong, luminous, pure spirit, so when he prayed for them and mentioned them with good, effects from his spiritual strength stirred upon (p. 96) their spirits, and by this cause their spirits were illuminated, their inner selves were purified, and they passed from darkness to light and from the corporeal to the spiritual. Shaykh Jamal al-Din Abu Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Sulayman, known as Ibn al-Naqib, said in his book al-Tahrir wa-al-Tahbir: al-Razi's statement is a philosophical statement in which he alludes to the idea that the powers of the souls are influential and efficacious, and that is not permissible according to the approach of the people of tafsir. End of quote. Al-Hasan and Qatada said, concerning these acknowledging ones from whom charity was taken: they are other than the three who were left behind. The Two Brothers (Ibn Kathir? no; ʿĀṣim's transmitters and Hafs) read: "inna salataka" here, and in Hud "salataka" in the singular, while the rest of the seven read it in the plural. "And Allah is All-Hearing" of their acknowledgment, "All-Knowing" of their regret and their repentance.

﴿Did they not know that Allah is He who accepts repentance from His servants and takes charities, and that Allah is the Accepter of Repentance, the Merciful?﴾ Those among the stayers-behind who had not repented said: These ones were with us yesterday, not spoken to or sat with, so it was revealed. In the codex of Ubayy, and in a reading of al-Hasan with a variant from him, it reads: "Did you not know" with the ta' as an address, so it is possible that it is an address to the stayers-behind who said: "What is this special status by which these people are singled out?" It is also possible that it means: say to them, O Muhammad; and that it is an address by way of iltifat (shift of address) without an implied "say," and that its intended referents are the repentant, as in the reading of the majority with the ya'. It is a specification and an affirmation that it is within Allah's nature to accept the repentance of whoever repents, as if it were said: Did they not know, before they were turned to and their charities were accepted, that He, exalted is He, accepts sincere repentance and accepts charities whose intention is purely for Allah? It has been said: The reason for the specification by "He" (huwa) is that accepting repentance and taking charities belong to Allah alone and not to other than Him, so intend Him and direct them to Him. Al-Zajjaj said: Taking charities means accepting them, and traditions have come in which acceptance is expressed figuratively, that charity falls into the hand of Allah, exalted is He, before it falls into the hand of the beggar, and that charity may be the size of a morsel, and Allah takes it in His right hand and makes it grow until it is like a mountain. Ibn Atiyya said: The meaning is that He commands it and legislates it, as you say: "The sultan took such-and-such from the people," meaning he compelled them to pay it. "'An" (from) is in the sense of "min" (from), and these two often serve in the same place. You say: "There is no charity except from (an) wealth and from (min) wealth," and "So-and-so did that out of (min) his own accord and out of (an) his own gaze." End of quote. It has also been said: the word "min" and the word "an" are close in meaning, except that "an" conveys distance. So when one says: "He sat to the right (an yamin) of the commander," it conveys that he sat on that side, but with a kind of distance. So it conveys that the penitent must believe of himself that he is far from Allah's acceptance of his repentance because of that sin, so that there arises in him the brokenness of a servant whom his master has expelled and whose distance from his presence is established. Thus the word "an" serves as an alert that this meaning must be present in the penitent. End of quote. What appears from the basic meaning of "an" is that it indicates passing beyond. If you say: "I took knowledge from (an) Zayd," its meaning is that it passed over to you; if you say: "from (min) Zayd," it indicates the starting point, that your taking began from Zayd. "An" is more eloquent because the transfer is evident with it, and it is not as evident with "min." It seems that when their repentance passed beyond them to Allah, He, exalted is He, was described as the One who turns in forgiveness toward them. Do you not see His saying: "And that Allah is the Accepter of Repentance, the Merciful," so each of the two is described with repentance, even though the directions of the relation differ. Do you not see what has been transmitted: "Whoever draws near to Me by a span, I draw near to him by a cubit; whoever draws near to Me by a cubit, I draw near to him by a fathom; and whoever comes to Me walking, I come to him running."

﴿And say: Act, and Allah will see your deed, and His Messenger and the believers, and you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He will inform you of what you used to do.﴾ It is an imperative form that contains a warning. "Those who excuse themselves," the penitent among the stayers-behind, are the ones addressed. It is said: they are the excusers who did not repent. It is said: they are the believers and the hypocrites. "Then Allah will see" to the end: its explanation has already been given for a similar expression. If the pronoun refers to the excusing ones who mixed their deeds and repented, which is the apparent meaning, then they are presented by His saying "Then Allah will see your deed" in the manner of presenting the hypocrites to whom it was said: "Do not make excuses; we will not believe you. Allah has already informed us of your news, and Allah will see your deed" [al-Tawba 9:94], and so on, as a diminishing of their state and a deterrence from what they fell into of staying behind from the Messenger, and that even if they repent, they are not like those who strove with him with their wealth and their selves, who do not, out of their own selves, turn away from his self.

(p-97) ﴿And others are deferred to the command of Allah: either He will punish them or He will turn to them in forgiveness. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrimah, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Qatadah, and Ibn Ishaq said: it was revealed concerning the three who were left behind before their repentance was accepted: Hilal ibn Umayya al-Waqifi, Murarah ibn al-Rabiʿ al-ʿAmiri, and Kaʿb ibn Malik. It was also said: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites who refused to repent, together with their building of the Masjid al-Dirar (the mosque of harm). Al-Hasan, Talhah, Abu Jaʿfar, Ibn Nassah, al-Aʿraj, Nafiʿ, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs read (مُرْجَوْنَ) and (تُرْجِي) without hamzah. The rest of the seven read them with hamzah, and both are dialectal variants. (لِأمْرِ اللَّهِ) means: for His judgment. (إمّا يُعَذِّبُهم) means: if they persist and do not repent. (وإمّا يَتُوبُ عَلَيْهِمْ) means: if they repent. Al-Hasan said: they are a group of hypocrites whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ deferred from his presence. Al-Asamm said: it refers to the hypocrites whom Allah deferred, and He did not inform about them what He knew of them, and He warned them with this verse if they did not repent. The meaning for which "إمّا" is originally put is that one of two things, or among things, is the case; it follows from this that it may be for doubt or for something else. So here it is on its original usage, which is the common element present in all the meanings that they claimed it was placed for by way of shared usage (ishtirak). (وَاللَّهُ عَلِيمٌ) with what their affair will come to, (حَكِيمٌ) in what He does to them.

﴿And those who took a mosque for harm and disbelief and to cause division among the believers, and as a station for whoever had waged war against God and His Messenger before. They will surely swear, "We intended nothing but good," but God bears witness that they are liars.﴾ ﴿Do not ever stand in it. A mosque founded upon piety from the first day is more worthy that you stand in it. In it are men who love to purify themselves, and God loves those who purify themselves.﴾

When He mentioned the blameworthy ways of the categories of hypocrites, in their words and deeds, He mentioned that among them were those who went to extremes in evil, to the point that they built a gathering place for the hypocrites, where they could plot whatever evil they wished, and they called it a mosque.

When Amr ibn Awf built the mosque of Quba', they sent word to the Messenger (ﷺ), and he came, prayed in it, and invoked blessings for them. Their cousins, the Banu Ghanm ibn Awf and the Banu Salim ibn Awf, envied them. Abu Amr, the sinner (al-Fasiq), incited them to build their own, when he fled to Syria after the battle of Hunayn. He sent messages to them about building it, saying: "Build a mosque for me, for I am going to Caesar to bring an army of Romans to expel Muhammad and his companions." They built it beside the mosque of Quba'. The builders were twelve men from among the hypocrites: Khidham ibn Khalid, from whose house the mosque was taken out; Tha'laba ibn Hatib; Mu'attib ibn Qushayr; Harithat ibn Amir; his two sons Mujammi' and Zayd; Nabtal ibn al-Harith; Abbad ibn Hunayf; Nijad ibn Uthman; Wadi'a ibn Thabit; Abu Hanifa al-Azhar; Bahzaj ibn Amr; and a man from the Banu Dubay'a. They said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "We have built a mosque for the sick, for those in need, for rainy and cold nights, and we love for you to pray in it for us and invoke blessings for us with barakah." He (ﷺ) said: "I am on the verge of a journey and busy with affairs, but when we return, God willing, we will pray in it." Their imam was Mujammi' ibn Jariya, who was a young man, a reciter of the Qur'an, with a beautiful voice, and he was among those whose Islam was sound. Umar appointed him as imam of the mosque of Quba' after some discussion, then sent him to Kufa to teach them the Qur'an.

When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) returned from the expedition to Tabuk, he halted at Dhu Awan, a place between him and Medina at a distance of an hour's journey in the daytime. The Qur'an was revealed to him concerning the mosque of harm. He summoned Malik ibn al-Dukhshum, Ma'n, and Asim, the two sons of Adi. It was said that he sent Ammar ibn Yasir and Wahshi, the slayer of Hamza, to demolish and burn it. It was demolished and burned with fire on palm fronds, and it was made into a rubbish heap where carrion and refuse were thrown.

Ibn Juraij said: They prayed Friday, Saturday, and Sunday in it, and it collapsed on Monday and was not burned.

Nafi', Abu Ja'far, Shayba, and others, and Ibn Amir, recited "alladhina" (those who) without a waw, as it is in the codices of Medina and Syria. This may be a substitution (badal) for His words, "and others await God's command" (al-Tawba 9:106); or it may be the predicate of an inchoative, with the implied sense "they are those who"; or it may be the subject (mubtada'). Al-Kisa'i said the predicate is "do not ever stand in it." Ibn Atiyya said: it is possible with an implied element, either at the beginning of the verse or at its end, meaning "do not stand in their mosque." Al-Nahhas and al-Hawfi said the predicate is "their building will not cease to be a cause of doubt" (la yazal bunyanuhum). Al-Mahdawi said the predicate is omitted, meaning "they will be punished" or something similar.

The majority of reciters recited "wa-alladhina" (and those who) with waw, as a conjunction to "wa-akharun" (and others), meaning "and among them are those who took..." It may also be a subject whose predicate is the same as that of the form without waw, if it is parsed as a subject. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, what is the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of "wa-alladhina ittakhadhu"? I say: its position is accusative by way of specification (ikhtisas), like His words, "and those who establish prayer" (al-Nisa' 4:162). It was also said that it is a subject whose predicate is omitted, its meaning being "concerning those we have described, [it is] those who took..." like His words, "and the thief, male and female" (al-Ma'ida 5:38).

"Dirarah" (harm) is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), meaning: to harm their brothers, the people of the mosque of Quba', and out of enmity, and disbelief, and to strengthen hypocrisy, and to cause division among the believers, because they used to pray together in the mosque of Quba', and it was crowded with them. So they wanted to split away from it and to divide their word, since whoever passed by their mosque would be drawn to it, and that would lead to turning him away from faith. It may also be accusative as a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal). Abu al-Baqa' permitted it to be a second object of "ittakhadhu" (took), and "wa-irsadan" (and as a station) means "as a preparation." It was prepared for the one who warred against God and His Messenger, namely Abu Amir the monk. They prepared it for him so that he might pray in it and gain ascendancy over the Messenger of God (ﷺ). He had been a worshipper in the pre-Islamic period, and was therefore called "the monk." The Messenger (ﷺ) named him "the sinner" (al-Fasiq). He was a chief among his people, a peer and close associate of Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul. When God brought Islam, he became a hypocrite and never ceased openly displaying that. After a dispute, he said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "I find no people fighting you except that I will fight you alongside them." He continued fighting him and rallied the confederates (al-ahzab) against the Messenger of God (ﷺ). When God repelled them in their rage, he stayed in Mecca openly displaying enmity. When the conquest came, he fled to al-Ta'if. When the people of al-Ta'if embraced Islam, he fled to Syria, seeking Caesar's help against the Messenger. He died alone, expelled, and a stranger at Qinnasrin. He had invoked curses on the disbelievers, and the Messenger said "amin" to his supplication, and it came to pass as he had prayed. Concerning him, Ka'b ibn Malik said:

"God forbid, from a wicked deed like your effort against your tribe, O Abd Amr,
And you said that for me there is honor and renown, *** but you have followed faith with disbelief."

Al-A'mash recited "wa-irsadan li-alladhina harabu Allaha wa-rasulahu" (and as a station for those who warred against God and His Messenger). The apparent sense is that "min qablu" (before) is connected to "harab" (warred), meaning at the battle of the confederates and other occasions, that is, before the taking of this mosque. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, with what does His words "min qablu" connect? I say: with "ittakhadhu," meaning they took a mosque before these people became hypocrites by staying behind. End of quote. It is not apparent, and "al-khalif" is one who does not go out, that is, for the expedition.

[They said:] "We intended by building this mosque nothing but good, and expansion for us and for those who are weak or unable to travel to the mosque of Quba'." Al-Zamakhshari said: "We did not intend by building this mosque anything but the good quality, or for the purpose of good, which is prayer, the remembrance of God, and the widening of space for worshippers." End of quote. It seems that in his words "except the good quality" he made it the object, and in his words "or for the purpose of good" he made it a cause. It seems he gave "arada" (intend) the meaning of "qasada" (aim at), meaning: we aimed in building it at nothing but the purpose of good, which is prayer. This is a strained interpretation.

So God refuted them in their claim, and forbade him to stand in it, saying: "Do not ever stand in it." He forbade him because its builders had deceived the Messenger (ﷺ). The Messenger (ﷺ) was determined to go with them, and he called for his garment to rise, so the verse was revealed: "Do not ever stand in it." The expression "standing" is used to refer to prayer in it.

Ibn Abbas, a group of the Companions, and the Successors said: "The mosque founded upon piety" is the mosque of Quba', which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) founded, and he prayed in it during the days he stayed at Quba', namely Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday, and he went out on Friday. This is preferable, because the comparison between the mosque of Quba' and the mosque of harm is more fitting than that between the Messenger's mosque and the mosque of harm, and that suits the narrative. It is also reported from Zayd ibn Thabit, Abu Sa'id, and Ibn Umar that it is the Messenger's mosque. It is related that he (ﷺ) said, when asked about the mosque founded upon piety: "It is this mosque of mine." If this report is sound, no disagreement with it is possible. From here, "min" entered upon the time expression. The Kufans used this as evidence that "min" can denote the starting point (ibtida' al-ghayah) in time. The Basrans interpreted it by omitting a modifier, meaning "from the foundation of the first day," since in their view "min" does not govern time expressions. The verification of this is in the science of grammar. Ibn Atiyya said: "It seems good to me that one may dispense with an assumed element, and that 'min' governs the word 'awwal' (first), because it carries the sense of beginning, as if he said: from the beginning of the days." This that I have chosen has been related to me from some of the leading grammarians. End of quote. "Ahaqqu" (more worthy) means "haqiq" (deserving), and it is not a comparative elative (af'al al-tafdil), since the two mosques do not share in the right. The "ta'" in "an taquma" (that you stand) is a second-person address to the Messenger (ﷺ).

Abd Allah ibn Yazid recited "fihi" with a kasra on the ha', and the second "fihu" with a damma on the ha', combining the two dialects. The original form is the damma. The "fihi" serves to remove the assumption of emphasis, and it raises "rijal" (men). "Fayaqumu" (so he stands): "fihi" the first is in the position of the accusative, and the second is in the position of the nominative. They permitted, in "fihi rijal," that it be an attribute of "masjid" (mosque), or a circumstantial clause (hal), or a resumptive new sentence (isti'naf).

It is reported in a hadith that he said to them: "O assembly of the Ansar, I see that God has praised you for purity; what do you do?" They said: "O Messenger of God, we saw our Jewish neighbors purifying themselves with water, meaning cleaning after relieving themselves with water, so we did the same. When Islam came, we did not abandon it." He said: "Then do not abandon it." In some wordings of this hadith there is additional material and variation.

The scholars have differed over whether cleaning after relieving oneself should be done with stones or with water, which of the two is better. One group saw the combining of both as best. Ibn Habib held an unusual view, saying: one should not clean with stones where water is available. According to what is reported in this hadith, purification is an expression for using water to remove impurity during cleaning after relieving oneself. It was also said that it is general to all impurities. Al-Hasan said: "Purification" means purifying oneself from sins through repentance. It was also said: they loved to purify themselves through the fever which expiates sins, so they all had fever. In the Dala'il al-Nubuwwa of al-Bayhaqi: "The people of Quba' complained of fever, and he said: 'If you wish, I will pray to God to remove it from you, or if you wish, I will make it a purification for you.' They said: 'Rather, make it a purification for us.'" The meaning of their love for purification is that they prefer it and are eager for it, as a lover is eager for the thing he desires in many respects. God's love for them means that He does good to them, as a lover does with his beloved.

Ibn Misarrif and al-A'mash recited "yattahharu" (they purify themselves) with assimilation (idgham). Ibn Abi Talib recited "al-mutatahhirin" (those who purify themselves).

﴿And those who took a mosque for harm and disbelief and to cause division among the believers, and as a station for whoever had waged war against God and His Messenger before. They will surely swear, "We intended nothing but good," but God bears witness that they are liars.﴾ ﴿Do not ever stand in it. A mosque founded upon piety from the first day is more worthy that you stand in it. In it are men who love to purify themselves, and God loves those who purify themselves.﴾

When He mentioned the blameworthy ways of the categories of hypocrites, in their words and deeds, He mentioned that among them were those who went to extremes in evil, to the point that they built a gathering place for the hypocrites, where they could plot whatever evil they wished, and they called it a mosque.

It may also be accusative as a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal). Abu al-Baqa' permitted it to be a second object of "ittakhadhu" (took), and "wa-irsadan" (and as a station) means "as a preparation." It was prepared for the one who warred against God and His Messenger, namely Abu Amir the monk. They prepared it for him so that he might pray in it and gain ascendancy over the Messenger of God (ﷺ). He had been a worshipper in the pre-Islamic period, and was therefore called "the monk." The Messenger (ﷺ) named him "the sinner" (al-Fasiq). He was a chief among his people, a peer and close associate of Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul. When God brought Islam, he became a hypocrite and never ceased openly displaying that. After a dispute, he said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "I find no people fighting you except that I will fight you alongside them." He continued fighting him and rallied the confederates (al-ahzab) against the Messenger of God (ﷺ). When God repelled them in their rage, he stayed in Mecca openly displaying enmity. When the conquest came, he fled to al-Ta'if. When the people of al-Ta'if embraced Islam, he fled to Syria, seeking Caesar's help against the Messenger. He died alone, expelled, and a stranger at Qinnasrin. He had invoked curses on the disbelievers, and the Messenger said "amin" to his supplication, and it came to pass as he had prayed. Concerning him, Ka'b ibn Malik said:

"God forbid, from a wicked deed like your effort against your tribe, O Abd Amr,
And you said that for me there is honor and renown, *** but you have followed faith with disbelief."

Al-A'mash recited "wa-irsadan li-alladhina harabu Allaha wa-rasulahu" (and as a station for those who warred against God and His Messenger). The apparent sense is that "min qablu" (before) is connected to "harab" (warred), meaning at the battle of the confederates and other occasions, that is, before the taking of this mosque. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, with what does His words "min qablu" connect? I say: with "ittakhadhu," meaning they took a mosque before these people became hypocrites by staying behind. End of quote. It is not apparent, and "al-khalif" is one who does not go out, that is, for the expedition.

[They said:] "We intended by building this mosque nothing but good, and expansion for us and for those who are weak or unable to travel to the mosque of Quba'." Al-Zamakhshari said: "We did not intend by building this mosque anything but the good quality, or for the purpose of good, which is prayer, the remembrance of God, and the widening of space for worshippers." End of quote. It seems that in his words "except the good quality" he made it the object, and in his words "or for the purpose of good" he made it a cause. It seems he gave "arada" (intend) the meaning of "qasada" (aim at), meaning: we aimed in building it at nothing but the purpose of good, which is prayer. This is a strained interpretation.

So God refuted them in their claim, and forbade him to stand in it, saying: "Do not ever stand in it." He forbade him because its builders had deceived the Messenger (ﷺ). The Messenger (ﷺ) was determined to go with them, and he called for his garment to rise, so the verse was revealed: "Do not ever stand in it." The expression "standing" is used to refer to prayer in it.

Ibn Abbas, a group of the Companions, and the Successors said: "The mosque founded upon piety" is the mosque of Quba', which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) founded, and he prayed in it during the days he stayed at Quba', namely Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday, and he went out on Friday. This is preferable, because the comparison between the mosque of Quba' and the mosque of harm is more fitting than that between the Messenger's mosque and the mosque of harm, and that suits the narrative. It is also reported from Zayd ibn Thabit, Abu Sa'id, and Ibn Umar that it is the Messenger's mosque. It is related that he (ﷺ) said, when asked about the mosque founded upon piety: "It is this mosque of mine." If this report is sound, no disagreement with it is possible. From here, "min" entered upon the time expression. The Kufans used this as evidence that "min" can denote the starting point (ibtida' al-ghayah) in time. The Basrans interpreted it by omitting a modifier, meaning "from the foundation of the first day," since in their view "min" does not govern time expressions. The verification of this is in the science of grammar. Ibn Atiyya said: "It seems good to me that one may dispense with an assumed element, and that 'min' governs the word 'awwal' (first), because it carries the sense of beginning, as if he said: from the beginning of the days." This that I have chosen has been related to me from some of the leading grammarians. End of quote. "Ahaqqu" (more worthy) means "haqiq" (deserving), and it is not a comparative elative (af'al al-tafdil), since the two mosques do not share in the right. The "ta'" in "an taquma" (that you stand) is a second-person address to the Messenger (ﷺ).

Abd Allah ibn Yazid recited "fihi" with a kasra on the ha', and the second "fihu" with a damma on the ha', combining the two dialects. The original form is the damma. The "fihi" serves to remove the assumption of emphasis, and it raises "rijal" (men). "Fayaqumu" (so he stands): "fihi" the first is in the position of the accusative, and the second is in the position of the nominative. They permitted, in "fihi rijal," that it be an attribute of "masjid" (mosque), or a circumstantial clause (hal), or a resumptive new sentence (isti'naf).

It is reported in a hadith that he said to them: "O assembly of the Ansar, I see that God has praised you for purity; what do you do?" They said: "O Messenger of God, we saw our Jewish neighbors purifying themselves with water, meaning cleaning after relieving themselves with water, so we did the same. When Islam came, we did not abandon it." He said: "Then do not abandon it." In some wordings of this hadith there is additional material and variation.

The scholars have differed over whether cleaning after relieving oneself should be done with stones or with water, which of the two is better. One group saw the combining of both as best. Ibn Habib held an unusual view, saying: one should not clean with stones where water is available. According to what is reported in this hadith, purification is an expression for using water to remove impurity during cleaning after relieving oneself. It was also said that it is general to all impurities. Al-Hasan said: "Purification" means purifying oneself from sins through repentance. It was also said: they loved to purify themselves through the fever which expiates sins, so they all had fever. In the Dala'il al-Nubuwwa of al-Bayhaqi: "The people of Quba' complained of fever, and he said: 'If you wish, I will pray to God to remove it from you, or if you wish, I will make it a purification for you.' They said: 'Rather, make it a purification for us.'" The meaning of their love for purification is that they prefer it and are eager for it, as a lover is eager for the thing he desires in many respects. God's love for them means that He does good to them, as a lover does with his beloved.

Ibn Misarrif and al-A'mash recited "yattahharu" (they purify themselves) with assimilation (idgham). Ibn Abi Talib recited "al-mutatahhirin" (those who purify themselves).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verses 109–110:

﴿Is one who founded his building upon piety from Allah and approval better, or one who founded his building upon the edge of a crumbling cliff, so it collapsed with him into the fire of Hell? And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾: Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read (أسَّسَ بُنْيانَهُ, "was founded" – passive) in both places, in the passive voice. The rest of the seven and a group read it in the active voice, with (بُنْيانَ) in the accusative. 'Umara ibn 'A'idh read the first in the passive and the second in the active. Nasr ibn 'Ali, and it is narrated from Nasr ibn 'Asim, read: (أسَّسَ بُنْيانَهُ). It is also narrated from Nasr ibn 'Ali, Abu Haywa and Nasr ibn 'Asim, likewise: (أساسُ), the plural of (أُسّ, "foundation"). It is narrated from Nasr ibn 'Asim: (أُسُسَ), with a fatha on the hamza and a damma on the sin. It is also read: (إساسُ) with a kasra, which are plurals considered as annexed to (البُنْيانِ, "the building"). It is read: "أساسُ" with a fatha on the hamza, and "أُسُّ" with a damma on the hamza and shadda on the sin; these are two singular forms annexed to (البُنْيانِ). Thus there are nine readings. In the book al-Lawami' (of Nasr ibn 'Asim): (أفَمَن أسَسُ) with tanwin and raf', (بُنْيانِهِ) with jarr as an annexed construction, so (أسَسُ) is the verbal noun of (أسَّ الحائِطَ يَؤُسُّهُ أسًّا وأسَسًا, "he founded the wall"). And it is also narrated from Nasr: (أساسُ بُنْيانِهِ) likewise, except that it has the alif; and (أسٌّ وأسَسٌ وأساسٌ) are all verbal nouns. End of quotation. (البُنْيانُ, "building") is a verbal noun like (الغُفْرانُ, "forgiveness"), applied to the thing built, as (الخَلْقُ, "creation") is used in the sense of "the created thing". It is also said that it is a plural whose singular is (بُنْيانَةٌ). The poet said:

كَبُنْيانَةِ القارِيِّ مَوْضِعُ رَحْلِها وآثارُ نِسْعَيْها مِنَ الدَّفِّ أبْلَقُ

Isa ibn 'Umar read: (عَلى تَقْوًى) with tanwin, and Sibawayh transmitted this reading, but people rejected it. Ibn Jinni said: its analogy is that its alif is for extension, like (أرْطى). A group, among them Hamza, Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr, read: (جُرْفٍ) with a sukun on the ra', while the rest of the seven and a group read it with a damma; both are dialectal forms. It is said the original is the damma. In the Mushaf of Ubayy: (فانْهارَتْ بِهِ قَواعِدُهُ في نارِ جَهَنَّمَ, "its foundations collapsed with it into the fire of Hell"). The apparent meaning is that this statement clarifies the state of the two mosques: the Mosque of Quba' or the Mosque of the Messenger (ﷺ), and the Mosque of Harm, and denies their equality and differentiates between them; so said many of the exegetes. Jabir ibn 'Abdullah said: "I saw smoke coming out of the Mosque of Harm, and it collapsed on Monday." Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated that when the Messenger (ﷺ) sent for its demolition, smoke was seen coming out of it. It is also narrated that a man would put a palm frond into it and take it out black and burnt, and that he would dig that place which had collapsed, and smoke would come out of it. It is said this is a parable, meaning: whoever founded his building on Islam is better, or whoever founded his building on polytheism and hypocrisy; and it clarifies that the building of the disbeliever is like a building on the edge of a crumbling cliff, whose people topple into Hell. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is said rather that this is literal, and that this very mosque collapsed into the fire of Hell; this was said by Qatadah and Ibn Jurayj. And (خَيْرٌ, "better") does not involve a shared comparison between the two matters unless from the view of the builder of the Mosque of Harm, and according to that belief the comparative is valid.

al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning is: Is one who founded the building of his religion upon a strong, firm foundation, which is the truth, namely the piety of Allah and His Messenger, better; or one who founded it upon a foundation that is the weakest of foundations, the feeblest and least lasting, which is falsehood and hypocrisy, whose likeness is the likeness of the edge of a crumbling cliff in lack of stability and holding? The edge of the cliff is placed in contrast to piety; it is not made a metaphor for what contradicts piety. If you say: what is the meaning of His saying: (فانْهارَ بِهِ في نارِ جَهَنَّمَ, "so it collapsed with him into the fire of Hell")? I say: when the crumbling cliff was made a metaphor for falsehood, it was said (فانْهارَ بِهِ, "it collapsed with him") in the sense: falsehood collapsed with him into the fire of Hell; but he extended the metaphor, so the word "collapse" that belongs to the cliff was used, and given the image that falsehood, as if it had founded its building on the edge of a cliff of the valleys of Hell, that cliff collapsed with it, so it plunged to its bottom. We see no more eloquent statement than this, nor one more indicative of the reality of falsehood and the essence of its matter. The doer of (فانْهارَ, "collapsed") is: the building, or the edge, or the cliff, "with him", that is, with the founder who built; (p-101) or the edge or the cliff collapsed "with it", that is, with the building; it entails the collapse of the edge and the building, but the collapse of one of them does not necessarily entail the collapse of the other. (وَاللَّهُ لا يَهْدِي القَوْمَ الظّالِمِينَ, "And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people") is an indication of their transgression and placing a thing in other than its place, in that they built the Mosque of Harm; since mosques are the houses of Allah, in which the intention and purpose must be made sincere for the sake of Allah and His worship; but they built it out of harm, disbelief, and division among the believers, and as an ambush for whoever fought Allah and His Messenger.

﴿The building which they built will not cease to be a doubt in their hearts, unless their hearts are cut to pieces. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾: It may be that (البُنْيانُ, "the building") here is a verbal noun, meaning that this act, namely the building, will not cease; and it may be intended as the thing built, in which case there is an omitted modifier, meaning: the construction of the building will not cease. Ibn 'Abbas said: "They will not cease to be doubters." Habib ibn Abi Thabit said: "Rage in their hearts," that is, a cause of rage. It was said: "Disbelief in their hearts." 'Ata' said: "Hypocrisy in their hearts." Ibn Jubayr said: "Regret and remorse." Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil said: "Grief and remorse, because they regretted its building." Qatadah said: there is an ellipsis in the speech, its estimated form being: the demolition of their building which they built will not cease to be a doubt, that is, a sore and rage in their hearts. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Which they built" is an emphasis and an explicit statement of the matter of the mosque and the removal of ambiguity. Doubt (ريبة) is uncertainty; the term "ريبة" may also be applied to corruption of belief and its disturbance, and to wavering and confusion regarding a matter. The sore (حزازة) comes from it; and even if it is not doubt, one who is not doubtful may still feel uneasy, but in common usage it goes with doubt. The meaning of "ريبة" in this verse encompasses the grudge, and the belief in the correctness of their act, and similar things, all of which lead to doubt regarding Islam. So the purpose of the speech is: this building which was demolished for them will continue to leave in their hearts a sore and a trace of evil. Ibn 'Abbas interpreted "ريبة" here as doubt, while al-Suddi interpreted it as disbelief. It was said to him: "Did Mujammi' ibn Jariyah disbelieve?" He said: "No, but it is a sore." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Mujammi', may Allah have mercy on him, swore to 'Umar that he did not know the inner state of the people, and did not intend evil. The verse only refers to those who concealed evil, and Mujammi' was not among them. It may be that the meaning is: they will continue to be doubters because of their building, in which their hypocrisy became clear. The sum of this is that doubt in the verse encompasses many meanings, each hypocrite taking from them according to his measure of hypocrisy. Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi said: He made the building itself a doubt, because it was the cause of it; and its being a cause of it is that when he ordered the destruction of what they had rejoiced in building, this weighed heavily upon them, and their hatred for him increased, and their doubt regarding his prophethood; or they believed its demolition was out of envy, so their faith departed and they feared that he would strike them with killing and plunder; or they remained doubtful: "Will Allah forgive them that disobedience?" End of quotation, and there is an abridgment in it.

Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and Hafs read: ﴿إلّا أنْ تَقَطَّعَ قُلُوبُهُمْ﴾ with a fatha on the ta', meaning (يَتَقَطَّعَ, "they be cut to pieces"), while the rest of the seven read it with a damma, as the imperfect of (قَطَّعَ, "to cut into pieces") in the passive voice. It is also read: (يَقْطَعَ) with lightness. Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah and Ya'qub read: (إلى أنْ نَقْطَعَ, "until We cut"), and Abu Haywa: (إلى أنْ تُقَطِّعَ) with a damma on the ta', a fatha on the qaf, a kasra on the ta' (shadda), and (قُلُوبَهَمْ) in the accusative, addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ), meaning: you kill them; or there is in it the pronoun referring to the doubt. In the Mushaf of 'Abdullah: (ولَوْ قُطِّعَتْ قُلُوبُهم, "even if their hearts were cut to pieces"), and likewise his companions read it. Abu 'Amr narrated this reading: (إنْ قَطَعْتَ) with lightness of the ta'. Talhah read: (ولَوْ قَطَّعْتَ قُلُوبَهم), addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ), or to every addressee. In the Mushaf of Ubayy: (حَتّى المَماتِ, "until death"), and in it: (حَتّى تُقْطَعَ, "until they are cut"). As for whoever reads with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the ta' and the accusative of the hearts, the meaning is: by killing. As for whoever reads it in the passive voice, Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Ibn Zayd and others said: by death, that is, until they die. 'Ikrimah said: until whoever is in the graves is resurrected. Sufyan said: until they repent of what they did, so they will be like one whose heart has been cut. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is not apparent, unless it is interpreted as their repenting a sincere repentance, with which there will be regret and anguish that cut the hearts with grief. al-Zamakhshari said: their doubt will continue to show itself as a cause of doubt and hypocrisy beyond their doubt and hypocrisy; its mark will remain in their hearts, and its matter will not disappear, unless their hearts are cut into pieces and divided into parts; then they will ask about it; but as long as they are whole and united, doubt remains in them, firmly established. It is also possible that what is meant is the literal cutting of them and what will happen from that by killing them, or in the graves, or in the Fire. It was said: its meaning is: unless they repent a repentance by which their hearts are cut with regret and grief over their negligence. (واللَّهُ عَلِيمٌ, "And Allah is All-Knowing") of their circumstances, (حَكِيمٌ, "All-Wise") in what judgments He applies to them; or All-Knowing of their intentions, All-Wise in their punishments.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Mujammi', may Allah have mercy on him, swore to 'Umar that he did not know the inner state of the people, and did not intend evil. The verse only refers to those who concealed evil, and Mujammi' was not among them. It may be that the meaning is: they will continue to be doubters because of their building, in which their hypocrisy became clear. The sum of this is that doubt in the verse encompasses many meanings, each hypocrite taking from them according to his measure of hypocrisy. Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi said: He made the building itself a doubt, because it was the cause of it; and its being a cause of it is that when he ordered the destruction of what they had rejoiced in building, this weighed heavily upon them, and their hatred for him increased, and their doubt regarding his prophethood; or they believed its demolition was out of envy, so their faith departed and they feared that he would strike them with killing and plunder; or they remained doubtful: "Will Allah forgive them that disobedience?" End of quotation, and there is an abridgment in it.

Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and Hafs read: ﴿إلّا أنْ تَقَطَّعَ قُلُوبُهُمْ﴾ with a fatha on the ta', meaning (يَتَقَطَّعَ, "they be cut to pieces"), while the rest of the seven read it with a damma, as the imperfect of (قَطَّعَ, "to cut into pieces") in the passive voice. It is also read: (يَقْطَعَ) with lightness. Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah and Ya'qub read: (إلى أنْ نَقْطَعَ, "until We cut"), and Abu Haywa: (إلى أنْ تُقَطِّعَ) with a damma on the ta', a fatha on the qaf, a kasra on the ta' (shadda), and (قُلُوبَهَمْ) in the accusative, addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ), meaning: you kill them; or there is in it the pronoun referring to the doubt. In the Mushaf of 'Abdullah: (ولَوْ قُطِّعَتْ قُلُوبُهم, "even if their hearts were cut to pieces"), and likewise his companions read it. Abu 'Amr narrated this reading: (إنْ قَطَعْتَ) with lightness of the ta'. Talhah read: (ولَوْ قَطَّعْتَ قُلُوبَهم), addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ), or to every addressee. It was said: its meaning is: unless they repent a repentance by which their hearts are cut with regret and grief over their negligence. (واللَّهُ عَلِيمٌ, "And Allah is All-Knowing") of their circumstances, (حَكِيمٌ, "All-Wise") in what judgments He applies to them; or All-Knowing of their intentions, All-Wise in their punishments.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verses 111–112:

﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their wealth in exchange for their having Paradise. They fight in the way of Allah, so they kill and are killed. That is a true promise binding upon Him in the Torah, the Gospel, and the Qur'an. And who is truer to his covenant than Allah? So rejoice in the bargain you have made, and that is the great triumph.﴾

It was revealed concerning the Second Pledge, which is the Pledge of al-ʿAqabah al-Kubra (the Great Pledge of al-ʿAqabah). In it, men of the Ansar (the Helpers) numbered seventy, and the youngest of them in age was ʿUqbah ibn ʿAmr. The reason is that they gathered with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at al-ʿAqabah, and they said: "Stipulate for yourself and for your Lord." The one who spoke was ʿAbd Allah ibn Rawahah. So the Prophet (ﷺ) stipulated that they protect him from what they protect themselves from, and he stipulated for his Lord the adherence to the Shariʿah (the sacred law) and the fighting of the red and the black (all people) in defense of the sanctuary (ḥawzah). They said: "What will we have in return for that?" He said: "Paradise." They said: "Yes, the bargain is profitable. We will not seek its cancellation, nor will we ask for its cancellation." In some narrations it says: "Nor will we seek to annul it." So it was revealed.

The verse is general, encompassing everyone among the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) who strives in the way of Allah until the Day of Resurrection. It is narrated from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah: "It was revealed while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was in the mosque, and the people shouted takbir. A man of the Ansar came forward, having folded the end of his riding gear over one of his shoulders, and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, was this verse revealed?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'A profitable bargain! We will not seek its cancellation, nor will we seek to annul it.'" In some narrations: "So he went out to the campaign and was martyred." Al-Hasan said: "No, by Allah, there is no believer on earth who has not renewed his pledge." ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab and al-Aʿmash recited: "and their wealth for Paradise (bi-l-jannah)," meaning that Allah, exalted is He, described their reward with Paradise in return for their expending their lives and wealth in His way, by way of an exchange (bi-l-shirāʾ). He placed lives before wealth, beginning with what is most noble and with what has no substitute once lost. In the word (ishtará, "purchased") there is a subtle point: it expresses the purchaser's desire for what he has bought and his satisfaction with it. The construction did not say "the believers sold," and the apparent meaning is that this purchase is with those who strive (mujāhidīn). Ibn ʿUyaynah said: "(He purchased from them their lives) means that they will not use them except in obedience, and (their wealth) means that they will not spend it except in the way of Allah. On this view the verse is more general than killing in the way of Allah." On this view, (yuqātilūn, "they fight") is a resumed statement (mustaʾnaf), mentioning their greatest states and drawing attention to their most noble station. According to the apparent meaning and the view of the majority, (yuqātilūn) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). Al-Hasan, Qatadah, Abu Raja', the two ʿArabiyyān, the two Ḥaramiyyān (the two readers of Mecca and Medina), and ʿĀṣim read the first (yuqtalūn, "they kill") in the active voice and the second (yuqtalūn, "they are killed") in the passive voice. Al-Nakhaʿi, Ibn Wathhab, Talhah, al-Aʿmash, and the two Akhawan (the two brothers, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾi) read the opposite of that, and the meaning is one, since the purpose is that the believers are fought against, and some of them are taken who are killed, some of them kill, some of them have both happen to them, and some of them experience neither but are engaged in fighting. Al-Zamakhshari said: "(yuqātilūn) carries the sense of a command, because of His saying: ﴿You strive in the way of Allah with your wealth and your lives﴾ [al-Saff: 11]." End of quotation. On this view the clause is not in the position of a circumstantial clause, because what has the meaning of a command cannot be a circumstantial clause. (waʿdan, "a promise") is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar) emphasizing the content of the clause, because the meaning of (ishtará ... bi-anna lahumu al-jannah, "purchased ... that for them is Paradise") is that Allah promised them Paradise in return for striving in His way. The apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿in the Torah, the Gospel, and the Qur'an﴾ is that every community that was commanded to strive and was promised Paradise in return for it, so (fī al-tawrāh, "in the Torah") is connected to (ishtará). It is also possible that it is connected to an implied mentioned statement, and it is a descriptive phrase (ṣifah) whose governing element is omitted, meaning: a promise binding upon Him, mentioned in the Torah. In that case, this promise of Paradise is the guidance of this community, which has been mentioned in the Torah, the Gospel, and the Qur'an. It was also said: the command to strive and fight exists in all the sacred laws.

(Wa-man awfā, "And who is truer") is an interrogative in the form of affirmation (taqrīr), meaning: no one. When He emphasized the promise with His saying (ʿalayhi ḥaqqan, "binding upon Him as a truth"), He presented it here in the form of a covenant (ʿahd), which is more emphatic and more binding than a promise, since a promise made by someone other than the Truth (Allah) may be broken, while a covenant may not be violated except by fulfilling it, since it is more emphatic than a promise. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿And who is truer to his covenant than Allah?﴾ because breaking a promise is ugly, and noble people among creation do not undertake it, though it is permissible for them because of their need, so how then with the Self-Sufficient (al-Ghaniyy), for whom no ugliness is ever permissible? And you will not find an exhortation to striving more excellent or more eloquent than this. End of quotation. In this there is the hidden doctrine of the Muʿtazilah, and the use of (qaṭṭ, "ever") in other than its proper context, since he used it with His saying: "for whom no ugliness is ever permissible." (Qaṭṭ) is a past-tense adverb, so only a past-tense verb governs it. Then He said: (fa-istabshirū, "so rejoice"). He addressed them by a shift (iltifāt, "turning of address") from third person to second person, because His addressing them directly honors them, and this is the wisdom of the shift here. (Istafʿala, here) is not for the sense of request, but has the sense of (afʿala), like (istawqada, "he kindled") and (awqada). (Alladhī bāyaʿtum bihi, "the bargain you have made") is a descriptive qualifier for emphasis, referring back to the previous pledge. Then He said: (wa-dhālika huwa al-fawz al-ʿaẓīm, "and that is the great triumph"), meaning: success in obtaining complete profit, and felicity in the bargain through the removal of sins and entry into Paradise.

﴿The repentant, the worshippers, the praisers, the wanderers, the bowers, the prostrators, those who enjoin right and forbid wrong, and those who keep the limits of Allah. And give good news to the believers.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: "When ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers﴾ was revealed, a man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, even if he commits fornication, even if he steals, even if he drinks wine?' Then ﴿the repentant﴾ was revealed, to the end of the verse." These are the attributes of the perfected among the believers, which Allah mentioned so that His servants would hasten to adorn themselves with them, and so that they would reach the highest degrees of perfection. The verse ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased﴾ is independent in itself, and it stipulates nothing besides faith, so every believer who fights so that the Word of Allah may be supreme falls under it, even if he does not possess these attributes. Martyrdom erases every sin, to the extent that it is narrated that He, exalted is He, bears the wrongs of the servants on behalf of the martyr and compensates them on his behalf. Another group said: these attributes are a condition for the one who strives. The two verses are connected, so only the believers who possess these attributes and expend their lives in the way of Allah enter into the pledge. A man asked al-Dahhak about His saying: (Indeed, Allah has purchased) and said: "I will charge against the polytheists and fight until I am killed." Al-Dahhak said: "Woe to you! Where is the condition: ﴿the repentant, the worshippers﴾ to the end of the verse?" This statement contains constriction and narrowing. Upon these two views, the grammatical analysis (iʿrāb) of (al-tāʾibūn, "the repentant") is determined. It was said: it is a subject (mubtadaʾ) whose predicate is mentioned, namely (al-ʿābidūn, "the worshippers"), and what follows it is a predicate after a predicate, meaning: the truly repentant are those who combine these qualities. It was said: its predicate is (al-āmirūn, "those who enjoin"). It was said: its predicate is omitted after the completion of the attributes, and its estimated form is: "they are among the people of Paradise also, even if they did not strive," as al-Zajjaj said, just as He said: ﴿And to each Allah has promised the best﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 95]. For this reason it came: (wa-bashshir al-muʾminīn, "and give good news to the believers"). On these grammatical analyses, the verse's meaning is separate from the meaning of what precedes it. It was said: (al-tāʾibūn) is the predicate of an implied subject, its estimated form being: "They are the repentant," meaning: those who pledged to Allah are the repentant, so it is a detached descriptive phrase for praise (ṣifah maqṭūʿah li-l-madḥ). This is supported by the reading of Ubayy, ʿAbd Allah, and al-Aʿmash: (al-tāyibīn, "the repentant," with a ya in place of the hamza), through to (wa-al-ḥāfiẓīn, "and those who keep"), in the accusative for praise. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also permissible for it to be an attribute of the believers." Ibn ʿAṭiyyah also said this. It was also said: (al-tāʾibūn) may be a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in (yuqātilūn, "they fight"). Ibn ʿAbbas said: "The repentant are those who repent from polytheism." Al-Hasan said: "from polytheism and hypocrisy." It was said: "from every act of disobedience." It is also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas: "the worshippers" means those who worship through prayer, and also from him: "those who obey through worship." From al-Hasan: they are those who worshipped Allah in ease and in hardship. From Ibn Jubayr: "the monotheists who wander." Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿAbbas, and others said: "the fasting ones," who were compared to wanderers in the land because of their restraint from their desires. From ʿĀʾishah: "The wandering (siyāḥah) of this community is fasting," and Abu Hurayrah narrated it from the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Azhari said: the fasting person is called a wanderer, because one who wanders in the land is a devotee with no provision with him, and he abstains from eating, and the fasting person abstains from eating. ʿAṭāʾ said: "the wanderers are those who strive." From Abu Umamah: "A man asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for permission to wander, and he said: 'The wandering of my community is striving in the way of Allah.'" Abu Muhammad ʿAbd al-Haqq declared it sound. It was said: the intended meaning is wandering in the land. It was said: they are those who migrated from Mecca to Medina. It was said: those who travel to seek hadith and knowledge. It was said: those who travel in the land to look at the signs of Allah and the wonders of His dominion with a view to taking lessons. It was said: those who roam with their thoughts through the power of Allah and His sovereignty.

When attributes are repeated and are for praise, blame, or pity, it is permissible to follow the qualified noun in them, or to detach them, in all of them or in some of them. When the two attributes differ from one another, conjunction (ʿaṭf) is permissible. Since commanding is the opposite of forbidding, as commanding is a request for an action and forbidding is a request to abstain from an action, the conjunction in His saying (wa-al-nāhūn, "and those who forbid") is good. The claim of an additional element (ziyādah) or the "eighth conjunction" (wāw al-thamāniyah) is weak. The arrangement of these attributes is in the highest degree of excellence, for He began first with what concerns the person himself, arranged according to what he strove for, then with what extends from these attributes from the person to others, which is commanding right and forbidding wrong, then with what includes both what concerns himself and what extends to others, which is keeping the limits of Allah. When He, exalted is He, mentioned the whole of these attributes, He commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to give good news to the believers. In the verse before it, (fa-istabshirū, "so rejoice"), He commanded them to rejoice, so they attained the complete distinction that Allah commanded them to rejoice, and commanded His Messenger to give them good news.

Al-Azhari said: the fasting person is called a wanderer, because one who wanders in the land is a devotee with no provision with him, and he abstains from eating, and the fasting person abstains from eating. ʿAṭāʾ said: "the wanderers are those who strive." From Abu Umamah: "A man asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for permission to wander, and he said: 'The wandering of my community is striving in the way of Allah.'" Abu Muhammad ʿAbd al-Haqq declared it sound. It was said: the intended meaning is wandering in the land. It was said: they are those who migrated from Mecca to Medina. It was said: those who travel to seek hadith and knowledge. It was said: those who travel in the land to look at the signs of Allah and the wonders of His dominion with a view to taking lessons. It was said: those who roam with their thoughts through the power of Allah and His sovereignty.

When attributes are repeated and are for praise, blame, or pity, it is permissible to follow the qualified noun in them, or to detach them, in all of them or in some of them. When the two attributes differ from one another, conjunction (ʿaṭf) is permissible. Since commanding is the opposite of forbidding, as commanding is a request for an action and forbidding is a request to abstain from an action, the conjunction in His saying (wa-al-nāhūn, "and those who forbid") is good. The claim of an additional element (ziyādah) or the "eighth conjunction" (wāw al-thamāniyah) is weak. The arrangement of these attributes is in the highest degree of excellence, for He began first with what concerns the person himself, arranged according to what he strove for, then with what extends from these attributes from the person to others, which is commanding right and forbidding wrong, then with what includes both what concerns himself and what extends to others, which is keeping the limits of Allah. When He, exalted is He, mentioned the whole of these attributes, He commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to give good news to the believers. In the verse before it, (fa-istabshirū, "so rejoice"), He commanded them to rejoice, so they attained the complete distinction that Allah commanded them to rejoice, and commanded His Messenger to give them good news.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verses 113–114:

﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they were close relatives, after it has become clear to them that they are companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾ ﴿The asking of forgiveness by Abraham for his father was only because of a promise he had made to him. But when it became clear to him that he was an enemy of Allah, he disassociated himself from him. Indeed, Abraham was tender-hearted and forbearing.﴾

Al-Jumhur (the majority) said: its transmission rests on Ibn al-Musayyab, al-Zuhri and Amr ibn Dinar: "It was revealed concerning Abu Talib when he was at the point of death. The Prophet (ﷺ) admonished him and said: 'O uncle, say: There is no god but Allah, a word by which I may argue on your behalf before Allah.' Abu Jahl and Abdullah ibn Abi Umayya were present, and they said to him: 'O Abu Talib, do you turn away from the religion of Abd al-Muttalib?' Abu Talib said: 'O Muhammad, were it not that I fear my sons will be reproached for it after me, I would have consoled your eye by it.' Then he said: 'I am upon the religion of Abd al-Muttalib,' and he died. So it was revealed: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾ (p-105). The Prophet (ﷺ) then said: 'I will surely ask forgiveness for you as long as I am not forbidden from it.' He continued to ask forgiveness for him until this verse was revealed, and so he abandoned asking forgiveness for Abu Talib."

It is also narrated that when the believers saw him asking forgiveness for Abu Talib, they began to ask forgiveness for their dead. Therefore they are mentioned in His saying: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe﴾.

Fudayl ibn Atiyya and others said: When he conquered Makkah, he went to the grave of his mother and stood by it until the sun heated it. He kept desiring to be permitted to ask forgiveness for her, but he was not permitted. So he was informed that he had been permitted to visit her grave, but was forbidden to ask forgiveness for her, and the verse was revealed.

A group said: it was revealed because of his saying: "By Allah, I will surely increase beyond seventy [times in asking forgiveness]." Ibn Abbas, Qatada and others said: it was revealed because of a group of believers who said: "We will ask forgiveness for our dead as Abraham asked forgiveness for his father."

His saying ﴿It is not for the Prophet﴾ — the verse includes a prohibition against asking forgiveness for them in any state, even if they are close relatives. So His saying ﴿even if they were﴾ is a clause conjoined to a presumed circumstantial state. The discussion of this kind of construction has already preceded us: that "wa law" (even if) comes to emphasize the inclusion of what follows within what precedes, which without it would not have included it.

The verse indicates an extreme emphasis on displaying disavowal of the polytheists and the hypocrites, and prohibiting association with them, even if they were in the greatest closeness. It also draws attention to the noble attribute of prophethood and faith, and that it is incompatible with asking forgiveness for one who died upon its opposite, which is associating partners with Allah.

The meaning of ﴿after it has become clear﴾ is: it became evident to them that they are companions of the Blazing Fire, because they died upon polytheism. The clarification comes through the information from Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾ (4:48). Apparently, the asking of forgiveness here means seeking forgiveness, and the occasions of revelation converge on this.

Ata ibn Abi Rabah said: the verse is about the prohibition of prayer over the polytheists, and asking forgiveness here means prayer. They said: asking forgiveness for a living polytheist is permissible, since his becoming Muslim is hoped for. From this is the saying of Abu Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him): "May Allah have mercy on a man who asked forgiveness for Abu Hurayra and his mother." It was said to him: "And for his father?" He said: "No, because my father died as a disbeliever." If a text from Allah is revealed concerning someone that he is among the people of the Fire while he is still alive, like Abu Lahab, asking forgiveness for him is forbidden. Thus the clarification of the polytheist's state, that he is among the companions of the Blazing Fire, is a deception (?) upon polytheism, and by the explicit text of Allah concerning him while he is alive, that he is among the people of the Fire.

It also bears on the permissibility of asking forgiveness for disbelievers while they are alive, because their becoming Muslim is hoped for, as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) related about a prophet before him whose people had wounded him, so the Prophet (ﷺ) would report about him that he said: "O Allah, forgive my people, for they do not know."

Since Abraham's asking forgiveness for his father was in a position to be followed, and for this reason a group of believers said: "We will ask forgiveness for our dead as Abraham asked forgiveness for his father" — He explained the reason for Abraham's asking forgiveness for his father, and mentioned that when his enmity to Allah became clear to him, Abraham disassociated himself from him. The promise Abraham made to his father is His saying: ﴿I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord﴾ (19:47) and His saying: ﴿I will surely ask forgiveness for you﴾ (19:47 variant). The pronoun subject in (wa'adaha) refers back to Abraham. His father was still alive, so he hoped for his faith. When it became clear to him through revelation from Allah that he was an enemy of Allah, and that he would die a disbeliever, and his hope from him was cut off, he disassociated himself from him and ceased asking forgiveness for him.

What indicates that the subject in (wa'ada) is a pronoun referring to Abraham is the reading of al-Hasan, Hammad al-Rawiya, Ibn al-Sumayqa, Abu Nahik and Mu'adh al-Qari: (wa'adaha abahu) [with the object being his father]. It was also said: the subject is the pronoun of Abraham's father, and "iyyahu" (him) is the pronoun of Abraham. His father promised him that he would become a believer, so Abraham's hope for his faith became strong, and that led him to ask forgiveness for him, until he was prohibited from it.

Talha recited: (wa ma istaghfara Ibrahimu) [the past tense without the object], and from him: (wa ma yastaghfiru Ibrahimu) [the present tense], as a narration of the state. What appears to be the case is that Abraham's asking forgiveness for his father took place during the life of this world. Do you not see His saying: ﴿And forgive my father, for indeed he was among the misguided﴾ (26:86), and His saying: (My Lord, forgive me and my parents) (14:41)? The view of Ibn Jubayr is weakened, that all of this will be on the Day of Resurrection: that Abraham will meet his father, recognize him, and remember his saying: "I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord." Then he will say to him: "Hold to my waistband (hiqwi), for I will not leave you today for anything." He leaves him until they come to the Sirat, and when he turns to him, he has been transformed into a hyena (dib'an); then he disassociates himself from him at that time. This concludes what Ibn Jubayr said, and its connection to the Hereafter does not appear.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: it was hidden from Abraham (peace be upon him) that asking forgiveness for a disbeliever is impermissible, until he promised him? I say: It is possible that he thought that as long as faith was still hoped for him, asking forgiveness for him was permissible. Furthermore, the impermissibility of asking forgiveness for a disbeliever is known only through revelation, because reason permits that Allah may forgive a disbeliever. Do you not see the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I will surely ask forgiveness for you as long as I am not forbidden from it." And from al-Hasan: it was said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "So-and-so asks forgiveness for his polytheist parents," and he said: "And we ask forgiveness for them." And from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him): "I saw a man asking forgiveness for his two parents while they were polytheists, so I said to him..." and he said: "Did not Abraham ask forgiveness?" End of quote. His saying "because reason permits that Allah may forgive a disbeliever" is a return to the view of the people of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah, the followers of the prophetic tradition).

Al-awwah (أوّاه) is: one who supplicates much, or a believer, or a jurist, or merciful, or a repentant believer, or one who glorifies Allah, or one who remembers Him much, or one who recites the Book of Allah, or one who says "awwah" out of fear of Allah, one who repeats that, or one who gathers and humbles himself, or a believer in Abyssinian, or one who teaches goodness, or one who fulfills, or one who asks forgiveness upon mentioning sins, or one who is compassionate, or one who turns back from everything Allah dislikes. These are sayings of the early generations (al-salaf), and we have mentioned its meaning in lexicography in the discussion of the vocabulary (in our work on the Mufradat). Al-Zamakhshari said: "Awwah" (أوّاه) — he said: from awwaha, like lali' (لَآلٍ) from lu'lu' (pearls), meaning one who frequently sighs (al-ta'awwuh), and its meaning is that out of his excessive compassion, tenderness and forbearance, he would show kindness to his disbelieving father and ask forgiveness for him, despite his harshness toward him and his saying: "I will surely stone you" (19:46). End of quote. His comparison of awwah (أوّاه) from awwaha to lali' (لَآلٍ) from lu'lu' (لُؤْلُؤ) is not good, because the root of awwaha exists in the form awwah (أوّاه), whereas the root of lu'lu' (لُؤْلُؤ) is absent in lali' (لَآلٍ) because of the difference in structure: lali' is triliteral, while lu'lu' is quadriliteral, and the condition of derivation is agreement in the root letters.

They interpreted al-halim (الحليم) here as: one who pardons sins, one who endures harm, one who is patient, one who is wise, one who is a lord (sayyid), and one who is tender-hearted and very compassionate.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verses 115–116:

﴿And Allah would not let a people go astray after He had guided them until He makes clear to them what they should fear. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾ ﴿Indeed, to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He gives life and causes death. And you have, besides Allah, neither a guardian nor a helper.﴾ A people died whose deeds were based on the earlier ruling, such as facing Bayt al-Maqdis (in prayer) and drinking wine. Then some people asked the Messenger about that after the abrogation (naskh) had come and the obligations had been revealed, and so this was revealed. Al-Karmani said: Some Bedouins embraced Islam and acted on what they saw the Messenger doing: praying toward Bayt al-Maqdis and fasting the white days. Then they came to him and found him praying toward the Ka'bah and fasting Ramadan. They said: "O Messenger of Allah, after you we went astray; you are upon one matter and we are upon another." So this was revealed. It was also said: some of the believers feared seeking forgiveness for the polytheists without permission from Allah, so this verse was revealed as reassurance, meaning: Allah would not, after having guided them to Islam and saved them from the Fire, cause them to be lost through that, nor let their people go astray for committing a sin that had not been preceded by a prohibition against it. But when He has made clear to them what they should guard against of the command and avoid of things, then whoever commits (it) after the prohibition deserves punishment. Al-Zamakhshari said: He means what Allah has commanded them to guard against and avoid, such as seeking forgiveness for the polytheists and other things He has forbidden, and He has made clear that it is prohibited. He does not hold His servants accountable for it, those whom He has guided to Islam, nor does He call them misguided or forsake them, except if they undertake it after the prohibition has been made clear to them and they know that it must be guarded against and avoided. Before knowledge and clarification, there is no blame upon them, just as they are not held accountable for drinking wine or for selling a sa' for two sa's before the prohibition. This is an explanation for the excuse of those who feared being held accountable for seeking forgiveness for the polytheists before the prohibition came. In this verse there is a severe warning that must not be overlooked: that the one guided to Islam, when he turns to some of Allah's prohibited matters, falls under the ruling of misguidance. The meaning of "what they guard against" is what must be guarded against because of a prohibition. As for what is known by reason, such as truthfulness in reports and returning a deposit, it does not depend on revelation. End. In this last part of his words, and in his words earlier in explaining (liyudilla): "nor does He call them misguided or forsake them," there is a trace (dasisah) of Mu'tazilism. His speech is also verbose; it is an expansion of what Mujahid said. He said: "He would not lead you astray through seeking forgiveness for the polytheists after He had guided you to faith, until He first forbids that and makes it clear to you so that you guard against it." End. The reasons for revelation mentioned earlier, which explain the verse, were already discussed: the question about one who died while having prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis and drank wine, and the story of the Bedouins.

What appears to be the connection of this verse to what precedes it, and its explanation, is this: when Allah, exalted is He, made clear that He does not ask forgiveness for the polytheists even if they were close relatives, there was in this verse and the one after it a clarification of the difference between kinship, until they were prevented from seeking forgiveness for them. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was prevented from seeking forgiveness for his uncle Abu Talib, who had taken charge of his upbringing, support, and protection until he died. Abraham was prevented from seeking forgiveness for his father, who was the origin of his upbringing and his educator. Likewise the Muslims were prevented from seeking forgiveness for the polytheists, whether relatives or not. It is as if it were said: do not be surprised at the difference among these: this is the Friend of Allah, and this is the Beloved of Allah, while the relatives specifically mentioned are the enemies of Allah. The misguidance of these people did not occur except after Allah had guided them to the path of truth through the proofs of reason that He placed within them, which they neglected, and through clarifying what they should guard against by way of revelation. The rational and revealed proofs thus converged upon them, yet they did not believe nor follow what the messengers brought from Allah, the Exalted. For this reason He concluded with His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things﴾, so He misguides whom He wills and singles out for guidance whom He wills. The meaning is: Allah would not perpetuate the misguidance of a people He had guided to the right path until He makes clear to them what they should guard against, that is, avoid, so that it has no effect on them, and then their misguidance would persist. When He mentioned His knowledge of all things, He knows what suits each person and what has been prepared for him in pre-eternity, He mentioned what indicates His overwhelming power: that to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, so He disposes of His servants as He wills. Then He mentioned among the greatest of His dispositions giving life and causing death, that is, bringing into existence and annihilating. Al-Tabari's interpretation here of His words "He gives life and causes death" as an indication that believers must not panic before an enemy however numerous, nor fear anyone, for the dreaded death and the decreed life are only in Allah's hand, is not appropriate here, even if in itself it is a correct statement. The explanation of His words: ﴿And you have, besides Allah, neither a guardian nor a helper﴾ [al-Baqarah: 107] was already given in al-Baqarah.
