As for what is known by reason, such as truthfulness in reports and returning a deposit, it does not depend on revelation. End. In this last part of his words, and in his words earlier in explaining (liyudilla): "nor does He call them misguided or forsake them," there is a trace (dasisah) of Mu'tazilism. His speech is also verbose; it is an expansion of what Mujahid said. He said: "He would not lead you astray through seeking forgiveness for the polytheists after He had guided you to faith, until He first forbids that and makes it clear to you so that you guard against it." End. The reasons for revelation mentioned earlier, which explain the verse, were already discussed: the question about one who died while having prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis and drank wine, and the story of the Bedouins.

What appears to be the connection of this verse to what precedes it, and its explanation, is this: when Allah, exalted is He, made clear that He does not ask forgiveness for the polytheists even if they were close relatives, there was in this verse and the one after it a clarification of the difference between kinship, until they were prevented from seeking forgiveness for them. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was prevented from seeking forgiveness for his uncle Abu Talib, who had taken charge of his upbringing, support, and protection until he died. Abraham was prevented from seeking forgiveness for his father, who was the origin of his upbringing and his educator. Likewise the Muslims were prevented from seeking forgiveness for the polytheists, whether relatives or not. It is as if it were said: do not be surprised at the difference among these: this is the Friend of Allah, and this is the Beloved of Allah, while the relatives specifically mentioned are the enemies of Allah. The misguidance of these people did not occur except after Allah had guided them to the path of truth through the proofs of reason that He placed within them, which they neglected, and through clarifying what they should guard against by way of revelation. The rational and revealed proofs thus converged upon them, yet they did not believe nor follow what the messengers brought from Allah, the Exalted. For this reason He concluded with His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things﴾, so He misguides whom He wills and singles out for guidance whom He wills. The meaning is: Allah would not perpetuate the misguidance of a people He had guided to the right path until He makes clear to them what they should guard against, that is, avoid, so that it has no effect on them, and then their misguidance would persist. When He mentioned His knowledge of all things, He knows what suits each person and what has been prepared for him in pre-eternity, He mentioned what indicates His overwhelming power: that to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, so He disposes of His servants as He wills. Then He mentioned among the greatest of His dispositions giving life and causing death, that is, bringing into existence and annihilating. Al-Tabari's interpretation here of His words "He gives life and causes death" as an indication that believers must not panic before an enemy however numerous, nor fear anyone, for the dreaded death and the decreed life are only in Allah's hand, is not appropriate here, even if in itself it is a correct statement. The explanation of His words: ﴿And you have, besides Allah, neither a guardian nor a helper﴾ [al-Baqarah: 107] was already given in al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verses 117–118 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Allah has certainly turned in forgiveness toward the Prophet and the Emigrants and the Helpers who followed him in the hour of hardship, after the hearts of a group of them had nearly swerved. Then He turned toward them in forgiveness. Indeed, He is Kind and Merciful to them.﴾ ﴿And toward the three who were left behind, until when the earth became confining for them despite its vastness, and their souls became confining for them, and they thought that there was no refuge from Allah except in Him. Then He turned toward them in forgiveness so that they might repent. Indeed, Allah is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾ [p. 108] When the discourse had preceded concerning the condition of the hypocrites and their staying behind from the expedition of Tabuk, and it digressed to the division of the hypocrites into Bedouins and others, and mentioned what they did regarding the mosque of harm, and mentioned the believers' pledge to Allah in jihad and praised them, and that they should disassociate from the polytheists, even those of them who had died, by abandoning seeking forgiveness for them, it returned to mentioning what remained of the conditions of the expedition of Tabuk. This is the customary way of Arabic speech: they begin with a matter, then mention after it related things and elaborate on them, then return to that matter they had begun with.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Repentance from Allah is His returning to His servant from one state to a state higher than it. It is mostly a return from the state of disobedience to the state of obedience, and it may be a return from a state of obedience to one more complete than it. This is His repentance in this verse toward the Prophet ﷺ, because He returned him from a state before attaining the expedition and bearing its hardships, to a state after that more complete than it. As for His repentance toward the Emigrants and the Helpers, its state is open to being a return from deficiency to obedience and diligence in the expedition and in supporting the religion. As for His repentance toward the group, it is a return from a state of being brought low to a state of forgiveness and good pleasure.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Allah turned toward the Prophet" is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That Allah may forgive you your earlier and later sins﴾ [al-Fath: 2] and ﴿and ask forgiveness for your sin﴾ [Ghafir: 55]. It is an exhortation to the believers to repentance, and that there is no believer but that he is in need of repentance and seeking forgiveness, even the Prophet, the Emigrants and the Helpers; and it is a manifestation of the excellence of repentance and its worth before Allah, exalted is He, and that the attribute of those who repent much is the attribute of the prophets, just as He described them as the righteous so that the virtue of righteousness might appear. It was said: its meaning is that Allah turned toward Him (the Prophet) from His permission to the hypocrites to remain behind from him, according to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah pardon you! Why did you grant them permission?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 43]. End of quote. It was also said: it is not far-fetched that there proceeded from the Emigrants and the Helpers various kinds of violations, but He, exalted is He, turned toward them and pardoned them because they bore the hardships of that journey. Then He, exalted is He, joined the mention of the Messenger ﷺ with their mention, as an indication of the greatness of their ranks in accepting repentance.

﴿ittaba'uhu﴾ means: they followed his command, so this is a figurative ellipsis (majaz al-hadhf). It is also permissible that he himself began the going forth and they went forth after him, in which case "following" is literal.

﴿sa'at al-'usrah﴾ means: at the time of hardship. The word "sa'ah" (hour) is used metaphorically for unrestricted time, just as they used "ghadah" (morning), "'ashiyyah" (evening) and "yawm" (day). A poet said:

"In the morning when the flags of Bakr ibn Wa'il hovered, and in the evening when we fought Judham and Himyar."

Another said:

"When my heir comes to me one day seeking wealth..."

That expedition of Tabuk was called the expedition of hardship. It is also permissible that by "the hour of hardship" he means the hour in which their resolve and their readiness to bear the difficulty occurred, since the whole journey follows that hour, and by it and in it the reward from Allah occurs and the intention is bound. Whoever resolves to join the expedition while in straitened circumstances has spent in an hour of hardship; and if it happened that wealth came to them during the rest of their journey, that would not undermine their being followers in the hour of hardship. "Al-'usrah" means constriction, severity and want. This is the army of hardship concerning which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever equips the army of hardship, for him is Paradise." Uthman ibn Affan equipped it with a thousand camels and a thousand dinars. It is related that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ turned the dinars over with his hand and said: "Nothing will harm Uthman what he does after this." And a man of the Helpers brought seven hundred wasq of wheat. Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Hasan said: The hardship reached them to the point that ten of them would take turns on one camel because of the scarcity of mounts, and to the point that they divided a date between two men, and a group would take one date, and one of them would suck it and drink water after it, and then all of them would do the same with it. Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: In some part of it a severe thirst befell them, so that they began to slaughter the camels and drink what was in their stomachs of water, [p. 109] and squeeze the dung, until the Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked for water. He raised his hands in supplication, and he did not lower them until a cloud poured down. They drank, stored water, and then departed, and the cloud had not left the camp. In this expedition, from hunger, they resolved to slaughter the camels, so he ordered the collection of the surplus of their provisions, until a small amount gathered on the leather mat. He invoked blessing upon it, then said: "Take in your vessels," and they filled them until no vessel remained. All the people ate until they were satisfied, and some surplus remained. The army was thirty thousand and more, and this was his last expedition. In it he left 'Ali behind in Medina. The hypocrites said he left him out of hatred for him, so he informed him of their statement, and he said: "Are you not content that you stand to me in the position of Harun to Musa?" He ﷺ reached the outskirts of the enemy's lands, dispatched detachments, and the people of Adhruh, Aylah and others made peace with him on payment of the jizyah, and he returned.

﴿yazighu qulubu fariq﴾: al-Hasan said: a group resolved to turn back because of the hardship they encountered. It was also said: their swerving was through suspicions that gave them bad thoughts about the Messenger's resolve for that expedition, because of what they saw of the severity of the hardship, the scarcity of provisions, the distance of the journey, and the strength of the enemy targeted. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Tazigu" means they deviated from the truth in the pledge. The word "kada" (nearly) indicates proximity, not actual involvement in the swerving. Hamzah and Hafs read "yazigu" with the ya', so it is necessary that the pronoun in "kada" be the pronoun of the matter (ism al-sha'n), and the raising of "qulub" is by "tazigu", because it is impossible for "qulub" to be the subject of "kada" with "tazigu" in the position of the predicate, since the intended order would be delayed. It is not permissible to say: "min ba'di ma kada qulubun yazigu" with the ya'. The rest of the seven read with the ta', so it is possible that "qulub" is the subject of "kada" and "tazigu" is the predicate, with an element placed between them, just as is done with "kana". Abu 'Ali said: This is not permissible with "'asa". It is also possible that the subject of "kada" is a pronoun referring to the plural that the mention of the Emigrants and Helpers implies, meaning: after what he (i.e. the group) nearly did, that is, the group. Ibn 'Atiyyah and Abu al-Baqa' supposed the nominative of "kada" to be an explicit noun, namely "the people", as if he said: after what the people nearly did. Each of these three analyses raises a difficulty according to what is established in the science of grammar: that the predicate of verbs of approximation (af'al al-muqarabah) must only be an imperfect verb raising a pronoun referring to its subject. Some made this general, and some restricted it to verbs other than "'asa", and it cannot be a causal clause. This differs from "kana", for its predicate raises a pronoun, and the causal clause is for the subject of "kada". So if we assume a pronoun of the matter in it, the clause is in the position of an accusative predicate, and the nominative is not a pronoun referring to the subject of "kada", nor a causal clause for it. This also applies to the reading with the ya'. As for placing the predicate in the middle, it is based on the permissibility of such a construction in examples like "kana yaqumu Zaydun", and this is disputed, and the correct view is prohibition. As for the other analysis, it is very weak, because it posits in "kada" a pronoun that has no referent except by assumption, and because the predicate of "kada" would be a causal clause. These difficulties are resolved by holding that "kada" is redundant (za'idah), its meaning intended but having no governing effect on a subject or predicate, so it is like "kana" when it is redundant: its meaning is intended and it has no effect. This interpretation is supported by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "min ba'di ma zaghat" without "kada". The Kufans went to the view that it is redundant in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿he could hardly see it﴾ [al-Nur: 40], despite its effect on the governed element and its own governing. So it is more fitting to claim its redundancy here, since it is neither governing nor governed.

Al-A'mash and al-Jahdari read "tuzigu" with a damma on the ta'. Ubayy read: "min ba'di ma kadat tazigu".

﴿thumma taba 'alayhim﴾: the pronoun in "'alayhim" refers either to the former group or to the party, so the sentence is repeated for emphasis. Or the first refers to the initiation of repentance and the second to its continuation. Or, since He mentioned that a group of them had nearly had their hearts swerve, He stated the repentance a second time to remove the suspicion that they were left unmentioned regarding repentance; then He mentioned the cause of repentance, which is His compassion toward them and His mercy for them.

The three who were left behind, their names have already been mentioned. The meaning of "khullifu" (were left behind) is from the expedition, the expedition of Tabuk, as said by Qatadah. Or they were left behind from Abu Lubabah and his companions, when repentance was accepted for them after the repentance of Abu Lubabah and his companions, and the postponement of their matter for fifty days, after which He accepted their repentance. Ka'b ibn Malik himself rejected Qatadah's interpretation, saying: The meaning of "khullifu" is that they were left aside from accepting the excuse, and it is not about our staying behind from the expedition. The majority read "khullifu" with a shaddah on the lam, in the passive voice. Abu Malik read it likewise but with the lam unstressed. 'Ikrimah ibn Harun al-Makhzumi, Dhirr ibn Hubaysh, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, Mu'adh al-Qari' and Humayd read it with the lam unstressed in the active voice, and it is related from Abu 'Amr; that is: they left the fighters behind in Medina, or they corrupted, from "al-khalifah" (corruption). Abu al-'Aliyah and Abu al-Jawza' read it likewise with the lam stressed. Abu Zayd, Abu Mijlaz, al-Sha'bi, Ibn Ya'mar, 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, and his two sons Zayd and Muhammad al-Baqir, and his son Ja'far al-Sadiq read "khalafu" with an alif, meaning: they did not agree to the expedition. Al-Baqir said: Had they been left behind, it would not have been for them. Al-A'mash read "wa 'ala al-thalathati al-mukhallafina" (the three who were made to stay behind), and perhaps he read it that way as an explanation, since this reading differs from the written text of the codex.

﴿hatta idha dagat 'alayhimu al-ardu bima rahubat﴾: the explanation of its parallel has already been given in this surah, in the story of Hunayn. "And their souls became confining for them" is a metaphor, because grief and sorrow filled them so that no comfort or joy could fit in them, and they went beyond the extreme of loneliness and distress.

﴿wa-zannu﴾ means: they knew. So said al-Zamakhshari. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: they were certain, as they said in the verse of the poet:

"So I said to them: Be certain of two thousand armored men, their chiefs in coats of mail woven of Persian fabric."

Some said: "zann" here is in its usual sense of preponderance of one of two possibilities, because their matter had been left to revelation, and they were not certain that a Qur'an would come down concerning them; or they were certain, but they considered that the period of their remaining in hardship might be prolonged, so the "zann" returned to considering that period to be short. These sentences came under "idha" in the utmost beauty and order. He mentioned first the narrowness of the earth for them, which is a metaphor for their being shunned and people turning away from speaking to them. Second: ﴿and their souls became confining for them﴾, which is a metaphor for the constant succession of worry and grief on their hearts, until nothing in them remained of expansiveness and spaciousness. So He mentioned first the narrowness of the place, then second the narrowness of the state within it, because a place may be narrow while the soul remains expansive.

ﾠ"Sammu al-khiyat ma'a al-mahbubi maydanu" (the eye of the needle, with the beloved, is a wide field).

Thirdly, when they despaired of the creatures, they placed their affairs in the hands of Allah and turned to Him exclusively. They knew that none relieves them of hardship or removes it except the Exalted. ﴿Then, when adversity touches you, to Him you cry for help﴾ [al-Nahl: 53]. As for "idha" (إذا, "when"), if it is conditional (shartiyyah), its answer (jawab) is omitted. Its estimated sense is "He turned to them in repentance," and His saying ﴿then He turned to them﴾ is similar to His saying ﴿Allah has certainly turned in forgiveness to the Prophet﴾ [al-Tawbah: 117], and the rest of the verse. The claim that "thumma" (ثُمَّ, "then") is superfluous and that the answer of "idha" is what follows "thumma" is very far-fetched. The use of "thumma" as superfluous is not established in the language of the Arabs. As for one who holds that "idha" after "hatta" (حَتّى, "until") may be stripped of the conditional sense and remain merely for the sense of time, so that it requires no answer but serves as the endpoint (ghayah) of the verb preceding it, which is His saying "they were left behind" (khullifu), meaning "they were left behind until this time," then ﴿He turned to them that they might repent﴾. Then He returned to them with acceptance and mercy once more, so that they might remain steadfast in their repentance and turn back in penitence. Or it means that they should repent also in the future, should any wrongdoing proceed from them, knowing that Allah is ever-Relenting toward whoever repents, even if he returns to it a hundred times a day. It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿that they might repent﴾ is that they might persist in repentance and not return to what nullifies it. It has also been said: ﴿that they might repent﴾ means that they might return to their former state and custom of mixing with the believers, and their souls would be at ease thereby. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Since this statement is an enumeration of His favors, He began its arrangement with the side that comes from Allah, the Exalted, so that this would alert to receiving the blessing from Him, there being no lord other than Him. Had the statement been an enumeration of a sin, the beginning would have been with the side that comes from the sinner, as the Exalted said: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [al-Saff: 5], so that this would more firmly establish the sin upon them. This is among the eloquence of the Qur'an, its wondrous composition, and its inimitable coherence. The explanation of this verse and the positions of its words is completed by reading the narration of the three who were left behind. Al-Bukhari and Muslim have transmitted their hadith in full, and it is found in the biographies (al-siyar). Therefore I have abridged its presentation. Their sin was grave, and they deserved this because the Law demands from them a strict standard (hadd) in accordance with their ranks and their precedence in it, since they were a model and a proof for the hypocrites and the detractors, Ka'b being one of the people of 'Aqabah, and his two companions being of the people of Badr. This implies that the learned man who is taken as a model has less excuse for falling short than anyone else. Al-Awza'i wrote to al-Mansur Abu Ja'far in the final part of a letter: "Know that your kinship to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ will only increase Allah's right over you in greatness, his obedience in obligation, and the people's denunciation of you for whatever opposes that." Peace. Al-Qadi al-Tanukhi spoke well in his saying:
"Blame clings to the great, and the great are greatly blamed."
It is related that some of the believers stayed behind from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Among them were those who later changed their minds and joined them, like Abu Khaythamah, and among them were those who remained and did not join them, namely the three. Abu Bakr al-Warraq was asked about sincere repentance (al-tawbah al-nasuhah), and he said: "That the earth becomes constricted upon the penitent despite its vastness, and his own soul becomes constricted upon him, as with the repentance of Ka'b ibn Malik and his two companions."

These difficulties are resolved by holding that "kada" is redundant (za'idah), its meaning intended but having no governing effect on a subject or predicate, so it is like "kana" when it is redundant: its meaning is intended and it has no effect. This interpretation is supported by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "min ba'di ma zaghat" without "kada". The Kufans went to the view that it is redundant in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿he could hardly see it﴾ [al-Nur: 40], despite its effect on the governed element and its own governing. So it is more fitting to claim its redundancy here, since it is neither governing nor governed.

Al-A'mash and al-Jahdari read "tuzigu" with a damma on the ta'. Ubayy read: "min ba'di ma kadat tazigu".

﴿thumma taba 'alayhim﴾: the pronoun in "'alayhim" refers either to the former group or to the party, so the sentence is repeated for emphasis. Or the first refers to the initiation of repentance and the second to its continuation. Or, since He mentioned that a group of them had nearly had their hearts swerve, He stated the repentance a second time to remove the suspicion that they were left unmentioned regarding repentance; then He mentioned the cause of repentance, which is His compassion toward them and His mercy for them.

The three who were left behind, their names have already been mentioned. The meaning of "khullifu" (were left behind) is from the expedition, the expedition of Tabuk, as said by Qatadah. Or they were left behind from Abu Lubabah and his companions, when repentance was accepted for them after the repentance of Abu Lubabah and his companions, and the postponement of their matter for fifty days, after which He accepted their repentance. Ka'b ibn Malik himself rejected Qatadah's interpretation, saying: The meaning of "khullifu" is that they were left aside from accepting the excuse, and it is not about our staying behind from the expedition. The majority read "khullifu" with a shaddah on the lam, in the passive voice. Abu Malik read it likewise but with the lam unstressed. 'Ikrimah ibn Harun al-Makhzumi, Dhirr ibn Hubaysh, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, Mu'adh al-Qari' and Humayd read it with the lam unstressed in the active voice, and it is related from Abu 'Amr; that is: they left the fighters behind in Medina, or they corrupted, from "al-khalifah" (corruption). Abu al-'Aliyah and Abu al-Jawza' read it likewise with the lam stressed. Abu Zayd, Abu Mijlaz, al-Sha'bi, Ibn Ya'mar, 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, and his two sons Zayd and Muhammad al-Baqir, and his son Ja'far al-Sadiq read "khalafu" with an alif, meaning: they did not agree to the expedition. Al-Baqir said: Had they been left behind, it would not have been for them. Al-A'mash read "wa 'ala al-thalathati al-mukhallafina" (the three who were made to stay behind), and perhaps he read it that way as an explanation, since this reading differs from the written text of the codex.

﴿hatta idha dagat 'alayhimu al-ardu bima rahubat﴾: the explanation of its parallel has already been given in this surah, in the story of Hunayn. "And their souls became confining for them" is a metaphor, because grief and sorrow filled them so that no comfort or joy could fit in them, and they went beyond the extreme of loneliness and distress.

﴿wa-zannu﴾ means: they knew. So said al-Zamakhshari. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: they were certain, as they said in the verse of the poet:

"So I said to them: Be certain of two thousand armored men, their chiefs in coats of mail woven of Persian fabric."

Some said: "zann" here is in its usual sense of preponderance of one of two possibilities, because their matter had been left to revelation, and they were not certain that a Qur'an would come down concerning them; or they were certain, but they considered that the period of their remaining in hardship might be prolonged, so the "zann" returned to considering that period to be short. These sentences came under "idha" in the utmost beauty and order. He mentioned first the narrowness of the earth for them, which is a metaphor for their being shunned and people turning away from speaking to them. Second: ﴿and their souls became confining for them﴾, which is a metaphor for the constant succession of worry and grief on their hearts, until nothing in them remained of expansiveness and spaciousness. So He mentioned first the narrowness of the place, then second the narrowness of the state within it, because a place may be narrow while the soul remains expansive.

ﾠ"Sammu al-khiyat ma'a al-mahbubi maydanu" (the eye of the needle, with the beloved, is a wide field).

Thirdly, when they despaired of the creatures, they placed their affairs in the hands of Allah and turned to Him exclusively. They knew that none relieves them of hardship or removes it except the Exalted. ﴿Then, when adversity touches you, to Him you cry for help﴾ [al-Nahl: 53]. As for "idha" (إذا, "when"), if it is conditional (shartiyyah), its answer (jawab) is omitted. Its estimated sense is "He turned to them in repentance," and His saying ﴿then He turned to them﴾ is similar to His saying ﴿Allah has certainly turned in forgiveness to the Prophet﴾ [al-Tawbah: 117], and the rest of the verse. The claim that "thumma" (ثُمَّ, "then") is superfluous and that the answer of "idha" is what follows "thumma" is very far-fetched. The use of "thumma" as superfluous is not established in the language of the Arabs. As for one who holds that "idha" after "hatta" (حَتّى, "until") may be stripped of the conditional sense and remain merely for the sense of time, so that it requires no answer but serves as the endpoint (ghayah) of the verb preceding it, which is His saying "they were left behind" (khullifu), meaning "they were left behind until this time," then ﴿He turned to them that they might repent﴾. Then He returned to them with acceptance and mercy once more, so that they might remain steadfast in their repentance and turn back in penitence. Or it means that they should repent also in the future, should any wrongdoing proceed from them, knowing that Allah is ever-Relenting toward whoever repents, even if he returns to it a hundred times a day. It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿that they might repent﴾ is that they might persist in repentance and not return to what nullifies it. It has also been said: ﴿that they might repent﴾ means that they might return to their former state and custom of mixing with the believers, and their souls would be at ease thereby. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Since this statement is an enumeration of His favors, He began its arrangement with the side that comes from Allah, the Exalted, so that this would alert to receiving the blessing from Him, there being no lord other than Him. Had the statement been an enumeration of a sin, the beginning would have been with the side that comes from the sinner, as the Exalted said: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [al-Saff: 5], so that this would more firmly establish the sin upon them. This is among the eloquence of the Qur'an, its wondrous composition, and its inimitable coherence. The explanation of this verse and the positions of its words is completed by reading the narration of the three who were left behind. Al-Bukhari and Muslim have transmitted their hadith in full, and it is found in the biographies (al-siyar). Therefore I have abridged its presentation. Their sin was grave, and they deserved this because the Law demands from them a strict standard (hadd) in accordance with their ranks and their precedence in it, since they were a model and a proof for the hypocrites and the detractors, Ka'b being one of the people of 'Aqabah, and his two companions being of the people of Badr. This implies that the learned man who is taken as a model has less excuse for falling short than anyone else. Al-Awza'i wrote to al-Mansur Abu Ja'far in the final part of a letter: "Know that your kinship to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ will only increase Allah's right over you in greatness, his obedience in obligation, and the people's denunciation of you for whatever opposes that." Peace. Al-Qadi al-Tanukhi spoke well in his saying:
"Blame clings to the great, and the great are greatly blamed."
It is related that some of the believers stayed behind from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Among them were those who later changed their minds and joined them, like Abu Khaythamah, and among them were those who remained and did not join them, namely the three. Abu Bakr al-Warraq was asked about sincere repentance (al-tawbah al-nasuhah), and he said: "That the earth becomes constricted upon the penitent despite its vastness, and his own soul becomes constricted upon him, as with the repentance of Ka'b ibn Malik and his two companions."

O you who believe, fear God and be with the truthful. This is an address to the believers, commanded to be with the people of truthfulness after the mention of the story of the three whose truthfulness benefited them and freed them from the noose of hypocrisy. This sentence was inserted as an alert to the rank of truthfulness, and it is enough of its merit that it comes second to the rank of prophethood in His words: ﴿Those are with the ones whom God has blessed among the prophets and the truthful ones﴾ [an-Nisa: 69]. Ibn Juraij and others said: "Truthfulness here means truthfulness of speech." Al-Dahhak and Nafi' said, in substance: "The wording is more general than truthfulness of speech. It means soundness in religion and steadfastness in goodness, as the Arabs say, 'a man of truthfulness' (rajul sidq)." This group said: "Be with Muhammad, Abu Bakr, Umar and the best of the Emigrants (Muhajirun), who were truthful to God in Islam." It was also said: "They are the three," meaning: be like these in their truthfulness and their steadfastness. Al-Zamakhshari said: "They are those who were truthful in their faith and in their covenant with God and His Messenger, from His words: ﴿There are men who were true to what they covenanted with God﴾ [al-Ahzab: 23]. They are those who were truthful in the religion of God in intention, speech and action." End of quote. It was also said: the address "those who believe" is directed at those among the Tulaqa' (the freed ones, i.e., those freed at the Conquest) who stayed behind from the expedition of Tabuk. From Ibn Abbas: the address is to those among the People of the Book who believed, meaning: be with the Emigrants and the Helpers (Ansar). The word "with" (ma'a) requires companionship in the present state and sharing in the attribute that merits praise. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas read: (min al-sadiqin) ("from the truthful"), and it was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ). Ibn Mas'ud used to interpret it as truthfulness of speech and said: "Lying is not fit from anyone, whether in earnest or in jest, nor that any one of you promise his child and then not fulfil it. Recite, if you wish: ﴿And be with the truthful﴾." The author of al-Lawami' said: "'Min' is more general than 'ma'a', because whoever is from a people is with them in the meaning commanded, but the reverse does not hold." Zayd ibn Ali, Ibn al-Sumayqa', Abu al-Mutawakkil and Mu'adh al-Qari recited: ﴿ma'a al-sadiqin﴾ with a fatha on the qaf and a kasra on the nun, in the dual form (ma'a al-sadiqayn, "with the two truthful ones"). It appears that the two are God and His Messenger, based on His words: ﴿When the believers saw the confederates, they said: "This is what God and His Messenger promised us, and God and His Messenger spoke the truth"﴾ [al-Ahzab: 22], and because of what preceded: ﴿and they knew that there is no refuge from God except in Him﴾ [at-Tawbah: 118]. They were commanded to be with God and His Messenger by complying with the command and avoiding what is forbidden, just as it is said: "Be with God, and He will be with you."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verses 120–121:

﴿It was not for the people of Medina and those Bedouins around them to remain behind from the Messenger of Allah, nor to prefer themselves over his own self. That is because they will not suffer thirst, nor fatigue, nor hunger in the way of Allah, nor tread on any ground that enrages the disbelievers, nor gain anything from an enemy except that a righteous deed is recorded for them thereby. Indeed, Allah does not waste the reward of the good-doers.﴾ ﴿And they do not spend any expenditure, small or great, nor cross any valley, except that it is recorded for them, that Allah may reward them with the best of what they used to do.﴾ (p-112) They were revealed concerning those of the people of Medina who stayed behind from the expedition of Tabuk, and concerning those Bedouins around them who stayed behind, from Muzaynah, Juhaynah, Ashja', Aslam and Ghifar. Its connection to what precedes it: when He commanded the believers to fear Allah, and commanded them to be with the truthful, and the best of the truthful is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), then the Muhajirun and the Ansar, this required accompanying the Messenger and keeping company with him wherever he went of the campaigns and battlefields. So whoever stayed behind from the Messenger in a campaign was severely reproached, and this command required companionship with him and the sacrifice of souls in his defence. Al-Zamakhshari said: that they should accompany him in hardship and adversity, and they were commanded to endure with him the terrors with eagerness, energy and gladness, and to cast themselves into hardships as he (ﷺ) himself encountered them, knowing that his soul is the most honoured and dearest soul to Allah the Exalted. So when it is exposed, along with its honour and dignity, to plunging into hardship and ease, it becomes obligatory upon all other souls that they rush toward what it has been exposed to, and their owners should not be concerned for them, nor give them any weight, and they should be the lightest and least thing for them, let alone that they should refrain from following and accompanying them, and grudge them against what he granted his own soul. This is an emphatic prohibition, along with a censure of their matter and a rebuke to them for it, and an incitement to follow him with pride and zeal. Al-Karmani said: this is a negation whose meaning is a prohibition, and these were singled out for mention, though all people are equal in this, because of their nearness to him and because his departure is not hidden from them. Qatadah said: this obligation was specific to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the response to going forth to fight when he himself went out. This ruling did not remain for anyone else among the caliphs. Zayd ibn Aslam said: this command and obligation was during the weakness of Islam and the need for the joining of hands, then it was abrogated when Islam became strong, by His saying: ﴿It is not for the believers to go forth all together﴾ [al-Tawbah: 122]. He said: all of this concerns setting out to fight an enemy for the sake of entering Islam. As for when the enemy attacks a region, it becomes obligatory upon every individual to repel and confront it. The indication by that is to what the negation of staying behind includes of the obligation to go out with him and to sacrifice the self in his defence, as if it were said: that obligation to go out and sacrifice the self is because of what Allah has prepared for them of great reward for the hardships that befall them, and for what is accomplished at their hands of harming the enemies of Islam. Al-Zama'ah (thirst) is thirst. Ubayd ibn Umayr read (ظِماءٌ) with a long vowel, like سَفِهَ سِفاهًا. Since thirst is the most difficult of the harmful things for the traveller, through much movement and the disturbing of the soul, especially in the severe heat such as the expedition of Tabuk, it was mentioned first. He followed it with نَصَب, which is weariness, because it is the exhaustion that reaches the traveller and the fatigue arising from thirst and travel. And he came third with hunger, because it is a state that can be endured for many periods, unlike thirst and weariness, which lead to ruin and cutting off from the journey. So the report of what befalls the traveller came first, then second, then third. And مَوْطِئًا is a noun of place or of the verbal noun from وَطِئَ; it may be a place, and it may be a verbal noun. The subject in (يَغِيظُ) refers back to the noun: either to مَوْطِئٍ if it is a verbal noun, or to what is understood from مَوْطِئٍ if it is a place, meaning: their treading upon it enrages the disbelievers. He left مَوْطِئًا unrestricted when it is a place, to include every place whose treading enrages the disbelievers, whether it is one of the places of the disbelievers or one of the places of the Muslims, if its traversal causes them rage. Treading includes treading with hooves, hoofs and feet. Zayd ibn Ali read (يُغِيظُ) with a dammah on the ya'. The word نَيْل is a verbal noun, and it may remain on its original meaning, and it may be intended as the thing gained. He left نَيْلًا unrestricted to include the little and the much of what distresses them: killing, capture, booty, or defeat. The ya' in نَيْل is not a substitution for a waw, contrary to the claim of one who asserts it; rather نال has two roots: one from the waw-form: نِلْتُهُ أنُولُهُ نَوْلًا ونَوالًا meaning a gift, and from it التَّناوُل; and the other is this one from the ya'-form: نِلْتُهُ نالَهُ نَيْلًا when it reaches and overtakes him. In these two sentences also he began with the earlier, which is treading, then followed with gaining from the enemy. The generality in (الكُفّارِ) comes with the definite article, and in "مِن عَدُوٍّ" because it is in the context of negation. (p-113) He began first with what urges the traveller in jihad within himself, then second with what follows from enduring those hardships: the enragement of the disbelievers and gaining from the enemy. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible that by treading is meant overwhelming and annihilation, not treading with feet and hooves, as in his saying, peace be upon him: "The last trampling that Allah trampled upon Wajj." The writing here may be taken literally, that is, it is recorded in the scrolls or in the Preserved Tablet, so that he may be recompensed for it on the Day of Resurrection. It may also be a metaphor, expressing establishment by writing, since whoever wishes to establish something writes it down. The clause "كُتِبَ" is in the position of a circumstantial clause, and for this reason the pronoun is singular, treating it as the demonstrative, as if it were said: except that a righteous deed is recorded for them thereby, that is, by the befalling of thirst, weariness, hunger, treading and gaining. In a hadith: "Whoever has his feet covered in dust in the way of Allah, Allah forbids him from the Fire." Ibn Abbas said: for every fright that befalls them in the way of Allah, seventy thousand good deeds. Small expenditure: Ibn Abbas said: like a date and the like, and great is what exceeds it. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿small﴾ even if a date, even if the lash of a whip, ﴿nor great﴾ like what Uthman spent in the army of hardship. End. He placed ﴿small﴾ first out of concern, like His saying: ﴿leaves out nothing small or great﴾ [al-Kahf: 49], ﴿nor smaller than that nor greater﴾ [Yunus: 61]. If the reward of the small is recorded, then the reward of the great is more deserving. The object of ﴿كُتِبَ﴾ is an implied pronoun referring back to the verbal noun understood from ﴿يُنْفِقُونَ﴾ and ﴿يَقْطَعُونَ﴾, as if it were said: it was recorded for them, that is, the spending and the crossing. It is also permissible that it refers to the previously mentioned ﴿عَمَلٌ صالِحٌ﴾. These two sentences were delayed and those preceding sentences were placed first, because they are more burdensome on the soul and more painful to the enemy, while these two are easier, since they concern wealth and crossing land to the enemy, whether or not the enragement of the disbelievers and the gaining from the enemy occur. So this is more general and that is more specific. The explanation of the former is more emphatic, since it came with the nominal sentence emphasized by "إنَّ", and mentioned the reward in it. The word ﴿al-muhsinin﴾ is to alert that they have attained the ranks of excellence which are the highest ranks of the believers. In these two sentences the particle of purpose (لام العلة) is used, and it is connected to (كُتِبَ). The estimated meaning is: the best reward for what they used to do, because their deed has a good reward, and it has a better reward, and here the reward is the best reward. Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: ﴿the best of what they used to do﴾ has two aspects. The first: that "أحسن" is a description of their action, and in it is what is obligatory and recommended, but not what is permissible. End of this aspect. So it is possible that ﴿أحسن﴾ is a substitute for the pronoun in ﴿لِيَجْزِيَهُمُ﴾ as a substitute of inclusion, as if it were said: that Allah may reward the best of their actions with the best of reward, or with whatever reward He wills. It is also possible that this is by elision of a noun, so the estimate would be: that He may reward them the reward of the best of their actions. The second: that the "أحسن" is a description of the reward, that is, He rewards them with a reward that is better than their deeds and more majestic and excellent, namely the reward. End of this aspect. If "أحسن" is a description of the reward, then how is it added to the deeds when no part of them is from them? And how does the superlative occur then between the reward and the deeds, without being stated with "مِن"?

The object of ﴿كُتِبَ﴾ is an implied pronoun referring back to the verbal noun understood from ﴿يُنْفِقُونَ﴾ and ﴿يَقْطَعُونَ﴾, as if it were said: it was recorded for them, that is, the spending and the crossing. It is also permissible that it refers to the previously mentioned ﴿عَمَلٌ صالِحٌ﴾. These two sentences were delayed and those preceding sentences were placed first, because they are more burdensome on the soul and more painful to the enemy, while these two are easier, since they concern wealth and crossing land to the enemy, whether or not the enragement of the disbelievers and the gaining from the enemy occur. So this is more general and that is more specific. The explanation of the former is more emphatic, since it came with the nominal sentence emphasized by "إنَّ", and mentioned the reward in it. The word ﴿al-muhsinin﴾ is to alert that they have attained the ranks of excellence which are the highest ranks of the believers. In these two sentences the particle of purpose (لام العلة) is used, and it is connected to (كُتِبَ). The estimated meaning is: the best reward for what they used to do, because their deed has a good reward, and it has a better reward, and here the reward is the best reward. Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: ﴿the best of what they used to do﴾ has two aspects. The first: that "أحسن" is a description of their action, and in it is what is obligatory and recommended, but not what is permissible. End of this aspect. So it is possible that ﴿أحسن﴾ is a substitute for the pronoun in ﴿لِيَجْزِيَهُمُ﴾ as a substitute of inclusion, as if it were said: that Allah may reward the best of their actions with the best of reward, or with whatever reward He wills. It is also possible that this is by elision of a noun, so the estimate would be: that He may reward them the reward of the best of their actions. The second: that the "أحسن" is a description of the reward, that is, He rewards them with a reward that is better than their deeds and more majestic and excellent, namely the reward. End of this aspect. If "أحسن" is a description of the reward, then how is it added to the deeds when no part of them is from them? And how does the superlative occur then between the reward and the deeds, without being stated with "مِن"?

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verse 122:

﴿It was not for the believers to go forth all together. Why should not a group from every division of them go forth, so that they might gain understanding of the religion, and warn their people when they return to them, so that they may beware?﴾: When they heard ﴿It was not for the people of Madinah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 120] and the rest of the verse, it concerned them, so they set out for Madinah to the Messenger, and this verse was revealed. It was also said that when the verse ﴿It was not for the people of Madinah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 120] was revealed, the hypocrites said: "This applies to the people of the desert too," so this verse was revealed. It was also said that when the Messenger (ﷺ) invoked a curse upon Mudar with years of drought, they were struck by famine, so they set out for Madinah in search of sustenance, and they nearly corrupted it. Most of them were not sound in faith, and hunger alone had brought them, so the verse was revealed, and it said: "It was not for those weak in faith to set out in such a departure", meaning: these people are not believers. According to these views, the departure is not for military campaign (ghazw), and the pronoun in ﴿li-yatafaqqahu﴾ (so that they may gain understanding, *liyatafaqqahu*) refers to the departing group. This is the apparent meaning. Ibn Abbas said: the verse concerns the detachments (bu'ut) and expeditions (saraya). The preceding verse remains in effect when the Messenger goes out on a campaign, and this verse remains in effect when he does not go out, meaning: when he does not go out, it is obligatory that people not all depart together, so that he remains alone. Rather, it is fitting that a group depart while another group remains, so that this remaining group gains understanding of the religion and warns those who depart when they return to them. A group said: this verse abrogates (naskh) everything that obliges all people to depart and fight. According to this view and the view of Ibn Abbas, the pronoun in ﴿li-yatafaqqahu﴾ refers to the group remaining with the Prophet (ﷺ), and the meaning of ﴿wa-li-yundhiru qawmahum﴾ (and that they may warn their people) is: the group departing for the campaign informs them of what new rulings of the Shari'ah and its obligations have arisen. There was an omitted clause indicated by its division, meaning: "Why did not a group from every division of them go forth, while another group stayed behind, so that they might gain understanding?" It was also said: on the basis that the departure is for military campaign, it is valid for the pronoun in ﴿li-yatafaqqahu﴾ to refer to those who depart, and their gaining understanding (tafaqquh) occurs in the campaign through what they see of God's support for His religion and His granting victory to the small group of believers over the numerous unbelievers. This is evidence for the truth of Islam and for the Messenger's report that this religion would prevail. What appears to be the case is that this verse came only to urge the seeking of knowledge and gaining understanding of God's religion, and that it is not possible for all the believers to travel in this way, leaving their lands bare of them so that their enemies seize them and their offspring. So why did not a group of them travel for gaining understanding of the religion and for warning their people? Here He mentions the reason for the departure, which is gaining understanding first, then informing their people of what they have learned of the matters of the Shari'ah. Meaning: why did not a small group from every large community depart, so that they would suffice the departure, and each would take up a concern: this group guarding their lands and fighting their enemies, and that group learning knowledge and conveying it to those who remain when they return to them.

The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that both departures are in the way of God and the revival of His religion: this one by knowledge, and that one by fighting. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿li-yatafaqqahu fi'l-din﴾ (so that they may gain understanding in the religion) means that they should take upon themselves the effort of understanding it, and endure hardships in acquiring and attaining it, ﴿wa-li-yundhiru qawmahum﴾ (and warn their people) and make their aim and the goal of their resolve in understanding the warning of their people, guiding them, and counseling them, ﴿la'allahum yahdharun﴾ (so that they may beware), meaning that they may beware of God Most High, and thus do righteous deeds. Another aspect: when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent out a detachment after the Battle of Tabuk, and after the severe verses concerning those who stayed behind had been revealed, all the believers, every one of them, rushed to the departure, and they all cut themselves off from revelation and from gaining understanding of the religion. So they were commanded that a group from every division should depart to jihad, while their remnants remain gaining understanding, so that they would not be cut off from the understanding which is the greater jihad, because jihad by proof is greater in matter than jihad by the sword. As for His saying ﴿li-yatafaqqahu﴾, the pronoun in it refers to the divisions remaining after the departing groups, and ﴿wa-li-yundhiru qawmahum﴾ (and let them warn their people) means that the remaining divisions should warn their people who departed, when they return to them, of the knowledge they gained during their absence. On the first view, the pronoun refers to the group departing to Madinah for gaining understanding.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verse 123:

﴿O you who believe, fight those of the disbelievers who are near you, and let them find in you harshness; and know that Allah is with the God-fearing.﴾: When the Exalted commanded seeking understanding in the religion (tafaqquh fi al-din) and urged a group of the believers to set out in pursuit of it, the Exalted commanded all the believers to fight those of the disbelievers who are near them. Thus He combined in jihad both the jihad of argument (jihad al-hujjah) and the jihad of the sword (jihad al-sayf). Some of the poets said on this:

"Whoever is not straightened by the Qur'an, for him there is straightening by humiliation and by the Indian swords."

It has been said: it was revealed before the command to kill the disbelievers entirely, so it belongs to the gradual stages that were in the early period of Islam. This view is considered weak, because this verse is among the last of what was revealed. Another group said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would sometimes pass over a people of the disbelievers while campaigning against others farther away than them, so Allah commanded fighting the nearer ones first, then the nearer to Medina. Another group said: the verse clarifies the form of fighting in general; it is therefore connected with the command to fight the disbelievers entirely, and its meaning is that Allah the Exalted commanded in it the believers that each group among them should fight the army of the disbelievers that presses upon it. This is the fighting for the Word of Allah and the repelling of harm from Islam. As for when the enemy inclines toward one region of the lands of the Muslims, it is an obligation (p-115) upon those believers who are connected to it to suffice against the enemy of that region, even if the abode is distant and the lands far apart. Those who held this view said: the verse was revealed pointing to fighting the Romans in Syria, because they were on that day the enemy who is nearby and close, since the Arabs had been overtaken by Islam, while Iraq was distant. Then, when the scope of Islam expanded, the obligation to fight the Persians, the Daylam and others of the nations became incumbent. A man asked Ibn Umar about fighting the Daylam, and he said: "Stick to the Romans." Ali ibn al-Husayn and al-Hasan said: they are the Romans and the Daylam, meaning in their time. Ibn Zayd said: what is intended by this verse at the time of its revelation was the Arabs; when they were finished with, it was revealed concerning the Romans and others: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah nor in the Last Day﴾ [al-Tawbah: 29] to its end. It has been said: they are the Qurayzah, al-Nadir, Fadak and Khaybar. Some said: they were reluctant to fight their relatives and neighbours, so they were commanded to fight them.

﴿Yalunakum﴾: its apparent meaning is nearness in place. It has been said: it is general, covering nearness in place and in lineage, and beginning with fighting those who are nearest; because it is impossible to fight all of them at once, and we have been commanded to fight all of them, so preference by proximity became obligatory, as in other important matters such as invitation (da'wah), commanding good and forbidding evil. Also, the expenses in it, and the need for mounts and equipment, are less; also, fighting the more distant exposes the Muslims to the risk of turmoil (fitnah); also, if they are weak, subjugating them is easier and the arrival of non-Islam is more facile; and if they are strong, their assault upon the abode of Islam is more severe. Also, knowledge of those nearby is more pressing than knowledge of those far away, for the purpose of understanding their conditions, their equipment and their numbers. Thus beginning with fighting those nearby was preferred over fighting those far away.

The Exalted commanded the believers to be harsh and severe toward the disbelievers, as the Exalted said: ﴿Strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be harsh with them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 73]. This is so that it would be more awe-inspiring and more effective in instilling terror in their hearts. And He said: ﴿Humble toward the believers, mighty against the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 54]. In a hadith: "Meet the disbelievers with scowling faces." And the Exalted said: ﴿Do not weaken and do not grieve﴾ [Al 'Imran: 139], and He said: ﴿So they did not weaken for what befell them in the way of Allah, nor did they become feeble, nor did they submit﴾ [Al 'Imran: 146]. The ghilzah (harshness) combines boldness and steadfastness in fighting and intensity of enmity. Ghilzah is literally said of bodies, and here it is used figuratively for severity in war.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿ghilzah﴾ with a kasrah on the ghayn, and this is the dialect of Asad; al-A'mash, Aban ibn Tha'lab and al-Mufaddal, both from 'Asim, read it with a fathah, and this is the dialect of the Hijaz; Abu Haywah, al-Sulami, Ibn Abi Ablah, al-Mufaddal and Aban also read it with a dammah, and this is the dialect of Tamim; and from Abu 'Amr there are three dialects. Then He said: ﴿And know that Allah is with the God-fearing﴾, to draw attention to the fact that what should motivate fighting and the existence of harshness is only the fear of Allah the Exalted; and whoever fears Allah, Allah is with him by way of victory and support, and he does not intend by his fighting spoils, nor boasting, nor the display of bravery.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 9, verses 124–127:**

﴿When a surah is revealed, some of them say: "Which of you has had its faith increased by this?" As for those who believed, it has increased their faith, and they rejoice.﴾ ﴿As for those in whose hearts is a disease, it has added defilement to their defilement, and they died while they were disbelievers.﴾ Ibn Abbas said: These two verses, and the second, were revealed about the hypocrites. Whenever a surah was revealed that contained the faults of the hypocrites, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would address them and allude to them in his sermon. Some of them would look at others, wanting to flee, and would say: "Does anyone see you if you stand up?" If no one saw them, they would leave the mosque. When [the discourse] digressed from the account of the expedition to battle and the reproach of those who stayed behind from the Messenger, to the expedition of seeking understanding of the religion, and then commanded fighting those of the disbelievers nearest to them and being harsh toward them, it returned to mention the disgraceful deeds of the hypocrites, since most of the surah was revealed about them. The verse before it contained an allusion to harshness toward the disbelievers, and the hypocrites are among them. Their saying: ﴿Which of you has had its faith increased by this?﴾ may be the speech of some hypocrites to others, in denial and mockery of the believers. It may also be that they said this to their believing relatives, approaching them and hoping to return them to hypocrisy. The meaning of their saying is in the manner of belittling the surah and making light of it, as you say: "What strangeness is there in this?!" and "What proof is there in this?!" Regarding the [word] al-Ghuniyan, it was said: it is the saying of the believers, for the purpose of inquiry and alerting. The majority read ﴿Ayyukum﴾ (p-116) with a nominative *ḍamma*. Zayd ibn Ali and Ubayd ibn Umayr read *Ayyakum* with a *fatḥa*, in the construction of *ishtighal* (a construction in which the verb is occupied with a pronoun referring back to the noun), and the accusative is, according to al-Akhfash, more eloquent here, like the pronoun after the interrogative particle, as in: *azaydan ḍarabtahu* (Zayd, did you strike him?). The division implies that the address from those mocking hypocrites is general to both the hypocrites and the believers. The increase of faith is an expression for the occurrence of a particular assent that did not exist before the revelation of the surah, [arising from] a narrative and the renewal of a ruling from Allah the Exalted; or it is an expression for alerting to a proof that the surah contains, where the knowledge of Allah had been acquired through proofs, and this surah alerted him to a proof that added to his proofs; or it is an expression for the removal of a slight doubt or a passing, non-firm misgiving, so that doubt disappears and misgiving is lifted by that surah. As for the view of those who call obedience faith, which is a metaphor according to Ahl al-Sunnah (the people of the Sunnah), the increase is produced by the surah, since it contains rulings. Al-Rabi said: ﴿it increased them in faith﴾ means: in fear (of Allah); he named the thing by one of its fruits. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿it increased them in faith﴾ because it is more increasing for the God-fearing in steadfastness and more soothing to the hearts; or ﴿it increased them in action﴾, for the increase of action is an increase in faith, since faith applies to belief and action. End of quotation. This is a Mu'tazilite tendency.

﴿And they rejoice﴾ at what it contains of the mercy and good pleasure of Allah. As for ﴿those in whose hearts is a disease﴾, they are the hypocrites. Health and disease belong to bodies, and it has been transferred metaphorically to belief. The *rijs* is filth, and *rijs* is also punishment. Its increase is an expression of their going deep into disbelief and their floundering in misguidance. When they disbelieve in a surah, their disbelief increases, becomes firmly established, and their punishment multiplies. Qutrub and al-Zajjaj said: he means disbelief added to their disbelief. Muqatil said: sin added to their sin. Al-Suddi and al-Kalbi said: doubt added to their doubt. Ibn Abbas said: he means what has been prepared for them of disgrace and punishment, renewed upon them at every time, in this world and the Hereafter. The revelation of the surah produced two things for the believers: an increase of faith and rejoicing at what awaits them with Allah. For those in whose hearts is a disease, there is an increase of defilement, and their dying upon disbelief means that their original disbelief has brought them to it, and the increase continued until they died in disbelief.

﴿Do they not see that they are tested every year once or twice? Then they do not repent, nor do they take heed﴾: When he mentioned that by their death upon disbelief they are headed to the punishment of the Hereafter, he mentioned that they also do not escape the punishment of this world. The pronoun in (*yarawna*, they see) refers back to ﴿those in whose hearts is a disease﴾, according to the reading of the majority with *yā'*. Hamza read it with *tā'*, as an address to the believers. The seeing may be seeing of the heart or seeing of the eye. Ubayy, Ibn Mas'ud and al-A'mash read (*a-wa-la tara*, "Do you not see?"), meaning: you, O Muhammad? And from al-A'mash also: (*a-wa-lam tarawā*, "Did they not see?"). Abu Hatim reported from him: (*a-wa-lam yarawā*, "Did they not see?"). Mujahid said: ﴿yuftanuna﴾ means they are tested by drought and hunger. Al-Naqqash reported from him: once or twice of illness. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: they are tested by the command to jihad. Ibn Atiyyah said: What appears from what precedes the verse and what follows it is that the trial and testing are only by Allah's exposing their secrets and disclosing their beliefs; this is the testing upon which the proof is established, by their seeing it and abandoning repentance. As for jihad or hunger, what we have mentioned does not follow from them. So the meaning of the verse according to this is: Will not those whose inner secrets are exposed every year, once or twice, according to each individual, be restrained, and know that this is from Allah, and so repent, and remember the promise and threat of Allah? End of quotation. Muqatil also said this in brief, saying: they are disgraced by the exposure of their hypocrisy. As for the testing by illness, it is for the believers. Al-Hasan used to recite:

*Is it every year an illness, then a convalescence? How long, how long, and until when?*

Another group said: the meaning of ﴿they are tested﴾ is by what the polytheists spread against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of lies and rumors, and that the kings of Rome were intending to come against them with their armies and hosts; and to this refers His saying: ﴿If the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease do not desist...﴾ [al-Ahzab: 60]. So those in whose hearts is a disease were tested by that. Al-Tabari transmitted this view from Hudhayfah, and it is a strange meaning. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿they are tested﴾ means they are afflicted with illness and famine and other trials of Allah the Exalted, and then they do not desist nor repent of their hypocrisy, nor do they remember or learn a lesson, nor do they look into their affair; or they are tested with jihad alongside the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), witnessing his affair and what Allah the Exalted sends down to him of victory and support; or Satan tempts them, so they lie and break covenants with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he kills them and punishes them, yet they do not restrain themselves. Ibn Mas'ud read: (*wa-la hum yatadhakkarun*, "nor do they remember").

﴿When a surah is revealed, some look at others: "Does anyone see you?" Then they turn away. Allah has turned their hearts away, because they are a people who do not understand﴾: He first mentioned what was said by them, in the manner of mockery, and then he mentioned secondly what proceeded from them of action in the manner of mockery, which is gesturing and winking with the eyes, in denial of the revelation and in derision, saying: "Does anyone of the Muslims see you, so that we may withdraw? For we cannot bear to listen to it, and laughter overcomes us, and we fear exposure among them." Or they exchanged glances, consulting about arranging to leave and slipping away furtively, saying: "Does anyone see you?" The apparent sense is the surah without restriction, whatever surah it was. It was also said: *thumma* is an omitted qualifier, meaning: a surah that exposes them and mentions their disgraceful deeds.

﴿Some look at others﴾ in the manner of confirmation; from that glance is understood the confirmation: "Does one who reports about you see you? Does anyone see you when you plan your affairs?" ﴿Then they turned away﴾, that is, from the path of guidance. This is because when the uncovering of their secrets and the informing of the unseen matters of their affairs is made clear to them, they inevitably experience astonishment, hesitation and reflection; so if they were guided, that moment would be the occasion for correct reflection and guidance. Al-Dahhak said: "Has anyone among them noticed your secrets, out of fear of being killed?"

﴿Then they turned away﴾: if it is literal, the meaning is: they stood up from the place where the surah was recited; or if it is figurative, the meaning is: they turned away from faith, which is at the time of their returning to it and turning toward it, as al-Kalbi said; or they returned to mockery, or to disparagement of the Qur'an and denial of it and of the one who brought it; or [they turned away] from acting upon what they were hearing; or from the path of guidance after it had been made clear to them, and its proof had been established. This view returns to the view of al-Kalbi.

﴿Allah has turned their hearts away﴾: its form is a report, and it is a supplication against them, that Allah turn their hearts away from what is in the hearts of the people of faith. This was said by al-Farra'. The apparent meaning is that it is a report, since the discourse, being in the context of the mention of denial, began with the act attributed to them, which is His saying: ﴿Then they turned away﴾; then He mentioned His action toward them as a recompense for their action, like His saying: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [al-Saff: 5]. Al-Zajjaj said: He misguided them. It was also said: [He turned them away] from understanding the Qur'an and believing in it. Ibn Abbas said: from every right direction, good and guidance. Al-Hasan said: He sealed upon their hearts because of their disbelief. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Allah has turned their hearts away﴾ is a supplication against them for abandonment, and He turns their hearts away from what is in the hearts of the people of faith of expansion and openness.

﴿Because they are a people who do not understand﴾: this may be connected to ﴿turned away﴾ or to ﴿has turned﴾, and it would then be of the type of *i'mal* (the construction in which one of two verbs governs the same complement), meaning: because of their turning away; or Allah turned their hearts away because they do not reflect upon the Qur'an, so they do not understand what it contains of matters that necessitate their faith and their stopping before it.

When [the discourse] digressed from the account of the expedition to battle and the reproach of those who stayed behind from the Messenger, to the expedition of seeking understanding of the religion, and then commanded fighting those of the disbelievers nearest to them and being harsh toward them, it returned to mention the disgraceful deeds of the hypocrites, since most of the surah was revealed about them.
