**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 9, verse 128:**

﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves. It grieves him that you suffer hardship. He is eager for your guidance, and to the believers he is kind and merciful.﴾

When he began the surah with the declaration of innocence (bara'ah) of Allah and His Messenger from the polytheists, and recounted the conditions of the hypocrites bit by bit, he addressed the Arabs by enumerating the blessings upon them and bestowing favor upon them, in that a Messenger had come to them from their own kind, or from their own lineage, an Arab and a Qurashi, who conveys to them from Allah, possessing the beautiful qualities: that his hardship grieves him when they face the evil consequence of falling into punishment, that he is eager for their guidance, that he is compassionate toward them, and that he shows mercy to them. Ibn 'Abbas said: "There is no tribe of the Arabs but that the Prophet ﷺ was born into it." So it is as if he said: "O assembly of the Arabs, there has certainly come to you a Messenger from the sons of Isma'il." It is also possible that the address is to those present in his presence from the people of the religions and sects, and it is possible that it is an address to the children of Adam, and the meaning is that he was not of a kind other than the children of Adam, because of the incompatibility between the species, as in His saying: (p-118) ﴿And had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾ [al-An'am: 9]. Since the ones addressed are general, either all the Arabs or all the children of Adam, the address came in general terms with His saying: ﴿It grieves him that you suffer hardship, he is eager for you﴾, meaning: for your guidance, so that no one departs from following him and perishes.

Since compassion (ra'fah) and mercy (rahmah) are specific, their object came specific, which is His saying: ﴿to the believers he is kind and merciful﴾. Do you not see His saying: ﴿Strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be stern with them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 73], and His saying: ﴿humble toward the believers, mighty against the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 54], and His saying concerning the fornicators among the believers: ﴿And let not pity for them overtake you in the religion of Allah, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [al-Nur: 2].

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: His saying ﴿from among yourselves﴾ implies praise of the lineage of the Prophet ﷺ, and that he is of the pure core of the Arabs and their most noble. This meaning is also reflected in the saying of the Prophet ﷺ, peace be upon him: "Indeed Allah chose Kinanah from the offspring of Isma'il, and chose Quraysh from Kinanah, and chose Banu Hashim from Quraysh, and chose me from Banu Hashim." And from it is his saying ﷺ: "I am from a marriage, and not from fornication" — meaning that his lineage ﷺ, traced back to Adam, peace be upon him, had no offspring in it except through marriage, and there was no adultery in it. End of quote.

Allah described His Prophet, peace be upon him, with six attributes: Prophethood (risalah), which is the attribute of human perfection, because of what it contains of the perfection of the Messenger's essence and the purity of his pure soul, and his being among the chosen such that he was fitted to be an intermediary between Allah and His creation. Since this attribute is the most noble, it was mentioned first. And his being from among themselves, which is an attribute that influences the conveying of the message, understanding from him, and feeling at ease with him. If the address is to the Arabs, then in this attribute there is an alert to their nobility and an incitement to follow him. If the address is to the children of Adam, then in it there is an honoring of them and gentleness in delivering the news to them, and that he is known among them for truthfulness, trustworthiness, chastity and purity. His being one for whom what is hard on you is grievous is a consequence of the message. From his being from among themselves, because whoever is from you wishes you good and finds it hard to convey to you what harms you. His being eager for their guidance is also a consequence of the message, because he was sent so that Allah may be worshipped and singled out in divinity. His being kind and merciful to the believers are two attributes that are consequences of following him and entering the religion of Allah.

﴿The believers are but brothers﴾ [al-Hujurat: 10]. "The believer to the believer is like a building, one part of it strengthening the other," until you love for your believing brother what you love for yourself.

Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Dahhak, Ibn Muhaysin, Mahbub from Abu 'Amr, 'Abd Allah ibn Qusayt al-Makki, and Ya'qub from some of his transmissions, read: (مِن أنفَسِكم) with a fatha on the fa'. This reading is narrated from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and from Fatimah and 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with them both. The meaning is: from the most noble of you and the most esteemed of you, and that is from preciousness (nafasah), and it returns to the meaning of breath (nafas), for it is the most precious of things. The apparent view is that "ma" is a verbal-source particle (masdariyyah) in the position of the subject of ﴿'azīz﴾, meaning: his suffering is grievous to him, as the poet said:

It grieves a man that the nights pass, and their passing is for him a passing.

That is: the passing of the nights grieves a man. It is also permissible that ﴿ma 'anittum﴾ be a subject (mubtada', grammatically the topic of a nominal sentence), meaning: your distress is grievous to him, and its predicate (khabar) has been placed first; but the first analysis (i'rab) is more correct. Al-Hawfi permitted that ﴿'azīz﴾ be the subject, and ﴿ma 'anittum﴾ the predicate, and that "ma" be in the sense of "alladhi" (which), and that it be a verbal-source particle; and this is an analysis (i'rab) below the two preceding ones. Ibn al-Qushayri said: ﴿'azīz﴾ is an attribute of the Prophet ﷺ, and he was described with honor (al-'izzah) only because of his being central among his people, the nobility of his lineage, and the goodness of his origin. Then he resumed and said: ﴿upon him is what you suffer﴾, meaning: your affair concerns him. End of quote.

Al-'Anat: its explanation was given earlier in al-Baqarah in His saying: ﴿would have put you in hardship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 220]. Ibn 'Abbas said: here it means your hardship. Al-Dahhak said: your sin. Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah said: your misguidance. Al-'Utbi said: what harms you. Ibn al-Anbari said: what destroys you. It was also said: what distresses you. The better view is that something be supplied in ﴿'alaykum﴾, meaning: upon your guidance and your faith, as in His saying: ﴿If you are eager for their guidance﴾ [al-Nahl: 37], and His saying: ﴿And most people, even if you were eager, would not be believers﴾ [Yusuf: 103]. It was also said: he is eager to bring good things to you in this world and the Hereafter. Al-Farra' said: the eager one (al-harīs) is the stingy one (al-shahih), and the meaning is that he is stingy upon you (p-119) that you should enter the Fire. It was also said: he is eager for your entering Paradise. The supplying was needed because eagerness (al-hirs) does not attach to essences (al-dhawat).

The phrase ﴿bil-mu'minin﴾ may be connected to ﴿ra'ūf﴾, and it may be connected to ﴿raḥīm﴾, in which case it falls under the grammatical dispute (al-tanazu', the two verbs or adjectives competing for one complement). On the permissibility of placing the complement of the two competing words first, there is a view: most do not mention any fronting of it before both, but some grammarians permitted the fronting, so one says: "Zaydan I struck and I insulted" under the tanazu'. The apparent view is that the two attributes connect to all the believers. Some said: it is distributed, ra'ūf toward the obedient and raḥīm toward the sinners. It was also said: ra'ūf toward whoever sees him, raḥīm toward whoever does not see him. It was also said: ra'ūf toward his close relatives, raḥīm toward others. Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: Allah did not combine for any prophet two of His names except for our Prophet ﷺ, for He said: ﴿to the believers kind and merciful﴾, and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed Allah is to the people most kind and merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143].

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 9, verse 129:

﴿Then if they turn away, say: "Allah is sufficient for me. There is no god but Him. In Him I have put my trust, and He is the Lord of the Mighty Throne."﴾: That is, if they turn away from faith after this state in which Allah has blessed them through your being sent to them and your possessing these beautiful attributes.

﴿Say: "Allah is sufficient for me"﴾, that is, He is sufficient for me in everything. ﴿"In Him I have put my trust"﴾, that is, I have entrusted my affair to Him and not to anyone else. Allah has indeed sufficed him against their evil and granted him victory over them, since there is no god but Him. This is a blessed verse because it is among the last things revealed. He singled out the Throne for mention because it is the greatest of the created things. Ibn 'Abbas said: "No one can estimate the measure of the Throne." End of quotation. It was mentioned in the context of explaining the power and greatness of Allah. The disbelievers used to hear the report of the existence and greatness of the Throne from the Jews and the Christians, and it is not far-fetched that they had heard this from their forebears.

Ibn Muhaysin read (al-'Azim) with a raised mim (ḍamma), as an attribute of "the Lord" (rabb), and it is narrated from Ibn Kathir. Abu Bakr al-Asamm said: "This reading is more pleasing to me, because making (al-'Azim) an attribute of Allah the Exalted is preferable to making it an attribute of the Throne." The greatness of the Throne lies in the largeness of its body and the vastness of its sides, as mentioned in the reports, while the greatness of the Lord lies in His being exalted above corporeality (al-hajmiyya), parts, and components, in the perfection of His knowledge and power, and in His being far above being imagined in illusions or reached by comprehensions.

From Ibn 'Abbas: the last thing revealed was ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 128] to its end. From Ubayy: the Qur'an's most recent connection with Allah is the two verses ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 128]. These two verses were not found when the mushaf was compiled, except in the memory of Khuzayma ibn Thabit, the one with the two testimonies (dhu al-shahadatayn). When he brought them, many of the Companions recalled them. Zayd knew them, and that is why he said: "I lost two verses from the end of Surat al-Tawbah." Had he not known them, we would not have known whether something had been lost or not. The verse was established by consensus, not by Khuzayma alone.

'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "The revelation of 'Bara'a' was not finished until we thought that none of us would remain without something being revealed concerning him."

In Sunan Abi Dawud, from Abu al-Darda', who said: "Whoever says, when he reaches the morning and when he reaches the evening: 'Allah is sufficient for me; there is no god but Him; in Him I have put my trust, and He is the Lord of the Mighty Throne,' seven times, Allah the Exalted will suffice him for whatever concerns him."
